units.la: ANTIQVA NOBILITATE AC VIRTUTE CLARO VIRO, D. Ioanni im Thurn, amplissimę reipublicæ Scaphusianæ Senatori & Quæstori, Iosias Simlerus Gratiam & pacem à Deo patre & D. N. Iesu Christo precatur.
units.tr: To the noble and virtuous Mr. Johann im Thurn, senator and treasurer of the most distinguished Republic of Schaffhausen, Josias Simler wishes grace and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: MVLTISiam annis V. CL. hoc vnice omnium exoptarunt viri boni & quibus incolumitas ecclesiarum cordi est, ut tandem ex verbo Dei componatur infelix ista controversia quæ ecclesias Germaniæ turbat: sed quando id, impedientibus credo nostris peccatis, hactenus impetrare non potuimus, quod proximum erat, silentio utrinque constituto hanc sopire conati sunt non pauci è præcipuis & Illustrissimis Germaniæ principibus. Verum interea neglecta principum auctoritate, proximis annis complura acerbissima scripta in publicum prodierunt, quibus non tantum certamina inueterata renouantur, sed omnis etiam via pacis constituendæ, si modo magistratus horum A auctoritatem sequi voluerint, praecluditur. Nam nostras ecclesias Mahometanismi accusant, in quibus non plus Christo tribuatur quam illi Mahometus in suo Alcorano tribuat: & constanter afferunt omnes eos qui negant ubiquitatem essentialem carnis Christi, quam ipsi nouo Maiestatis titulo ornant, in caeteris quoque dogmatibus nihil recte de Christo credere. Quis autem tales doctores & ecclesias non abominetur, & ut ipsi hortatur, ad Turcas relegados esse censeat? Quoniam vero haec non tantum domi e sacra cathedra declamitant, sed libellis utraque lingua editis in vulgus spargunt, necessitas nos urget ut doctrinae nostrae iustam defensionem rupto tandem silentio suscipiamus, & ecclesiarum nostrarum innocentiam aduersus vanissimas calumnias asseramus: ne perpetuo silentio optimam causam prodere videamur. Ac dolet quidem nobis plurimum tam atroces calumnias passim per Germaniam de nobis spargi, cum tamen nos de ecclesiis Germaniae sem per optime existimauerimus, & nunquam nisi honorificam illarum mentionem in nostris scriptis scriptis fecerimus. Sed speramus viros moderatos & amantes pacis, quales Dei beneficio plurimi sunt in aulis Illustrissimorum principum & amplissimis Germaniae vrbibus, non probare hanc Doctorum quorundam conuiciatricem & maledicam Theologiam,& longe rectius quàm illos de nostris ecclesijs iudicare. Etsi enim in dogmate de cœna Domini nõ per omnia consentimus, tamen facile animad uertere possunt vniuersam nostram doctrinam sacris literis, veteri ecclesia,& cum ipsa Augustana confessione, vna hac de cœna Domini controuersia excepta, per omnia optime consentire. Cum contra aduersariorum nostrorum doctrinam περὶ παντα-χυσίας damnent plurimi per Germaniam qui Augustanam confessionem probant,& quidem non e plebe doctorum, sed vere lumina Germaniae. Itaque nemo iniquo animo ferre debet quod nostrae doctrinae veritatem,& nostrarum ecclesiarum existimationem contra accusationes grauissimas quorundam theologorum publice defendimus. Neque enim his scriptis controuersias augere, aut ab ecclesia in rempublicam transferre cupimus, sed id potius ca- vere ne certamina ex ecclesia in rempub. trans- ferantur. Praesentem vero libellum hoc consilio scriptum sub tuo nomine vir Clarissime in lucem edere volui, primum quidem quod te eum esse sciam qui de huiusmodi gravissimis controver- sijs iudicium facere possit: nam cum civilium rerum usu, literas & artium atque linguarum cognitionem coniunxisti: & non tantum huma- narum disciplinarum, sed sacrarum litera- rum, quae solae hominem ad veram & solidam pietatem erudire possunt, semper studiosus fuisti. Itaque cum vestra familia vetusta ac nobilis multis ornamentis hactenus clara fuerit, hoc tamen novum ornamentum literarum, hactenus temporum no hominum culpa neglectum, in illam primus intulisti, dum tua etiam exemplo fratres tuos nobilissimos aemulatione honesta ad eadem studia excitas: Deinde honestissimus dignitatis locum obtines in amplissimum Scaphusianorum republica, qui pagus Helvetiae nostrae vri Tigurinis regionis vicinia, ita etiam eiusdem religionis professione coniunctissimus est. Nam ab eo tempore tempore quo Dei beneficio clarior lux Euan-gelij nobis illuxit, summa semper fuit, vestrae ecclesiae cum nostra, cum in doctrina tum etiā in administratione ecclesiae & externis ritibus consensio: atque vt arctissima coniunctio fuit eorum ministrorum qui primi has ecclesias vtrinque instituerunt, ita eandem nobiscum conseruant & quotidie augent viri optimi & doctissimi qui nunc ecclesiae vestrae inseruiunt. Comunis etiam vtriusq; ecclesiae & rei publicae confessio publice extat, quare omnes hae calumniae quae nunc de nostris ecclesijs iactantur, non minus pertinent ad vos quàm ad nos qui Tiguri in ea ecclesia quā Zuinglius in stituit Christo inseruimus. Et eo magis quia in aditu Germaniae positi estis, vt nihil mali ex discordia ecclesiarū oriri possit quod nō primo omniū ad vos perueniat: rursus eandem ob causam ac mutua commercia, omniū commodissime poteritis innocentiam nostrarū ecclesiarum bonis ac moderatis viris demonstrare. Et quia pacis & concordiae studium ad vos maxime pertinet qui rebus publicis moderandis diuinitus praefecti estis, non tantum in republica, sed in ecclesia quoque eius prosecurationem suscipere debetis, ne tandem ἐρις seu potius Erinnys & rabies certandi ex ecclesia in rempublicam, & a calamis, quod Deus avertat, ad arma transferatur. Postremo humanitatem tuam expertus in alio studiorum genere (conscribenda historia patriae nostrae) e cuius medio cursu me trasfuerfum quasi alio importunitas adversariorum abripuit, volui hoc officij genere animum gratum & memorem tuorum beneficiorum ostendere. Atque hoc unice V. CL. a te peto ut hanc meam nuncupationem aequo animo accipias, & cum libelli huius si forte opus fuerit, tum etiam rei ipsius de qua agitur patrocinium suscipias. Nam id ingenue testari possum, me in illo conscribendo primum Dei gloriam, & puram doctrinae conservationem, deinde pacem & concordiam in ecclesia & republica potissimum quaesivisse. Precor autem Deum ut his tristibus temporibus nostris misertus tandem diem illam exoptatam nobis illucescere patiatur, qua discussa omnium errorum caligine, graves illae controversiae quae tadiu ecclesiam turbarunt, harunt, ex Verbo ipsius componantur, & suauissima pax diu desiderata aliquando afflictæ ipsius ecclesiæ restituatur. Id nobis præstet Dominus noster Iesus Christus, unicus veræ pacis auctor: qui te quoq; V. CL. ad nominis sui gloriam, & ecclesiæ atq; communis patriæ utilitatem, quam diutissime incolumem conseruare velit. Tiguri
units.tr: For many years good men have longed for one thing above all: that this unhappy controversy, which troubles the churches of Germany, might at last be settled from the Word of God. But since, as I believe, our sins have stood in the way, we have not yet been able to obtain this. The next best thing was attempted: by mutual silence, several of the leading and most illustrious princes of Germany tried to quiet the dispute. Meanwhile, however, the authority of the princes has been disregarded, and in recent years many very bitter writings have appeared in public. These not only renew old quarrels but also shut off every way of restoring peace, if the magistrates are willing to follow their authority. For they accuse our churches of Mohammedanism, claiming that Christ is given no more honour among us than Muhammad gives him in his Alcoran. They keep asserting that all who deny the essential ubiquity of Christ's flesh, which they adorn with the new title of majesty, believe nothing rightly about Christ in other doctrines either. Who would not abhor such teachers and churches, and think they ought to be sent back to the Turks, as they themselves urge? Since they not only declaim this at home from the sacred chair but also scatter it among the public in books published in both languages, necessity presses us to break our silence at last, to defend our teaching justly, and to assert the innocence of our churches against the most empty calumnies. Otherwise we might seem to betray our very good cause by silence forever. It truly grieves us greatly that such atrocious calumnies are spread about us everywhere in Germany, since we have always thought very well of the churches of Germany and have never mentioned them in our writings except with honour. But we hope that moderate men who love peace, of whom by God's kindness there are very many at the courts of the most illustrious princes and in the most distinguished cities of Germany, will not approve this reviling and slanderous theology of certain doctors, and will judge our churches far more rightly than those men do. For although we do not agree with them in every point on the doctrine of the Lord's Supper, nevertheless they can easily see that our whole teaching agrees in every respect with the Holy Scriptures, with the ancient Church, and with the Augsburg Confession itself, except for this one controversy over the Lord's Supper. On the other hand, many in Germany who approve the Augsburg Confession condemn our opponents' teaching [περὶ πανταχυσίας], concerning ubiquity, and these are not from the common crowd of teachers but are truly the lights of Germany. Therefore no one should take it ill that we publicly defend the truth of our teaching and the good name of our churches against the most grave accusations of certain theologians. For we do not wish to increase the controversies by these writings, nor to carry the matter from the Church over into the commonwealth; rather, we wish to take care that the quarrels are not carried from the Church into the commonwealth. I wanted to publish this little book, written with this purpose, under your name, most distinguished sir, first because I know you to be the man who can pass judgment on controversies of such weight. For you have joined the knowledge of letters, arts and languages to your experience of civil affairs, and you have always been devoted not only to the human disciplines but also to the Holy Scriptures, which alone can train a man to true and solid piety. Therefore, although your ancient and noble family has hitherto been famous for many distinctions, you were the first to add this new distinction of learning to it, a thing neglected until now through the fault of the times and not of men. You have also stirred your most noble brothers to the same studies by your example and by an honourable rivalry. Then you hold the most honourable office in the most distinguished commonwealth of Schaffhausen, a town of our Helvetia that lies near the region of Zurich and is therefore most closely joined to it in the profession of the same religion. For from the time when, by God's kindness, the clearer light of the Gospel shone upon us, there has always been the greatest agreement between your church and ours, both in doctrine and in the administration of the Church and its outward rites. And just as the ministers who first established these churches on both sides were most closely united, so the most excellent and learned men who now serve your church keep the same union with us and increase it every day. The common confession of both churches and commonwealths is also published openly, so that all these calumnies now being hurled against our churches pertain to you no less than to us, who in Zurich serve Christ in that church which Zwingli founded. And all the more so because you stand at the entrance to Germany, so that nothing evil arising from discord among the churches can fail to reach you first of all. Again, for the same reason and because of mutual trade, you will be best placed of all to demonstrate the innocence of our churches to good and moderate men. And since the zeal for peace and concord pertains most of all to you, who have been divinely appointed to govern the commonwealths, you ought to take up this care not only in the commonwealth but also in the Church, lest at last strife, or rather Discord and the rage of contention, be carried from the Church into the commonwealth, and from pens, which God forbid, to arms. Finally, having experienced your kindness in another kind of study (the writing of the history of our homeland), from the middle of which the importunity of our adversaries has dragged me away, as if across my course to another task, I wished to show by this kind of duty a grateful and mindful spirit for your favours. And this, most distinguished sir, is the only thing I ask of you: that you receive this dedication of mine with a calm mind, and, if this little book should perhaps need it, that you take up its defence and that of the matter itself which is under discussion. For I can honestly testify that in writing it I sought above all the glory of God and the pure preservation of the doctrine, and then peace and concord in the Church and the commonwealth. And I pray God that, having pity on our sorrowful times, he may at last allow that longed-for day to dawn upon us, on which, with the darkness of all errors dispelled, those grave controversies that have so long troubled the Church may be settled from his own Word, and the sweetest peace, long desired, may at last be restored to the afflicted Church itself. May our Lord Jesus Christ, the sole author of true peace, grant this to us, and may he wish to preserve you also, most distinguished sir, safe for as long as possible, to the glory of his name and the usefulness of the Church and of our common fatherland. Zurich

units.la: ORTHODOXA ET BREVIS EXPOSITIO VERAE PRAESENTIAE Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qua in his terris praesens est.
units.tr: An Orthodox and Brief Exposition of the True Presence of Our Lord Jesus Christ, by Which He Is Present on This Earth.

units.la: INTER ea de quibus hodie in scholis Theologorum disceptatur, non puto quicquam magis controversum esse quam doctrinam de sacrosancta coena Domini nostri Iesu Christi: Aliter enim de illa docet Papistę, aliter Lutherani, aliter illi quos Zuinglianos & Caluinianos vocant, aliter Anabaptistę: alia postremo est sententia Brentianorum, qui quamuis & ipsi Lutherani videri velint, tamen aliter quàm plerunque; Lutherus docuerit, & Lutherani atque ipse Brentius olim scripserit, nunc de coena Domini docent. In tanta autem opinionum varietate quotidie plurimi libelli vbiq; in publicum prodeunt, plurimi etiam iamdudum à doctissimis viris nostrarum ecclesiarum qui nunc in Domino quiescunt, editi sunt, quibus haec controversia copiose & perspicue explicatur, & quae sit vera sententia ex scripturis & Patribus firmis rationibus demonstratur. In tanta autem librorum huius argumenti copia, nihil minus haftenus in animo habui, quam hanc quæstionem aliqua ex parte attingere: sed nunc vt aliter statuerem commouit me, non iniusta, vt arbitror, animi indignatio: nam non tantum de præsentia Christi in cœna Domini nunc contenditur, verum in genere de præsentia Christi in his terris secundum humanam naturam quæritur, & Vbiquitas seu Omnipræsentia carnis Christi veritas incognita asseritur, atq; ad hanc stabiliendam noua doctrina de Incarnatione Filij Dei, & eius Ascésione in cœlos, & sessione ad dextera Dei, ecclesiæ cum magna multorum infirmorū offensione proponitur. Deinde prodeunt subinde in publicum noua scripta calumnijs salsissimis aduersus nostras ecclesias referta, quibus ea dogmata impudentissime nobis affinguntur, quæ neper somnium quidem vnquam nobis in mentem venerunt: & nos Arianos atque etiam Mahumetanos esse clamant, cum ipsorum conscien tiæ eos calumniæ & mendacij arguant: optime enim norunt qua fide & diligentia nostrę ecclesiæ sese haftenus Arianorum furoribus opposuerint, & quantum à tatis blasphemijs abhorreamus & semper abhorruerimus. In tanta igitur calumniandi petulantia existimaui officij mei esse, puram doctrinā quam haftenus cum alijs pijs & doctis viris in his scholis & ecclesijs tradidi, publico scripto cōtra apertas calumnias defendere, & simul innocentiam nostrarum ecclesiarum aduersus falsas & horrendas criminationes aduersa-riorum afferere. Neque existimo quenquam hoc mihi vitio posse vertere, quasi noua certamina pacatis ecclesijs attrahere, aut vetera dissidia renouare & augere velim, quando ego nullam contentionem moueo sed tantum tela immissa repello, & illis respondeo qui pacem ecclesiarum ferre non possunt. Etenim scripta quorundã, & nominatim Iacobi Andreæ complura, & nuper ad Viadrum editæ Musculi propositiones, satis ostendunt plerosque huius factionis plurimum in eo elabo-rare, vt viros doctos & moderatos qui pacem nobiscum seruare, & tristem hanc atque diuturnam controuersiam sacramentariam tollere & sopire cuperent, in odium & inuidiam apud Principes & vulgus adducant, & eos sal-sis criminibus grauent, atque ita omnem pacis & concordiæ rationem tollant.
units.tr: Among the matters debated today in the schools of the theologians, I think nothing is more contested than the doctrine of the most holy Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Papists teach one thing about it, the Lutherans another, those whom they call Zwinglians and Calvinists another, and the Anabaptists another. Finally, there is the opinion of the Brentians, who, although they wish to appear Lutherans themselves, nonetheless teach about the Lord's Supper in a way different from how Luther taught it, and different from how the Lutherans and Brenz himself once wrote. Amid such variety of opinions, very many pamphlets appear in public every day everywhere. Many have also long since been published by the most learned men of our churches, who now rest in the Lord, in which this controversy is explained fully and clearly, and which true opinion is demonstrated from Scripture and the firm testimony of the Fathers with solid arguments. Given such an abundance of books on this subject, until now I had no intention of touching this question in any way. But what has moved me to decide otherwise is, I think, a not unjust indignation of mind. For the dispute now concerns not only the presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper, but in general the question of the presence of Christ on this earth according to his human nature. The truth of the Ubiquity, or Omnipresence, of Christ's flesh is asserted as something previously unknown, and to establish it a new doctrine about the Incarnation of the Son of God, his Ascension into heaven, and his sitting at the right hand of God is put forward to the Church, with great offence to many weak people. Then, from time to time, new writings appear in public, filled with the most foul calumnies against our churches, in which those doctrines are shamelessly fastened upon us which never once entered our minds, not even in a dream. They shout that we are Arians and even Mohammedans, while their own consciences convict them of this calumny and falsehood. For they know very well with what faith and diligence our church has until now opposed itself to the furies of the Arians, and how far we abhor, and always have abhorred, such blasphemies. Therefore, in the face of such wanton slandering, I judged it my duty to defend in a public writing, against open calumnies, the pure doctrine which until now I have taught, together with other pious and learned men, in these schools and churches, and at the same time to assert the innocence of our churches against the false and horrible accusations of our adversaries. Nor do I think anyone can charge me with this fault, as if I wished to stir up new contests in peaceful churches, or to renew and enlarge old quarrels, since I am not provoking any strife but merely repelling missiles hurled at me, and answering those who cannot bear the peace of the churches. Indeed, the writings of certain men, especially the many of Jacob Andreae, and the recently published propositions of Musculus at Frankfurt on the Oder, show well enough that most of this faction labour greatly to bring into hatred and ill will, before princes and the common people, men learned and moderate who wish to keep peace with us and to remove and quiet this sad and long-lasting sacramentarian controversy, and to burden them with false charges, and so to destroy every means of peace and concord.

units.la: Ac dolendū est homines theologos quos maximè omnium pacis studiosos esse opor-tebat, tantopere ab ea abhorrere, vt vix nomen eius ferre posse videantur, quorum tanta est pugnandi rabies, vt si his magistratus gladium traderet aut eum horū arbitrio strin-geret, breui non minus principes & respubli-cæ armis & ferro, quam theologi calamo inter se contenderent. Elaborarunt in hac re
units.tr: And it is to be lamented that theologians, who above all others ought to be eager for peace, shrink so greatly from it that they seem scarcely able to bear even its name. Their rage for fighting is so great that, if the magistrate were to hand them the sword, or to draw it at their direction, before long princes and commonwealths would be fighting one another with arms and steel no less than theologians fight with the pen. They have laboured in this matter

units.la: Illustrissimi aliquot Germaniæ principes, & amplissimarum vrbium magistratus, multi quoque eximiæ eruditionis viri, vt quando hanc tristem Sacramentariam contentionem componere nō possent, saltem amicitiam inter partes conciliarent, & ab vtrisq; impetrarent, vt à concertationibus & rixis & conuitiis abstinerent. Existimabāt enim cum alioqui maledicentia Christiano theologo indigna sit, & dissidia bonis omnibus fugienda sint, tum maximè in hac quæstione id faciendum esse, quod turpissimum sit Christianis idipsum esse belli materiam, quod pacis vinculum esse Christus voluit, præsertim cum vtraq; pars circa præcipua capita quæ in cœna spectantur consentiat. Nam his qui absque affectu & præiudicio nostra scripta legunt manifestum est, nos neque præsentiam Christi in sua cœna, neque communionem corporis & sanguinis eius negare, solum in eo controuersiam omnem positam esse, quis sit modus præsentiæ, qua Christus cœnæ suę adest, & nos verum eius corpus & sanguinem percipimus.
units.tr: Several most illustrious princes of Germany, and magistrates of the most important cities, and many men of outstanding learning, since they could not settle this sad sacramentarian contention, have tried at least to reconcile the parties in friendship, and to obtain from both that they abstain from disputes, quarrels and reproaches. For they thought that, since slander is in any case unworthy of a Christian theologian, and quarrels are to be avoided by all good men, this ought above all to be done in this question. It is most shameful for Christians that this should be the matter of war which Christ willed to be the bond of peace, especially since each side agrees on the chief points which are considered in the Supper. For it is plain to those who read our writings without partiality and prejudice that we deny neither the presence of Christ in his Supper nor the communion of his body and blood, and that the whole controversy lies only in this: what is the manner of the presence by which Christ is present at his Supper, and by which we receive his true body and blood.

units.la: Ea autem quæ de modo præsentiæ & communionis docemus, pia & consentanea esse doctrinæ sacratum literarum negare non possunt moderati homines etiam aduersę partis: nam etsi à nobis dissentiant, tamen modum præsentiæ & communionis quem nos statuimus nequaquam negant, sed praeter hunc alium quoq; substantialem asserunt, & non in eo arguunt quod falsa doceamus, sed quod non cuncta quæ ( vt ipsi iudicant) docenda & asserenda erat affirmemus. Ac quoniam modus ille præsentiæ corporis Christi quem ipsi affirmant, nusquam disertis verbis sacrarum literarum traditur & definitur, vti etiam nonnulli aduersariorum fatentur, existimarunt boni viri nobis iniuriam fieri, si huius quæstionis gratia ab amicitia & fraterna charitate excludamur. Sed nouis istis theologis hæc bonorum virorum consilia politica esse videntur, quod scilicet compositio quæratur in re fidei, vbi nihil est iuris nostri quod concedere possimus, sed verbo Dei stan dum sit, & integritas fidei coseruanda, quam cuerti a nobis clamitant. Quasi vero euicerint verbum Dei a se stare, aut nos fidei quicquam contrarium docere: nam quod nos negare aiunt Dei omnipotentiam, personamq; Christi diuidere, meræ sunt calumniæ dudum refutatæ. Attamen aliqui e vehementibus istis theologis qui tam seueri sunt in Sacramentarios, Flaccium, quem hi qui quondam sui gregales erant Manichaicos furores renouare affirmant, ferunt, & fratris loco habent, quia Vbiquitati eorum vbique patrocinatur. Vt merito zelum hunc suum contra Sacramentarios suspectum faciant, nam si gloriæ Dei
units.tr: As for what we teach concerning the manner of the presence and of the communion, moderate men even of the opposing side cannot deny that it is pious and consistent with the doctrine of the sacred letters. For although they dissent from us, they by no means deny the manner of presence and communion which we set forth; rather, they assert besides it another, substantial one, and they accuse us not of teaching falsehoods but of failing to affirm everything which, as they judge, ought to be taught and asserted. And since that manner of the presence of Christ's body which they affirm is nowhere stated and defined in plain words of the sacred letters, as some of the adversaries themselves admit, good men have thought that we are being wronged if, on account of this question, we are shut out from friendship and brotherly charity. But to these new theologians such counsels of good men seem merely political, namely that an agreement should be sought in a matter of faith, where we have no right which we could concede, but the Word of God must stand and the integrity of the faith must be preserved, which they loudly claim we are overturning. As if they had proved that the Word of God stands on their side, or that we teach anything contrary to the faith! For what they say, that we deny the omnipotence of God and divide the person of Christ, are mere calumnies, refuted long ago. Yet some of these vehement theologians, who are so severe against the Sacramentarians, bear with Flacius, whom those who were once his fellow-members affirm to be reviving Manichaean frenzies, and they regard him as a brother, because he defends their Ubiquity everywhere. So they rightly make their zeal against the Sacramentarians suspect.

units.la: Zelum adversariorum inæqualis. riæ Dei studio hos odissent, Flaccium cuius quoq; doctrinam damnant æque ac illos nul lo modo ferre possent.
units.tr: The unequal zeal of the adversaries. For if they hated these men out of zeal for the glory of God, they could in no way tolerate Flacius, whose doctrine they condemn just as they condemn those others.

units.la: Sed quando illis omnia bene habent si Sacramentarijs nullus sit locus, nos, quos immerito eo nuncupant nomine quod in ipsos magis quadrat, omissis his à quibus ius æquum impetrare nunquam potuimus, causam nostram, quam iustissimo iudici ipsi Domino & Seruatori nostro Iesu Christo approbatam esse confidimus, bonis quoq; & moderatis viris approbare conabimur. Quia vero non tam tu nunc quæritur de præsentia corporis Christi in Eucharistia, sed huius controuersiæ occasione coeptum est disputari de absoluta præsentia Christi secundum humanam naturam, quam ad illam alteram præsentiam carnis Christi in cœna afferendam, vbique non minus quam ipsam diuinitatem præsentem esse volunt, visum est mihi quoq; in genere de præsentia Christi secundum humanitatem in his terris scribere, initio tamen facto à præsentia eius in Eucharistia, & interpretatione verborum Cœnæ, HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, HIC EST SANGVIS MEVS. Nam reuera hoc est caput totius controuersiæ, & quia sibi persuaserunt his verbis statui realem & corporalem præsentiam carnis & sanguinis Christi in cœna sacra, vt hanc opinionem semel male conceptam tueri possint, & nulla lum tropum in his verbis admittere cogantur, suam vbiquitatem excogitarunt, ac inauditos tropos, & nouas interpretationes symboli & locorum scripturae quam plurimorum, etiam illas quę grauissimis erroribus vel patrocinantur vel periculosam occasionem praebent, approbare non dubitant.
units.tr: But since everything goes well for them if there is no place for the Sacramentarians, we, whom they unjustly name with that title which fits them far better, will, setting aside those from whom we could never obtain a fair hearing, seek to win over good and moderate men to our cause, which we trust has been approved by our most just Judge, the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ himself. But since the present question is not so much about the presence of Christ's body in the Eucharist, but the dispute, begun on the occasion of this controversy, has turned to the absolute presence of Christ according to his human nature, which they want to be present everywhere, no less than the deity itself, in order to support that other presence of Christ's flesh in the Supper, it seemed right to me to write also in general about the presence of Christ according to his humanity on this earth. Yet I have made a beginning with his presence in the Eucharist and the interpretation of the words of the Supper, THIS IS MY BODY, THIS IS MY BLOOD. For in truth this is the heart of the whole controversy, and because they have persuaded themselves that these words establish a real and corporeal presence of the flesh and blood of Christ in the holy Supper, and so, in order to defend this opinion once badly conceived, they cannot admit any trope in these words, they have devised their Ubiquity, and they do not hesitate to approve unheard-of tropes and new interpretations of the creed and of many passages of Scripture, including those which either support very grave errors or offer a dangerous occasion for them.

units.la: Aduersarios non seruare τὸ ῥητὸν verborum Coenae Domini.
units.tr: The adversaries do not keep the literal sense [τὸ ῥητόν] of the words of the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Quoniam igitur aduersarij, hoc subinde iactant, & idem vbique repetit Musculus, se verba Christi accipere vt sonant, κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν iuxta verum, genuinum & grammaticum sensum, quem certa ipsorum significatio, natura & vsitata grammatica reddit, atque omnes interpretationes verborum Christi quae figuratam locutionem in coena statuunt, damnant, primum omnium de sensu verborum Christi agemus, quaerentes quod sit τὸ ῥητὸν seu genuinus & grammaticus sensus, & hunc non seruari ab aduersarijs demonstrabimus.
units.tr: Since the adversaries often boast of this, and Musculus repeats it everywhere, that they take Christ's words as they sound, according to the literal sense [κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν], that is, according to the true, genuine and grammatical meaning which their own clear signification, nature and ordinary grammar yield, and since they condemn all interpretations of Christ's words that posit a figurative mode of speech in the Supper, we shall first deal with the sense of Christ's words. We shall ask what the literal sense [τὸ ῥητόν], that is, the genuine and grammatical sense, is, and we shall show that the adversaries do not keep it.

units.la: Verba Christi in hunc modum ab Euangelistis & Paulo apostolo nobis tradita sunt, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum postquam agnum paschalem cum discipulis suis edit, in illa vltima coena, accepisse panem, & quum benedixisset siue gratias egisset, fregisse & dedisse discipulis, dicendo, accipite, comedite, HOC EST CORPVS MEVM: quod pro vobis datur, vel frangitur, hoc facite in mei commemorationem. Similiter accepto poculo & gratijs actis id dedisse eis ac dixisse, Bibite ex eo omnes HOC EST ENIM SANGVIS MEVS NOVI TESTAMENTI; qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum, vel HOC POCVLVM EST NOVVM ILLVD TESTAMENTVM in meo sanguine, seu per sanguinem meum, qui pro vobis effunditur: hoc facite quotiescunque bibe-ritis ad mei commemorationem. Quotiescunque enim ederitis panem hunc, & poculum hoc biberitis, mortem Domini annuntiabitis vsque quo venerit. Horum verborum genuinus simplex & grammaticus sensus est, Panem esse corpus Christi, & Poculum esse novum testamentum seu sanguinem nou i testamenti. Nam pronomen demonstratiuum Hoc, panem ostendit: id enim quod accepit, quod fregit, super quo gratias egit, quod dedit discipulis & comedere iussit, hoc vocat Corpus suum: Panem autem accepit, panem fregit (corpus enim Christi proprie non frangitur) Panem benedixit, seu super eo gratias egit, hoc dedit discipulis & comedere iussit: Itaque panis in hac oratione subiectu est, de quo praedicatur corpus Christi, est id quod corpus Christi esse dicitur. Veteres etiam id sensérunt pronomen Hoc ad panem referri, & Christum Panem corpus suum vocasse. Tertullianus contra Iudaeos, inquit Christus
units.tr: The words of Christ have been handed down to us in this form by the Evangelists and by the apostle Paul. Our Lord Jesus Christ, after he ate the paschal lamb with his disciples on that final evening, took bread, and when he had blessed it, or given thanks, he broke it and gave it to the disciples, saying: "Take, eat, THIS IS MY BODY, which is given, or broken, for you; do this in remembrance of me." Likewise, having taken the cup and given thanks, he gave it to them and said: "Drink of it, all of you: THIS IS MY BLOOD OF THE NEW COVENANT, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins"; or THIS CUP IS THAT NEW COVENANT in my blood, or through my blood, which is poured out for you; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me. For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes. The genuine, plain and grammatical sense of these words is that the bread is the body of Christ, and the cup is the new covenant, or the blood of the new covenant. For the demonstrative pronoun This points to the bread: that which he took, which he broke, over which he gave thanks, which he gave to the disciples and bade them eat, this he calls his body. He took bread, he broke bread (for the body of Christ is not properly broken), he blessed bread, or gave thanks over it, and this he gave to the disciples and bade them eat. Thus in this sentence the bread is the subject, of which the body of Christ is predicated; it is that which is said to be the body of Christ. The ancients also understood that the pronoun This refers to the bread, and that Christ called the bread his body. Tertullian, against the Jews, says that Christ

units.la: Hoc; de pane dicitur.
units.tr: This; it is said of the bread.

units.la: Lib. 4. panem corpus suum appellasse. Origenes, Deum Verbum inquit panem corpus suum fateri, & potum sanguinem suum. Iustinus Panem & poculum coenae Dominicae nominat alimoniam sacratam, & haec inquit esse illius Iesu incarnati carnem & sanguinem. Irenaeus Panem eum in quo gratiae actae sint ait esse corpus Domini, & calicem sanguinis eius. Chrysostomus. Quid nam est panis? Corpus Christi. Quid autem fiunt qui accipiunt? Corpus Christi. Augustinus. Quod ergo vidistis panis est & calix, quod etiam oculi vestri renuntiant, quod autem fides vestra postulat instrueda, panis est corpus Christi & calix sanguis. Item corpus & sanguine Christi dicimus illud quod ex fructibus terrae acceptum, & prece mystica consecratum recte sumimus ad salutem spiritualem, in memoriam Dominicae passionis. Quin etiam Lutherus in Defensione verborum HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, ait verba Christi de pane sonare seu panem notare, ideo necesse esse corpus Christi in pane inesse: Et in breui confessione Wer nicht gloubt wil ...
units.tr: Book 4: that he called the bread his body. Origen says that the Word of God acknowledges the bread as his body and the drink as his blood. Justin calls the bread and cup of the Lord's Supper a sacred food, and says that these are the flesh and blood of that incarnate Jesus. Irenaeus says that the bread over which thanks have been given is the body of the Lord, and the cup is the blood of him. Chrysostom: What then is the bread? The body of Christ. And what do those who receive it become? The body of Christ. Augustine: What you saw is bread and cup, as your eyes also report; but what your faith requires to be taught is that the bread is the body of Christ and the cup the blood. Likewise we rightly call the body and blood of Christ that which, taken from the fruits of the earth and consecrated by a mystical prayer, we receive for our spiritual salvation, in memory of the Lord's passion. Indeed Luther, in his Defence of the words THIS IS MY BODY, says that the words of Christ sound about the bread, or designate the bread, and therefore the body of Christ must be in the bread. And in his short confession: "Whoever will not believe that the blood of the Lord in the Supper is his true, natural body, which the wicked man or Judas receives orally just as well as St Peter and all the saints, let him alone and leave him in peace," etc.

units.la: Wer nicht gloubt wil Das Deß Herren Blot im abentmal sey/sein rechter natürlicher lyb/ welchen Der gottlose oder Judas eben so wol mundtlich empfehet/ als S. Petrus vnnd alle heiligen/ Der laß mich nur zu fryden/&c. Qui noluerit credere panem Domini in coena eius verum & naturale corpus esse quod impius seu Iudas non minus oraliter percipiat quam Petrus & omnes sancti, hic a me faceßat: attamen mox suas vsitatas interpretationes adhibet. Sunt tamen aliqui veteres & recentiores Sophistæ qui negant pro nomen demonstrationum HOC panem indicare: & quamuis alioqui iurati sint in verba Lutheri, tamen hic illi contradicunt, & fingunt Identicam propositionem, vbi ipsum subiectum sit prædicatum: ac alij quidam vagum quoddam indiuiduum demonstrant, quorum opinionem aduersarij nostri ipsi quoque improbant, alij volunt simul cum pane demonstrari corpus Christi, neque hoc panem proprie demonstrari à Christo, quem alioqui manifeste cernebant Apostoli vt non necesse fuerit eius præsentiam demonstrare, sed ipsum Christi corpus, sicut etiam de sanguine dicitur HIC EST SANGVIS, ac aiunt similem esse locutionem vt si quis ferrum tandens ostendat, ac dicat hoc est ignis, aut cantharum vino plenum & dicat hoc est vinum. Sed hæc similia nihil eos iuuant, nam cantharus & ferrum ostenduntur, sed cantharus vinum figurate dicitur, eo quod continës accipit nomen contentis, & ita ferrum candens ignis dici potest, quia ignitum est, vt sit permutatio causæ & effectus, aut partium: at illi nullam figuram hic ferunt. Deinde si concedamus hæc absque figura accipi posse, & demonstrari non Cantharum sed vinū Can*tharo contentum:tamen in huiusmodi locu*tionibus oportet duorum realem coiunctio*nem praecedere, vt haec demonstratio vere lo*cum habeat, nisi enim antea cantharus vino plenus fuerit non recte dicetur hoc esse vinū: at in sacramento coenae non poni potest alia antecedens coiunctio panis & corporis Chri*sti, vt manu ad panem porrecta indicetur corpus Christi, sed ex ipsa institutione sacramen*ti panis hoc accipit demum vt dicatur Chri*sti corpus. Nam etiamsi ponatur Vbiquitas corporis Christi, qua semper vbique adsit & ita etiam pani coniunctum sit, tamen nihilo*minus ab ipsis quoq; peculiarem aliquā con*iunctionem Christi cum pane, nempe sacra*mentalem, ex institutione Christi statui opor*tet, alioquin eodē modo de quouis pane, imo de quauis re uere dici posset, hoc est corpus Christi. At si demonstratiua particula HOC ad panem simul & corpus refertur, vt si quis cantharum vino plenum ostendés dicat, hoc est vinum, & ita vtroq; demonstrato alterum tantum nominatur, tum certe fuerit tropica locutio & synechdoche in verbis Christi, & tamen contendunt nullum prorsus tropum in verbis testamenti admittendum. Et quoniam a nobis exigunt vt aliis locis scripturae nostrum tropum probemus, eodem iure ab illis petitur vt suum tropum aliis locis probent. bent & non id quod in quæstione est pro argumento sumant. Atque posita synechdoche nihilominus quæritur quomodo coniungantur panis & corpus Christi, an substantialiter, an per relationem, ut nos dicimus. Quod si pronomen demonstrativum non demonstrat panem, quid quæso distribuit Christus, quid in manus accepit & fregit? Si panè non ostendit & hunc dicit esse suum corpus, sed suum ipsius corpus tantum ostendit, & de hoc dicit HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, quis visus panis in cœna, cur Paulus Panem communionem corporis Christi vocat? Et si pronomen HOC panem non demonstrat, tamen aperte poculum monstratu esse à Christo Lucas & Paulus testantur. Neque ab his dissentit Matthæus, sed eius verbis vim faciut qui ea ita interpretantur HIC SANGVIS EST NOVI TESTAMENTI, quasi Sanguinis vox sit subiectum in propositione. Nam in Græco est τοῦτο HOC, quod Lucas & Paulus explicant HOC POCVLVM. Quare à simplicitate verborum & genuino & Grammatico sensu recedunt qui demonstrativum pronomen alio violenter quàm ad panem & poculum detorquent, hæc enim Iesum accepisse, benedixisse, fregisse, distribuisse discipulis, iussisse accipere & edere & bibere Paulus & Euangelistæ omnes testantur, ideoque de his quoque dixit corpus suum & sanguinem suum esse. Porro nulla quoq; ambiguitas est in nomine corporis, non enim sic figuratum aut spirituale aliquod corpus Christo affingi mus, sed fatemur haec eius verba de vero suo & naturali corpore loqui, nā addit quod pro vobis frāgitur, fractionis nomine passionem intelliges, & de sanguine qui pro vobis effun ditur. Hic cardo controuersiae est quomodo panis sit corpus Christi, quomodo & cur panem hunc Christus suū corpus nominet.Mul culus qui gloriatur se simplicem genuinū & grammaticum sensum verborum Christi retinere, hunc sensum verborum Christi esse vult, quod his stabiliatur realis & substantialis praesentia veri corporis & sanguinis Christi, sic ut praesens ipse manu ministri mediante corpus verum, substantiale, naturale, & sanguinem verum in pane & vino & cum pane & vino sumentibus praebeat dignis & indignis, atque hic ipsam carnem quae nata est ex virgine, & passa in cruce, & resurrexit a mortuis, fide & ore percipi atque manducari ait. Nam esse vnionem incompre hensibilem panis & corporis Christi, nō quidem naturale, personalem aut formalem, sed sacramentalem & supernaturale, qua statuatur in coena praesens corpus Christi realiter, substantialiter, naturaliter, sed admirando & adorando & supernaturali modo, & accipi ac manducari non visibiliter nec sensibiliter, sed incomprehensibiliter, inuisibiliter, supernaturali & corporali manducatione. Hæc est illa simplicitas verborum Christi, hic genuinus & grammaticus sensus, vbi seruatur τὸ ῥητὸν. Etsi autem apparet cuiuis non prorsus occæcato multum recedi à simplicitate verborum Christi, id tamen nunc omittentes dicamus de rationibus ob quas nullam interpretationem nullum tropum & figuram in his verbis admittendam putant. Verba inquiunt sunt testamenti Christi, ideo simpliciter & absque figura accipi debent. An non autem verba Christi quæ in cruce pendens dixit, sunt verba testamenti ipsius, quando suo sanguine sanciuit Nouum Testamentum? Atqui tum videns matrem & discipulum cruci astantes, dixit matri suæ, Mulier ecce filius tuus: & discipulo, Ecce mater tua. Num dicemus Ioannem verè filium fuisse beatæ virginis? Imo vltima verba seruatoris in cruce pendentis non carent tropo: Pater in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum: nisi enim Anthropomorphitæ esse voluerimus, tropū hic agnoscere oportet. n ipsa cœna, vt demus in his verbis HOC EST CORPVS MEVM nullū esse tropū, tamen ea quæ poculo dicuntur absq; tropo intelligi & exponi nō possunt, HOC POCVLVM EST NOVVM TESTAMENTVM, neque enim senquam ita desipere puto vt poculū putes. vere & substantialiter esse nouum Testamen-tum. Nolunt hic tropum agnoscere, & ascen-sionem Christi in coelos, sessionem ad dexte-ram Patris, locos scripturae de absentia & dis-cessu Christi ex hoc mundo, & alios multos tropice aut allegorice exponunt, noua more tantum ne hic tropum admittere cogantur. Nolunt tropum in verbis testamenti admit-tere, interim ex tabulis diuini foederis inte-grum praeceptum eradunt, de non faciendis & adorandis imaginibus. Apostolos fingunt simpliciter credidisse panem esse corpus Chri-sti substantialiter, seu in pane sibi praeberi cor-pus Christi vere & essentialiter, ideoq; Domi-num non interrogasse, quorum exemplum nobis quoque imitandum sit. Sed audiamus quid Chrysostomus de Apostolis scribat:
units.tr: "Whoever does not believe that the Lord's blood in the Supper is his true, natural body, which the wicked man or Judas receives orally just as well as Peter and all the saints, let him be left in peace, etc." Whoever will not believe that the bread of the Lord in his supper is his true and natural body, which the impious man or Judas receives orally no less than Peter and all the saints, let him go his own way with me; yet at once he brings out his usual interpretations. There are, however, some older and more recent Sophists who deny that the word HOC points out the bread. Although otherwise they swear by Luther's words, here they contradict him and invent an identical proposition in which the subject is itself the predicate. Others point out some vague individual thing, an opinion which our opponents themselves also reject. Others want the body of Christ to be pointed out together with the bread, and not the bread itself to be properly pointed out by Christ, whom the apostles plainly saw, so that there was no need to point out his presence; rather the body of Christ itself is pointed out. It is said in the same way of the blood, HIC EST SANGVIS, and they claim the expression is like someone who, holding out a glowing iron, says "this is fire," or who, showing a tankard full of wine, says "this is wine." But such examples do them no good. For the tankard and the iron are shown, but the tankard is figuratively called wine, because the container takes the name of the contents, and so the glowing iron can be called fire because it is on fire; there is an exchange of cause and effect, or of parts. But they bring no figure here. Next, even if we grant that these words can be taken without a figure, and that what is pointed out is not the tankard but the wine contained in the tankard, still in expressions of this kind a real joining of the two things must come first, for the demonstration to hold true. For unless the tankard was already full of wine, it would not be rightly said, "this is wine." But in the sacrament of the Supper no prior joining of the bread and the body of Christ can be posited, so that by holding out a hand to the bread the body of Christ is pointed out; rather, from the very institution of the sacrament, the bread receives this, that it is called the body of Christ. For even if we posit the ubiquity of Christ's body, by which it is always everywhere present and so is also joined to the bread, nevertheless they too must set up from Christ's institution a particular joining of Christ with the bread, namely a sacramental one; otherwise, in the same way, this could be truly said of any bread, indeed of any thing at all: this is the body of Christ. But if the demonstrative particle HOC refers both to the bread and to the body, as when someone showing a tankard full of wine says "this is wine," and so, with both things pointed out, only one of them is named, then surely this would be a tropical expression and a synecdoche in the words of Christ; and yet they contend that no trope at all is to be admitted in the words of the testament. And since they demand that we prove our trope from other passages of Scripture, by the same right it is demanded of them that they prove their trope from other passages, and not take as proof the very thing that is in question. And even granting a synecdoche, the question still remains how the bread and the body of Christ are joined: substantially, or by relation, as we say. But if the demonstrative pronoun does not point out the bread, what, I ask, did Christ distribute, what did he take into his hands and break? If he did not point out the bread and say that this is his body, but only pointed out his own body and said of this, HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, what bread was seen in the Supper? Why does Paul call the bread the communion of the body of Christ? And if the pronoun HOC does not point out the bread, yet Luke and Paul testify that the cup was plainly pointed out by Christ. Nor does Matthew disagree with them; but they do violence to his words who interpret them as HIC SANGVIS EST NOVI TESTAMENTI, as if the word blood were the subject of the proposition. For in the Greek it is τοῦτο [HOC], which Luke and Paul explain as HOC POCVLVM [this cup]. Therefore those who twist the demonstrative pronoun violently away from the bread and the cup, instead of taking it as it stands, depart from the simplicity of the words and from the genuine and grammatical sense. For Paul and all the evangelists testify that Jesus took these things, blessed them, broke them, distributed them to the disciples, and commanded them to take, eat and drink; and therefore he said of these also that they were his body and his blood. Furthermore, there is no ambiguity in the word body either. For we do not attach to Christ some figurative or spiritual body; rather we confess that these his words speak of his true and natural body. For he adds, which is broken for you, and you will understand the breaking to mean his passion; and, of the blood which is poured out for you. Here is the crux of the controversy: how the bread is the body of Christ, and how and why Christ calls this bread his body. He who boasts that he keeps the simple, genuine and grammatical sense of Christ's words wants this to be the sense of Christ's words: that by them the real and substantial presence of the true body and blood of Christ is established, so that Christ himself, present through the hand of the minister, offers the true, substantial, natural body and the true blood in the bread and wine, and with the bread and wine, to those who take them, worthy and unworthy alike; and here, he says, the very flesh that was born of the virgin, suffered on the cross and rose from the dead is received and eaten by faith and by the mouth. For he says there is an incomprehensible union of the bread and the body of Christ, not natural, personal or formal, but sacramental and supernatural, by which the body of Christ is held to be present in the Supper really, substantially and naturally, yet in a wondrous and adorable and supernatural manner; and it is received and eaten not visibly nor sensibly, but incomprehensibly, invisibly, by a supernatural and yet bodily eating. This is that simplicity of Christ's words, this is the genuine and grammatical sense, where τὸ ῥητὸν [the literal sense] is kept. Although it is plain to anyone not completely blinded that much is departed from the simplicity of Christ's words, let us nevertheless set that aside for now and speak of the reasons for which they think no interpretation, no trope and no figure is to be admitted in these words. "The words," they say, "are the words of Christ's testament, therefore they must be taken simply and without figure." But are not the words which Christ spoke while hanging on the cross also words of his testament, since he ratified the New Testament with his own blood? And yet, seeing his mother and the disciple standing by the cross, he said to his mother, Woman, behold your son, and to the disciple, Behold your mother. Shall we say that John was truly the son of the blessed virgin? Indeed, the last words of the Saviour hanging on the cross are not free of a trope either: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit. For unless we want to be Anthropomorphites, we must recognise a trope here. Moreover, even granting that in the Supper itself there is no trope in the words HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, still the things said of the cup cannot be understood and explained without a trope: HOC POCVLVM EST NOVVM TESTAMENTVM. For I never suppose that anyone is so foolish as to think the cup itself is truly and substantially the New Testament. They refuse to recognise a trope here, while the ascension of Christ into heaven, his sitting at the right hand of the Father, and the passages of Scripture about the absence and departure of Christ from this world, and many others, they expound tropically or allegorically; they do this in a new way, merely so that they will not be forced to admit a trope here. They refuse to admit a trope in the words of the testament, while in the meantime they erase from the tablets of the divine covenant the entire precept about not making and worshipping images. They pretend that the apostles simply believed that the bread was substantially the body of Christ, or that the body of Christ was really and essentially offered to them in the bread, and therefore that the Lord did not ask them, and that this is an example for us to imitate. But let us hear what Chrysostom writes about the apostles:

units.la: Quomodo turbati non fuerunt cum audis-sent (accipite, edite hoc est corpus meum?) Quia multa iam & magna de hoc ante diffe-ruit. Quapropter nec illud quod iam crebro perceperant confirmauit. Ipse quoque bibit ex eo, ne auditis verbis illis dicerent: Quid igi-tur sanguinem bibimus & carnem edimus, ac ideo perturbarentur. Nam & quado prius de his verba fecit, multi solummodo propter ver-ba scandalum passi sunt. Ne igitur tunc id quoque accideret, primus ipse hoc fecit, vt tranquillo animo ad communicationem my-steriorum induceret. Vult Chrysostomus Apostolos
units.tr: How they were not troubled when they heard (take, eat, this is my body?). For he had already spoken much and at length about this before. Therefore he did not even confirm what they had already often grasped. He himself also drank of it, so that, on hearing those words, they would not say: "Why then do we drink blood and eat flesh?" and so be disturbed. For even when he spoke of these things before, many were offended by the words alone. Lest then this also happen at that time, he himself did this first, so that he might bring them to the communion of the mysteries with a calm mind. Chrysostom wishes that the Apostles

units.la: Quomodo haec verba intellexerint.
units.tr: How they understood these words.

units.la: Apostolos verba Christi intellexisse ex illa concione prius habita à Christo, quæ loan.6. describitur: Vbi certe non statuitur corporalis, sed spiritualis manducatio corporis Christi. Quod si primo intuitu corporalis præsentia & manducatio statui videretur, tamen nō statim hic sensus recipiendus erat sed conse- rendi prius alij loci, & videndum an talis sensus analogiæ fidei congruat, neque enim sem per est natiuus sensus verborum scripturæ is quem primo intuitu verba præse ferunt, præsertim vbi mysticus sermo est, vt in sacramentis omnibus. Nunc quando ipsa verba non lo quuntur de corporali manducatione, nō posse fumus eos ferre qui tantopere illam vrgent, ac si euicissent hūc esse sensum verborū Christi. Paulus optimus est interpres verborum Domini qui 1.Cor. 10. scribit: Poculum benedictionis cui benedicimus, nonne communio sanguinis Christi est? Panis quem frangimus nonne communio corporis Christi est? In eo igitur nobis vtrinque conuenit, quod vtriq; agnoscimus communionem veri corporis & sanguinis seruatoris nostri Iesu Christi: nobis enim manifestam iniuriam faciunt, ne dicam turpissime mentiuntur, qui aiunt nos omnem præsentiam & communionem corporis Christi negare, Christum cœna excludere, & nullo modo agnoscere præsentem secundum humanam naturam, & merum panem. & vinû seu nuda & vacua tantû signa in coe‑na Domini agnoscere: & tamè Zuinglius & Oecolampadius aperte semper testati sunt, se nunquam negasse corpus Christi à nobis edi, & sanguinem eius bibi, sed hoc fieri spiritua‑liter per fidé. Imo Lutherus ipse in amarulen‑tissimo scripto, quod breue Confessionem in scripsit, ait ipsos in colloquio Marpurgi, reli‑​cto veteri errore concessisse nô esse merum panem & vinû in coena Domini, verum etiam corpus & sanguinem Domini, sed tantû spiritualiter nô corporaliter. Vbi rectè quidem de eorum sententia scribit, attamen ipsis iniuriam facit quasi ante colloquiû Marpurgense aliter docuerint, cum scripta eorum testetur eos antea quoq; sic docuisse, vt facile constat ex Actis disputationis Bernae habitae, & ex responsio‑nibus Zuinglij & Oecolampadii ad Lutheri li‑brum de verbis Domini. Sophistice etiā nos‑bisci agunt, qui aiût nos Christo aliud quod dâ nouû & spirituale corpus affingere, quan‑do dicimus id spiritualiter à nobis edi in coena: cum vox spiritualiter nô de natura aut es‑sentia corporis Christi dicatur, sed modû pręsentiæ & manducationis exprimat. Itaq; non de corporis Christi præsentia & manducatione, sed de præsentiæ & manducationis modo controuersia est. Scio quidem aduersarios dicere, modum præsentiæ incomprehensibilē & ineffabilem esse, sed interim ipsi multis verbis hunc definire & exprimere conantur. Aiunt enim adesse corpus Christi corporali ter, realiter, substantialiter, naturaliter, sacra mentaliter, non tamen naturali, sed supernaturali modo, non localiter, non quantitatiue, non qualitatiue non circumscriptiue, sed definitiue, personaliter, aut repletiue, & ita volunt adesse vt vniatur pani no personaliter aut local iter, sed sacramentaliter & supernaturaliter, ita vt cum pane, in pane, sub pane, iuxta pane manu ministri porrigatur, & non tantum fide, sed ore quoq; a pijs & impijs equaliter sumatur. Certe his verbis modum exprimere volunt, quamuis reuera non exprimant, quoniam haec quae dicunt inter se pugnant & se mutuo euertunt. Porro cum claram explicationem sententiae suae ab ipsis petimus, quomodo corpus Christi praesens sit, ad modum ineffabile confugiunt & quia nihil habent quod respondere possint, accusant nos quod impia quadam curiositate haec quaeramus, & hanc quaestione QVOMODO aiunt Iudaicam & Capernaitica esse. Sed si omnis interrogatio QVOMODO vitiosa esset, oporteret damnare Mariam virginem interrogantem angelum, Quomodo erit istud quando quidem virum non cognosco? Damnandi essent Abrahamus, Gedeon, Samuel, qui hac quaestione vsi sunt. Quorum exemplo constat, quando non reuelarit Dominus aliquid secus futurum, aut sa
units.tr: That the Apostles understood the words of Christ from that earlier sermon given by Christ, which is described in John 6. There certainly it is not laid down that the eating is bodily, but spiritual, of the body of Christ. But even if a bodily presence and eating seemed to be asserted at first glance, this sense should not have been accepted immediately; rather, other passages ought first to be compared, and one should see whether such a sense agrees with the analogy of faith. For the natural sense of the words of Scripture is not always the one that the words first present at first glance, especially where the language is mystical, as in all the sacraments. Now since the words themselves do not speak of bodily eating, we cannot tolerate those who press it so hard, as if they had proved this to be the sense of Christ's words. Paul is the best interpreter of the Lord's words, who writes in 1 Corinthians 10: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" In this we agree with one another on both sides, that both of us acknowledge the communion of the true body and blood of our Saviour Jesus Christ. For they do us a manifest injury, not to say that they lie most shamefully, who say that we deny all presence and communion of the body of Christ, exclude Christ from the Supper, and in no way acknowledge him present according to his human nature, and that we recognise in the Lord's Supper only bare bread and wine, mere empty signs. Yet Zwingli and Oecolampadius have always openly testified that they never denied that the body of Christ is eaten and his blood drunk by us, but that this is done spiritually, through faith. Indeed Luther himself, in his most bitter writing, which he called a Short Confession, says that they at the colloquy of Marburg, having abandoned their old error, conceded that in the Lord's Supper there is not mere bread and wine, but also the body and blood of the Lord, only spiritually and not bodily. Here he indeed writes rightly of their opinion, yet he does them an injury, as if they had taught otherwise before the Colloquy of Marburg, when their writings testify that they had also taught this before, as is easily established from the Acts of the disputation held at Bern, and from the replies of Zwingli and Oecolampadius to Luther's book on the words of the Lord. They also act sophistically towards us, who say that we attribute to Christ some new and spiritual body other than his own, when we say that it is eaten spiritually by us in the Supper; for the word "spiritually" is not said of the nature or essence of the body of Christ, but expresses the mode of presence and of eating. Therefore the controversy is not about the presence and eating of the body of Christ, but about the mode of presence and eating. I know indeed that our opponents say the mode of presence is incomprehensible and ineffable, yet meanwhile they themselves try to define and express it in many words. For they say that the body of Christ is present corporeally, really, substantially, naturally, sacramentally, yet not in a natural but in a supernatural mode; not locally, not quantitatively, not qualitatively, not circumscriptively, but definitively, personally, or repletively; and they want it to be present so that it is united to the bread not personally or locally, but sacramentally and supernaturally, so that it is given by the hand of the minister with the bread, in the bread, under the bread, beside the bread, and is taken equally by the godly and the ungodly, not only by faith but also by the mouth. Certainly with these words they wish to express the mode, although in truth they do not express it, since what they say fights among themselves and overturns one another. Furthermore, when we ask them for a clear explanation of their opinion, how the body of Christ is present, they flee to the ineffable mode, and since they have nothing they can answer, they accuse us of asking these things with a certain impious curiosity, and they say this question HOW is Jewish and Capernaite. But if every question HOW were faulty, it would be necessary to condemn the Virgin Mary for asking the angel, "How shall this be, since I do not know a man?" Abraham, Gideon and Samuel would have to be condemned, who used this question. By their example it is clear that, when the Lord has not revealed that something will happen otherwise, or that...

units.la: Modus praesentia quae aduersarij statuunt.
units.tr: The mode of presence which our opponents maintain.

units.la: An liceat quaerere Quomodo? stum esse, quàm ordinaria ratione agatur, liì cere modum quaerere atque exigere, non quidem dubitando, sed instructionem petendo. Et si Deus aliquem horum modorum verbo suo definiret, sciremus absque vlla hæsitatione aut contradictione credendum, nunc autem cum ipsi hæc dicant, neque suam sententiam verbo Dei confirment, cur non licebit nobis interrogare quomodo hæc sint & fiant? Atqz vt ad ipsa verba Christi redeamus,
units.tr: Whether it is lawful to ask "How?" ...is done in a more ordinary way, it is lawful to ask about and demand the mode, not indeed doubting but seeking instruction. And if God had defined any of these modes in his Word, we would know that it must be believed without any hesitation or contradiction; but now, since they say these things and do not confirm their opinion by the Word of God, why should it not be lawful for us to ask how these things are and come about? And so, to return to the very words of Christ:

units.la: Vtrinque agnoscimus hæc verba Christi esse, & vera eo sensu quo à Christo dicta sunt, quis autem hic sensus sit quæritur. Fatemur verù Christi corpus in cœna manducari & sanguinem bibi, sed de modo manducationis inter nos non conuenit. Aduersarij dicunt hunc esse sensum verborum quod Christus corpus suum realiter & substantialiter & naturaliter præsens cum pane & vino porrigat ore corporis manducandum. Nos dicimus Christum in sacra cœna, cum pane & vino exteris symbolis, verum corpus & sanguinem sacramentaliter coniuncta, porrigere ad manducandum, non quidem ore corporis, sed spiritualiter per fidem: ita vt sicut pane & vino corpora nostra aluntur quoad hanc vitam, sic corpore
units.tr: On both sides we acknowledge that these words of Christ are true, in the sense in which Christ spoke them; but what this sense is, is the question. We indeed confess that the body of Christ is eaten and his blood drunk in the Supper, but we do not agree about the mode of eating. Our opponents say that the sense of the words is that Christ, really, substantially and naturally present, gives his body with the bread and wine to be eaten by the mouth of the body. We say that Christ in the holy Supper, with bread and wine as the outward symbols, offers to be eaten the true body and blood, sacramentally joined, not indeed by the mouth of the body, but spiritually through faith; so that, just as our bodies are nourished by bread and wine for this life, so the whole man is spiritually fed to eternal life by the body of Christ given for us, which is the heavenly and life-giving bread.

units.la: Quis sensus verborum, & modus præsentiæ. corpore Christi pro nobis tradito, qui est panis cœlestis & viuificus, homo totus spiritualiter alatur ad vitam æternam. Neque tantum communione meriti aut efficacię Christi statuimus, quoniam fides nostra respicit Christum totum, neq; meritum a persona separat, non magis quàm lucem a corpore Solis, eum que totum agnoscit caput nostrum esse, & ita nos cum ipso Christo vnitos & coniunctos. Interea tamen profitemur ad hanc communionem quæ fide fit, non esse necessariam essentialem naturalem & corporalem præsentiam corporis Christi, qua cum pane essentialiter præsens ore corporis manducetur: imo hunc præsentiæ modum vt naturæ sacramentorū, articulis fidei, & plurimis locis scriptrarum, contrariū recipere non possumus. Nam quo ad verba Christi quorū simplicé & grāmaticū sensum se seruare falso iactā t manducatio corporis Christi inde confici potest, non autē oralis manducatio, & corporalis naturalisq; præsentia. Verba Christi sonant Panè esse corpus Christi, & Paulus panè ait esse communionem corporis Christi, & cū in verbis Christi duodisparata Panis & corpus Christi de se prædicentur, non potest hæc prædicatio simpliciter & identice intelligi, itaque & Papistæ per Transubstantiationem ea explicant, & isti nescio quam consubstantiationem fingentes à verbis Christi recedunt, & cum dicunt cum pane, & in pane, & sub pane corpus Christi realiter & naturaliter praesens esse, simplicem verborum & grammaticum sensum non expri- munt, sed eam quam ipsi putant esse διάνοιαν verborum Christi, & velint nolint tropum in verbis Christi agnoscere coguntur: nam Brentius & Iacobus Andreae docent Synechdochen esse in verbis Christi. Similiter cum nos negamus corporalem naturalemque praesentiam corporis Christi, & oralem eius mandu-cationem, ac spiritualiter & per fidem manducari Christi corpus dicimus, panem autem dici corpus Christi sacramentaliter, quia est signum, symbolum & figura corporis Christi, quo exterius sumpto ore corporis, fides sumit & percipit corpus Christi, non ideo negamus verba Christi, aut de eorum veritate dubitamus, sed horum sententiam & interpretationem idque non ex nostra mente sed ex scripturis adferimus.
units.tr: What the sense of the words is, and the mode of presence. Nor do we posit only a communion of merit or efficacy of Christ, since our faith looks to the whole Christ, and does not separate the merit from the person, any more than light from the body of the sun, and it acknowledges him whole to be our head, and so we are united and joined with Christ himself. Meanwhile, however, we profess that for this communion which takes place by faith, a necessary essential, natural and bodily presence of the body of Christ is not required, by which it is eaten by the mouth of the body while essentially present with the bread. Indeed we cannot receive this mode of presence as contrary to the nature of the sacraments, the articles of faith, and very many places of the Scriptures. For as regards the words of Christ, by whose simple and grammatical sense the eating of the body of Christ is falsely claimed to be kept, the eating that can be made from them is not an oral eating and a bodily and natural presence. The words of Christ sound that the bread is the body of Christ, and Paul says the bread is the communion of the body of Christ; and since in the words of Christ two disparate things, bread and the body of Christ, are predicated of each other, this predication cannot be understood simply and identically. And so the Papists explain it by transubstantiation, and these men, inventing I know not what consubstantiation, depart from the words of Christ; and when they say that the body of Christ is really and naturally present with the bread, in the bread and under the bread, they do not express the simple and grammatical sense of the words, but the meaning which they themselves think is the meaning of Christ's words, and whether they wish it or not they are compelled to recognise a trope in the words of Christ: for Brenz and Jakob Andreae teach that there is synecdoche in the words of Christ. Similarly, when we deny a bodily and natural presence of the body of Christ, and an oral eating of it, and say that the body of Christ is eaten spiritually and through faith, and that bread is called the body of Christ sacramentally, because it is the sign, symbol and figure of the body of Christ, which, when the outward thing is taken by the mouth of the body, faith takes and receives the body of Christ, we do not thereby deny the words of Christ or doubt their truth, but we bring forward their sense and interpretation, and this not from our own mind but from the Scriptures.

units.la: Confirmatio nostrae interpretationis.
units.tr: Confirmation of our interpretation.

units.la: Primum hoc inter nos & adversarios convenit, esse inter panem & corpus Christi unionem sacramentalem, ideoque locutionem sacramentalem esse, quando panis corpus Christi nominatur, quia illi super naturalem incomprehensibilem & ineffabil esse aiunt: quod ex parte aliqua verum est. Nam quia symbo-la haec non naturaliter significant & repræsen-tant res signatas, sed ex Dei institutione, re-ète illa vnio dicitur supernaturalis, solius es-nim Dei est sacramenta instituere: præterea si spectamus operationem internam divinae virtutis in mentibus fidelium, per quam vere fruuntur non tantum signis, sed ipsis rebus si-gnificatis, est haec efficacia quodam modo in-comprehensibilis & ineffabilis. At non ideo sacramentalis vnio est substantiarum panis & vini cum corporis & sanguinis Christi sub statialis vnio & ineffabilis quaedam cosubstan-tiario, sed in omnibus sacramētis duo statuū-tur, signum & res signata, sacramentum & res sacramenti, quæ vt Dialecticorum more lo-quamur, relatione mutua coniunguntur, qua fit vt signum accipiat nomen rei signatae. Au- gustinus ad Bonif. Si sacramenta earum re-rum quarum sunt sacramenta similitudinem non haberent, vtique sacramenta non essent. Ex hac autem similitudine plerunq; etiam ip-sarum rerum nomina accipiunt. Item contra Maximinum lib.3. cap.22. In sacramentis non quid sint, sed quid ostendant attenditur: quia signa sunt rerum aliud existentia & aliud significantia Sic illa Abrahae mandata circum-cisio foedus nominatur, & agnus mactatus di-citur Pascah seu transitus, & hostia pro pec-cato nominatur peccatum. Lapis etiam quē
units.tr: First, we and our opponents agree that there is a sacramental union between the bread and the body of Christ, and that the expression is therefore sacramental when the bread is called the body of Christ. They say this union is supernatural, incomprehensible and ineffable, and in some respect that is true. These symbols do not signify and represent the things they signify by nature but by God's institution, so the union is rightly called supernatural, since it belongs to God alone to institute sacraments. Moreover, if we consider the inward working of divine power in the minds of the faithful, by which they truly enjoy not only the signs but the things signified, that efficacy is in a certain way incomprehensible and ineffable. But the sacramental union is not a substantial union of the substances of bread and wine with the body and blood of Christ, nor some ineffable co-substantiation. In all sacraments two things are set down, the sign and the thing signified, the sacrament and the thing of the sacrament, which, to speak as the dialecticians do, are joined by a mutual relation, so that the sign receives the name of the thing signified. Augustine, to Boniface: If sacraments did not have a likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would certainly not be sacraments. From this likeness, however, they very often also receive the names of the things themselves. Likewise, against Maximinus, book 3, chapter 22: In sacraments what matters is not what they are but what they show, for they are signs, existing as one thing and signifying another. So that circumcision commanded to Abraham is called a covenant, the lamb slain is called the Passover or passing over, and the sin offering is called sin. The stone also that

units.la: Iacob statuit in symbolum Bethel vel domus Dei, ipsa domus Dei vocatur, locus ipse domus Dei & Deus de Bethel dicitur. Arca foederis symbolum praesentiae & auxilij diuini Iehoua exercituum saepe nominatur. In nouo foedere Baptismus dicitur ablutio peccatorum & regeneratio spiritualis: item in Baptismo dicitur indui Christus, & nos ei commori & sepeliri dicimur, quae omnia non realiter & substantialiter, sed symbolice & sacramentaliter explicanda sunt. Ac monet Theodoretus non contemnendus author, ideo in sacramentis signis tribui nomen rei signatae, vt qui diuina sumunt mysteria, non ad ipsam naturam rerum sub aspectu cadentium obstu pescerent, sed hac permutatione nominum adducerentur ad incomprehensibilem Dei gratiam contuendam. Est autem hic tropus in communi ratione loquendi frequens & vsitatus, praesertim in pactorum & foederum ratione. Ita signa solennia contractuū saepe nomina ipsa contractuum sortiuntur, & monumenta earum rerum quarum sunt monumenta, sic statuam Caesaris Caesarem nominamus, & saepe propter similitudinem nomina permutantur. Christus agnus dicitur, & petra, & rursus Petra diserte erat Christus. Sic etiam Christus se panem nominat: & tamen cum rei signatae symboli nomen tribuitur tropum omnes facile agnoscunt, sed cum rursus symbolo pari ratione nomen rei significatæ imponi∗ tur, tantopere (quod mirum est) à tropo abhorrent. Dauid cum tres è numero heroum exercitus sui irruissent in castra Palæstinorum, & attulissent illi aquam è cisterna Bethlehemitica, quàm desiderauerat, noluit illam bibere dicens: Absit à me Iehoua vt faciam hoc. Num bibam sanguinem virorum qui abierunt cum periculo vitæ suæ? Hic aquam sanguinem appellat, quia testabatur periculo effundendi sanguinis illos se exposuisse, & mirantur aliqui in Eucharistia vinum sanguinem dici, vbi testatur seruatorem nostrum se non tantum exposuisse periculo, sed etiam reuera sanguine fudisse. Porro nostrum argumentum non est tale vt quidam fingunt, Scriptura, in quibusdam locis tropicè loquuntur ergo verba cœnæ tropicè accipienda sunt. Sed hæc est argumenti summa. In omnibus sacra mentis veteris & noui Testamenti signa per tropum accipiunt nomen rerum significarum, & signum ac res significata relatione coniunguntur, non autem realiter & substantialiter idem sunt. Ergo etiam in cœna panis per tropum corpus Domini vocatur, & non substantialiter, sed relatiue cum corpore Christi coniunctum est. In hoc autem modum sacra mentaliter verba cœnæ vetus ecclesia semper intellexit, & interpretata est nomine signi, symboli, figuræ, typi, &c. id quod Patrum in-
units.tr: Jacob set up as a symbol at Bethel is called the house of God itself, the place is called the house of God, and it is said to be God of Bethel. The ark of the covenant is often called the symbol of the presence and help of the LORD of hosts. In the new covenant baptism is called the washing away of sins and spiritual regeneration; likewise in baptism we are said to put on Christ, and to die and be buried with him. All these things are to be explained not really and substantially, but symbolically and sacramentally. Theodoret, no contemptible author, observes that the name of the thing signified is given to the signs in sacraments so that those who receive the divine mysteries should not fix their gaze on the nature of the things that fall under the senses, but by this exchange of names be led to contemplate the incomprehensible grace of God. This trope is common and usual in ordinary speech, especially in the case of pacts and covenants. Thus the solemn signs of contracts often take on the very names of the contracts, and the memorials of things take the names of those things; so we call the statue of Caesar Caesar, and names are often exchanged because of likeness. Christ is called a lamb, and a rock, and again the Rock was plainly Christ. So also Christ calls himself bread. Yet when the name of the thing signified is given to the symbol, everyone readily recognises the trope, but when, by the same reasoning, the name of the thing signified is given to the symbol, they recoil from the trope, remarkably so. When David's three men from among the heroes of his army had broken into the camp of the Philistines and brought him water from the cistern of Bethlehem, which he had longed for, he refused to drink it, saying: Far be it from me, O LORD, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of these men who went at the risk of their lives? Here he calls the water blood, because he testified that those men had exposed themselves to the danger of shedding blood. And some marvel that in the Eucharist the wine is called blood, where we testify that our Saviour not only exposed himself to danger but actually shed his blood. Our argument, moreover, is not of the kind some invent: Scripture speaks figuratively in some places, therefore the words of the Supper must be taken figuratively. Rather, the sum of our argument is this: in all the sacraments of the Old and New Testament the signs receive by a trope the names of the things they signify, and sign and thing signified are joined by relation, not really and substantially the same. Therefore also in the Supper the bread is called by a trope the body of the Lord, and is joined with the body of Christ not substantially but relatively. The ancient Church always understood the words of the Supper in this sacramental way and interpreted them by the name of sign, symbol, figure, type and so on, which can be shown from almost innumerable testimonies of the Fathers.

units.la: C numeris pene testimonijs ostendi potest. Tertullianus: Acceptum panem & distribuutm discipulis corpus suum illum fecit,hoc est corpus meũ dicdo: hoc est figura corporis mei. Ambrosius, Fac nobis hanc oblationem ascriptam, rationabilem, acceptabilem, quod est figura corporis & sanguinis Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Beda. Christus pro carne & sanguine agni,suę carnis sanguinisq; sacramentũ in panis ac vini figura substituit. Bertramus, Panis ille vinumque figurate Christi corpus & sanguis existit.Ité:In pane illo nō solũ corpus Christi,verũm corpus etiam in eum credentis populi figuratur. Et corpus Christi quod in ecclesia per mysterium geritur,secundum quendam modum corpus Christi esse cognoscitur,& modus iste in figura est & imagine. D.
