Augustinus luda adhibuit ad conuiuiũ,in quo corporis & sanguinis sui figurā, discipulis suis commendauit. Idem: Non enim Dominus dubitauit dicere, Hoc est corpus meum cum daret signum corporis sui. Idem de verbis cœnæ in libro 3. de doctrina Christiana scribit. Figura est ergo,præcipiens passioni Domini esse communicandum, & suauiter atque vtiliter recondendum in memoria quod pro nobis caro eius crucifixa & vulnerata sit. Omitto hic Græcos qui typum & antitypum,symbolum,mysterium corporis & sanguinis Christi nominant. Ideoque nostra interpretatio nec aliena est, cum eadē ratio sit omnium sacramentorum, nec detorta & violenta, cum non recedat a loquendi ratione spiritui sancto vsitata, neque etiam nova, cum vetus Ecclesia verba Christi in hunc modum intellexerit & interpretata sit.
units.tr: Tertullian: Taking the bread and distributing it to the disciples, he made it his body, saying, "This is my body," that is, "This is a figure of my body." Ambrose: Make this oblation for us inscribed, reasonable, acceptable, which is a figure of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Bede: Christ, in place of the flesh and blood of the lamb, substituted the sacrament of his flesh and blood under the figure of bread and wine. Bertram: That bread and wine figuratively are the body and blood of Christ. Again: In that bread not only the body of Christ but also the body of the believing people is figured. And the body of Christ which is performed in the church through the mystery is known to be the body of Christ in a certain manner, and that manner is in figure and image. Augustine: Judas was admitted to the feast, at which he commended to his disciples the figure of his body and blood. The same: For the Lord did not hesitate to say, "This is my body," when he gave the sign of his body. The same, in book 3 of On Christian Doctrine, writes on the words of the Supper: It is therefore a figure, commanding that communion be shared in the passion of the Lord, and that it be sweetly and profitably kept in memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us. I omit here the Greeks, who call the body and blood of Christ type and antitype, symbol and mystery. Therefore our interpretation is neither foreign, since the same reasoning applies to all sacraments, nor distorted and forced, since it does not depart from the manner of speaking used by the Holy Spirit; nor is it new, since the ancient Church understood and interpreted the words of Christ in this way.

units.la: Deinde neminem putamus ambigere vtriusque signi in cœna sacra parem rationem esse, at quæ de poculo scribuntur ea omnino tropice accipiēda sunt. Calix enim dicitur nouum Testamentum, neque tamen poculum neq; quod eo continetur vinum est reipsa nouum Testamentum. Neq; dici potest per synechdochen, qua continēs nomen accipit rei quæ continetur, calice sanguinem Christi & nouum Testamentum nominari. Negant enim sanguinem ita poculo contineri sicut vinum cantharo continetur: testamentum autem calice contineri nemo puto dixerit. Et quum alij Euangelistæ inquiunt τῦτό ἐστι τὸ αἷμά μου eodē tropo quo Paulus & Lucas vtuntur; nam τῦτο nihil aliud referre potest quàm poculum, quod Christus in manus accepit, & Apostolis dedit, & Paulus expresso subiecto docet quo pronomen demonstratiuum referri debeat. Atque vt sequamur eorum interpretationem, tamen hoc dictum HIC EST SANGVIS MEVS idem valebit, atque hoc Pauli & Lucæ, Hoc poculum est nouum Testamentum in sanguine meo. nisi velint Matthęu & Marcúa Paulo & Luca dissentire. Quod si par est ratio utriusque symboli, idem erit HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, atq; si dixisset, Hoc est nouū Testamentum in corpore meo, vel hoc est corpus noui Testamenti. Quin etiā ipsum noui Testamenti nomen docet qualem praesentiā corporis & sanguinis Christi, & qualem mandu-cationem statuat Christus: non aliam scilicet quam quatenus noui Testamenti corpus & sanguis sunt. Sed corpus Christi ad noui Testamenti confirmationem refertur quatenus victima fuit qua Deus nobis reconciliatus est, & sanguis quatenus effusus est in remissione peccatorum. Corporis aut & sanguinis Christi societate participes reddimur noui Testamenti, nō corporali horū exhibitione, sed in effabili illa vnione Christi capitis cum membris suis, atq; cōmunicatione virtutis ac effica-cię, quae ex viuifica illorū substantia manat, & spiritualiter a nobis percipitur, vt Christus docet Ioannis 6. cap.
units.tr: Next, we think no one doubts that the reasoning about both signs in the holy supper is the same, but what is written about the cup must be taken wholly figuratively. For the cup is called the new covenant, yet neither the cup nor the wine contained in it is in fact the new covenant. Nor can it be said by synecdoche, by which the container takes the name of the thing contained, that the blood of Christ and the new covenant are named by the cup. For they deny that blood is contained in a cup as wine is contained in a goblet, and I think no one would say that a covenant is contained in a cup. And when the other evangelists say this is my blood [τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ αἷμά μου], they use the same trope that Paul and Luke use; for this (touto) can refer to nothing other than the cup, which Christ took in his hands and gave to the apostles, and Paul, by expressly naming the subject, teaches what the demonstrative pronoun must refer to. And even if we follow their interpretation, this saying, THIS IS MY BLOOD, will have the same force as Paul's and Luke's, This cup is the new covenant in my blood, unless they wish Matthew and Mark to disagree with Paul and Luke. But if the reasoning of both symbols is equal, THIS IS MY BODY will be the same as if he had said, This is the new covenant in my body, or this is the body of the new covenant. Indeed, the very name of the new covenant teaches what kind of presence of the body and blood of Christ, and what kind of eating, Christ appoints: namely, none other than insofar as they are the body and blood of the new covenant. But the body of Christ is referred to the confirmation of the new covenant insofar as it was the victim by which God was reconciled to us, and his blood insofar as it was poured out for the remission of sins. We are made partakers of the new covenant by fellowship with the body and blood of Christ, not by a bodily exhibition of them, but by that ineffable union of Christ the head with his members, and by the communication of virtue and efficacy which flows from the life-giving substance of them and is received spiritually by us, as Christ teaches in John chapter 6.

units.la: Praeterea Christus sacramentum cœnae instituens iussit hoc facere in sui memoriam seu cōmemorationē. At D. Augustus scribit: Nemi-nem recordari alicuius rei, nisi quae in praesentia non sit posita. in Psal. 37. Itaq; sacrificium Christi a cœna distinguit, quod illud promitte-batur veteribus, per ipsam veritate reddeba-tur in passione, nunc vero eius memoria celebratur bratur.Contra Faustum lib.20.cap.21. & lib. 6.cap.5. Multo aūt clarius à D.Bernardo memoria & realis præsentia corporis & sanguinis Christi in cœna opponūtur; statuit enim hoc discrimen inter nos & angelos, quod illi reali præsentia Christi fruantur,cum nos memoria tantum fide ac spiritu quasi per speculum in ænigmate Christum intueamur. Neq; tamen propterea ab illo nuda signa constituuntur,sed fatetur Christum ipsum nobis proponi, sed sub sacramenti cortice velatum. Est enim etiam certa veritas realiter quoque absentium rerum quarum hypostasis est fides.
units.tr: Moreover, when Christ instituted the sacrament of the Supper, he commanded that this be done in his memory or remembrance. But Augustine writes: no one recalls anything unless it is not present. (On Psalm 37.) Thus he distinguishes Christ's sacrifice from the Supper: the sacrifice was promised to the ancients and was accomplished in reality through his passion itself, whereas now its memory is celebrated. (Against Faustus, bk. 20, ch. 21, and bk. 6, ch. 5.) Much more clearly, Bernard opposes memory to the real presence of Christ's body and blood in the Supper. He draws this distinction between us and the angels: the angels enjoy the real presence of Christ, while we, having only memory, behold Christ by faith and spirit, as through a mirror in an enigma. Yet on that account he does not make the elements bare signs. He confesses that Christ himself is set before us, but veiled under the bark of the sacrament. For there is also a certain truth in things that are really absent, whose substance is faith.

units.la: Apostolus etiam iubet in celebratione huius sacramenti annuntiare mortem Domini donec veniat, & ita interpretatur verba Christi iubentis hæc in sui memoriam facere, nempe vt non curiose quæramus corporalem præsentiam, quando corporaliter extremo demū die venturus est ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos, sed vt beneficium hoc quod morte sua nobis præstitit,& hoc ritu efficaciter impertit,semper animo intueamur, & de ipsius gratia & auxilio minimè dubitemus, & ita fide manducemus corpus pro nobis traditum, & sanguinem pro nobis fusum bibamus. Quod si annuntianda est mors Domini donec venerit, is autem realiter in cœna adest, debet igitur cœna cessare, & hac ratione eius vsus tolleretur.
units.tr: The Apostle also bids us, in celebrating this sacrament, to proclaim the Lord's death until he comes, and he so interprets the words of Christ commanding us to do this in remembrance of him: namely, that we should not curiously seek a bodily presence, since he will come bodily at the last day to judge the living and the dead. Rather, we should always keep before our minds, with the eye of the soul, the benefit he bestowed by his death and imparts effectively through this rite, and should not doubt his grace and help at all. Thus by faith we eat the body given for us and drink the blood shed for us. But if the death of the Lord is to be proclaimed until he comes, and yet he is really present in the Supper, then the Supper ought to cease, and by this reasoning its use would be taken away.

units.la: Præterea vbi Christus panem corpus suũ & vinum sanguine suum in sacra cœna nominat, non absolute de corpore suo loquitur, sed quatenus corpus pro nobis traditur, & sanguis pro nobis funditur. Quatenus seipsum obtulit vt esset victima pro peccatis nostris ad reconciliandũ nobis patrem cœlestẽ, & abluęda peccata, hactenus corpus suum & sanguinem nobis offert in cibũ & potũ, vt aut fruamur hoc beneficio non necesse est statui realem coniunctionem cum pane & vino, & corporalem manducationẽ. Sicut Solem præsentẽ habemus quatenus illuminat oculos nostros, neq; tamẽ necesse est corpus Solis absolute præsens realiter adesse oculis nostris. Absoluta caro & absolutus sanguis nõ possunt cibũ & potũ præstare animabus nostris, quæ nõ nutriũtur corporata aliqua substantia: itaq; cũ Christus nobis dederit corpus suũ in cibũ, & sanguinẽ in potũ, non dedit hæc quatenus sunt corporea substantia, sed quatenus sunt pro nobis effusa & tradita. Et eo tempore quo Christus cœnam instituit, corpus nondum in morte traditũ erat neq; sanguis effusus, & tamen nihilominus Christus tanquã de re præsenti loquitur, Quod datur inquit & frągitur, & qui effunditur, ostendens se dare donum non actu, sed virtute & efficacia præsens.
units.tr: Moreover, when Christ in the holy Supper calls the bread his body and the wine his blood, he is not speaking of his body absolutely, but insofar as his body is given for us and his blood poured out for us. Insofar as he offered himself to be the victim for our sins, to reconcile the heavenly Father to us and to wash away our sins, so far he offers us his body and blood as food and drink. That we may enjoy this benefit, it is not necessary to posit a real union with the bread and wine, or a bodily eating. We have the sun present insofar as it lights our eyes, yet it is not necessary that the body of the sun itself be really present to our eyes. Flesh considered absolutely and blood considered absolutely cannot provide food and drink to our souls, which are not nourished by any corporeal substance. So when Christ gave us his body as food and his blood as drink, he did not give them insofar as they are corporeal substance, but insofar as they were poured out and given for us. And at the time Christ instituted the Supper, his body had not yet been given in death, nor his blood shed; yet nevertheless Christ speaks as of a present thing: "This is given," he says, "and broken," and "which is poured out." He shows that he gives the gift not in act but present in power and efficacy.

units.la: Cõmuni etiam consensu theologorũ receptum est, sacramentũ esse visibile verbũ Dei, & eandem esse præsentiam Christi in verbo & sacramentis: atque veteres, vt Origenes & Hieronymus, statuunt duas rationes edendi- & bibendi corpus & sanguinē Domini, in verbis, &in sacramentis seu in mysterio. Et inter recentiores, vt alios nunc omittam, idē docuit Brētius, qui in Exegesi in Ioanně scribit. Iam quemadmodum per verba Euangelij, credentibus offeruntur & communicantur dona Dei, ita & per sacramenta verbo affixa. Sunt enim sacramenta ob hanc causam vero boadiecta, vt sint media instrumenta, vna cum verbo, quibus credentibus dona Dei communicarentur. Sed verbo scriprurarum non est coniunctum corpus Christi aliter quam significatione, verba enim notæ & signa sunt: quare non aliam quoque corporis Christi cum externis symbolis coniunctionem statuere debemus.
units.tr: It is also received by the common consent of theologians that the sacrament is the visible word of God, and that the presence of Christ is the same in the word and in the sacraments. The ancients, such as Origen and Jerome, hold that there are two ways of eating and drinking the body and blood of the Lord: in the words, and in the sacraments or the mystery. Among more recent writers, to pass over others for now, Brentius taught the same, who writes in his Exegesis on John: "Just as the gifts of God are offered and communicated to believers through the words of the Gospel, so also through the sacraments joined to the word. For the sacraments are added to the word for this reason, that they may be instruments, together with the word, by which the gifts of God are communicated to believers." But the body of Christ is not joined to the words of Scripture otherwise than by signification, for words are marks and signs. Therefore we ought not to posit any other conjunction of the body of Christ with the external symbols.

units.la: Statuuntur etiā ab omnibus veteribus duę tantum partes sacramentorum signum & res signata, signum visibile & inuisibilis gratia, & hæ non res terrena & cœlestis, quę non realiter coniuncta sunt, alioqui omnes signum percipientes cœlestis quoq; inuisibilis gratię participes essent, quod aduersarij non concedunt, qui impios percipere volunt corpus Christi, non tamen gratiæ & viuificationis esse participes. Itaq; videntur tria statuere, externa symbola, deinde corpus & sanguinem Christi, & gra-
units.tr: All the ancients also establish only two parts of the sacraments: the sign and the thing signified, the visible sign and the invisible grace. These are not earthly and heavenly things that are really joined together. Otherwise all who receive the sign would also be partakers of the heavenly and invisible grace, which our opponents do not concede, since they want the wicked to receive the body of Christ yet not to be partakers of grace and quickening. Thus they seem to posit three things: the external symbols, then the body and blood of Christ, and the invisible grace.

units.la: Hæc non realiter coniuncta. tiam inuisibilem : atque ita à simplicitate orthodoxæ doctrinæ recedunt.
units.tr: These are not really joined together, and thus they depart from the simplicity of orthodox doctrine.

units.la: Postremo scriptura docet, mãducari Christi corpus & bibi sanguinem eius, spiritualiter & per fidē Ioā.6.ca.Itaq; cum in cœna iubemur corpus Christi edere & sanguine eius bibere:quod ad ipsum corpus Christi & sanguinem pertinet, non instituitur aliud manducationis genus in cœna quam quo fideles corpus Christi edunt per fidem:adduntur tamen in cœna externa symbola quibus fides communicantium provocetur, oftendaturq; quid manducatio spiritualis corporis Christi conferat, nempe id quod panis in cibū sumptus,& vinum in potū,vitæ comedentiū & bibentium præstare solent. Ideoq; non modo Chrysost. sed alij quoque patres verba cœnæ per verba Christi Ioā. 6. interpretātur. Quod aūt aliam manducationē corporis Christi in cœna quidā statuūt, præter Dei verbū faciūt. Editur Christi corpus in cœna in sacramēto, quādo sacramentū seu signū quod etiam symbolicōs corpus Christi nominatur, ore percipimus, & ita veteres dixerunt Christum in sacramento edi. At ipsam Christi carnem verā & substantialem pro nobis traditam, & sanguine pro nobis effusum, aliter quàm per fidem manducari ex verbo Dei ostendi non potest: nam si obijciunt verba hæc: Accipite, edite, hoc est corpus meum: vtuntur elencho Petitionis principij: verba enim Christi nos iubent corpus eius edere & sanguinem bibere, at oralis & corporalis manducatio nusquã ne verbulo quidem innuitur: ea autem quam nos docemus, & aliis scripturæ locis & Patrum testimonijs confirmatur.
units.tr: Finally, Scripture teaches that the body of Christ is eaten and his blood drunk spiritually and through faith (John 6). Therefore, when in the Supper we are bidden to eat Christ's body and drink his blood, as far as the body and blood of Christ themselves are concerned, no other kind of eating is established in the Supper than that by which the faithful eat the body of Christ through faith. Yet external symbols are added in the Supper, by which the faith of the communicants is stirred up, and it is shown what the spiritual eating of Christ's body confers. That is, what bread taken as food and wine taken as drink are accustomed to provide to those who eat and drink: life. Hence not only Chrysostom but other Fathers too interpret the words of the Supper through the words of Christ in John 6. But those who posit some other eating of Christ's body in the Supper, besides the word of God, go beyond God's word. The body of Christ is eaten in the Supper in the sacrament, when we receive with the mouth the sacrament or sign, which is also called symbolically the body of Christ; and so the ancients said that Christ is eaten in the sacrament. But that the very flesh of Christ, true and substantial, given for us, and his blood, poured out for us, is eaten in any way other than by faith, cannot be shown from the word of God. For if they object these words, "Take, eat; this is my body," they use the fallacy of begging the question. Christ's words bid us eat his body and drink his blood, but oral and corporal eating is nowhere indicated, not even by a syllable. The eating that we teach, however, is confirmed by other passages of Scripture and by the testimonies of the Fathers.

units.la: Quare præsentiam carnis Christi corporalem reijciamus.
units.tr: Why we reject the corporeal presence of Christ's flesh.

units.la: Porro ne statuamus realem & naturalem præsentiam corporis & sanguinis Christi in pane & vino cœnæ Dominicæ, & eorū oralé manducationem, mouent nos absurda quæ hinc consequuntur, quæ non tantū rationi absurda sunt, sed cū scripturis & fide pugnant.
units.tr: Furthermore, to avoid affirming a real and natural presence of the body and blood of Christ in the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper, and their oral eating, we are moved by the absurdities that follow from it. These are not only absurd to reason but also clash with the Scriptures and with faith.

units.la: Primum realis præsentia corporis Christi in pane aut cum pane, qua vel vbique, vel simul innumeris locis præsens sit realiter & substantialiter & naturaliter, abolet humanæ naturæ veritatem in Christo seruatore nostro, & doctrinam incarnationis, quæ est fundamentum salutis nostræ euertit. Christū enim ex scripturis didicimus veritatem humanæ naturæ ita assumpsisse, vt nobis per omnia similis factus sit excepto peccato. At vero humanum corpus definitum & circunscriptum non potest simul in multis locis præsens esse. Et Christum ante & post resurrectionē suam a mortuis, ita in vno loco corpore suo præsen tem fuisse, vt alibi eodem tempore corpore suo non adesset, sacræ literæ aperte testantur. Porro vbique præfentem esse diuinæ naturæ ita propriü est, vt hinc firmissimè Patres probauerint deitatem Spiritus sancti: & non dubitarint afferere diuinam naturâ fi corporea effet, circumscriptam quoque & in loco fore. Quare fi Christo tribuitur omniprefentia corporis, veritas corporis in eo aboletur. Et omissa iam omnipræsentia, ex illa reali præfentia qua multis simul in locis præfens fit æque multa absurda consequuntur. Exempli enim causa illam ipsam cœnā consideremus quam Christus cũ discipulis sumpsit. Assedit Christus corpore suo vero mensæ vna cum disci-pulis,idque vere,realiter,aspectabiliter: & tamen iuxta horum sententiam suum verum corpus realiter & inuisibiliter discipulis sub pane & cum pane manducandũ dedit: & corpus eius mortale & patibile tum erat, & illud ipsum impatibiliter & supernaturaliter edebant discipuli. Itaq; sequitur Christi corpus simul & eodé tempore visibile & inuisibile, patibile & impatibile,mortale & immortale, fractum & integrum tũ fuisse,imo Christum plura habuisse corpora, illud quod videbant discipuli & illud quod accipiebat, illud quod porrigebat illis panem & poculum, & illud quod vna cum pane & poculo porrigebatur. Hæc an non humanæ naturæ veritatem tollunt? Scio omnia absurda huiusmodi repelli abads
units.tr: First, a real presence of Christ's body in the bread, or with the bread, by which it is present really, substantially and naturally either everywhere or at the same time in countless places, abolishes the truth of human nature in Christ our Saviour and overturns the doctrine of the incarnation, which is the foundation of our salvation. For we have learned from the Scriptures that Christ assumed the truth of human nature so as to be made like us in all things except sin. But a human body, defined and circumscribed, cannot be present in many places at once. The sacred letters clearly testify that Christ, both before and after his resurrection from the dead, was present with his body in one place in such a way that at the same time he was not with his body elsewhere. Moreover, being present everywhere is so proper to the divine nature that the Fathers firmly proved the deity of the Holy Spirit from this, and did not hesitate to affirm that if the divine nature were corporeal it would also be circumscribed and in a place. Therefore, if omnipresence is attributed to Christ's body, the truth of that body is abolished. Even setting aside omnipresence, from that real presence by which he is present in many places at once, many absurdities follow. Let us consider, for example, that very supper which Christ ate with his disciples. Christ sat at the table with his disciples in his true body, truly, really and visibly. Yet, according to these men's opinion, he really and invisibly gave his true body to the disciples to be eaten under the bread and with the bread; and that body was then mortal and passible, and the disciples ate that very same body impassibly and supernaturally. It follows, then, that Christ's body was at the same time and in the same moment both visible and invisible, passible and impassible, mortal and immortal, broken and whole; indeed, that Christ had several bodies: the one the disciples saw, the one that took the bread, the one that offered them the bread and cup, and the one that was offered along with the bread and cup. Do not these things destroy the truth of human nature? I know that the adversaries repel all absurdities of this kind with the shield of divine omnipotence, but we must have recourse to omnipotence only when we are sure of the will of God.

units.la: ab aduersarijs clypeo diuinæ omnipotentiæ, sed primum ad omnipotentiam confugiendum est vbi nobis de voluntate Dei constat. Nondum probarūt Christū voluisse nobis in cœna corpus suū realiter & corporaliter in pane dare. Sæpe enim diximus id nequaquā effi¦ci his verbis HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, de quorū sensu cum sit controuersia, ipsi tamē subinde sophistico more id quod controuersum & in quæstione positum est pro argumē-to sumunt. Deinde omnipotetia Dei non implicat contradictionē, alioqui veritati diuinæ aduersaretur. Neq; omnipotentia Dei facit vt eodē tempore actu & reipsa aliquid sit & non sit, vt corpus Christi eodē tempore sit infinitum simul & circumscriptū, eodem tempore sit patibile & impatibile, adsit & non adsit: idq; realiter, substantialiter & naturaliter. Neq; enim quærimus an naturaliter loco definiatur, per energiam autē præsens sit, aut persona-liter præsens. Sed quæstio hactenus fuit de reali & substantiali & corporali præsentia corporis Christi, an sacerdos manu porrigat & percipiens sacramentū ore sumat ipsum corpus Christi verum & naturale, realiter, substantialiter, corporaliter. Scimus quibus verbis & Lutherus vsus sit & alij adhuc vtantur.
units.tr: They have not yet proved that Christ willed to give us his body in the supper really and corporeally in the bread. We have often said that this is by no means effected by the words THIS IS MY BODY, and since their meaning is in dispute, they nevertheless, in their sophistical manner, take as an argument what is itself disputed and in question. Next, the omnipotence of God does not involve contradiction, otherwise it would be opposed to divine truth. Nor does the omnipotence of God make it so that something is and is not at the same time, in act and in fact, so that the body of Christ would be at once infinite and circumscribed, at once passible and impassible, present and not present; and all this really, substantially and naturally. For we do not ask whether he is naturally defined by place, or present by his power, or present personally. The question so far has been about the real, substantial and corporeal presence of Christ's body: whether the priest, offering with his hand and the communicant receiving the sacrament with his mouth, takes in the true and natural body of Christ itself, really, substantially, corporeally. We know in what words both Luther and others still in use have spoken.

units.la: Pugnat deinde realis præsentia corporis Christi cum articulis fidei nostræ & plurimis scripturarum locis. Credimus enim secundum scripturas Christum corpore suo in cœlos ascendisse, & inde demum extremo die venturum ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos. Non est autem dubium Ecclesiam semper articu- lum hunc intellexisse, quod in locum cœle- stem corporali & physica locatione ascende- rit. Nostra demum ætate ad corporalem in cœna præsentiam asserendam, alij ascensio- nem transparitionem quandam fecerunt & allegorice interpretati sunt: alij ad omnipo- tentiam confugientes volunt corpus Christi in cœlo simul & in terra in pane præsens es- se, neq; hic contradictionem esse, quam tamen omnes nisi ipsorum more excæcati vident: a- lij corpus Christi in cœlo certo loco esse vo- lunt physice, attamen modo maiestatis aut dexterę Dei seu personaliter in cœna præsens esse. Ita ne vnum tropum in verbis cœnæ ad- mittere cogantur, nouas interpretationes ar- ticulorum fidei, nouos loquendi modos, & insolitos in alijs locis tropos confingunt. Ea- dem ratio est plurimorum locorum scripturę in quibus testatur Christus se non amplius corporaliter in terris præsentem fore, id quod plurimis agit in illa çoncione quam in vlti- ma cœna habitam Ioannes copiose descripsit. Et in alijs locis, vt cum inquit: Pauperes sem- per habebitis, me autē semper non habebitis.
units.tr: Furthermore, the real presence of Christ's body conflicts with the articles of our faith and with very many passages of Scripture. For we believe, according to the Scriptures, that Christ ascended into heaven in his body, and that from there he will at last come on the last day to judge the living and the dead. There is no doubt that the Church has always understood this article to mean that he ascended to a heavenly place by corporeal and physical location. In our own age, some, in order to assert a corporeal presence in the supper, have made the ascension into a kind of transparition and interpreted it allegorically; others, having recourse to omnipotence, want the body of Christ to be present in heaven and at the same time on earth in the bread, and say there is no contradiction here, which, however, all see except those blinded in their own way; others want the body of Christ to be physically in a certain place in heaven, yet to be present in the supper personally, by the mode of the majesty or right hand of God. Thus, so that they are not forced to admit even one trope in the words of the supper, they invent new interpretations of the articles of faith, new modes of speaking, and unusual tropes in other places. The same reasoning applies to very many passages of Scripture in which Christ testifies that he will no longer be present on earth in body, which he does at length in that sermon which John described fully as given at the last supper; and in other places, as when he says: "You will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me."

units.la: Præterea hoc quoq; absurdū ex aduersa- riorū sententia cōsequitur; vt si in pane realiter
units.tr: Moreover, the following absurdity also follows from the opposing opinion: if the body of Christ is really

units.la: adest corpus Christi, & in vino sanguis vt dicamus in pane aut simul adesse sanguinem aut non adesse, & itidem de corpore vt simul adsit vel non adsit cum sanguine in vino: si adesse simul negant, sequitur realis distractio corporis & sanguinis Christi, quam afferere impium est: si simul adesse dicunt, corpus & sanguinem congeminant, & bis vtrunque in communione præbent, semel sub pane, & iterum in vino.
units.tr: present in the bread, and the blood in the wine, then we must say either that the blood is present in the bread at the same time, or is not, and likewise concerning the body, whether it is present at the same time as the blood in the wine or not. If they deny that they are present together, there follows a real separation of the body and blood of Christ, which it is impious to assert. If they say they are present together, they double the body and the blood, and give each of them twice in communion: once under the bread, and again in the wine.

units.la: Adhæc, Christus ipse docet corporalem hanc manducationem inutilem esse Ioan.6. Cum enim prolixa cócione docuisset veram & salutarem sui corporis manducationē quæ fide fiat, Capernaitæ verba Christi de edenda carne sua & sanguine suo bibendo non intelligentes, quærebant, Quomodo potest hic nobis carnem suā dare qua vescamur? Quidam etiam ex discipulis offensi dicebāt, Durus est hic sermo: quis potest eum audire? Iesus autem sciens eos de hoc murmurare dixit, Hoc vos offendit? Quid si igitur conspiceritis filium hominis ascendentem eo ubi erat prius? Spiritus est qui viuificat, caro non prodest quicquam: Verba quæ ego loquor vobis spiritus sunt & vita: sed sunt quidam ex vobis qui non credunt. Etsi autem Christus alio tempore cœnam suam instituit, id tamē non obstat quo minus ea quæ hic de manducatione corporis sui tradit ad cœnam referamus, nam non alia est manducatio corporis Christi iñ fe quam ea quæ Ioannis 6. docetur, in cœna autem ad hanc accedit externa & oralis manducatio, quando in sacramento & symbolo manducatur, ibi namque ex Christi institutione non tantum fide manducatur corpus Christi, sed ore sumitur externum symbolum, quod sacramentum est veri corporis, & ideo etiam corpus Christi nominatur. Atque ita plærique veterum verba Christi intellexerunt & ad cœnam accommodarunt: atque tradidere nonnulli ideo beatum Ioannem Euangelistam non descripsisse institutionem cœnæ dominicæ, quod capite 6. satis explicasset manducationem corporis Christi, sic vt concio Christi ab eo tradita, debeat esse loco interpretationis eorum verborum quibus in cœna Christus corpus suum ad edendum & sanguinem ad bibendum porrexit. Si concio illa ab aliquo Apostolorum habita fuisset, dubitare possemus an ad cœnam pertinet, sed cum Christus qui optime norat quibus verbis cœnam instituere vellet, hæc docuerit, & vtrobique iubeat corpus suum edere & sanguinem suum bibere, neque discrimen ponat vllum, cur nos faceremus aliam manducationem veri & realis corporis Christi ab illa quam Ioan. 6. tradidit & docuit fide fieri. Neq; vero tantum docuit manducationem hanc spiritualem esse, sed carnalem man-ducationem ducationem nihil prodesse ait. Quod enim ait, Caro nihil prodest: non potest de carne Christi absolute dici, quis enim piorum ferat ut dicamus carnem Christi, quę vere est cibus vitæ æternæ, nihil prodesse. Neque hic carnis nomine Vetus homo intelligitur. Opponun tur quidem aliquando Caro & spiritus, vt carnis nomine vetus homo significetur, sed hoc non est perpetuum in hac oppositione, vt falso aduersarij afferunt: nam cum Christus dicitur mortuus carne, viuificatus spiritu, Caro & spiritus opponuntur, neque tamen carnis nomen veterem Adamum significat. Sic etiam hoc loco caro & spiritus opponuntur, sed quia de carne Christi verba fiunt, hæc de carne eius accipienda sunt, non quidem absolute, abest: sed cū de carne Christi manducanda quæstio esset verba hæc ad manducationem carnis Christi pertinent. Caro igitur Christi non absolute dici debet nihil prodesse, hoc enim blasphemia esset, sed carnaliter manducata & separata a spiritu, sicut manducandam putabant Capernaitæ, nihil prodest. Atq; Augustinus ita interpretatur verba Christi. Spiritus est qui viuificat, caro autem nihil prodest: verba quæ locutus sum vobis, spiritus est & vita. Spiritualiter intelligite quod locutus sum vobis. Non hoc corpus quod videtis, manducaturi estis, & bibituri illum sanguinem, quem fusuri sunt qui me crucifigent.Sacramētum aliquod vōbis commendaui,(spiritualiter intellectum vivificabit vos. Neque se tueri aduersarij possunt quod à Capernaitis differant, quoniam illi existimarint carnem Christi costam, aut in frusta cōcisam comedendam esse, & quod iudicarint eo modo comedendam quo carnibus in macello emptis vescimur: nā Capernaitarum falsa opinio qualis fuerit, ex his verbis apparet: Quomodo potest hic nobis carnem suam dare ad manducandum? Et Patres testantur eis horrendum visum humana carne vesci: item eos putasse corpus Christi dentibus atteri, & ventre absorberi. Et certe ex contraria mäducatione quam Christus docet, apparet quæ illorum fuerit opinio. Nam Capersnaiticæ manducationi opponitur à Christo spiritualis manducatio, quæ fit per fidem: Itaque etiamsi non omnino eundem modum manducationis cum Capernaitis asserant, docent tamen carnem Christi realiter & corporaliter ore corporis manducandam, & dentibus atterendam idq; sensualiter, si modo confessionem Nicolai Papæ quam Berengario præscripsit, quam etiam Lutherus probauit, retinere voluerint: hæc autem manducatio prorsus contraria est illi quam Christus docuit, Ioan. 6. Nam spiritus & spiritualis manducatio non tantum opponitur manducationi carnali quæ particulatim fit, sed omni carnali
units.tr: Besides, Christ himself teaches that this corporeal eating is useless (John 6). For after he had taught, in a lengthy sermon, the true and saving eating of his body, which is done by faith, the Capernaites, not understanding Christ's words about eating his flesh and drinking his blood, asked: "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" Some of the disciples also, offended, said: "This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?" But Jesus, knowing that they murmured about this, said: "Does this offend you? What if then you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit and life; but there are some among you who do not believe." Although Christ instituted his supper at another time, this does not prevent us from referring what he teaches here about the eating of his body to the supper, for the eating of the body of Christ in itself is not other than that which is taught in John 6. In the supper, however, external and oral eating is added to this, since in the sacrament and symbol it is eaten; for there, by Christ's institution, the body of Christ is not only eaten by faith, but the external symbol is taken with the mouth, which is a sacrament of the true body, and therefore is also called the body of Christ. And so most of the ancients understood the words of Christ and applied them to the supper; and some have handed down that the blessed John the Evangelist did not describe the institution of the Lord's Supper because in chapter 6 he had sufficiently explained the eating of Christ's body, so that the sermon of Christ delivered by him ought to serve in place of an interpretation of those words by which Christ, at the supper, offered his body to be eaten and his blood to be drunk. If that sermon had been delivered by one of the apostles, we might doubt whether it belongs to the supper; but since Christ, who knew best with what words he wished to institute the supper, taught these things, and in both places commands that his body be eaten and his blood drunk, and makes no distinction at all, why should we make a different eating of the true and real body of Christ from the one which he taught in John 6 is done by faith? Nor did he teach only that this eating is spiritual, but he also says that carnal eating profits nothing. For when he says "the flesh profits nothing," this cannot be said absolutely of the flesh of Christ; for who of the pious could bear us saying that the flesh of Christ, which is truly the food of eternal life, profits nothing? Nor is the old man meant here by the name of flesh. Flesh and spirit are indeed sometimes opposed so that the old man is signified by the name flesh, but this is not perpetual in this opposition, as the adversaries falsely assert; for when Christ is said to have been put to death in the flesh and made alive in the spirit, flesh and spirit are opposed, and yet the name flesh does not signify the old Adam. So also in this passage flesh and spirit are opposed, but because the words concern the flesh of Christ, they must be taken of his flesh; not absolutely, but since the question is about eating the flesh of Christ, these words pertain to the eating of Christ's flesh. Therefore the flesh of Christ ought not to be said absolutely to profit nothing, for that would be blasphemy; but flesh eaten carnally and separated from the Spirit, as the Capernaites thought it was to be eaten, profits nothing. And Augustine interprets the words of Christ thus: "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. Understand spiritually what I have said to you. You are not going to eat this body that you see, nor to drink that blood which those who crucify me are going to shed. I have commended to you a sacrament; understood spiritually, it will give you life." Nor can the adversaries defend themselves by saying that they differ from the Capernaites, since those men thought that Christ's flesh was to be eaten as a joint or cut into pieces, and judged that it was to be eaten in the way we eat meat bought at the butcher's. For the false opinion of the Capernaites, of what kind it was, appears from these words: "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" And the Fathers testify that it seemed horrible to them to feed on human flesh; likewise that they supposed the body of Christ was to be ground by the teeth and absorbed by the stomach. And certainly the contrary eating which Christ teaches shows what their opinion was. For spiritual eating, which is done by faith, is set by Christ against Capernaitic eating. Therefore, even if they do not assert exactly the same mode of eating as the Capernaites, they nevertheless teach that the flesh of Christ is to be eaten really and corporeally with the mouth of the body, and ground by the teeth, and this sensually, if indeed they wish to retain the confession of Pope Nicholas which he prescribed to Berengar, and which Luther too approved. But this eating is wholly contrary to that which Christ taught in John 6. For spirit and spiritual eating are opposed not only to carnal eating which is done piecemeal, but to all carnal

units.la: Aduersarij sunt Capernaitæ. nali & corporali mäducationi. Ac nostri ad⁠uersarij asserentes carnem Christi non minus à Iuda quàm à Petro,ab impijs & infidelibus, quàm pijs & credentibus in cœna Domini manducari, an non eam à Spiritus viuifica⁠tione seiungunt,& meram carnalem manducationem statuunt?
units.tr: Our adversaries are the Capernaites, who hold to carnal and corporal manducation. Do our adversaries, who assert that the flesh of Christ is eaten in the Lord's Supper no less by Judas than by Peter, by the wicked and unbelieving no less than by the godly and believing, not separate it from the life-giving Spirit and maintain a mere carnal manducation?

units.la: Porrò impiorum manducatio quam perti naciter defenduñt,videtur quidem ipsis neces saria ad stabiliendam realem præsentiam car- nis Christi, sed opinio hæc prorsus absurda est,& scripturis atq; veteris Ecclesiæ doctrinę repugnat. Christus enim inquit: Quisquis cœderit carnem suam, & biberit sanguinem suũ hunc viram habere, & in se manere, atq; se in illo. Impij autem neq; vitam in se habent, neque Christo coniuncti sunt, non igitur Christi carnem edunt & sanguinem eius bibunt. Neq; hic distinctione aliqua opus est, an non enim clara & perspicua sunt Christi verba: an non vitæ perceptione cum corporis sui manducatione coniungit: corpus Christi viuificum est, vt autem hæc spiritualis & viuifica uis à carne eius separari non potest, ita etiam hæc duo in perceptione corporis Christi non sunt diuellenda. Lutherus in libro de verbis Cœnę,scribit de carne Christi: Hic cibus eum à quo manducatur suæ natu æ participem facit & spiritualem. Eodem libro scribit, Corporalem manducationem carnis Christi pro⁠
units.tr: Moreover, the manducation of the wicked, which they stubbornly defend, seems to them necessary for establishing the real presence of the flesh of Christ. But this opinion is wholly absurd and contrary to the Scriptures and to the doctrine of the ancient Church. For Christ says: "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has life in him and abides in him, and he in him." The wicked, however, have no life in them and are not joined to Christ. Therefore they do not eat the flesh of Christ or drink his blood. Nor is any distinction needed here. Are not the words of Christ clear and plain? Does he not join the reception of life with the eating of his body? The body of Christ gives life, and just as this spiritual and life-giving power cannot be separated from his flesh, so these two things must not be torn apart in the reception of the body of Christ. Luther, in his book on the words of the Supper, writes of the flesh of Christ: "This food makes spiritual the one by whom it is eaten, and a partaker of his nature." In the same book he writes that the corporal manducation of the flesh of Christ profits nothing for the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: D desse ad remissionem peccatorum. Hinc autem sequeretur, impiosque iuxta aduersariorum sen tentiam carnem Christi corporaliter, realiter, substantialiter, comedút spirituales esse & peccatorum remissionem habere. Dicūt impios corpus Christi sumere sibijpsis ad iudicium, & sicut Euangelium aliquibus odor est mortis ad mortem, ita non mirum esse si corpus Christi ad mortem sumatur ab impijs, Christum nanq; non tantum saluatorem sed iudicem esse. Sed hęc sunt dissimilia, quibus enim Euangelium est odor mortis, hi non percipiunt rem ipsam quæ Euangelio offertur, exter nam tantum prædicationem ad sui condemnationem audiunt: at in sacramento impij non tantum symbola sed rem ipsam iuxta ipsorum sententiam accipiunt. Christum iudicem esse quis negat, sed cum in pane & vino corpus & sanguis percipienda offerūtur, an ea in iudicium offeruntur, an vero vt viuifica alimonia? Instituant igitur sumptionem talem qualis aliquādo in Papatu recepta fuit, dare corpus Christi ad iudiciū siue ad probationem. Apostolus inquit eos qui panem hūc ederint, aut poculum biberint, reos teneri corporis & sanguinis Domini, & sibijpsis damnationem edere & bibere, quia non discernant corpus Domini. Non dicit impios ipsum corpus Christi edere & sanguinē bibere, sed quia non discernunt corpus Domini reos esse, illi corpus Domini nō percipiūt, sed illis in sym⁠bolo oblatum negligunt & tanquam rem ali quā vilem contemnunt. Neq; necesse est illis realiter præsens esse corpus, quasi alioqui in il lud non peccare possint, cum alibi de impijs apostatis scribatur eos proculcare filiū Dei, & sanguinem fœderis profanum æstimare & Christum denuo crucifigere: qui tamen non ideo realiter præsens corpus Christi habue⁠re. Mirum autem est aduersarios ne corpus à pane, cui sacramentaliter vnitum est, diuellat, Christi corpus à viuifica sua vi seiungere, ita vt Christum in se habentes eius efficaciā non sentiant. Veteres etsi aliquando videntur im⁠pijs tribuere quod sumant corpus Christi, quod scilicet id sumunt in sacramento, signū corporis accipientes quod nomen rei signat̄ habet, nihilominus seipsos optime interpre⁠tantur, & distincte docent quid de impiorum sumptione sentiendū sit. Augustinus: Escam vitę accipit, & æternitatis poculum bibit: qui in Christo manet: & cuius Christus habita⁠tor est: nam qui discordat à Christo, nec car⁠nem eius manducat nec sanguinem bibit, etsi tantæ rei sacramentum ad iudicium suæ præ⁠sumptionis quotidie indifferenter accipiat. Idem alibi scribit Apostolos panē Dominum edisse, Iudā panem Domini contra Dominū. In Ioan. tract.59. Item aliud esse sacramētum, aliud virtute sacramenti, ac eum qui non ma⁠ net in Christo, non manducare spiritualiter carnem eius, licet carnaliter & visibiliter premat dentibus sacramentum corporis & sanguinis Christi. Hieronymus eos qui non sunt sancti corpore & spiritu, asserit non comedere carnem Iesu & bibere sanguinem eius.
units.tr: Hence it would follow, according to the opinion of our adversaries, that the wicked eat the flesh of Christ corporally, really and substantially, and yet are spiritual and have the forgiveness of sins. They say that the wicked take the body of Christ to their own judgment, and that just as the Gospel is to some a savour of death unto death, so it is no wonder if the body of Christ is taken to death by the wicked, since Christ is not only Saviour but also Judge. But these things are not alike. Those to whom the Gospel is a savour of death do not receive the thing itself that is offered in the Gospel; they hear only the preaching, to their own condemnation. But in the sacrament the wicked, according to their opinion, receive not only the signs but the thing itself. Who denies that Christ is judge? But when the body and blood are offered to be received in the bread and wine, are they offered for judgment, or rather as life-giving nourishment? Let them therefore institute such a reception as was once in use under the Papacy, of giving the body of Christ for judgment or for proof. The Apostle says that those who eat this bread or drink the cup are guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, and eat and drink damnation to themselves, because they do not discern the body of the Lord. He does not say that the wicked eat the body of Christ itself and drink his blood, but that because they do not discern the body of the Lord they are guilty; they do not receive the body of the Lord, but neglect what is offered to them in the sign and despise it as some worthless thing. Nor is it necessary that the body be really present to them, as if otherwise they could not sin against it, since elsewhere it is written of wicked apostates that they trample under foot the Son of God, count the blood of the covenant unholy, and crucify Christ anew; yet they did not on that account have the body of Christ really present. It is strange, moreover, that our adversaries fear to separate the body from the bread to which it is sacramentally united, and so sever the body of Christ from its life-giving power, so that those who have Christ in them do not feel his efficacy. The ancients, though at times they seem to ascribe to the wicked that they take the body of Christ, mean that they take it in the sacrament, receiving the sign of the body, which bears the name of the thing signified. Nevertheless they explain themselves very well and teach plainly what is to be thought of the reception by the wicked. Augustine: "He receives the food of life and drinks the cup of eternity who abides in Christ, and in whom Christ dwells. For whoever is at odds with Christ neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even though he receives the sacrament of so great a thing every day, to his judgment, through his presumption." He writes elsewhere that the Apostles ate the bread of the Lord, but Judas ate the bread of the Lord against the Lord. On John, tractate 59. Likewise, that the sacrament is one thing and the power of the sacrament another, and that he who does not abide in Christ does not eat his flesh spiritually, although he carnally and visibly presses with his teeth the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ. Jerome asserts that those who are not holy in body and spirit do not eat the flesh of Jesus or drink his blood.

units.la: Postremo etsi pudet nos hoc obijcere, & licet impietatis nos arguant qui tam crasse de sacro corpore Christi loquamur, tamen eorum crassa opinio nos haec loqui cogit: & revera non de Christi corpore haec dicta volumus, sed de ipsorum opinione: & eo modo accipienda quo veterum anathema in Deum Mahumeti: non enim execrabantur Deum creatorem coeli & terrae, sed Deum quem falso hoc nomine vocabat Mahumet, qui no Deus sed idolum & figmentum illius pseudopropheta erat. Ita nos haec nequaquam de Christi carne vivifica dicta volumus, sed de aduersariorum opinione vbi fingunt reale quoddam corpus Christi, quod non est Christi corpus, sed ipsorum figmentum. Aiunt corpus Christi oraliter manducari: & quando Lutherum sequuntur qui Papae sententiam se probare aliquoties in suis scriptis testatur, non possunt improbare Berengarij confessionem a Papa illi praescriptam, nempe verum corpus & sanguinem Christi sensualiter & in veritate manibus sacerdotum tractari, frangi & fidelium dentibus atteri. Iam vero haec non nostra sed Christi verba sunt, Quicquid ingreditur in os in ventrem cedere & per latrinam eijci. Porro quid hinc cóficiatur manifestum est:sed tantæ huius absurditatis & impietatis cuius nos arguunt,& ob quâ ad Christi tribunal vocât,ipsi causa sunt, non nos qui hæc illis obijcimus. Propositio argumenti nó est nostra, sed verba Christi sunt clara, perspicua in suo sensu genuino. Assumptio argumenti corpus Christi ore manducari & per os ingredi, ipsorũ est inuentum, Nusquam scripturæ ita loquuntur: & vbi Christus nos iubet manducare carnem suam,ipse se explicat de qua mäducatione, spirituali nempe per fidem loquatur: Et Augustinus oratione figuratam esse inquit, quoniam alioqui facinus & flagitiū pręciperetur. Porro ne ex præmissis absurda illa cõclufio quam effari nolo, conficiatur, non Maior argumēti ipsis immutanda est, cum sint verba Christi, sed oralis manducatio quam extra & præter scripturas confinxerunt,tollenda erit.
units.tr: Finally, although we are ashamed to bring this charge, and although they accuse us of impiety for speaking so crudely of the sacred body of Christ, their crude opinion compels us to speak thus. And in truth we do not wish these things to be said of the body of Christ, but of their opinion. They are to be understood in the way the ancient anathema against the god of Mahomet is understood: they did not curse God the creator of heaven and earth, but the god whom Mahomet falsely called by that name, who was not God but an idol and a fiction of that false prophet. So we do not wish these things to be said of the life-giving flesh of Christ, but of the opinion of our adversaries, where they feign a certain real body of Christ, which is not the body of Christ but their own fiction. They say that the body of Christ is eaten orally; and when they follow Luther, who in several of his writings testifies that he approves the opinion of the Pope, they cannot disapprove the confession of Berengar prescribed to him by the Pope, namely that the true body and blood of Christ are handled sensually and in truth by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful. Now these are not our words but the words of Christ: "Whatever enters the mouth passes into the belly and is cast out into the privy." What follows from this is plain. But the great absurdity and impiety of which they accuse us, and for which they summon us to the tribunal of Christ, is their own doing, not ours who object these things to them. The major premise of the argument is not ours but the clear and plain words of Christ in their genuine sense. The minor premise, that the body of Christ is eaten by the mouth and enters through the mouth, is their own invention. The Scriptures nowhere speak so. And where Christ bids us eat his flesh, he himself explains of what manducation he speaks: a spiritual one, namely through faith. Augustine also says that this is said figuratively, since otherwise a crime and a disgrace would be commanded. Moreover, so that the absurd conclusion, which I am unwilling to name, may not follow from the premises, the major premise need not be changed, since it is the words of Christ; rather the oral manducation, which they have fashioned outside and beyond the Scriptures, must be removed.

units.la: Porro hic denuo repetendum est, quando negamus Realem, corporalem & naturalem præsentiam carnis & sanguinis Christi,& horum substantialem coniunctionem cum externis symbolis panis & vini, atque oralem horum manducationem, nos propterea communionem veri corporis Christi non tollere, aut Christum omnimodo à sua cœna absentem facere,& nuda signa statuere, ita vt fides les tantum panem & vinum in cœna Domi‑ni accipiant, sicut Iacobus Andreæ & alij falso de nobis scribunt. Docemus enim coniunctionem seu communionem spiritualem, veram tamen cum corpore & sanguine Christi: licet enim hæc in cœlis & nō in his terris reaā liter & substantialiter præsentia sint, tamen nostræ cum Christo coniunctioni locorum distantia non obstat: hæc autē edi & bibi credimus, non ore corporis, sed animi, spiritu & fide imbuti: fide enim constare hanc mandu cationem Christus docuit Ioan. 6. Fides autem nostra non in phantasma aut rem sistam, neque tantum in meritum Christi, sed in ipsum Christum dirigitur, & corpus Christi verum & naturale quod Verbum ex Virgine assumpsit ampleƈitur: vnde iniuriam faciunt nobis qui communionem & percepti onem veri & substantialis corporis Christi nos negare aiunt. Corpus Christi à cœna quo ad realem & corporalem præsentiam abesse confitemur, sed ipsam carnem & sanguinem Christi nobis præsentia esse credimus, ἐνεργείᾳ sua, spiritu, gratia, meritis & admirabilibus fructibus quæ inde in nos deriuantur, ita vt non tantum hæc animis nostris præsentia sint spiritualiter & per fidem, sed corpora etiam nostra beatæ resurrectionis capacia inde reddantur, credendo enim corpus & sanguinem Domini esse pretia nostræ salutis, iustificamur, & regeneramur, vel augemur & confirmamur in ipsa iustificatione & regeneratione, hæc autem principia sunt nostræ immortalitatis. Libenter audirem recipimus locutiones Veterum, qui dicunt nobis dari gratiam corporis Christi, uitæ atq; immortalitatis alimoniam. Nos manducare vitam & bibere vitam: recipere nos gratiam & veritatem inuisibilem: gratiam & societatem membrorum corporis Christi. Senti re Dominum præsentem in gratia. Recipere cibum cœlestem & superne venientem. Proprietatem naturalis cōmunionis, Natura carnis, & benedictionē viuificatiuam in pane & vino: virtute propriæ carnis Christi, vitam & gratia corporis, vnigeniti proprietatem, id est vitam. Fatemur nos recipere mysticum Christi aduentum, gratiam & veræ naturæ virtutem: item veræ carnis sacramentū, corpus per gratiam. Carnem spiritualem, sed alia ab ea quæ crucifixa est. Gratiam influentem in sacrificium & spiritus gratiam. Fatemur secundum id haberi in sacramento cœnæ Dominicæ corpus Christi, videlicet quod sit in eo spiritus Christi, id est, diuini potentia verbi, quæ non solum animam pascit, verum etiam purgat. Quod si quidam his non contenti sunt, & exiſtimant, nullam posse fieri veram communionem carnis & sanguinis Christi nisi hæc substantialiter & corporaliter præsens tia sint, hi fidei naturam non bene expen-dunt, & quod nobis obijciunt ipsi faciunt, potentiae Dei parum tribuunt, nimisque crasse & philicè de rebus diuinis & spiritua-libus existimant: nam alioqui salua humanae naturae veritate & proprietate, facile absque reali coniunctione & quasi physico contactu, veram & spiritualem veri corporis & sangui nis Christi communionem quam fide percia pimus vna nobiscum defenderent.
units.tr: Here again it must be repeated: when we deny a real, corporal and natural presence of the flesh and blood of Christ, and their substantial conjunction with the outward signs of bread and wine, and their oral manducation, we do not on that account remove the communion of the true body of Christ, or make Christ wholly absent from his Supper and set up bare signs, so that faith receives only bread and wine in the Lord's Supper, as Jacob Andreae and others falsely write about us. For we teach a conjunction or communion that is spiritual yet true, with the body and blood of Christ. For although these are in heaven and not on this earth really and substantially present, the distance of places does not hinder our conjunction with Christ. We believe that they are eaten and drunk, not by the mouth of the body but by the mind, imbued with the Spirit and with faith; for Christ taught in John 6 that this manducation consists in faith. Our faith is directed not to a phantasm or a thing set before us, nor only to the merit of Christ, but to Christ himself, and it embraces the true and natural body of Christ, which the Word assumed from the Virgin. Hence they do us wrong who say that we deny the communion and reception of the true and substantial body of Christ. We confess that the body of Christ is absent from the Supper as to its real and corporal presence; but we believe that the flesh and blood of Christ themselves are present to us by their energy [ἐνεργείᾳ], by the Spirit, by grace, by merits, and by the wonderful fruits that flow from them into us. Thus they are present to our souls spiritually and through faith, and our bodies too are made capable of the blessed resurrection. For by believing that the body and blood of the Lord are the price of our salvation, we are justified and regenerated, or increased and confirmed in justification and regeneration itself; and these are the beginnings of our immortality. I would gladly accept the expressions of the Ancients, who say that the grace of the body of Christ is given to us, the nourishment of life and immortality. We eat life and drink life; we receive grace and invisible truth; grace and fellowship of the members of the body of Christ; we feel the Lord present in grace; we receive heavenly food that comes down from above; the property of natural communion, the nature of the flesh, and life-giving blessing in the bread and wine, by the power of the proper flesh of Christ, the grace and life of the body, the property of the only-begotten, that is, life. We confess that we receive the mystical coming of Christ, grace, and the power of his true nature; likewise the sacrament of the true flesh, the body through grace; a spiritual flesh, but other than that which was crucified; grace flowing into the sacrifice, and the grace of the Spirit. We confess that according to this the body of Christ is had in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper, namely because the Spirit of Christ is in it, that is, the power of the divine Word, which not only feeds the soul but also cleanses it. But if some are not content with these things and think that no true communion of the flesh and blood of Christ can be made unless these are substantially and corporally present, they do not weigh the nature of faith well. What they object to us they themselves do: they attribute too little to the power of God and judge divine and spiritual things too crudely and carnally. For otherwise, with the truth and property of human nature preserved, they could easily defend, without a real conjunction and a kind of physical contact, the true and spiritual communion with the true body and blood of Christ, which we receive by faith, along with them.

units.la: Qualem vbiquitatem corporis Christi aauerfarij do cant, & an inde probetur praesentia realis corporis Christi in pane & vino.
units.tr: What kind of ubiquity of the body of Christ the adversaries teach, and whether the real presence of Christ's body in the bread and wine is proved from it.

units.la: Controuersia de praesentia reali corporis Christi in coena Domini diu disceptata est hac ratione, vt tantum eam vi verborum coenae afferere conarentur, sicut & Papistae docuerunt: quoniam vero animaduertebant hoc praesidium infirmum esse, quia de sententia verborum quaestio mouebatur, neque verba ipsorum sensum simpliciter prae se ferebant, & veritas finitae & circumscriptae carnis in Christo ipsorum sententiae obstabat, aliud fir-mamentum causae suae excogitarunt & dixe-runt, Corpus Christi vbiq; praesens esse, ideo-que etiam adesse in pane coenae Dominicae. Hac autem ratione non iam de praesentia cor-poris & sanginis Christi in coena Domini, sed in vniuersum de Christi seruatoris nostri, secundum carnem aut humanam naturam præsentia in his terris cœptum est disputari. Ac Lutherus quidem tantum ad præsentiam realem carnis & sanguinis Christi in cœna stabiliendam multis in locis Vbiquitatem hanc asseruit: alibi tamen verba Christi vult esse causam huius præsentiæ, & Christum in quit definitiue esse in cœna: nonnunquam vero eum modum præsentiæ probat quem Papistæ tenent, qui hanc Vbiquitatem nunc quam agnouerunt. At Brentius & huius successores Vbiquitatem hanc studiose docuerunt, in quorum partes multi Lutheranorum concedere videntur, tuentur autem illam prǫ cipue argumentis ab vnione personali duarum naturarum in Christo desumptis. De quibus antequam dicam duo prius breuiter notanda sunt, qualis Vbiquitas ab eis statuatur, &quæ sit huius vis in statuenda reali prǫ sentia corporis Christi. Negant illi se statuere crassam & localem omniprælentiam corporis, vt vel multa corpora tribuantur Christo, vel corpus statuatur quadam diffusione aut extensione vbiq; cum diuinitate cui conjunctum est præsens esse, sed id corporaliter aut localiter non nisi alicubi tantum esse, modo aut maiestatis & dextræ Dei & personali ter vbiq; præsens esse. Atq; admodum nobis irascuntur qui ipsos tam crassæ opinionis ac-
units.tr: The controversy over the real presence of Christ's body in the Lord's Supper has long been disputed. At first they tried to assert it only by the force of the words of the Supper, as the Papists also taught. But since they saw that this defence was weak, because the question turned on the meaning of the words, and the words did not plainly display their sense, and the truth of a finite and circumscribed flesh in Christ stood in the way of their view, they devised another support for their cause and said that the body of Christ is present everywhere, and therefore is also present in the bread of the Lord's Supper. By this reasoning the question was no longer only about the presence of Christ's body and blood in the Lord's Supper, but in general about the presence of Christ our Saviour on this earth according to the flesh, or human nature. Luther indeed, to establish the real presence of Christ's flesh and blood in the Supper, asserted this ubiquity in many places. Yet elsewhere he holds that the words of Christ are the cause of this presence, and says that Christ is definitively in the Supper. Sometimes he approves the mode of presence that the Papists hold, though they never acknowledged this ubiquity. Brentius and his successors have zealously taught this ubiquity, and many of the Lutherans seem to agree with them. They defend it chiefly by arguments drawn from the personal union of the two natures in Christ. Before I discuss these, two things must be briefly noted: what kind of ubiquity they set up, and what its force is in establishing the real presence of Christ's body. They deny that they set up a gross and local omnipresence of the body, either by attributing many bodies to Christ, or by holding that the body is spread or extended everywhere together with the divinity to which it is joined. Rather, the body is present not bodily or locally, but only in one place, while being present everywhere in the mode of majesty and of the right hand of God, and personally. They are very angry with us when we accuse them of so gross an opinion.

units.la: Quälis vbi quitas statuatur à Brentiano fertores credamus. Sed ipsi certè in culpa sunt vt ita de illis iudicemus: Brétius enim inquit, Corpus Christi posse, si non in omnib. locis simpliciter, certè in pluribus simul locis adesse. Item Christum humanitate sua etiā simpliciter in omnibus esse locis. Corpus itè Christi in quantū est corpus assumptum omnia implere. An vero corpus simpliciter aut absolute alicubi est non localiter & corporaliter. Idé Mirandū est (inquit) quod tanto odio aduersus corpus Christi feratur, vt nō concedant ei ex personali vnione, hoc est ex miraculo omnia miracula superante, tantam, vt ita dicam, subtilitatem, vti omnia impleat, & interim tamen maneat verum & naturale corpus. Si non adest corporaliter, quare oportet corpori dari nouā quandā subtilitatem qua omnia impleat? In lib. Maiestatis accusat Zuinglianos, quod negent omnipotentia Dei fieri posse, vt verū corpus, manens verū corpus, aut sit at spiritus, aut in omnia loca extendatur. Quorsum verò excogitarunt suā Vbiquitate, nonne vt probarent realem praesentiā corporis & sanguinis Christi in pane & vino coenę dominicę? At Lutherus cuius auctoritate isti omnes sequuntur, non docuit personalē aut maiestatis praesentiā in coena Domini, sed condit corpus Christi realiter, essentialiter, substantialiter, corporaliter, naturaliter praesens esse. Christus inquit, vult in coena corpus suum edcanū elcam nostrã corporaliter esse. Os manducat corpus Christi corporaliter. Nostra corpora PHYSICE percipientia Eucharıstiam corporis Christi,etiâ incorruptibilia &ç̧erna crút. Os & stomachum,inquit,manducare corpus Christi. Alibi(inquit)corpus Christi eadem quantitate forma & habitu in sacramëto præsens esse quo immolatū in cruce pepédit. Quare si eorū omniprætentia non est realis & corporalis, sed duntaxat personalis,frustra eam excogitarunt ad tuendam doctrinam Lutheri. Quod si dicunt Lutherum non tam crasse sensisse, sed seruore quodam certandi cõmo-tũ vehementioribus locutionibus vsum esse, cur non ipsi qui nouas loquendi formas ex-cogitant explicant Lutheri sententiam? cur ipsi qui tantum personaliter Christum secun dum humanitatem præsentem statuunt non autem naturaliter, non aperte reijciunt rea-lem & corporalem & naturalem præsentiam corporis Christi?&c. Cur damnant tot eccle-sias, tot viros doctos qui negant corporalem præsentiam, personalem præsentiam recte explicatam nunquam impugnarunt ? Cur quod in ipsis est, obstant ne pax & tranquil-litas ecclesijs per Germaniam restituatur? Etenim crassa illa corporali manducatio-ne & præsentia repudiata, spes aliqua con-cordiæ in hoc tam tristi certamine affulgere posset, personalem enim præsentiam modo sane intelligatur nunquam damnauimus. Interim ab hac loquendi formula vt inusitata & obscura, & ambigua cófulto abstinemus, & libenter retinemus locutiones consuetas veteri ecclesiae, quae nusquam personalem, sed sacramentalem praesentiam in coena Domini statuit. Sed non tam contentionum armantes fumus vt de verbo etiam inusitato litem mouere velimus, fi de reipfa inter nos conueniat. Interea vero dum illi naturalem & corporalem praesentiam sua Vbiquitate stabilire conantur, non aliter iudicare possumus quam hanc ipsam quoque corporalem esse: vtcunque obscuris loquutionibus non è scriptura aut veteris ecclesiae patribus, sed è philosophia desumptis, suam sententiam nō tam explicare quam inuoluere studeant. Praesertim cum idem alij non cessant crassius affirmare, corpus Christi verum substantiale & naturale non tantum realiter & substantialiter, sed etiam naturaliter adesse affirmantes, imo Christum iuxta omnem praesentiae modum totum in loco esse posse circumscriptiue, definitiue, repletiue.
units.tr: Let us take it that this is the ubiquity set up by Brentius's supporters. But they are certainly at fault if we judge them in this way. For Brentius says that the body of Christ can be present at the same time in many places, if not simply in all places. Likewise, Christ in his humanity is simply in all places, and the body of Christ, insofar as it is the assumed body, fills all things. But whether the body is simply or absolutely anywhere, it is not locally and bodily. He says: "It is to be wondered at that it is borne with such hatred against the body of Christ that they do not grant it, from the personal union, that is from a miracle surpassing all miracles, such subtlety, as I may say, that it fills all things and yet remains a true and natural body. If it is not present bodily, why must a new kind of subtlety be given to the body, by which it fills all things?" In his book On the Majesty he accuses the Zwinglians of denying that, by the omnipotence of God, a true body, while remaining a true body, can either be a spirit or be extended into all places. Why, then, did they devise their ubiquity, if not to prove the real presence of Christ's body and blood in the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper? But Luther, on whose authority all these men follow, did not teach a personal or majestic presence in the Lord's Supper. He asserted that the body of Christ is present really, essentially, substantially, bodily and naturally. Christ, he says, wills his body to be in the Supper bodily in our mouth. "The mouth eats the body of Christ bodily." "Our bodies, physically receiving the Eucharist of Christ's body, are made even incorruptible and eternal." "The mouth and stomach, he says, eat the body of Christ." Elsewhere he says that the body of Christ is present in the sacrament with the same quantity, form and habit in which it hung on the cross. Therefore, if their omnipresence is not real and bodily but only personal, they devised it in vain to defend Luther's doctrine. But if they say that Luther did not think so grossly, but was carried away by a certain zeal for contention and used more vehement expressions, why do they who devise new forms of speech not explain Luther's opinion? Why do they who posit only a personal presence of Christ according to his humanity, and not a natural one, not openly reject the real, bodily and natural presence of Christ's body? Why do they condemn so many churches and so many learned men who deny a bodily presence, when they have never attacked the personal presence, rightly explained? Why do they, as far as lies in them, stand in the way of peace and tranquillity being restored to the churches throughout Germany? For if that gross bodily eating and presence were rejected, some hope of concord might shine forth in this so sad a strife. For we have never condemned a personal presence, if it is understood in a sound sense. Meanwhile we deliberately abstain from this unusual, obscure and ambiguous form of speech, and gladly retain the customary expressions of the ancient Church, which nowhere posits a personal but a sacramental presence in the Lord's Supper. Yet we are not so armed with the smoke of contention that we want to raise a quarrel over an unusual word, if we agree about the thing itself. Meanwhile, while they try to establish a natural and bodily presence by their ubiquity, we cannot judge otherwise than that this too is bodily. However, by obscure expressions taken not from Scripture or the Fathers of the ancient Church but from philosophy, they strive not so much to explain their opinion as to wrap it up. This is especially so since others do not cease to affirm more crudely that the true, substantial and natural body of Christ is present not only really and substantially but also naturally, indeed that Christ, according to every mode of presence, can be wholly in a place circumscriptively, definitively and repletively.

units.la: Quod si maxime obtinuerint suam illam Vbiquitatem corporis Christi, tamen infirmum fundamentum iaciunt carnali reali & orali manducationi, cuius causa Vbiquitas haec inuenta est. Etenim si corpus Christi nō minus sua essentia vbique praesens est quam ipsa diuinitas, non magis prœsens dici poterit in pane cœnæ Domini quam in quouis alio pane, neque aliter quouis tempore quam in ipsa cœna ore manducabitur: non differet sanctus ille cibus & potus in sacramento Eucharistiȩ à quotidiano cibo & potu, vbi etiā cum pane & vino & quouis cibo & potu imo quacunque re corpus Christi huius Vbiquitatis ratione prœsens erit. Itaque necesse est vt dămnent Lutherum & alios qui docuerunt, verba cœnæ aut promissionem Christi causam esse prœsentiæ Christi in cœna sua. Neque valet eorum commentum Omnipræsentia hac statui corpus Christi prœsens, sed verbis cœnæ dispensari corpus Christi, & definiri & nobis prœsens fieri: nā si antea statuitur realis prœsentia, verbis cœnæ tribuunt tantum Relationem, & interim nos quando per relationem eadem explicamus damnant & Satanæ tradunt. Rursus tamen fatendum est nisi statuatur eam naturam esse corporis Christi vt possit pluribus in locis simul aut omnibus etiam prœsens esse, non posse constanter affirmari realem prœsentiam eius in pane & vino cœnæ Dominicæ. Itaque fundamentum hoc eorum est quodammodo asystaton, hac quidem ratione qua hactenus realem corporis prœsentiam in cœna & simul etiam eius Omnipræsentiam affirmarunt.
units.tr: Even if they fully obtain this ubiquity of Christ's body, they still lay a weak foundation for the carnal, real and oral eating, for the sake of which this ubiquity was invented. For if the body of Christ is present everywhere by its essence no less than the divinity itself, it could no more be said to be present in the bread of the Lord's Supper than in any other bread. Nor would it be eaten by the mouth at any time other than in the Supper itself. That holy food and drink in the sacrament of the Eucharist would then not differ from ordinary food and drink, since with bread and wine, with any food and drink, indeed with anything whatever, the body of Christ would be present by this reasoning of ubiquity. Therefore they must condemn Luther and the others who taught that the words of the Supper, or Christ's promise, are the cause of Christ's presence in his Supper. Nor does their invention hold, the claim that by this omnipresence the body of Christ is posited as present, but by the words of the Supper the body of Christ is dispensed, defined and made present to us. For if the real presence is first posited, they attribute to the words of the Supper only a relation, and meanwhile they condemn us, and hand us over to Satan, when we explain the same things by relation. Yet again it must be confessed that unless it is established that the nature of Christ's body is such that it can be present in many places at once, or in all places, it cannot be constantly affirmed that it is really present in the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper. So their foundation is in a way self-contradictory [ἀσύστατον], in that it is the same method by which they have hitherto affirmed both the real presence of the body in the Supper and, at the same time, its omnipresence.

units.la: DE PRAESENT. CHRISTI
units.tr: On the Presence of Christ

units.la: De hypostatica unione Verbi cum assumpta humanitate.
units.tr: On the hypostatic union of the Word with the assumed humanity.

units.la: Doctrina de vnione personali Dei verbi cum humana natura, fundamentum suum habet cum alia loca scripturae quae incarnationem Verbi docent, tum vel praecipue haec D. Ioannis Euangelistae verba: Verbum caro factum est & habitauit in nobis, Verbum autem non significare aliquid transitiuum ἀνννὸ σαρξ, sed Verbum esse hypostaticum atq; consubstantiale aeterno Patri, nulla est inter nos & aduersarios controuersia. Carnis etiam nomine vtrique intelligimus humanam naturam integram, corpus & animam mente praeditam, ac pariter Apollinarij delirium reijcimus. Cum vero dicitur Verbum caro factum esse: non docemus transmutatione Verbi in carnem, sed faciendi verbum per assumendi vocem interpretamur, quia Apostolus scribit, Filium Dei assumpsisse formam serui, item assumpsisse semen Abrahae. Ita autem assumpta est humana natura a Verbo, ut vna sit cum Verbo persona, & caro haec sit propria Dei verbo caro, idque semper, ut nulla unquam hic separatio fieri possit, manente nihilominus Verbo in sua natura, & carne suam naturam seruante, vt ita duae naturae integrae & perfectae, absque vlla mixtione aut confusione, mutatione, inseperabiliter in vna persona vnitae sint, sicut Patres contra NestoNestorium naturas separantem & Eutychen easdem confundentem pie & erudite ex fcri‑pturis sanctis definierunt. Atque hæc qui‑dem utrique profitemur: quamuis enim ad‑uerfarij multa tradant non consentanea huic doctrinæ, tamen verbis saltem hæc profiten‑tur,& vna nobiscum Neftorianam separatio‑nem & Eutychianam confusionem duarum naturarum damnant. De hoc controuersia est: Quid fit humanam naturam esse verbi propriam, & esse perfonaliter Verbo vniam, quæ inquam fit ratio tantæ vnionis vt hic Homo dicatur Deus, & hoc homine na‑scente & moriente dicatur Deus natus &paf‑sus,quamuis fecundum carnem,quod de Pe‑tro, Paulo,& alio sanctorum patiente dici no‑potest, in quibus tamen Deus etiam inhabi‑tat, & qui diuine naturæ participes dicuntur. Volunt igitur vnionis huius peculiaris & incomprehensibilis rationem in illo pofi‑tam esse, quod diuinitas in persona filij om‑nes suas proprietates in humanam naturam effuderit,& eam ita affumpserit, vt λόγῳ omnia faciat & operetur per hunc hominem af‑sumptum. In qua explicatione, cum ipsi quoque fundamentum idem nobiscum profite‑antur, Verbum carnem factum esse, miror qui fiat vt contrario ordine sibi incedendum putarint, nam Verbum carnem factum esse, idem est atque Deum hominem factum esse, Deum manifestatū esse in carne, Filium Dei formam assumpsisse serui: at ipsi de eo solo disserunt, Quomodo Homo Deus sit factus & transfusione donorū effectus omnipotens, omniscius,omnisapiens,omnipraesens. Cum autem alium ordinem explicandi seruet scri‐ptura, & eundem Patres retinuerint,non vi‐deo causam cur ab eo recedere debuerint,si de innouatione & immutatione veteris doctri‐nae nolunt suspectli esse. Nos scripturas secuti dicimus, Deo adiuuante, Quomodo Verbū carnem assumpserit, & qua ratione sibi pro‐pria fecerit quae carnis sunt,quomodo etiam quae Verbi sunt carni facta sint propria:inte‐rim fatemur mysterium hoc ineffabile esse & longè humanae mentis captum superare, quod Deus homo, & Verbum caro factum est,sed tamen liceat nobis reuerteer de his rebus balbutire, dum modo nusquam a scriptu‐ra & veteris ecclesiae orthodoxa doctrina recedamus.
