Verbum igitur suam personam assumptam humanam naturam ab aeterno habuit, sed humana natura (anima inquam illa cum corpore quod Verbum assumpsit) nunquam extra Verbum suam habuit subsistentiam, vt per se extra Verbum, hoc est antequam Verbum illam formaret simul & sibi vniret, vnquam fuerit aut dici potuerit homo,sed in persona Dei Verbi initium vt esset habuit; Verbum nanq; humanam naturam assumen‐
units.tr: The doctrine of the personal union of God the Word with human nature rests on other passages of Scripture that teach the incarnation of the Word, but chiefly on these words of the Evangelist John: "The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us." That the Word does not mean something transitive, not in place of flesh, but that the Word is hypostatic and consubstantial with the eternal Father, is not in dispute between us and our opponents. By the name flesh we both understand the whole human nature, body and soul endowed with mind, and likewise we reject the delirium of Apollinaris. When it is said that the Word was made flesh, we do not teach a change of the Word into flesh. We explain "made" as "assumed," because the Apostle writes that the Son of God took on the form of a servant and likewise took on the seed of Abraham. The human nature was so assumed by the Word that the flesh becomes the Word's own flesh, one person with the Word, and this always, so that no separation can ever take place here. Yet the Word remains in his own nature, and the flesh keeps its own nature. Thus two whole and perfect natures, without any mixture, confusion or change, are inseparably united in one person, as the Fathers, against Nestorius who separated the natures and against Eutyches who confused them, defined piously and learnedly from the holy Scriptures. This much both sides profess. Although our opponents teach many things that do not agree with this doctrine, yet in words at least they profess these things, and along with us they condemn the Nestorian separation and the Eutychian confusion of the two natures. The controversy is about this: what it means for the human nature to be the Word's own and to be united to the Word personally; what, I say, is the manner of so great a union that this man is called God, and that when this man is born and dies, God is said to be born and to suffer, though according to the flesh, which cannot be said of Peter, Paul or any other saint, in whom God nevertheless dwells and who are said to be partakers of the divine nature. They therefore want the peculiar and incomprehensible manner of this union to lie in this: that the deity in the person of the Son poured all its properties into the human nature and so assumed it that through this assumed man he does and works all things by the Word [λόγῳ]. In this explanation, since they too profess the same foundation as we do, that the Word was made flesh, I wonder why they thought they had to proceed in the opposite order. For that the Word was made flesh is the same as saying that God was made man, that God was made manifest in the flesh, that the Son of God took on the form of a servant. Yet they discuss only this: how man was made God, and by the transfusion of gifts became almighty, all-knowing, all-wise and everywhere present. But since Scripture keeps the other order of explanation, and the Fathers kept the same, I do not see why they should depart from it, if they do not wish to be suspected of innovating and changing the old doctrine. Following the Scriptures, we say, with God's help, how the Word assumed the flesh, and by what means he made the things of the flesh his own, and how also the things of the Word were made the flesh's own. Meanwhile we confess that this mystery is ineffable and far exceeds the grasp of the human mind, that God is man and the Word was made flesh. Yet we may be allowed to return to these matters and stammer about them, provided we never depart from Scripture and the orthodox doctrine of the ancient Church. The Word, then, had the assumed human nature in his own person from eternity; but the human nature (that soul, I mean, together with the body which the Word assumed) never had its own subsistence outside the Word, so that it was never, nor could it be called, a man by itself outside the Word, that is, before the Word formed it and at the same time united it to himself. Rather it had its beginning to be in the person of God the Word. For the Word, in assuming, formed the human nature, and in forming it, assumed or united it to himself, and so from the two natures Christ was made one.

units.la: Humanitas suâ subsistētiā in verbo habet. âssumendo formauit,&formādo sibi assump sit seu vniuit, atque ita ex duabus naturis vnus factus est Christus. Vnde Cassianus ait: Neque enim vnquam sine Deo fuerat homo ille,qui vtiq; hoc ipsum quod erat,esse à Deo coeperat. Omnes quidem hominest à Deo habent vt sint; nam in ipso viuimus, sumus & mouemur,sed ita formamur singuli, vt vnius cuiusque natura sua ipsius separatim sit, & quamuis Petrus non tantum formatus sit à Deo & diuina vi sustentetur, sed præterea etiam Deus habitat in ipso,non tamen propterea Deus pars est personæ Petri,aut Petrus in Deo ita subsistit vt cum eo vnum quiddam& singulum sit, neque etiam Petrum definiendo Deum illa definitione comprehendimus: At humana natura à Verbo ita assumpta est, non vt hæc natura hominis ipsius separatim esset, sed vt Verbo vniretur, esset Verbi proprium indumentum & inæstimabile vt ita quis dicat instrumentu,creata est vt Deus esset homo.Nā naturæ humanæ est esse animal rationale, hoc habet in se humana natura à Christo assumpta:at vt sit persona,subsistentia in quā indiuidua & incomunicabilis, hoc non in se habet,sed est in verbo fundata,ab eo assumpta sustētatur, vt iam sicut Athanasius scribit,Idem Deus & homo sit, Idem vtrumque simul,vt vnum quiddam & singulum & solum. Hanc personam Christum nomina mus, Deum Verbum incarnatum, non Verbum absque carne, multominus hominem solum absque Verbo, sed utrunque Deum & hominem. Non alius Deus, alius Homo, sed unus idemque Deus homo, aliud tamen diuinitas, aliud humanitas, sed haec tam arcte coniuncta ut persona unitas semper maneat, ut demonstrato homine Iesu nato ex Maria virgine, non demonstrari possit humana natura sola, quae non est per se indiuiduum subsistens, sed hypostasis in qua subsistit humana natura seu tota persona demonstretur quae diuina humanaque natura constat: rursus λόγος non potest demonstrari solus post assumptam carnem, ut non intelligamus & demonstremus etiam totam personam, quando humanitatem in suae personae unitatem inseparabiliter suscepit: atque ita totus Deus homo, & totus
units.tr: Hence Cassian says: "That man was never without God, for from the beginning he had received from God the very thing that he was. All men indeed have from God that they exist, for in him we live, move and have our being; but each one is so formed that the nature of each is his own, separately. And although Peter is not only formed by God and sustained by divine power, but God also dwells in him, yet for that reason God is not a part of the person of Peter, nor does Peter subsist in God so that he is one and single thing with him; nor, by defining Peter, do we comprehend God in that definition. But the human nature was so assumed by the Word that this nature was not separately its own man, but was united to the Word, and became the Word's own garment, and (so to speak) an inestimable instrument. It was created so that God might be man. For it belongs to human nature to be a rational animal, and this the human nature assumed by Christ has in itself. But to be a person, a subsistence which is individual and incommunicable, this it does not have in itself; rather it is grounded in the Word, and sustained by him who assumed it, so that now, as Athanasius writes, the same is God and man, the same both together, so that he is one thing, single and alone." We name this person Christ, God the Word incarnate, not the Word without flesh, much less the man alone without the Word, but both God and man. Not one God and another man, but one and the same God-man. Yet the deity is one thing and the humanity another, but they are so closely joined that the unity of the person always remains, so that when the man Jesus born of the virgin Mary is pointed to, the human nature alone cannot be pointed to, since it does not subsist of itself as an individual. Rather the hypostasis in which the human nature subsists, that is, the whole person, which consists of divine and human nature, is pointed out. Again, the Word cannot be pointed out alone after the flesh is assumed, without our also understanding and pointing out the whole person, since he has inseparably taken the humanity into the unity of his person. And so the whole God is called man by the ancients, and the whole man God, and the whole Christ is in God and the whole God in Christ, as Cassian puts it, so that no division or separation of the natures takes place, and so that, equally blasphemously, either man is believed to be entirely without God, or God without man.

units.la: Homo Deus dicitur a veteribus, & totus in Christo Deus, & totus in Deo Christus, ut Cassianus loquitur, ne diuisio aut separatio aliqua naturarum fiat, atque quod paris est blasphemiae, aut homo penitus sine Deo, aut Deus sine homine credatur. Arctissimam hanc unionem veteres similitudine animae & corporis explicare conati sunt, quae duae naturae in unam personam in homine conueniunt: meminit huius similitudinis Nazianzenus, & ante hunc Iustinus, qui tamen fatetur eam non per omnia huic mysterio conuenire, sed aliquo modo seu secundum quid. Atque Patres tantum vsi sunt hoc exemplo ad demonstrandam vnitatem personæ, quod vnus sit Christus, vnus Dominus, sed id postea Eutychiani & Acephali detorserūt ad afferendam vnam in Christo naturam: itaque à posterioribus diligenter annotatum est discrimen inter vnitionem Dei verbi cum assumpta humanitate, & vnionem animæ cum corpore. Anima & corpus non tantū vnam personam faciunt, sed vnam quoque naturam, sed Verbum & Caro non faciunt vnam naturam, sed vnum Christum, vnam personam. Deinde anima non extitit ante carnem, & carnis seu corporis informādi causa facta est, anima est proprij corporis gubernatrix, &ad hoc etiam subsistit, & quamuis corpore exuta subsistat, rursus tamen corpori excitato iungetur vt homo integer restituatur. At Verbū ab æterno suam hypostasim integram perfectamque habuit, neq; ad incarnandum & inhumanam dum substitit, sed alteram habet subsistendi causam, Imo Deus Verbum est creator & formator eius naturæ quam assumpsit, neq; illi aliquid perfectionis ex carne accessit, sed carnem ex gratia assumpsit. Anima & caro sunt duæ finitæ naturæ, at Verbum infinitum carnem finitæ naturæ assumpsit, & quamuis totum sit in humanitate assumpta, tamen non intra hanc cócluditur vt anima intra corpus, sed simul etiam totum est vbiq;. Ob hanc natuturarum infinitam distantiam, quae tamen nihilominus in vnam conuenere persona, maior dicitur esse vnitio Dei verbi & carnis assumptae in vna persona, quam animae & corporis quae non tantum vnam personam, sed vnam quoque naturam faciunt. Anima compatitur corpori, Deus Verbum nequaquam, Anima nullatenus foris a corpore suo habet operationis principium, Deus autem Verbu & in humanitate existens, in coelo & vbique consuetas operationes impleuit, licet quasdam & inaestimabiles & per corpus: atque alia est libertas Dei in carne & extra, & alia necessitas animae, quae obligata in corpore, secundum id habet eodem modo mouendi simplicis corporis potestatem. Sed quo melius tota ratio hypostaticae vnionis perspiciatur, non pigebit hic adscribere Elig Cretensis, verba ex commentarijs eius in Nazianzenum. Vnitio (inquit) κατὰ συνθεσιν siue per compositionem, quaedam est partium coeuntium quasi mutua complexio, facta citra partis utriusque interitum. Huiusmodi ea est, quam in coniunctione corporis & animi perspicimus, quam nonnulli ἑνωκραοιν vocant, hoc est, temperamentum, siue συμφωνιαν, naturalem nimirum coalitione. Atq; per compositionem vnitio hypostatica est, qua ex corporibus vnitis hypostasis vna efficitur, in qua naturae copulatae non extinguntur.
units.tr: The ancients tried to explain this most close union by the likeness of soul and body, in which two natures come together into one person in a human being. Gregory Nazianzen mentions this likeness, and before him Justin, who nevertheless admits that it does not fit this mystery in every respect, but in some way or in some respect. The Fathers used this example only to show the unity of the person, that Christ is one, one Lord; but later the Eutychians and Acephali twisted it to assert one nature in Christ. Therefore later writers have carefully noted the difference between the union of the Word of God with the assumed humanity and the union of soul with body. Soul and body make not only one person but also one nature. But the Word and the flesh do not make one nature, but one Christ, one person. Moreover, the soul did not exist before the flesh, and it was made for the sake of forming the flesh or body; the soul is the governor of its own body, and it subsists for this purpose; and although when stripped of the body it still subsists, yet it will be joined again to the raised body so that the whole man may be restored. But the Word had from eternity his whole and perfect hypostasis, and he did not subsist in order to be incarnate and made man, but has another cause of subsisting. Indeed God the Word is the creator and former of the nature which he assumed, and nothing of perfection came to him from the flesh; rather he assumed the flesh out of grace. The soul and the flesh are two finite natures, but the infinite Word assumed the flesh of a finite nature, and although he is wholly in the assumed humanity, yet he is not enclosed within it as the soul is enclosed within the body; rather at the same time he is wholly everywhere. Because of this infinite distance between the natures, which nevertheless came together into one person, the union of God the Word and the assumed flesh in one person is said to be greater than the union of soul and body, which make not only one person but also one nature. The soul suffers with the body; the Word of God does not suffer at all. The soul has no principle of action outside its own body; but God the Word, existing also in the humanity, carries out his accustomed operations in heaven and everywhere, though some of them are inestimable and done through the body. The freedom of God in the flesh and outside it is one thing, and the necessity of the soul, which is bound in the body, is another; it has, in the same way, the power of moving only the simple body. But so that the whole reasoning of the hypostatic union may be seen more clearly, it will not be tedious to add here the words of Elias of Crete from his commentaries on Gregory Nazianzen. "Union," he says, "by composition [κατὰ σύνθεσιν], or through composition, is a certain mutual embrace of the parts coming together, made without the destruction of either part. Such is the union which we see in the conjoining of body and mind, which some call a blending [ἑνωκραοιν], that is, a temperament or agreement [συμφωνίαν], by natural coalition. And union by composition is hypostatic when a single hypostasis is produced from the united bodies, in which the joined natures are not extinguished."

units.la: Quid sit in genere vnionis hypostatica. tur: sed vt earundem inter se discrimina & attributa propria nulla ex parte confusa neque mutata conseruantur: sic etiam inter se ratione hypostasis postquam coaluerunt nequaquam discerni possunt. Nam partium vnitarum differentiae characteristicae, hoc est de quibus singulae tanquam notis quibusdam agnoscuntur, & quae vnumquodque ab ijs, quae sunt eiusdem speciei separant: proprie vni hypostasi ambae efficiuntur, sicut de anima & corporis vnitione intelligitur, &c. Idem de vnione naturarum in Christo sic scribit. Caeterum personalis vnio est essentialis & quidem per se (ἀνθύπαρχος) duarum naturarum in vtero sanctae genitricis Dei concursus. Nec enim corpus ante Deum sermone ibi extitit, nec anima: sed simul caro, simul Deus sermo, simul caro animata rationis particeps. Quippe in ipso Deo sermone personam peculiare constituente(συνυποστάτω) exstitit. Quid igitur af sumpto potuit accidere maius, quā vt Deus fiat per vltranaturalem illam vnionem? Hoc autem modo Patres vtos esse similitudine animae & corporis, vt ostenderent conuentum hunc ineffabilem Verbi cum carne vnam solum constituisse personam, seu ita a Verbo carnem in vnitatem suę personae assumptam esse, vt Verbum & caro sint vna persona, vnus Filius, ex ipsis Patrum scriptis manifestum est. Nazianzenus, Si quis (inquit) duos filios, » alterum ex Deo & Patre, alterû ex matre, non » autem vnum atque eundem induxerit, is ab » ea quoque filiorum adoptione excidat, quæ » rectè credentibus promissa est. Quanquam e- » nim Deus & Homo duæ naturæ sunt, quem- » admodum & anima & corpus, non tamè duo » Filij nec Dij: sicut ne hic quidem duo homi- » nes, tametsi Paulus ad hunc modum interna » externamque hominis partem appellauerit. » Atque vt paucis rem complectar, aliud qui- » dem & aliud sunt ea, ex quibus Seruator còn » stat, non tamen alius atque alius, absit. Ambo » enim hæc copulatione vnum sunt, Deo nimi » rum humanitatem, atq; homine diuinitatem » suscipiente, aut quocunque tandem alio ver- » bo quispiam eam rem exprimedam duxerit.
units.tr: ...but just as their distinct characteristics and proper attributes are preserved without any confusion or change, so too, once they have come together, they cannot be told apart in respect of the hypostasis. For the characteristic marks of the united parts, that is, those by which each is recognized as by certain signs and which separate each from things of the same kind, both belong properly to the one hypostasis, as is understood of the union of soul and body, etc. He writes the same about the union of natures in Christ: "Moreover, the personal union is essential, and indeed per se [ἀνθύπαρχος], the concurrence of two natures in the womb of the holy mother of God. For there neither did the body exist before God the Word, nor the soul, but at once the flesh, at once God the Word, at once the animated flesh partaking of reason. Indeed, in the very Word of God, which constitutes a distinct person, it subsisted [συνυποστάτω]. What greater thing could happen to the assumed nature than that it should become God through that supernatural union?" That the Fathers used the likeness of soul and body in order to show that this ineffable meeting of the Word with the flesh constitutes only one person, or that the flesh is so assumed by the Word into the unity of his person that the Word and the flesh are one person, one Son, is plain from the writings of the Fathers themselves. Gregory Nazianzen: "If anyone should introduce two sons, one from God and the Father, the other from the mother, and not one and the same, he falls away from that adoption of sons which is rightly promised to believers. For although God and man are two natures, just as soul and body are, yet they are not two sons or two gods, just as there are not two men here, although Paul has called the inner and outer part of man by this name. And to sum up briefly: those things of which the Saviour consists are indeed different from one another, yet he is not a different one and another, God forbid. For both are one by union, God taking up humanity and man taking up divinity, or whatever other word someone may judge fit to express the matter."

units.la: Cyrillus: Filius coæternus Patri, qui natus est & ante omne seculum, postquam descendit in hominis naturam, non amisit esse quod e- » rat, nempe Deus, accepta humanitate intelli- » gitur merito & ex femine Dauid natus esse, » & recentem in humanitate habere natiuita- » tem. Porro quod assumptum non alienum » ab assumente, sed vere eius proprium repu- » tatum est, igitur quasi vnû cum ipso, quem- » admodum scilicet & hominis compositione » quis considerauerit. Nam ex dissimilibus, na- » tura animæ dico & corporis, composita est, » attamè vnus homo intelligitur, qui ex vtro- » que. Ita ab vna quidem carne interdum totum animal nominatur, interdum autem & anima nominata, intelligitur vtrunq;. Simili sane modo &de ipso Christo accipiemus. Nā si vnus Dominus &vn' filius Iesus Christus, & ante carne,& quando apparuit homo, eum qui nos redemit Dominū non negabimus, quāuis significetur interdū nobis per huma- nitatis proprietates, & humilitatis mensurā. Idé alibi ficscribit,Coniectare dicimus quod deceat cogitare ( quāuis minor fit oratio veri tate)talé esse adunationé Emanuel,qualé quis intelligat& animā ad suū corpus habere. A nima enim omnia quę sunt corporis reputat esse sua,licet per naturā propriā expers sit pas sionibus corporis,& quę extrinsecus partici- pant,&c. Subijcien' autem quomodo Deus impassibilis carnis infirmitates contudebat, eas tamen sui corporis esse ducebat,addit: Si- cut corpus est alterius naturæ præter animā, vnus tamen ex vtroque homo efficitur & vo catur:ita etiā ex perfecta Dei Verbi subsisten- tia & humanitate perfecta,vnus est Christus. Idem in eodem Deus simul homo:& sua qui- dem dicit Deus Verbum, ea quæ sunt carnis propria:quia ipsius est corpus & nō alterius. Communes autē facit tanquā cum sua carne diuinæ suæ maiestatis operationes, vt posset etiā viuificare mortuos & seruare infirmos. Idem quomodo Verbum caro factum fit,hoc modo exponit, Verbum inquit factum, esse
units.tr: Cyril: "The Son, coeternal with the Father, who was born even before all ages, after he descended into the nature of man, did not lose what he was, namely God. Having taken up humanity, he is rightly understood to have been born also of the seed of David, and to have a recent birth in his humanity. Moreover, what is assumed, not foreign to the one who assumes but truly reckoned his own, is therefore as one with him, just as anyone would consider in the composition of man. For he is composed of unlike things, I mean the nature of soul and of body, and yet one man is understood, who is of both. Thus the whole living creature is sometimes named from the one flesh, and sometimes, when the soul is named, both are understood. In a similar way we shall also understand concerning Christ himself. For if there is one Lord and one Son, Jesus Christ, both before the flesh and when he appeared as man, we shall not deny that he who redeemed us is the Lord, although it is sometimes indicated to us by the properties of humanity and the measure of humiliation." The same author writes elsewhere: "We say that we should conjecture (though the statement is less than the truth) that the union of Emmanuel is such as one would understand the soul to have with its body. For the soul reckons all the things of the body to be its own, although by its own nature it is free from the sufferings of the body, and those that come from outside it shares in, etc." Then, showing how God, who is impassible, bore the weaknesses of the flesh, yet counted them his own body, he adds: "Just as the body is of another nature apart from the soul, yet one man is made and is called from both, so also from the perfect subsistence of God the Word and the perfect humanity, Christ is one." And in the same work: "God is man at once; and God the Word calls his own the things that belong to the flesh, because the body is his and not another's. But he makes the works of his divine majesty common, as it were, with his own flesh, so that he could also quicken the dead and save the sick."

units.la: carnem, nihil est aliud, quã quod in carne ąę sanguine nobiscum similiter communicauit, ac nostrum corpus sibi proprium fecit, & homo prodijt ex muliere, interim nonabiecto quod Deus est & ex Patre genitū, sed, etiã in ipsa carnis assumptione, quòd erat retento. Hoc nusquã non contendit exactæ fidei dostrina. Hac fuisse sententia sanctos Patres inueniemus. De eodé mysterio sic scribit, Athanasius citante Maxentio. Verbū caro, non caro Verbum factū est. Verbum autē caro factū dicitur, quia Verbi facta est caro, & non alicuius hominis, hoc est, Deus homo factus est: & dicitur caro, ne prætereatis carnis nomē. Cur ergo non sufficit nobis naturalis vnitio Verbi ad propriam carnē, & quia Deus homo factus est. Item, Cyrillus apud eudē Maxentiū, Non enim dicimus quod Dei natura conuersa aut immutata, facta sit caro, vel quod in totum homine, qui est ex anima & corpore trāsformata sit: sed illud magis quod carnem animatā & animā rationalē sibi copulauerit Verbum, & Filius Dei substanstialiter, ineffabiliter, incomprehensibiliter factus sit homo, & nuncupatus sit Filius hominis. Nec nuda tantum voluntate, nec assumptione personæ, sed quod diuersæ quidam naturæ in vnū conuenerint, vnus tamen ex vtraq; Christus & Filius: non euacuata aut sublata naturarum diuersitate propter vnionem.
units.tr: The same author explains how the Word became flesh in this way: "That the Word was made flesh is nothing other than that he in flesh and blood likewise shared with us, and made our body his own, and came forth as man from a woman, yet not laying aside that he is God and was begotten of the Father, but, even in the very assumption of the flesh, retaining what he was. The doctrine of exact faith nowhere denies this." We find that the holy Fathers held this view. Athanasius, quoted by Maximus, writes thus about the same mystery: "The Word became flesh, not the flesh the Word. But the Word is said to have become flesh because the flesh became the Word's, and not that of some man; that is, God was made man; and it is called flesh, lest you pass over the name of flesh." Why then is the natural union of the Word with its own flesh not enough for us, and that God was made man? Likewise Cyril, also quoted by Maximus: "For we do not say that the nature of God was changed or transformed, so that it became flesh, or that it was transformed into the whole man, who consists of soul and body; but rather that the Word joined to himself animated flesh and a rational soul, and the Son of God was made man substantially, ineffably, incomprehensibly, and was called the Son of man. Not by bare will, nor by assumption of a person only, but because different natures came together into one, yet one Christ and Son is from both, the diversity of natures not being emptied or taken away by the union."

units.la: Possem plura testimonia adducere, sed ex his facile perspici potest quomodo vetus ecclesia de vnione hypostatica docuerit, pleraque etiam ex his quae attulimus, Aduersarij nostri concedunt, sed contendunt non esse plenam definitionem hanc vnionis hypostaticae, qua dicimus vnionem hypostaticam in Christo esse copulationem seu vnitionem Dei Verbi cum carne, in qua verbum carne assumpsit & ita sibi propriam fecit, vt saluis vtriusque naturae proprietatibus Verbum & caro vnam|personam vnum quid & singulum constituant.
units.tr: I could bring forward more testimonies, but from these it can easily be seen how the ancient Church taught concerning the hypostatic union. Many of the things we have cited our adversaries grant. But they contend that this definition of the hypostatic union is not complete, by which we say that the hypostatic union in Christ is the joining or uniting of God the Word with the flesh, in which the Word assumed the flesh and so made it its own, that, with the properties of each nature kept safe, the Word and the flesh constitute one person, one thing and one individual.

units.la: Primum enim quod dicitur vtraque natura suam proprietatem saluam retinere, id quia ita confirmatum est scripturis, & veteris ecclesiae consensu, negare quidem non audent aperte, sed tamen per cuniculos oppugnant: nam multa quae maxime propria sunt volunt accidentarias esse proprietates.
units.tr: For as to the statement that each nature keeps its own property safe, since this has been confirmed by the Scriptures and by the consent of the ancient Church, they do not dare to deny it openly, yet they attack it by underground tunnels; for they want many properties that are most proper to be accidental properties.

units.la: Deinde Marbachius, scribit extra vnionem personalem naturam vtranque suas proprietates seruare, neque quicquam alteri communicare, aut capacem esse proprietatem alterius naturae: at naturas in vnam personam vnitas, retinere quidem substantiam suam, sed proprietates realiter sibi mutuo communicare. Vbi omnino statuere videtur proprietates non manere integras facta vnione: atq; vt vt ipse cum alijs hoc fateatur, tamen oes contendunt vnionem personalem <bl>ἑνῳσέως</bl> & communicatione proprietatum definiendam esse: ac nisi vnio hæc reali effusione omnium proprietatum diuinæ naturæ in humanam defi-niatur, clamant Christum in ordinem sanctorum redigi, & deitate, potentia, gloria & maiestate omni spoliari, & tantum nomen nudum illi relinqui. An autem hæ sint veræ & specificæ differentiæ vnionis personalis quibus ipsi eam definiunt mox viderimus, nunc de reali communicatione quam tantopere vrgent aliquid dicamus. Hoc tamen prius omnes admonitos volumus vt bene expendant quæ à nobis allata sunt, nam tum facile animaduertent nulli creaturæ hanc definitionem nostram conuenire, sed soli huic vnioni Filij Dei cum assumpta sua carne. Etsi enim Deus in sanctis suis inhabitat, eos sustentat, & donis ornat, ita vt etiam suo modo diuinæ naturæ consortes facti dicantur, & ea quæ sanctis fiunt sibi fieri dicit, tamen illa inhabitatio aut conuentus Dei cum hominibus, toto genere differt ab hac copulatione aut vnione personali: nam exempli gratia Paulus etsi Christum in se habitantem & viuentem habet, tamen nō est vnum quiddam cum Christo aut Verbo, sed alius est Christus alius est Paulus: neque Deus ita sustentat Paulum, vt cum eo vnum quoddam & singulum fit, neque ita facta est humana natura Pauli, vt simul Verbo vniretur, sed ipsa in semetipsa suam habet sub- sistentiam, & ita creata est vt seperatim sua ipsius esset: aliam autem esse rationem huma- nitatis illius quam Verbum assumpsit, supra ostendimus. Ac mirum mihi videtur Aduer- sarios tribuere humanae naturae Christi quod variis modis & nobis incognitis praesens rea- liter esse possit, at ipsam Dei naturâ ita astrin- gere vt vno tantū modo ἰδίᾳ sua creaturis adef- se possit, & vt nō alia sit Dei in Christo quàm in creaturis reliquis omnibus praesentia, quae tantum ὑπερβάλλει differat: vbi hic est Dei omni- potentia? num illam circumscribere finibus aliquibus volunt? Nos constanter affirma- mus praesentiam Dei in assumpta humani- tate genere ipso differre à praesentia Dei qua vel omnibus rebus creatis vel peculiari etiam gratia sanctis suis adest & in illis habitat. Hàc autè cum Paulo ita exponimus, quod in Chri- sto sit omnis plenitudo Dei σωματικῶς, vt sit vt- num quasi σῶμα, vnum quiddam singulum & solum seu vna hypostasis: Dicimus cum Ioan- ne Verbum carnem factum esse: non autem inquit Verbum suas proprietates in carnem transfudisse, sed Verbum factum carnem, ita assumpsisse in vnitatem suae subsistentiae hu- manam naturam & carnem induisse ac sibi fecisse propriam, vt Verbum natum dicatur in carne & sit homo factum. Hanc vnionem Verbi infiniti & aeterni, cum humana finita
units.tr: Then Marbach writes that outside the personal union each nature keeps its own properties and communicates nothing to the other, nor is it capable of a property of the other nature; but that the natures, once united into one person, indeed retain their substance, yet really communicate their properties to one another. Here he seems to lay down that the properties do not remain whole once the union is made. And although he himself, with others, admits this, yet they all contend that the personal union must be defined by the communication of properties, and unless this union is defined by the real outpouring of all the properties of the divine nature into the human, they cry out that Christ is reduced to the rank of the saints and stripped of deity, power, glory and all majesty, and that only a bare name is left to him. Whether these are the true and specific differences of the personal union by which they define it, we shall soon see; now let us say something about the real communication, which they press so hard. Yet first we want everyone to weigh carefully what we have brought forward, for then they will easily notice that this definition of ours applies to no creature, but only to this union of the Son of God with his assumed flesh. For although God dwells in his saints, sustains them and adorns them with gifts, so that they are even said in their own way to have become partakers of the divine nature, and what is done to the saints he says is done to himself, yet that indwelling or fellowship of God with men differs in its whole kind from this personal joining or union. For example, although Paul has Christ dwelling and living in him, yet he is not one thing with Christ or with the Word; but Christ is one and Paul another. Nor does God so sustain Paul that he becomes one single thing with him, nor is Paul's human nature so made that it is simultaneously united to the Word; rather it has its own subsistence in itself and was so created that it would be separate and its own. We have shown above that the manner of that humanity which the Word assumed is another. And it seems strange to me that our adversaries attribute to the human nature of Christ that it can be really present in various ways, unknown to us, and yet bind the divine nature itself so that it can be present to creatures in only one way of its own, and that the presence of God in Christ is not different from the presence in all other creatures, differing only by an excess. Where, then, is God's omnipotence? Do they want to confine it within certain limits? We firmly affirm that the presence of God in the assumed humanity differs in kind from the presence by which God is present to all created things, or even by peculiar grace to his saints, and dwells in them. But we explain this with Paul, that in Christ there dwells all the fullness of God bodily [σωματικῶς], so that he is as it were one body, one single thing and only one, or one hypostasis. We say with John that the Word was made flesh; yet, he says, the Word did not pour its properties into the flesh, but the Word, having become flesh, so took the human nature into the unity of his subsistence and put on the flesh and made it his own, so that the Word is said to be born in the flesh and to have become man. This union of the infinite and eternal Word with finite human nature...

units.la: Cur de my- sterio hoc ineffabili scribamus. natura, ratione comprehendi aut verbis effa ri non posse,& omnium mysteriorum maxi* mum & prorsus ἀρρήτων esse, libenter agnosci* mus & profitemur, ac satius effet nos potius hæc mysteria venerari & adorare quam per* scrutari: sed quod de his differimus cogit nos Aduersariorum importunitas, qui hæc in quæstionem primi vocarunt, & repudiatis plerisque formis loquendi quibus ecclesia o* lim in explicatione horum mysteriorum vsa est, nouam doctrinam protulerunt, cui fi quis non per omnia aflentiatur, mox non tantum omnium hæreseon infamia aspergitur, sed prorsus Mahumetanus esse dicitur, & adTur cas relegatur. Cogimur itaque ostendere nos & cum veteri ecclesia sentire & loqui, & eam vnione docere qua nulli creaturæ alij sed tan* tum huic naturæ adfumptç Verbum vnitum fit, & Deus homo, ac homo Deus factus.
units.tr: Why we write about this ineffable mystery. We gladly acknowledge and profess that this mystery cannot be grasped by nature or reason, or expressed in words, and that it is the greatest of all mysteries and altogether unspeakable [ἀρρήτων]. It would be better for us to revere and adore these mysteries than to pry into them. But the importunity of our opponents compels us to discuss them. They have called these matters into question, and, rejecting most of the forms of speech by which the Church formerly explained these mysteries, they have brought forward a new doctrine. Whoever does not agree with it in every point is at once not only stained with the infamy of every heresy, but is said to be a Mahometan outright and is relegated to the Turks. We are therefore obliged to show that we both think and speak with the ancient Church, and that we teach the union by which the Word is joined to this assumed nature alone, and to no other creature, so that God becomes man and man becomes God.

units.la: De communione proprietatum.
units.tr: On the communion of properties.

units.la: Quoniam vero Aduersarij in communica tione ceu transfusione proprietatum diuinæ naturæ in humanam, vnionem hanc confi* stere volunt, de illa plura adhuc dicenda erùt. Cum autem proprietates essentiales ab ipsa natura separari non possint, non est alia con* ftituenda communicatio proprietatum ab ipsa naturarum communicatione.
units.tr: Since our opponents want this union to consist in a communication, or transfusion, of the properties of the divine nature into the human, more must still be said about this. But since the essential properties cannot be separated from the nature itself, the communication of properties must not be established as anything other than the communication of the natures themselves.

units.la: Porro naturæ ipsæ non sunt ἀκοινώνητοι, ne* que singulæ seorsim post vnionem factam subsistunt, ideo recte communicari dicuntur, non quod vna natura transfundatur in alteram, ita enim non manerent ambæ integræ, sed quod vniantur & vnius personæ sunt. Similimodo proprietates naturarum vnius personæ sunt, seu persona communicatur. Sicut etiam Theodoretus scribit, propria naturarum fiunt communia personæ. Atque hæc est vera & realis communicatio naturarum in persona, Exempli gratia, est Dei Verbi proprium esse æternum infinitum, omnipotentem, esse Deum; humanæ naturæ proprium est, corporeum & circumscriptum, & temporale seu in tempore originem habere: hæc non separatim tribuuntur naturis, sicuti nec actiones, ne soluatur personæ vnitas, sed prædicatur de persona in qua naturæ ambæ subsistunt, & sic Christus Deus & homo, visibilis, & inuisibilis, æternus & in tempore initium habens, corporeus & incorporeus, finitus & infinitus dicitur. Hæc enim quæuis contraria tamen vere & reipsa huic personæ conueniunt, non tamen eiusdem naturæ ratione. Nam vt Fulgentius scribit, vnus idemque Christus est, qui quod humanum est, habet Deus, in veritate humanæ, & quod diuinum est habeat homo, in veritate diuinæ naturæ. Et Augustinus similitudine animæ & carnis idem explicat, in quibus quod singulis est proprium commune fit amborum: proprium naturæ, commune personæ. Quare sicut ad vitandam separationem & exprimendâ vim verę vnionis hæc de persona tota prædicantur, & quidem vere, ita ne confusio aut transfusio facta credatur, ecclesia addidit exemplo sacrarū litterarum particulā distinguetem iuxta quam natura tale idioma aut actio personæ tribuatur, vt Christus est æternus secundū diuinam naturā, & idem in tempore esse coepit, secundum humanam naturā: consubstantialis est nobis secundum carnem, & consubstantialis est Patri secundum diuinam naturam: genitus est ex femine Dauid, sed secundū carnem, Illa enim persona Christus, quæ diuina & humana natura constat, & vere æterna est, sed tantum ratione τῆς λόγου, & vere etiam in tempore reinitium accepit, non quod λόγος in tempore initiū acceperit, sed ratione carnis assumptæ, quæ ante non extitit, & carne assumpta Verbum factum est caro Deus incarnatus seu manifestatus in carne. Itaque cum Christus in Euangelio loquitur de seipso, aliquando quidem vt homo loquitur, humana de se prædicans, vt cum se filium hominis nominat: & cur me quæritis interficere hominem qui veritatem locutus sum vobis: & cum de cruce & passione sua loquitur, &c. Aliquando autē de se ea dicit quæ diuina sunt, vt quum se Patri æqualem facit, & ante Abraham fuisse dicit: omnia
units.tr: Moreover, the natures are not unshared [ἀκοινώνητοι], nor does each subsist separately after the union has been made. They are therefore rightly said to be communicated, not because one nature is transfused into the other (for then both would not remain whole), but because they are united and belong to one person. Likewise the properties of the natures belong to one person, or the person is communicated. As Theodoret also writes, the properties of the natures become common to the person. This is the true and real communication of the natures in the person. For example, it is proper to the Word of God to be eternal, infinite, almighty, and God; it is proper to the human nature to be corporeal and circumscribed, and to have its origin in time, or temporal. These are not assigned to the natures separately, any more than the actions are, lest the unity of the person be dissolved. Rather, they are predicated of the person in whom both natures subsist. Thus Christ is called God and man, visible and invisible, eternal and having a beginning in time, corporeal and incorporeal, finite and infinite. For these contrary things truly and in fact belong to this one person, yet not by reason of the same nature. As Fulgentius writes, it is one and the same Christ who has, as God, what is human, in the truth of the human nature, and who has, as man, what is divine, in the truth of the divine nature. Augustine explains the same by the likeness of soul and flesh, in which what is proper to each becomes common to both: proper to the nature, common to the person. Therefore, in order both to avoid separation and to express the force of the true union, these things are predicated of the whole person, and truly so. And so that no confusion or transfusion is believed to have taken place, the Church has added, following the pattern of Holy Scripture, a distinguishing particle by which a given predicate or action is assigned to one nature rather than the other. For example: Christ is eternal according to the divine nature, and the same Christ began to exist in time according to the human nature; he is consubstantial with us according to the flesh, and consubstantial with the Father according to the divine nature; he was born of the seed of David according to the flesh. For that person, Christ, who consists of the divine and human nature, is truly eternal, but only by reason of the Word [τοῦ λόγου]. And truly he also received a beginning in time, not because the Word received a beginning in time, but by reason of the assumed flesh, which did not exist before; and with the flesh assumed, the Word became flesh, God incarnate, or manifested in the flesh. Accordingly, when Christ speaks of himself in the Gospel, sometimes he speaks as a man, predicating human things of himself, as when he calls himself the Son of Man, or: "Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth?" and when he speaks of his cross and passion, etc. At other times he says of himself things that are divine, as when he makes himself equal to the Father and says that he was before Abraham.

units.la: Distinctio secundum naturam. omnia autē hæc ad personam vnam pertinet, ad hunc qui hæc dixit, ad Iesum Christū, sed alia quidem secundum diuinā naturam, alia secundum humanam: omnia tamen vere & reipsa vnius Christi sunt. Hanc distinctionē proprietatū in vnitate personę secundū diffe-rentiam naturarum diligeter docet Cyrillus, necessarium scribens vt licet diuersa & minime inter se coueneintia acta esse dicantur, vt hæc secundum aliud & aliud in vno Christo accipiamus, & de vno eodemque constitua-mus, nulla diuisione admissa. Hæc arctissima copulatio assumptæ carnis cum assumente verbo, & ineffabilis illa vnio duarū naturarū in vna persona fundamentū est Communionis idiomatum. Dicitur autem communicatio idiomatum prædicatio, in qua proprietas vni naturæ conueniens ad alteram transfertur, in concreto propter vnionē hypostaticam. Hanc Cassianus explicat per synechdochen, quo tropo & a parte totum intelligitur, & a toto portio. Et Gelasius in hoc mysterio inquit, cum nulla necessitas impugnationis emergit, simpliciter vnam rem pro vtraque frequenter proferimus. Item vsitato compendio sæpe de qualibet rei parte dicimus, & totū quod est sine dubio profitemur. Nunquid cum verbū Dei dicitur non simul intelligitur & caro quod factum est?&c. Primum itaque quia ita in utero virginis vnitas est Deus carni,vt vnum fit ἑνυσάρκωνον, non pōs test vna in illo natura nominari quin simul intelligatur altera, quicquid enim de Christō dicitur de tota persona dicitur, & in filio Dei filius hominis, & in hominis filio Dei filius nuncupatur. Sic Ioannes Christum virum nō minat, & eunde ait post se venire, & ante se fuisse. Hic Christus vir nominatur, & quod humanæ naturæ est toti personæ tribuitur: atque hæc est synechdoche: eidem viro tri-buitur ante Ioannem fuisse, & post eum ve-nire quod vtrunque cum partis sit, hoc quidem humanę illud vero diuinæ naturæ, tamē vtrunque de tota persona per synechdochen prædicatur. Atq; in hunc sensum has loquen-di formas Cassianus explicat per synechdo-chen, hoc ipso exemplo vsus. Atque vt appa-ret geminata synechdoche statuitur, vna qua vnius naturę nomen concretum pro tota per-sona ponitur, altera qua toti personæ in con-creto tribuitur quod vnius tantum naturæ est. Atque idem est quando dicitur naturæ vni tribui in concreto, quod est naturæ alte-rius: nā vt Cassianus docet, nomen vnius na-turæ per synechdochen pro tota persona po-nitur: itaque quod de illa in concreto prædi-catur, non de ipsa natura sed de persona præ-dicatur. Boetius quoq; hāc naturarū vnioné, & quæ ex eo oritur prædicationū rationem, his verbis explicat. Fides catholica continet
units.tr: Distinction according to nature. All these things, however, pertain to one person, to the one who spoke them, Jesus Christ. Some belong to him according to the divine nature, others according to the human, yet all are truly and in reality the acts of the one Christ. Cyril teaches this distinction of properties within the unity of the person, according to the difference of natures, with care. He writes that it is necessary, although the things said to be done are diverse and by no means agree with one another, to understand them as belonging to one and another in the one Christ, and to ascribe them to one and the same, admitting no division. This most intimate joining of the assumed flesh with the assuming Word, and that ineffable union of the two natures in one person, is the foundation of the communion of idioms. The communication of idioms is the predication in which a property belonging to one nature is transferred to the other, in the concrete, on account of the hypostatic union. Cassian explains this by synecdoche, a trope by which the whole is understood from the part and the part from the whole. Gelasius, speaking of this mystery, says: when no necessity of refutation arises, we simply and often name one thing for both. Likewise, by a customary shorthand, we often speak of a part of anything and undoubtedly profess the whole that it is. Surely when the Word of God is spoken of, the flesh that was made is not also understood at the same time? And so on. First, therefore, since in the virgin's womb God is so united to the flesh that he becomes one [ἑνυσάρκωνον], one nature cannot be named in him without the other being understood at the same time. For whatever is said of Christ is said of the whole person: in the Son of God the Son of Man is named, and in the Son of Man the Son of God is named. Thus John calls Christ a man and says of him that he comes after him and was before him. Here Christ is called a man, and what belongs to the human nature is attributed to the whole person. This is synecdoche: to the same man is attributed that he was before John and comes after him. Both of these belong to a part, the one to the human nature, the other to the divine, yet both are predicated of the whole person by synecdoche. In this sense Cassian explains these forms of speech by synecdoche, using this very example. And so that the double synecdoche appears, one is set up by which the concrete name of one nature is put for the whole person, and the other by which what belongs to one nature only is attributed in the concrete to the whole person. It is the same when it is said that what belongs to the other nature is attributed in the concrete to one nature. For, as Cassian teaches, the name of one nature is put by synecdoche for the whole person, so that what is predicated of it in the concrete is predicated not of the nature itself but of the person. Boethius also explains this union of natures, and the rule of predications that arises from it, in these words: The catholic faith holds

units.la: » Not printed as a separate note; see text. eundem Christum hominem esse perfectum eundem Deum, eundemque qui homo sit perfectus atque Deus. Vnum esse Deum ac Dei filium, nec quaternitatem Trinitatis astrui, dum Homo addicitur supra perfectum Deum, sed vnam eandemque personam numerum Trinitatis explere. Vt cum humanitas passa sit Deus tamen passus esse dicatur. Non quod ipsa diuinitas humanitas facta sit : sed quod a Deitate fuerit assumpta. Item qui homo est Dei filius appellatur, non substantia diuinitatis sed humanitatis, quae tamen diuinitatu naturali vnitate coniuncta est. Et cum haec ita intelligentia discernantur permisceanturque, tamen vnus idemque & homo perfectus sit & Deus. Deus quidem quod ipse sit ex Patris substantia genitus, homo vero quia ipse ex Maria virgine sit procreatus. Itemque qui homo Deus eo quod a Deo fuerit assumptus: & qui Deus homo, quoniam vestitus homine fit: Cumque in eadem persona aliud sit diuinitas quae suscepit, aliud humanitas quam suscepit, idem tamen Deus atque homo est. Nam si homo minem intelligas, idem homo est atq; Deus: quoniam homo ex natura, Deus assumptione. Si vero Deum intelligas, idem Deus est atque homo, quoniam Deus est natura, homo assumptione: fitque in eo gemina natura geminaque substantia, quoniam homo Deus: vnaq; persona, quoniam idem homo atq; Deus,
units.tr: » Not printed as a separate note; see text. that the same Christ is perfect man and the same God, and that the same is who is perfect man and God. There is one God and the Son of God, and the number of the Trinity is not increased by adding a man above the perfect God, but one and the same person fills the number of the Trinity. So although the humanity suffered, God is nevertheless said to have suffered. Not that the divinity itself was made humanity, but that it was assumed by the Deity. Likewise, he who is man is called the Son of God, not in respect of the substance of the divinity but of the humanity, which is nonetheless joined to the divinity by natural unity. And although these are distinguished in understanding, and yet mixed, one and the same is both perfect man and God: God indeed because he is begotten of the substance of the Father, man indeed because he was born of the Virgin Mary. Likewise, he who is man is God because he was assumed by God, and he who is God is man because he is clothed with a man. And since in the same person the divinity that assumed is one thing and the humanity that was assumed is another, yet it is the same God and man. For if you understand man, the same is man and God, since he is man by nature and God by assumption. If you understand God, the same is God and man, since he is God by nature and man by assumption. Thus in him there is a twofold nature and a twofold substance, since he is man and God, and one person, since the same is man and God.

units.la: Multa huiusmodi de proprietatum communicatione, apud Cyrillum, Theodoretum, Vigilium, atque Fulgentium aliosque scriptores occurrunt. Verum inter nos & aduersarios de hoc controuersia est, quod harum praedicationum fundamentum nos quidem facimus vnitionem hypostaticam hac ratione, quod naturae proprietates suas in se seruer, sed quia vera est vnitio naturarum propter communionem naturarum & proprietatum in persona, haec quae vnius naturae sunt de altera praedicari. Contra aduersarij etiam ipsi harum praedicationum fundamentum faciunt vnitionem hypostaticam sed hoc modo, quod naturae ita vnitae sint, vt vna suâ proprietate transfundat reipsa in alteram, vt ita fiat realis & physica quaedam transfusio & communicatio Idiomatum.
units.tr: Many statements of this kind about the communication of properties occur in Cyril, Theodoret, Vigilius, Fulgentius and other writers. But between us and our opponents there is a controversy about this: we indeed make the hypostatic union the foundation of these predications, in such a way that each nature keeps its own properties, yet because the union of the natures is true, there is a communion of natures and properties in the person, so that what belongs to one nature is predicated of the other. The opponents, on the other hand, also make the hypostatic union the foundation of these predications, but in this way: that the natures are so united that one transfuses its property in reality into the other, so that a certain real and physical transfusion and communication of the attributes takes place.

units.la: Atque quod proprietates humanae naturae spectat, alij quidem nullam hic realem communicationem agnoscunt quod diuinitas ab humanitate nihil accipiat: sed Marpachius scribit humanitatem diuinitati suas proprietates actiones, & officia vere & realiter communicare; atq; hanc realem communionem aliquot pagellis in suo crasso volumine explicare & confirmare conatur. In qua eius explicatione hoc ab eo quaero, quo exemplo scriptor humanam naturam communicare suas proprietates diuinae naturae, & eam in suorum operum societate admittere & suscipere. Cyrillus tillus & alij veterum nunquam tribuunt humanitati quod illa comunicet sua, aut in comunionem & societatem suorum operum sufci piat diuinitatem : sed dicunt Verbum ea quae sunt carnis suae sibi propria facere. Dicat etiā nobis cur opera & officia Messiae quae vndecim ab ipso enumerantur, proprietates seu propria opera faciat humanae naturae, quae il la communicet diuinitati? Sunt autem haec opera seu officia quae comemorat, 1. Esse servi uu legis & eam implere. 2. Hominibus prędi care verbū Regni Dei. 3. Seipsum offerre in cruce pro peccatorū expiatione & recócilia-tione humani generis. 4. Parta victoria adversus morte Satanam & inferos, in coelum ascendere, sedere ad dexterā Dei, esse suorum fidelium mediatorem & intercessorem apud Deum Patrem. 5. Mittere Spiritum sanctum. 6. Conseruare ministeriū Verbi & fideles ministros excitare. 7. Exaudire preces eorum qui ipsum inuocant. 8. Ecclesiā aduersus Satanam & alios hostes defendere. 9. Extremo die ad iudicandū venire. 10. Resuscitare mortuos. 11. Vnicuique retribuere iuxta sua opera. Si haec sunt officia totius personae, cur ea facit humanae naturae propria? An verò hoc ferendum est quod humanae naturae propria officia facit missionem Spiritus sancti, consolationem ministerij, exauditionem precum, defensionem ecclesiae, iudicium totius orbis.
units.tr: As for the properties of the human nature, some indeed acknowledge no real communication here, that the divinity receives nothing from the humanity. But Marpach writes that the humanity truly and really communicates its own properties, actions and offices to the divinity; and in his thick volume he tries to explain and confirm this real communion over several pages. In this explanation I ask him this: by what example does the writer show that the human nature communicates its properties to the divine nature, and admits and receives it into the fellowship of its works? Cyril and the other ancients never ascribe to the humanity that it communicates its own things, or admits the divinity into the communion and fellowship of its works; rather they say that the Word makes the things of his flesh his own. Let him also tell us why the works and offices of the Messiah, which he lists as eleven, make the proper works of the human nature, which it communicates to the divinity. These works or offices which he recalls are: 1. To be a servant of the law and to fulfil it. 2. To preach the word of the kingdom of God to men. 3. To offer himself on the cross for the expiation of sins and the reconciliation of the human race. 4. Having won the victory over death, Satan and hell, to ascend into heaven, to sit at the right hand of God, and to be the mediator and intercessor of his faithful before God the Father. 5. To send the Holy Spirit. 6. To preserve the ministry of the Word and raise up faithful ministers. 7. To hear the prayers of those who call upon him. 8. To defend the Church against Satan and other enemies. 9. To come to judge on the last day. 10. To raise the dead. 11. To render to each according to his works. If these are offices of the whole person, why does he make them the proper things of the human nature? Or is it to be endured that the human nature performs the proper offices of sending the Holy Spirit, the consolation of the ministry, the hearing of prayers, the defence of the Church, and the judgment of the whole world?

units.la: F ★ refuscitationem mortuorū, & quidé ita pro‐pria vt hæc cōmunicet diuinæ naturæ, & il‐lam quasi in possessionem horum admittat? Iam quod dicit hæc ab humana natura vtà promisso Messia facta esse, non tamē esse tan‐tum opera filij hominis, sed communia etiam Filio Dei, hoc est toti personæ quæ est Deus & homo, ita vt non minus vere hæc de filio Dei quam de Filio hominis dici possint: vala de ambiguum est, ne quid grauius dicā. Nam primum videtur humanam tantum naturam Messiam facere, deinde ita loquitur de filio hominis, quasi alius sit Dei, alius hominis fi‐lius, qui tamen sint societate vnus filius & vna persona. Cum autem exponit causas cur humana natura suas proprietates & opera sua cōmunicet diuinitati has affert. Primum quia humana natura in se non subsistat sed in persona Verbi, quod Verbum vere & essen‐tialiter est Dei filius, itaque quę humanæ na‐turæ accidunt, vere prędicari etiam Filio Dei accidisse, quoniā humana natura ne momen‐to quidem separatur à persona quæ est Filius Dei. Deinde quia Diuinitas quę per se & sub statia sua impassibilis est, in morte & passio‐ne humanam naturam sustentat, & efficacem reddit ad superandum mortē & Satanā: atta‐men vt caro pati & mori posset Verbum iux‐ta Irenæum quieuit, non exeruit suam poten‐tiam in repellenda morte & passione. Verum hinc non conficitur communicatio in natura: Nam exempli gratia nasci,crucifigi,mori, proprie ad humanam naturā pertinent, hæc autem prædicantur etiā de diuina natura in concreto, non quod hæc ad ipsam naturam Deitatis pertingant,tum enim etiā in abstracto de Deitate dici possent,sed quod hęc uere pertingant ad personam quæ non tantum humanam naturam habet sed Deus est. Neque sequitur humanitas sustētatur à Deitate,ergo operationes & propria sua realiter Deitati cō municat:non enim ex humanitate & Deitate fit vna natura,sed vna persona,itaque tantum hinc conficitur hæc personæ propria esse,hactenus enim hæc ad alteram naturā pertinent quatenus vnum sunt inuicem, sunt autem vnum non natura sed persona. Est autē hic obiter considerandum, Abstracti & concreti nomen non recte à quibusdam vsurpari, Marpa chius interpretatur abstractum idem esse atq; extra personalem vnionem per se subsistere: sed veteres & recentiores vsitate per abstractum intelligunt naturam in vnione hypostatica per se consideratam, vel cogitatione seiunctam vt proprietas ipsi conueniens recte applicetur.Nam sic etiā Dialectici ipsam formam cogitatione separatam & per se considerat, abstractum appellant, vt sunt humanitas,iusticia,sanitas,&c. Deinde sicut illi subiectum in quo forma hæret, vt homo, iustus, fanus concretū vocant:ita concretum in theo logorum scholis nominatur, non ipsa vnio naturarum, sed vocabulum quod personam τὸ ὑφισάμενον notat, cuiuscunque tandem natu-ræ ratione id fiat, vt Deus,homo, filius Dei, filius hominis:tali enim nomine persona có-prehenditur, quæ vtranque naturam habet. Itaque quod illi dicunt Filium Dei vere na-tum, mortuum & passum esse, libenter da-mus,illa enim persona quæ est filius Dei pas-sa est,sed non in diuinitate, verū carne, vt D. Petrus loquitur. Patientibus sanctis dicitur etiam Christus, pati qui Saulo inquit, Quid me persequeris?& populus reijciens prophe-tas Dei dicitur Deum ipsum spreuisse:sed hæc tantum per relationem ad Deum pertinent, quod hi sunt legati Dei, membra ecclesiæ cu-ius caput est Christus : at longè alia ratio est Filij Dei patientis : ille enim qui in cruce pe-pendit vere fuit Filius Dei, neque potuit de-monstrari homo nudus in cruce pendens,aut eam homini nudo attribuere possumus, nisi personā Christi soluere velimus, non tamen propterea passio ad naturam diuinitatis per-tingit. Sed vt corpore moriēte anima nō mo-ritur, ita multo minus mors aut passio ad na-turam diuinitatis in Christo pertingit: ac ani-ma quidem compatitur suo corpori,non au-tem diuinitas humanitati assumptæ. Quosi si passiones assumptæ naturæ cōmunicarentur realiter diuinæ naturæ, assumptione humanitatis fuisset immutata natura diuina, in quâ tamen nulla mutatio cadit. Neque ideo nominetantum Deus natus: passus & mortuus est, nisi forte (quod absit) Christus nomine tantum Deus & Filius Dei est. Ita autem semper ecclesia sensit & docuit de morte & passione Filij Dei. Cyrillus citante Leone, Is qui ante secula omnia natus est ex Patre, etiã ex muliere carnaliter dicitur procreatus in tempore. Non quia diuina ipsius natura de sacra virgine sumpsit exordium, nec quod propter ipsum opus habuit secundo nasci post illã natiuitatem quã habebat ex Patre (est enim ineptum & stultum hoc dicere, quod is qui ante secula omnia est consempiternus Patri, secundæ generationis eguerit vt esse inciperet) sed quia propter nos, & propter nostram salutem naturam sibi copulauit humanã, & processit ex muliere, idcirco dicitur natus esse carnaliter. Neq; enim prius natus est homo communis de sancta virgine, & tunc demum habitauit in eo Verbum, sed in vulua vtroque virginali secum carnem coniunxit, & sustinuit generationem carnalem, carnis suæ natiuitatem suam faciens. Sic illum dicimus & passum esse & resurrexisse, non quia Deus Verbum in sua natura passus sit, aut plagas, aut clauorum transfixiones, aut alia vulnera (Deus nanque incorporalis extra passionem est)sed quia corpus illud quod ipsius proprium factum est, passum est, ideo haec omnia pro nobis ipse dicitur passus. Inerat namq; in eo corpore quod patiebatur Deus, qui pati non poterat. Similiter modo & mortem ipsius intelligimus. Immortale enim & incorruptibile est naturaliter, & vita & viuificans Dei Verbum. Sed quia corpus ipsius proprium, gratia Dei pro omnibus iuxta Pauli vocem mortem gustauit, idcirco ipse dicitur morte passus esse pro nobis. Non quod ipse morte effet expertus, quantum ad ipsius naturā pertinet (insania, n. est hoc vel sentire vel dicere) quod (vt supra diximus) vera caro ipsius mortem gustauit. Ita & resurgente carne, ipsius rursus resurrectionem dicimus: non quia in corruptionem ceciderit (quod absit) sed quia eius resurrexit corpus. Ita Christum vnum & Dominū confitemur, non tanquā homine cum Verbo coadorantes, ne diuisionis quaedā species inducatur, sed vnum iam & eundem adorantes, quia non alienum est à Verbo corpus suum, cum quo ipsi etiam assidet Patri. Nec hoc ita dicimus quasi duobus filijs assidentibus, sed vno cum carne per vnitatem; quia si talem copulationem factam per substantiam, aut quasi impossibilem, aut quasi parum decoram, noluerimus accipere, in id incidimus, vt duos filios esse dicamus. Necesse est enim discernere, & dicere hominem separatim fuisse sola {a}fe sola filij appellatione honoratũ, & rursum Verbum quod est ex Deo, & nomine & veri tate Filium Dei: sed discernere in duos filios non debemus vnũ Dominũ Iesum Christũ. Neq; enim id adiuuat rectam fidei rationem licet nonnulli, nescio quam perhibeant copu lationem personarum. Non enim dixit scri- ptura Verbum Dei personam hominis sibi assumpsisse,sed carnem factum esse. Id autem est ostendere Dei Verbũ,similiter ac nos par- ticipatũ habuisse carnis & sanguinis & cor- pus nostrum proprie suum fecisse, & homi- nem ex muliere processisse, non abiecta nec deposita Deitate, aut generatione illa quam habebat, sed mansisse etiã in assumptione car- nis Deum quod erat. Hoc vbique rectæ fidei ratio protestatur. In tali sensu sanctos Patres fuisse comperimus. Ideo non dubitarunt san- ctam Virginem dicere Theotocon,non quod Verbi natura, Deitasq; in sancta Virgine sum pserit exordium, sed quod ex ea natum fit sa- crum illud corpus animatum anima rationa- li cui substantialiter adunatum Dei Verbum carnaliter natum esse dicitur. Cum autem di- ligentissime de vnione Verbi cum assumpta carne Cyrillus disseruerit, nusquã tamen me- minit vllius transfusionis aut communicatio- nis qua in Diuinam naturam trãslatæ aut illi communicatæ sunt proprietates vel actiones humanæ naturæ. Verum ait Deum natum, quia in vtero virginis humanam naturam sibi copulauit & ita carnis suæ natiuitatem suam fecit, item Deum passum, quia inerat in eo corpore quod patiebatur Deus, & corpus quod passum est ipsius propriu factum est: Deus Verbu mortuus est, quia vera ipsius caro gustauit mortem: Deus resurrexit quia eius corpus resurrexit. Hæc omnia tribuuntur Dei filio, quia Verbum cum carne vnus est Dei filius, copulatione facta per substantiam, quod vna est substantia seu hypostasis Verbi & carnis: sicuti autem Cyrillus hoc loco explicat quomodo Deo humanæ passiones & infirmitates tribuantur, ita alibi passim in suis libris hoc idem vrget, nec vsquam realis communicationis qua vnius naturæ proprietates reipsa transfundantur in alteram meminit. Alij quoque patres quorum scripta extant cum Cyrillo consentiunt. Deum aiunt passum, quòd humanitas quæ passa est à Deitate assumpta fuit: dici passum & mortuum secundum vnionem, sed in sola carne, quia caro & Deus vnus est Christus. Cum humanum pateretur corpus, hæc eadem Verbum quòd corpori coniunctum erat ad se retulisse, & sibi vendicasse tanquam sua ipsius quæ propria erant corporis, eaque aliquo modo sustinuisse, eo quod cum prohibere posset non prohibuit. Eundem fuisse patientem & non patientem: patientem quidem quatenus ipsius proprium corpus,in quo erat,patiebatur: nō patientem,quatenus ex natura Deus impatı» bilis erat, ipseque incorporeus in corpore pa tibili existebat, corpusq; vicissim Filium Dei impatibilem retinebat, absumentem corpo«reas infirmitates.Ita Dominus maiestatis cru cifixus est,quia Dominus maiestatis filius ho minis & homo est: & filius hominis Deus est maiestatis,& homo Deus est.Christus pas sus est carne non Deitate, cū tamen ipsa Dei« tas totum suum faciat quicquid caro perpes« sa est, ac sub vna persona merito vnus ac idē dicitur pati, quicquid vt Deus homo patitur, non infirmitate & conditione passibili, sed di gnatione suam faciens passionis iniuriam, a« dunatione particeps, sed sine passibilitate cō« patiens, sicut vnus idemqúe virtutes operaa tur,quicquid vt homo Deus operatur. Sum« ma est: Diuinitas per se,in se,secundum suam naturam nec patitur nec moritur, sed tamen Deus passus & mortuus est,quia persona que passa & mortua fuit, non vt homo tātum,sed vt homo & Deus passa fuit, licet secundum alteram naturam tantum passa fuerit, cum al tera vere & in se pati ac mori non potuerit. In hunc modum nos quoque in nostris eccle sijs docemus: itaque nobis iniuriam faciunt, qui aiunt nos negare Deum pro nobis pas« sum, sed tantum cum Nestorio dici passum: quasi relatione, tantum Deus passus dicatur Christo patiente, sicut pati dicitur in Paulo aut Petro. Longe enim aliud est affirmare Divinam naturam non esse passam in se, quod nos dicimus, aliud negare Deum passum. Videant autem ipsi quomodo ostendere possint humanas passiones realiter communicatas divinae naturae, vere in ipsam redundasse: neque enim scripturae neque Patres sic loquuntur.
units.tr: ...the resurrection of the dead, and that too in such a way that these are proper to it, so that it imparts them to the divine nature and admits that nature, as it were, into possession of them? Now, as for his claim that these things were done by the human nature in fulfilment of the Messiah's promise, yet are not merely works of the Son of Man but also common to the Son of God, that is, to the whole person who is God and man, so that they may be said of the Son of God no less truly than of the Son of Man: this is ambiguous, to put it no more harshly. For first, he seems to make the Messiah only by the human nature; then he speaks of the Son of Man as though the Son of God were one thing and the Son of Man another, although by their union they are one Son and one person. Moreover, when he sets out the reasons why the human nature imparts its properties and works to the divinity, he gives these. First, because the human nature does not subsist in itself but in the person of the Word, and the Word truly and essentially is the Son of God; so whatever happens to the human nature is truly said to have happened also to the Son of God, since the human nature is not separated from the person who is the Son of God even for a moment. Second, because the Divinity, which is impassible in itself and in its own substance, sustains the human nature in death and suffering and makes it effective to overcome death and Satan; yet, so that the flesh might suffer and die, the Word, according to Irenaeus, kept quiet and did not put forth its power to repel death and suffering. But from this no communication in nature follows. For example, to be born, to be crucified, to die, pertain properly to the human nature; yet these are also predicated of the divine nature in the concrete, not because they reach the very nature of the Deity (for then they could be said of the Deity in the abstract as well), but because they truly reach the person who has not only a human nature but is God. Nor does it follow that, because the humanity is sustained by the Deity, therefore the Deity really communicates to itself its operations and properties; for a human nature and a divine nature do not make one nature but one person, and so this only shows that these are properties of the person, for they belong to the other nature only insofar as the two are one with each other, and they are one not in nature but in person. Here, in passing, it should be considered that the terms abstract and concrete are not rightly used by some people. Marpach interprets the abstract as the same as what subsists in itself outside the personal union; but the ancient and recent writers commonly understand by the abstract the nature considered in itself in the hypostatic union, or separated in thought, so that a property suited to it may be rightly applied. For in this way also the dialecticians call the form considered in itself and separated in thought an abstract, such as humanity, justice, health, and so on. Then, just as they call the subject in which the form inheres (a man, a just man, a healthy man) the concrete, so in the schools of the theologians the concrete is named not the union of the natures itself but the word that denotes the person, the one subsisting [τὸ ὑφισάμενον], by whatever reason of nature this comes about: God, man, Son of God, Son of Man. For by such a name the person is comprehended, who has both natures. Therefore, when they say that the Son of God was truly born, dead and suffered, we gladly grant it; for that person who is the Son of God suffered, but not in the divinity, rather in the flesh, as St. Peter speaks. Christ is also said to suffer in the saints, as he says to Saul, "Why do you persecute me?"; and the people who rejected the prophets of God are said to have despised God himself; but these things pertain to God only by relation, because these are the envoys of God, the members of the Church of which Christ is the head. But the case of the suffering Son of God is quite different: for he who hung on the cross was truly the Son of God, nor could a naked man hanging on the cross be pointed out, nor can we attribute it to a naked man, unless we wish to dissolve the person of Christ; yet for all that the suffering does not reach the nature of the divinity. But just as, when the body dies, the soul does not die, so much less does death or suffering reach the nature of the divinity in Christ; and the soul indeed suffers with its body, but the divinity does not suffer with the humanity assumed. For if the sufferings of the assumed nature were really communicated to the divine nature, by the assumption of the humanity the divine nature would have been changed, and yet no change falls upon it. Nor is it therefore only in name that God was born, suffered and died, unless perhaps (which God forbid) Christ is God and Son of God only in name. Yet the Church has always thought and taught this way about the death and passion of the Son of God. Cyril, citing Leo: He who was born of the Father before all ages is also said to have been carnally begotten in time of a woman. Not because his divine nature took its beginning from the holy Virgin, nor because for the sake of this work he needed to be born a second time after that birth which he had from the Father (for it is foolish and stupid to say this, that he who is coeternal with the Father before all ages needed a second generation in order to begin to be); but because for our sake, and for our salvation, he joined to himself a human nature and came forth from a woman, therefore he is said to have been carnally born. For the man was not first born as a common man of the holy Virgin, and only then did the Word dwell in him; but in the womb he joined flesh to himself from the virginal substance, and he endured a carnal generation, making the birth of his flesh his own. So we say that he also suffered and rose again, not because God the Word suffered in his nature, or the blows, or the piercing of the nails, or other wounds (for God, being incorporeal, is beyond suffering), but because that body which had become his own suffered; therefore he is said to have suffered all these things for us. For in that body which suffered there was God, who could not suffer. In a similar way we also understand his death. For the Word of God, who is life and life-giving, is naturally immortal and incorruptible. But because the body was his own, by the grace of God he tasted death for all, according to the words of Paul; therefore he is said to have suffered death for us. Not that he himself experienced death as far as his own nature is concerned (for it is madness either to feel or to say this), but, as we said above, his true flesh tasted death. So also, when the flesh rose, we say that he rose again; not because he fell into corruption (which God forbid), but because his body rose. Thus we confess Christ as one Lord, not adoring him as a man together with the Word, lest some kind of division be introduced, but adoring him as one and the same now, because his body is not alien to the Word, and with it he also sits beside the Father. Nor do we say this as though two sons were sitting there, but one Son with his flesh through unity; for if we were unwilling to accept such a conjunction as made in substance, either as impossible or as scarcely fitting, we would fall into saying that there are two sons. For it is necessary to distinguish, and to say that the man, separately, was honoured only by the title of Son, and again that the Word, which is from God, is the Son of God both in name and in truth; but we must not divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons. For this does not help the right account of the faith, even though some, I know not what, put forward a conjunction of persons. For Scripture did not say that the Word of God assumed to himself the person of a man, but that he became flesh. That in fact shows that the Word of God, just as we, had a share in flesh and blood, and made our body his own properly, and proceeded from a woman, not by laying aside or abandoning his Deity, or that generation which he had, but that he remained God, which he was, even in the assumption of the flesh. The right account of the faith everywhere testifies to this. We find that the holy Fathers were of this mind. Therefore they did not hesitate to call the holy Virgin Theotocos [Θεοτόκος], not because the nature of the Word and the Deity took their beginning in the holy Virgin, but because from her was born that sacred body, animated with a rational soul, to which the Word of God, substantially united, is said to have been carnally born. But although Cyril has most diligently discussed the union of the Word with the assumed flesh, he nowhere mentions any transfusion or communication by which the properties or actions of the human nature are transferred into the divine nature or communicated to it. Rather he says that God was born because he joined the human nature to himself in the womb of the virgin, and so made the birth of his flesh his own; likewise that God suffered, because God was in that body which suffered, and the body that suffered became his own: God the Word died, because his true flesh tasted death; God rose again, because his body rose. All these things are attributed to the Son of God, because the Word with the flesh is one Son of God, by a conjunction made in substance, since the substance or hypostasis of the Word and of the flesh is one. But just as Cyril here explains how human sufferings and infirmities are attributed to God, so elsewhere throughout his books he urges the same thing, and nowhere does he mention a real communication by which the properties of one nature are actually poured into the other. The other Fathers whose writings survive also agree with Cyril. They say that God suffered, because the humanity which suffered was assumed by the Deity; that he is said to have suffered and died according to the union, but in the flesh alone, because the flesh and God are one Christ. When the human body suffered, the Word, which was joined to the body, referred these things to itself and claimed them as its own, as the proper things of the body, and in some way bore them, because although it could prevent them, it did not prevent them. The same one was both suffering and not suffering: suffering indeed insofar as the body in which he was suffered what was properly his own; not suffering insofar as by nature God was impassible, and he himself, being incorporeal, existed in a passible body, and the body in turn kept the Son of God impassible, consuming the bodily infirmities. Thus the Lord of glory was crucified, because the Lord of glory is the Son of Man and man, and the Son of Man is God of glory, and man is God. Christ suffered in the flesh, not in the Deity; yet the Deity itself makes its own whatever the flesh has suffered, and under one person it is rightly said that the one and the same suffers whatever as man he suffers, not by infirmity and a passible condition, but by condescension, making the injury of the suffering its own, sharing by union, yet co-suffering without passibility; just as the one and the same performs powers whatever as God he performs as man. The sum is this: the Divinity in itself, in its own nature, neither suffers nor dies; yet God suffered and died, because the person who suffered and died suffered not as man only but as man and God, although he suffered according to the other nature only, since the other nature could not truly suffer and die in itself. In this way we also teach in our churches. Those therefore do us wrong who say that we deny that God suffered for us, but only say with Nestorius that he suffered, as though only by relation God is said to have suffered when Christ suffers, just as suffering is predicated of Paul or Peter. For it is one thing to affirm that the divine nature was not passible in itself, which is what we say; it is another to deny that God suffered.
