Let them see how they can show that human sufferings were really communicated to the divine nature and truly flowed into it; for neither Scripture nor the Fathers speak in this way.

units.la: Alterum genus communicationis idiomatum, quo divina humanitati attribuuntur, nunc considerandum est. Tenenda autem est visitata distinctio qua proprietates aliae dicuntur esse incommunicabiles, aliae communicabiles: vel ut alii distinguunt, ea de quorum communicatione quaeritur, vel sunt infinita et essentialia in Deo ut omnes proprietates divinae naturae, vel sunt dona Dei finita et creata. Atque de hoc posteriori genere et proprietatibus communicabilibus non est controversia, omnes enim fatentur humanam naturam a Verbo assumptam vere et realiter et in se ineffabilibus donis ornatam esse, quibus numero et gradu omnes creaturas quantumvis excellentes superet. Veluti quod concepta est ex Spiritu sancto, nata ex Virgine, quod absque peccato fuit, quod omnibus donis Spiritus sancti ornata fuit, quod denique finito tempore Exinanitionis donata est immortalitate, ineffabili luce, sapientia, virtute, potentia et supra omnes creaturas glorificata est. Solent let quidé Aduersarij nobis obijcere, quod faciamus Christum hominem impotentem, & quidem longe absurdiori vocabulo apud Germanos, ein onmåchtigen menschen/ vt ita apud vulgus in odium & inuidiam nos adducant: sed hæ sunt merę calumniæ quas refutant omnia nostra scripta, si modo illis locus aliquis daretur. Porro præter hæc dona creata & finita in se, etsi forte nobis quodámodo infinita videri possint, in quibus est quædam communio capitis & membrorum ita vt generE conueniant, quamuis gradu & numero ita superet humana Christi natura omnes sanctos vt ferè sit nulla comparatio, alia prærogatiua sunt & maiora quæ humanæ naturæ Christi per vnionem personalem collata sunt.
units.tr: The second kind of communication of idioms, by which divine attributes are ascribed to the human nature, must now be considered. The customary distinction must be kept, by which some properties are called incommunicable and others communicable; or, as others distinguish, the properties whose communication is in question are either infinite and essential in God, like all the properties of the divine nature, or they are finite and created gifts of God. Concerning this latter kind of communicable property there is no controversy, for all admit that the human nature assumed by the Word is truly and really adorned in itself with ineffable gifts, by which it surpasses all creatures, however excellent, in number and degree. Such are that it was conceived of the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin, that it was without sin, that it was adorned with all the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and that at the appointed time of the Humiliation it was endowed with immortality, ineffable light, wisdom, virtue and power, and was glorified above all creatures. Our opponents are wont to charge us with making Christ an impotent man, and indeed with an even more absurd term among the Germans, "ein onmächtiger Mensch," so that they may stir up hatred and envy against us among the common people. But these are mere calumnies, which all our writings refute, if only they were given any opening. Moreover, besides these created and finite gifts in themselves, which perhaps may seem in some way infinite to us, and in which there is a certain communion of head and members, so that they agree in kind (although the human nature of Christ surpasses all the saints in degree and number so greatly that there is almost no comparison), there are other prerogatives, and greater ones, which have been conferred on the human nature of Christ through the personal union.

units.la: Nam primum æternum Dei verbū hanc naturam in vnitatem personæ suæ assumpsit, neq; tantū per assistentiam quandā aut gratiam, aut relationem, aut affectum quendam sese huic societate quadā iunxit, sed eam inefabili vnione ita sibi vniuit vt Verbum & caro sint vnū & singulum & solum quid, & vt Ioannes inquit, Verbum caro factū est. Tanta dignitas nulli creaturæ alij cóigit, non angelos assumpsit sed semen Abrahæ: & quamuis in sanctis suis Deus semper inhabitarit, nullus tamen sanctorum fuit Emanuel: solus Christus est Emanuel, Deus nobiscum, ipse enim vnus & idē Verbū & Caro, Deus homo.
units.tr: For first, the eternal Word of God assumed this nature into the unity of his person. He did not join himself to it merely by some assistance, or grace, or relation, or a certain affection, in a kind of fellowship; rather he united it to himself by an ineffable union, so that the Word and the flesh are one and the same single thing, and, as John says, "the Word was made flesh." Such dignity has been granted to no other creature: he did not assume angels but the seed of Abraham. And although God has always dwelt in his saints, yet none of the saints was Emmanuel; Christ alone is Emmanuel, God with us, for he himself is one and the same Word and Flesh, God and man.

units.la: Quæ nā dā ta sint Christo per vnionē personalem.
units.tr: What things have been given to Christ through the personal union.

units.la: Hanc carnem suam Deus Verbum ita assum psit vt cum illa & per illam redemptione hu-mani generis perficeret, hac secum euexit in coelos, & ad dexteram patris, vt noster summus pontifex & rex vna cum assumpta carne con-sedit, & cum eadem a nobis adoratur. Omnes denique diuinae naturae proprietates huma-nae naturae in concreto attribuuntur, hic enim homo qui conceptus est ex Spiritu sancto & natus ex Maria virgine, est Deus, est omnipo-tens, omnisapiens, omnipraesens. Verum in-ter aduersarios nostros & nos de eo controuer-titur, an proprietates illae diuinae essentiales transfusae sint in humanam naturam, vt in ea quasi in subiecto insint, vt ita facta sit per co-municationem proprietatum exaequatio dua-rum naturarum. Huiusmodi realem & phy-sicam communionem negamus, quod hac po-sita fiat confusio naturarum: sed de his essen-tialibus proprietatatibus nostri haftenus do-cuerunt, eas non aliter communicari quam ipsam essentiam, & Christum secundum hu-manam naturam non aliter esse omnipoten-tem, omnipraesentem, omnisapientem quam quo modo Deus est. Est enim hoc axioma certum, & vsitatum veteri ecclesiae, ex natu-rarum vnione, ipsam quoque idiomatu com-municationem aestimandam esse. Cum enim omnipotentia, omnipraesentia, omnisapien-tia, &c. sint ipsa Dei essentia, non aliter haec data
units.tr: God the Word so assumed this flesh of his that with it and through it he accomplished the redemption of the human race. With it he carried himself up into heaven and sat at the right hand of the Father, so that as our high priest and king he sits together with the assumed flesh, and together with it is adored by us. Finally, all the properties of the divine nature are attributed to the human nature in the concrete: for this man who was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of Mary the virgin is God, is almighty, all-wise, all-present. But between our opponents and us the dispute is whether those essential divine properties have been poured into the human nature, so that they inhere in it as in a subject, and so that by the communication of properties there is made an equalization of the two natures. We deny such a real and physical communion, because if it were posited, a confusion of natures would result. Our people have taught hitherto that these essential properties are communicated in no other way than the essence itself, and that Christ according to his human nature is not omnipotent, omnipresent and all-wise otherwise than as God is. For this is a certain axiom, and one customary in the ancient Church, that the communication of idioms itself is to be judged from the union of natures. For since omnipotence, omnipresence, omniscience, and so on, are the very essence of God, they have not been given otherwise

units.la: Anfacta sit realis transfusio Idiom.
units.tr: Whether a real transfusion of the idioms is made.

units.la: Eadem est communicatio proprietatum & naturarum. data sunt humanæ naturæ quàm ipsa essen-tia seu diuinitas. Diuinitas autē humanæ na-turæ data est, per vnionē personalem, nō per transfusionē in essentiam humanā, neq; enim ex illa factitius Deus aliquis creatus est, sed per assumptionem personalē ita illi cōmuni-cata est diuinitas vt nihilominus omnes suas proprietates essentiales saluas & illæsas reti-neat. Simili ratione diuinæ proprietates essen-tiales & infinitæ cōmunicatæ sunt humanæ naturæ, non tamē ita vt in ipsa tanquā in sub-iecto quodam inhæreant, sed vt illi propter personalem vnionē adsint, quo modo nulli a-lij creaturæ insunt. Sicut autem humanitas Christi neque Deus est, neque diuinitas, sed homo Christus est Deus, & Deus iste est ho-mo; ita etiam homo Christus est omnipotēs, omnipræsens, quomodo Deus est, humanitas ipsa non est reuera & secundū essentiā omni-præsens & omnipotens, non enim ipsa est Deus aut diuinitas, sed assumpta à diuinitate in personæ vnitatem. Hac autem doctrina nō derogatur maiestati Christi seruatoris no-stri, vt aduersarij clamant, sed potius vera ea-ius maiestas & diuinitas asseritur. Quando enim quæritur de diuinitate Iesu Christi, seu quomodo homo natus ex Maria virgine fit Deus, respondetur eum vere & natura Deum esse, quoniā Christus, homo ille, siue illa per-sona constat tota Deitate inhabitante, & per-a festa natura humana inhabitata, atque ita verus & natura Deus est, idque respectu Deitatis inhabitantis. Si tribuatur humanæ naturæ diuinitas in se per effusionem proprietatum, vt hac ratione homo Christus fit Deus sequeretur eum tantum diuinum aut deificatu hominem esse, non vere & natura Deum.
units.tr: than the essence itself, or the deity, is given. Deity, however, has been given to the human nature through the personal union, not through transfusion into the human essence; for no created god is made out of it by that means, but by personal assumption deity has been so communicated to it that nonetheless it keeps all its essential properties safe and unimpaired. In a similar way the divine essential and infinite properties have been communicated to the human nature, yet not in such a way that they inhere in it as in some subject, but so that they are present to it on account of the personal union, in a way in which they inhere in no other creature. Just as the humanity of Christ is neither God nor deity, but Christ the man is God, and this God is man, so also Christ the man is almighty and omnipresent as God is; the humanity itself is not in truth and according to its essence omnipresent and almighty, for it is not itself God or deity, but was assumed by deity into the unity of the person. Now this doctrine does not detract from the majesty of Christ our Saviour, as our opponents cry out; rather its true majesty and divinity is asserted. For when inquiry is made about the divinity of Jesus Christ, or how the man born of the Virgin Mary is God, the answer is that he truly and by nature is God, since Christ, that man or that person, consists of the whole Deity dwelling in him, and is indwelt by the perfect human nature; and so he is true and natural God, and this with respect to the indwelling Deity. If divinity were attributed to the human nature in itself through an outpouring of properties, so that by this means Christ the man became God, it would follow that he was only a divine or deified man, and not truly and by nature God.

units.la: Deinde veteres quotiescunque de communicatione proprietatu loquuntur, non ponut aliam realem qua diuina in humanā naturam transfundantur, aliam verbalem tantum qua humana tribuantur Deo, sed ostendunt similiter fieri proprietatū communicatione in utraque natura. D. Augustinus, Ille qui erat filius Dei, factus est filius hominis in vnitate personæ, Vt anima & caro vnus est homo, ita Verbū & homo vnus est Christus. Carni enim ita vnitur anima, vt vna fit cū carne persona. Vnde salua naturę vtriusque proprietate, adijcitur seu attribuitur carni quod est animæ, & vicissim animæ quod est carnis, pro vnitate personæ, non pro diuersitate naturæ. Ire in vnitate personę Christi, ex diuina & humana natura, quælibet earū vocabulū etiam alteri impertit, & diuina humanę & humana diuinæ. Leporius apud Cassianū scribit, Ex tempore susceptæ carnis sic omnia quæ Dei erant transisse in homine, vt omnia quæ erat hominis in Deum venirent. vt sic ipse Deus Verbum, totū suscipiēs quod est hominis homo fit:
units.tr: Next, the ancients, whenever they speak of the communication of properties, do not posit one real communication by which divine things are transfused into the human nature, and another merely verbal one by which human things are ascribed to God. Instead they show that the communication of properties takes place similarly in both natures. Augustine: "He who was the Son of God became the Son of man in unity of person. As the soul and flesh is one man, so the Word and man is one Christ. For the soul is so united to the flesh that it becomes one person with the flesh. Hence, with the property of each nature preserved, what belongs to the soul is added to or ascribed to the flesh, and what belongs to the flesh to the soul, on account of the unity of person and not the diversity of nature. In the unity of the person of Christ, of the divine and human nature, each of the names also imparts itself to the other, both the divine to the human and the human to the divine." Leporius, in Cassian, writes: "From the time the flesh was taken up, all the things that were of God have passed over into the man, so that all the things that were of man have come into God; so that the Word of God himself, taking up all that is man, becomes man:

units.la: Similis communic. Idiom. in vtraque natura. De Trin. & Vnit. Dei cap. 2. Contra Maximi. lib. 3. cap. 20. Lib. 1. cap. 3. mo fit: & adsumptus homo totū accipiendo quod Deus est, aliud quā Deus esse non possit. Gelasius. Sicut enim legitur Dominus maiestatis Christus, sic vtique legitur etiā Filius hominis. Itaque & Dominus maiestatis Filius hominis est, & homo est, & Filius hominis, Deus est maiestatis, & homo Deus est: & quicquid Deitatis est, habet Filius hominis: & quicquid humanitatis est habet Dominus maiestatis. Item: Deitas totum suū facit quicquid caro perpessa est: sicut & Filius hominis suū habet totū, quicquid est Dei. Fulgentius, In vnitate persona hominis Dei in confusa veritate, sicut Christus Deus in homine nomen hominis accepit, sicidem homo Christus in Deo, vocabulū Deitatis accepit. Sic & alij Patres de communicatione in vtraque natura loquuntur, & communicatione qua naturæ sibi suas proprietates communicent damnāt. Vnde Vigilius. Impium inquit & sacrilegū est ea quæ sunt propria carnis Christi ad naturæ Verbi proprietatem referre, & quæ sunt propria Verbi, proprietati naturæ carnis adscribere. Et Damascenus. Diuinitatē igitur dicentes, non de illo nominamus ea quæ humanitatis sunt propria. Nō enim dicimus Deitatē aut passibilem aut creatā, neq; de carne, id est humanitate, prædicamus ea quæ deitatis sunt propria: nam neque dicimus carnē, id est humanitatem increatā. At vero de hy
units.tr: Similar communication of idioms in both natures (De Trin. et Unit. Dei cap. 2; Contra Maximinum lib. 3 cap. 20; lib. 1 cap. 3): and the assumed man, receiving all that God is, cannot be other than God." Gelasius: "Just as the Lord of majesty Christ is read of, so too is the Son of man read of. Therefore the Lord of majesty is also Son of man, and is man, and the Son of man is God of majesty, and man is God; and whatever belongs to deity the Son of man has, and whatever belongs to humanity the Lord of majesty has." Likewise: "Deity makes wholly its own whatever the flesh has suffered, just as the Son of man has wholly whatever is God's." Fulgentius: "In the unity of the person, as Christ God in the confused truth received the name of man, so likewise Christ man in God received the name of deity." So also the other Fathers speak of communication in both natures, and condemn the communication by which the natures would impart their own properties to each other. Hence Vigilius: "It is impious and sacrilegious," he says, "to refer what are proper to the flesh of Christ to the property of the nature of the Word, and to ascribe what are proper to the Word to the property of the nature of the flesh." And Damascene: "Therefore, when speaking of the deity, we do not name of it the things proper to humanity. For we do not say that deity is passible or created, nor do we predicate of the flesh, that is of the humanity, the things proper to deity; for we do not say that the flesh, that is the humanity, is uncreated. But concerning the hypostasis

units.la: G » postasi siue ex vtraq; siue ex vna naturarum » eam nominamus, vtriusque naturarum pro- » pria illi adijcimus. Nam Christus hoc quidē » est quod vtrunq; simul, & Deus & homo di‐ » citur, & creatus & increatus, & passibilis & impassibilis.Similiter scholastici,Communi‐ catio (inquiunt) Idiomatum fit in persona, non in natura, quia naturæ ipsæ idiomata sua non communicant, nec abstracta natura‐ rum de se inuicem prædicantur.
units.tr: "...in the person, or from both natures, or from one of the natures, we name it, and we attach to it the properties of both natures. For Christ is that which both together: he is called both God and man, both created and uncreated, both passible and impassible." Similarly the scholastics say: "The communication of idioms takes place in the person, not in the nature, because the natures do not themselves communicate their idioms, nor are the abstract natures predicated of one another."

units.la: Præterea scripturæ testantur humanā na‐ turam suas proprietates seruasse in Christo: nam ante glorificationem, salua nihilominus vnione personali, vere prædita fuit infirmita‐ tibus nostris naturalibus: & quāuis illas post glorificationem exuerit, seruauit tamen essen tiales humanæ naturæ proprietates. Sed si proprietates diuinæ in humanitatem realiter & physice transfusæ fuissent, tum oporteret humanas proprietates sublatas fuisse & abo‐ litas: vel sequeretur de vno & eodem subiecto contradicentia simul vere posse affirmari: ve‐ luti humanam Christi naturam, circumscri‐ ptam & incircumscriptam, corpoream & in‐ corporeā, visibilem & inuisibilem, æternam & temporariam,finitam & infinitam,&c. si‐ mul & semel esse:nam horum alterum conue niret humanæ naturæ essentiali proprietate, alterum proprietate diuinitatis realiter com‐ municata. Quam autem absurdum sit talia affirmare vident omnes, neque Deus sua omnipotentia efficit talia, vt alibi dictum est.
units.tr: Moreover, the Scriptures testify that the human nature kept its own properties in Christ. Before the glorification, the personal union remaining intact, he was truly endowed with our natural infirmities. And although after the glorification he put these off, he nonetheless kept the essential properties of human nature. But if divine properties had been really and physically poured into the humanity, then the human properties would have had to be removed and abolished. Otherwise it would follow that contradictory things could be truly affirmed at once of one and the same subject: for example, that the human nature of Christ is at the same time and together circumscribed and uncircumscribed, corporeal and incorporeal, visible and invisible, eternal and temporal, finite and infinite, and so on. For one of each pair would belong to the essential property of human nature, and the other to the property of divinity really communicated. That it is absurd to affirm such things, everyone sees; nor does God by his omnipotence make such things, as has been said elsewhere.

units.la: Postremo talis transfusio realis proprietatum essentialium diuinae naturae infinitae, infinitam & creatam naturam fieri non potest, scriptura testante, Ego Deus & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Proprietates namque nihil aliud sunt quam essentia, cum diuina natura sit simplicissima, haec si realiter effunditur in aliquam creaturam oportet vt illa quoque talis fiat qualis est natura, cuius proprietates transfusae sunt, sed nulla natura potest fieri diuinitati aequalis, alioqui, diuinitas non esset diuinitas, nam ea non est vera diuinitas cui res aliqua creata exaequari potest: Deus est summum maximum, huic si quid exequetur, non erit summum maximum, & no erit Deus, duo enim infinita esse non possunt. Quod autem dicitur exequationem fieri non ἴσος sed ἰσότης, non essentia sed potentia, non substantia sed maiestate, quid nihil est, cum potentia Dei sit ipsissima & simplicissima Dei essentia: & miror quosdam Schuecalfeldium reprehendere, qui potentiam Dei in rebus omnibus esse affirmet, essentia vero extra res collocet: cum illi pari modo potentiam & maiestatem ac gloriam transfundi dicant, & in his exaequari humanam naturam diuinae, non autem essentia. Nam quod addunt diuinam naturam haec ex se habere & humanae communicare, alteram vero accipere & ex dono
units.tr: Finally, such a real transfusion of the essential properties of the infinite divine nature cannot make a created nature infinite, since Scripture testifies: "I am God, and I will not give my glory to another." For properties are nothing other than essence, since the divine nature is most simple. If this were really poured into some creature, that creature would also have to become such as the nature is whose properties were transfused. But no nature can be made equal to deity, for otherwise deity would not be deity: that is not true deity to which some created thing can be made equal. God is the highest and greatest; if anything were made equal to him, it would not be highest and greatest, and would not be God, for two infinites cannot exist. As for their claim that the equality is not equal [ἴσος] but equality [ἰσότης], not essence but power, not substance but majesty, this is nothing, since the power of God is the very and most simple essence of God. I am surprised that some reprehend Schuecalfeldius, who affirms that the power of God is in all things but places the essence outside things, when they likewise say that power, majesty and glory are transfused, and that in these the human nature is made equal to the divine, but not in essence. As for their addition that the divine nature has these from itself and communicates them to the human nature, while the latter receives them as a gift,

units.la: { } Essentiales proprietates incommunicabiles creaturae. habere, efficit quidem respectu principij alia quam differentia, non autem respectu rei ipsius que formaliter vtrobiq; vna & eadem statuitur. Adhaec si eaedem sunt proprietates & tantum communicatio facit inaequalitatem essentiae, Arianorum sententia probanda erit, qui dicebant Christum minorem Patre & dissimilem quia illi esset communicata diuinitas: cum contra orthodoxi contenderent communicationem non efficere aliam essentiam, cum eadem integra & ab aeterno, Christo communicata sit. Existimant quidam physicam & realem transfusionem diuinarum proprietatum in humana Christi natura, confirmari verbis scripturae, quibus dicitur illi data omnis potestas: item Christu esse in forma Dei: in Christo omnes thesauros sapientiae & scientiae abscondito esse: in ipso inhabitare omne plenitudine Deitatis corporaliter: donatum illi nomen quod est supra omne nomen, ut ad nomen Iesu omne genu se flectat, caelestium ac terrestrium & subterraneorum, &c. Requirerent autem praeclara haec scripturae loca iustam explicationem, sed ea est alterius operae.
units.tr: { } Essential properties are incommunicable to a creature. To have them in this way indeed makes a difference with respect to the source, but not with respect to the thing itself, which is set up formally as one and the same on both sides. Moreover, if the properties are the same and communication alone makes an inequality of essence, then the opinion of the Arians must be approved, who said that Christ was less than the Father and unlike him because divinity had been communicated to him. The orthodox, on the contrary, contended that communication does not make another essence, since the same essence, whole and from eternity, has been communicated to Christ. Some think that a physical and real transfusion of the divine properties into the human nature of Christ is confirmed by the words of Scripture: that all power was given to him; that Christ is in the form of God; that in Christ all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden; that in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily; that the name which is above every name was given to him, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and so on. But these notable passages of Scripture would require a proper explanation, and that is another task.

units.la: Nos respondemus primum aduersarios male detorquere ad transfusionem donorum aut proprietatum quae de vera diuinitate Verbi Apostolus scripsit, nam per formam Dei vestas semper intellexit naturam diuinam, scilicet per formam serui naturam humanam: vera enim æqualitas Filij cum Patre qua non arbi tratus est rapinam se æqualem esse Deo, est æqualitas naturæ, quod est ὁμοούσιος, transfusio donorum non exæquat naturam humanā finitam & creatam suo creatori. Sic plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter habitans in Christo, est ipse λόγος, non communicata deitas alia quam qua λόγος Deus est: communicata enim deitas non est θεότης seu πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος, sed πλήρωμα θεό-τητος, plenitudo diuinarum rerū, sapientię, potentię, bonitatis, donorum Spiritus sancti. At Apostolus maius aliquid tribuit Christo, quod θεότης ipsa deitas seu diuina essentia, & quidem omnis plenitudo deitatis, tota deitas, vt nihil sit Deitatis in Patre quod non sit in Filio, ac proinde per omnia æqualis sit Patri filius, inhabitet σωματικῶς, non tantum per esse-cta, sed vt ex deitate & humanitate cōiunctis, vnus constet Christus, vnum σῶμα substantia seu hypostasis. Hanc interpretationem Pa-trum testimonijs confirmare non est necesse, nemo enim ignorat veteres & recētiores, qui diuinitatem æternam filij Dei contra hæreti-cos defenderunt, his testimonijs vsos esse. Ac dolendum est horum locorum sensum nunc in dubium vocari, & eos qui volunt soli maie-statis Christi assertores videri, apertissima testimonia deitatis Christi, ad communicatā quandam deitatē & carni propriā cum nouis Antitrinitarijs & Samosatenianis detorquere.
units.tr: We reply, first, that the opponents wrongly twist to a transfusion of gifts or properties what the Apostle wrote about the true divinity of the Word. For by "form of God" he always understood the divine nature, and by "form of a servant" the human nature. The true equality of the Son with the Father, by which he did not think it robbery to be equal to God, is equality of nature, which is homoousios [ὁμοούσιος]. A transfusion of gifts does not make the finite and created human nature equal to its Creator. So the fullness of the Godhead dwelling bodily in Christ is the Word himself [λόγος], not a communicated deity other than that by which the Word is God. For a communicated deity is not deity [θεότης] or the fullness of the deity [πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος], but a fullness of deity [πλήρωμα θεότητος], that is, a fullness of divine things: of wisdom, power and goodness, and of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. But the Apostle attributes something greater to Christ: that deity itself [θεότης], the divine essence, and indeed the whole fullness of deity, the entire Godhead, so that there is nothing of deity in the Father that is not in the Son; and therefore the Son is in all things equal to the Father. He dwells bodily [σωματικῶς], not only by effects, but so that from the conjoined deity and humanity Christ is one, one body [σῶμα] in substance or hypostasis. It is not necessary to confirm this interpretation by the testimonies of the Fathers, for no one is ignorant that the ancient and more recent writers who defended the eternal divinity of the Son of God against heretics used these testimonies. And it is to be lamented that the sense of these passages is now called into doubt, and that those who wish to be seen as the only asserters of the majesty of Christ twist the most open testimonies to the deity of Christ toward a certain communicated deity proper to the flesh, together with the new Antitrinitarians and the Samosatenes.

units.la: Secūdo in eo aberrāt aduersarij, quod omnia quæ Christo data dicūtur, interpretantur humanæ naturæ realiter cōmunicata, vt illa hæc in se habeat & quasi subiectū sit earū rerū quæ Christo data sunt. Diuina quidē natura nullius indiget, ideoq; proprie nihil accipit, non tamē inde cōficitur hæc quæ persona Christi secundū humanam naturā data sunt, transfusa esse in humanā naturā. Augustinus inquit, Quicquid cōuenit Filio Dei per naturā, conuenit Filio hominis per gratiā: hoc aūt Scholastici de vnionis gratia interpretātur, in qua humanitas Christi in Verbi persona assumpta in eo subsistit. Vnde eodē modo quo homini datum est, vt sit Deus Verbū, in ipsa videlicet persona Verbi, in qua geritur & sustentatur, ita etiam omnia quæ sunt Filij Dei, vt omnis potestas & plenitudo scientiæ & sapientię,&c. data sunt homini, per gratiā hanc vnionis, per quam quæcunque dicuntur de filio Dei secundū diuinam naturā, dicuntur etiam de filio hominis propter personæ vnitatem. Patres etiā sicut exinanitionem Christi interpretantur assumptione carnis, qua pau- per tas carnis Verbi propria facta est sicut ipsa caro, ita etiā exaltationem qua omnia Christo data dicuntur, interpretantur per dispensationē, qua humanitas vnum cum Deo Verbo facta est. Itaque Cyrillus in Ioannem de hac re sic scribit, Vnum est Filius cū Patre, idem
units.tr: Second, the opponents err in this: they interpret all the things said to be given to Christ as really communicated to the human nature, so that it has them in itself and is, as it were, the subject of those things which were given to Christ. The divine nature indeed needs nothing and so properly receives nothing; yet it does not follow from this that the person of Christ, given those things according to the human nature, has transfused them into the human nature. Augustine says: "Whatever belongs to the Son of God by nature belongs to the Son of man by grace." The scholastics interpret this of the grace of union, in which the humanity of Christ, assumed into the person of the Word, subsists in that person. Hence, just as it was given to the man to be God the Word, in the very person of the Word in which he is borne and sustained, so also all the things that belong to the Son of God, such as all power and the fullness of knowledge and wisdom, are given to the man through this grace of union. Through it, whatever is said of the Son of God according to the divine nature is also said of the Son of man, on account of the unity of the person. The Fathers also interpret the emptying of Christ as the assumption of flesh, by which the poverty of the flesh became the Word's own, just as the flesh itself did. In the same way they interpret the exaltation, by which all things are said to be given to Christ, as the dispensation by which the humanity was made one with God the Word. Thus Cyril, in his commentary on John, writes about this matter: "The Son is one with the Father, the same..."

units.la: {a} Non identitate essentiæ,quamuis in propria subsi-stentia sit. Verum quoniam propter nostram salutem à sua dignitate & claritate quasi exi-uit (hoc enim significat exinaniuit seipsum) ideo accepit rursus cum carne claritatem & gloriam,quâ semper habuit vt Deus. Quo-niam ergo templum quod à Virgine accepit, quamuis consubstantiale Deo Patri non sit, vnitum tamen ita cū verbo est, vt vna perso-na cum eo sit (vnus enim Christus & vnus Fi-lius est etiam homo factus.) Idcirco vnitatem cum Deo accepisse dicitur, quod templum suum, quod à se Deus non est, vnū cum Deo Verbo factum sit. Et vt breuius dicam & cla-rius,quod templo suo datū est, sibi datum es-se vnigenitus ait, datum videlicet à Patre per ipsum in spiritu. Non enim aliam viam ha-bet modus vnitatis cū Deo. Intelligitur enim in Christo,vnitate ineffabili caro sanctificata, absque vlla confusione ad vnitatem Verbi as-cendere, & per Verbum ad vnitatem Patris, habitudine scilicet quadam non naturaliter. Dantur ergo humanæ naturæ omnia quate-nus vnitate cum Deo accepit, quia caro vna persona est cum Verbo, hac vnitate sanctifi-cata est absq; tamen confusione Verbi & car-nis. Si sanctificationis dona transfunderentur physice in carnem fierent confusio, ideo vnita-te seu vnione personali hæc humanitati data asserit. Damnatur etiam sæpe à Cyrillo hæc adunationis ratio, qua dicitur homo adaptatus sibi à Deo communicatione dignitatis, gloriæ, honoris ac filiationis, vt hac ratione homo Deus & Christus & filius & Dominus dicatur.
units.tr: {a} Not by identity of essence, although in his own subsistence. But since for our salvation he went out, as it were, from his dignity and brightness (for this is what "emptied himself" signifies), therefore he received again with the flesh the brightness and glory which he always had as God. Since therefore the temple which he received from the Virgin, although not consubstantial with God the Father, is nevertheless so united with the Word that it is one person with him (for Christ is one, and the Son is one, even though made man), therefore he is said to have received union with God, because his temple, which is not God from itself, has been made one with God the Word. And to say it more briefly and clearly: what was given to his temple was given to himself, says the Only-begotten, given indeed by the Father through him in the Spirit. For the mode of union with God has no other way. For it is understood that in Christ, by an ineffable union, the sanctified flesh ascends without any confusion to the union of the Word, and through the Word to the union of the Father, by a certain relation, not a natural one. So all things are given to the human nature insofar as it has received union with God, because the flesh is one person with the Word; sanctified by this union, yet without confusion of Word and flesh. If the gifts of sanctification were physically transfused into the flesh, there would be confusion; therefore he asserts that these things are given to the humanity by union, that is, by personal union. Cyril also often condemns this manner of union, by which man is said to be joined to himself by God through the communication of dignity, glory, honour and sonship, so that by this reasoning man is called God, Christ, Son and Lord.

units.la: Etsi autem transfusionem realé & physicam negamus, non tamen Christum hominem proprietatibus diuinis spoliamus, sicut etiam hominé Christum vere & naturâ Deú agnoscimus, quâuis humanitas eius in se non sit Deus aut diuinitas. Si realis communio afferetur in concreto, quod homini Christo, hoc est huic personæ omnia data sint, ita vt hic homo, hæc persona sit vere & ab æterno & essentia Deus, omnipotes & omnisciens, atq; omnipresens, nemo contradiceret. Sed ipsi homini pro humana natura, concretum pro abstracto accipiût, & hominem Christû ideo faciunt Deum & omnipotente, quod assum-ptæ humanitati realiter communicata sit, & in eam transfusa deitatis plenitudo, vt illa hac communicata maiestate, non tantum vnione sit Deus. Videntur autè non male in illos convenire quæ Athanasius scribit contra quosdam qui sua ætate ita afferebant diuinitatem hominis Christi, vt etiam contenderent carnem esse consubstantialem diuinitati. Si ea, inquit, quæ ex natura diuinitas fuit, diuinitas efficitur, cur igitur incusatis Arianos, qui istiusmodi opinionem de Verbo in medium adferût quum tamen scriptura in contrarium dicat Verbum carnē factum esse, non carnem Ver-bum: ideoq; dictū est, Verbum carnem esse factum, quoniā caro Verbi caro facta est, & nō hominis alicuius: hoc est Deus homo factus est, & caro dicitur factus esse, ne omitteretis carnis vocabulum. Quod si igitur contenti non estis ista Verbi cum carne vnione: atque eo ipso quod Deus homo factus est, certe ne-que audire, neque credere coftituiftis, quum vobis satisfieri nequeat tam modesta, religio-saque super omnem commentationem dicen-di ratione, dum corpus Dei auditis esse, idque secundum eum qui dicit: Qui transfigurabit corpus nostrae humilitatis, vt sit conforme corpori gloriae ipsius. Qua in re argumetum futurae resurrectionis ostenditur: quod etiam tum appellatur corpus, cum iam corpus est gloriae eius, &c.
units.tr: Although we deny a real and physical transfusion, we do not strip Christ the man of his divine properties, just as we acknowledge that the man Christ is truly God by nature, even though his humanity in itself is not God or divinity. If a real communion were asserted in the concrete sense, that to the man Christ, that is, to this person, all things have been given, so that this man, this person, is truly and from eternity God by essence, almighty, all-knowing and everywhere present, no one would contradict. But they take the concrete for the abstract, saying that the man himself is God and almighty for the sake of his human nature. They make the man Christ God because the fullness of the deity has been really communicated to the assumed humanity and poured into it, so that by this communicated majesty it is God not merely by union. What Athanasius writes against certain people of his own time who so asserted the divinity of the man Christ that they even contended the flesh was consubstantial with the divinity seems not badly to fit these people. "If," he says, "what was from the nature of the divinity becomes divinity, why then do you accuse the Arians, who bring such an opinion of the Word into the open, when Scripture says the opposite, that the Word was made flesh, not the flesh the Word? Therefore it is said that the Word was made flesh, because the flesh of the Word became flesh, and not of some man: that is, God was made man, and he is said to have been made flesh, lest you omit the word flesh. But if you are not content with this union of the Word with flesh, and by the very fact that God was made man you have resolved neither to hear nor to believe, since you cannot be satisfied with so modest and religious a manner of speaking, above all contrivance, while you hear that the body of God exists, and this according to him who says: 'who will transform the body of our humility, that it may be conformed to the body of his glory' [Phil. 3]. In this matter the argument for the future resurrection is shown: for the body is called body even when it is already the body of his glory, etc."

units.la: Differentiæ specificæ vnionis personalis quas Brentius proponit, rem non vere explicant.
units.tr: The specific differences of the personal union which Brenz proposes do not truly explain the matter.

units.la: Exposita haftenus orthodoxa doctrina de vnione naturarum & communione proprie-tatum, dicam nunc de illis specificis differen-tijs vnionis hypostaticae quas Brētius adfert, & ostendam quae absurda, absurda inquam fidei & scripturis repugnātia inde consequan-tur. In libro de Maiestate vnionem persona-rum
units.tr: Having set out so far the orthodox doctrine of the union of the natures and the communion of properties, I shall now speak of those specific differences of the hypostatic union which Brenz brings forward, and I shall show what absurdities, absurdities I say, repugnant to the faith and to Scripture, follow from them. In his book on the Majesty, he defines the union of the persons

units.la: lem Vbiquitate definit. Verum idem alibi Vbiquitatem tribuit Sanctis ex sententia Hieronymi male intellecta. Parsimonius quoque Brentij discipulus, Concionis suae arg.6. Esse in coelis, significare inquit, vbiq; adesse & implere omnia. Sanctos autem in coelis esse nemo dubitat, quare etiam vbiq; aderunt & omnia implebunt. Itaq; si Vbiquitas constituit personalem vnionem, Christus hac re nihil a sanctis differet, neque magis Deus dici poterit quam Petrus aut Paulus, sed in ordine sanctorum manebit, quando sancti illi hac ratione a Brentio aequantur. Neque poterit dicere sanctos per alium, Christum per se vbique esse, quia ait tam Christum quam sanctos diuina virtute intime praesente agere & vbique adesse. Porro quod Andreas Brentium suum ita explicat, non tantum ab eo praesentia staturi, sed eam praesentiam vt per humanam naturam & cum ea λόγος faciat omnia, non satis est vt sit vnionis hypostaticae vera differentia, nam Deus Pater omnia facit per λόγον & tamen non est vna vtriusque persona.
units.tr: by ubiquity. Yet elsewhere he attributes ubiquity to the saints, on the basis of a badly understood opinion of Jerome. His disciple Parsimonius, too, in argument 6 of his sermon, says: "To be in heaven means to be present everywhere and to fill all things." No one doubts that the saints are in heaven, therefore they too will be everywhere present and will fill all things. So if ubiquity constitutes the personal union, Christ will differ in no way from the saints, and he could be called God no more than Peter or Paul, but will remain in the order of the saints, since those saints are equated with him by Brenz in this respect. Nor can he say that the saints are present by another, but Christ is everywhere through himself, since he says that both Christ and the saints act by divine power, intimately present, and are everywhere present. Moreover, that Andreas explains his Brenz thus, that he not only stands present by him, but makes all things through the human nature and with it the Word [λόγος], this is not enough to be a true difference of the hypostatic union, for God the Father makes all things through the Word [λόγον], and yet the two are not one person.

units.la: Aliam deinde differentiam vnionis hypostaticae proponit effusionem maiestatis diuinae in humanam naturam, siue communicationem omnium proprietatum, Discrimen inquit Christi & Petri non est sumendum simpliciter ab inhabitatione filij Dei, sed a communicatione proprietatum eius, Filius enim
units.tr: Next he proposes another difference of the hypostatic union: the outpouring of the divine majesty into the human nature, or the communication of all properties. He says: "The distinction between Christ and Peter is not to be taken simply from the indwelling of the Son of God, but from the communication of his properties. For the Son of God,

units.la: Dei etsi sua essentia implet Petrum, sicut & hominem Christum, non tamen communicat Petro omnes suas proprietates, sed tarum nonnullas. Filium vero hominis assumptum ex Maria virgine, ornat non aliquibus tantu, sed vniuersis suis donis, & communicat ipsi omnes suas proprietates. Item alibi, inquit, hominem Christu Deum dici no quia Deus in ipso, sed quia in assumptione carnis dedit huic homini omnem potestatem in coelo & in terra, communicauit ei omnia dona Spiri- tus sancti. Hominem Christum propter im- mensitatem & infinitatem donorum inquit Deo factum aequalem, &c. In hac autem eius sententia hoc primum reprehendimus quod Christus redigatur in ordinem sanctorum, si namq; vnio posita est in communione dono- rum, sancti etiam suo modo Deus erunt, qui-bus multa & ampla dona à Deo coferuntur. Neque est hoc sufficiens discrimen quod san-cti dimensa dona acceperint Christus immen-sa, nam ita nihilominus genere non differret, sed tantum secundum magis & minus, at illa inhabitatio Dei in sanctis & in homine as-sumpto genere toto differt. Conatur quis dem Iacobus Andreae suam sententiam pro- bare his verbis D. Augustini. Deus qui vbi- que est non in omnibus habitat: etiam in qui- bus habitat, non aequaliter habitat. Et vnde in omnibus sanctis sunt alij alijs sanctiores, nisi abundantius habendo habitanteDeum? Sed aliter homo ille in Deo, quoniam & aliter Deus ille in homine. Hæc ille adducit,sed quæ his coniuncta sunt, & sententiam absoluuunt omisit, manifesta fraude vsus. Integra Augustini sententia sic habet: Aliter homo ille in Deo, quoniam & aliter Deus ille in homine, proprio quodam & singulari modo. Vna enim persona Deus & homo est,&vtrüque est vnus Iesus, vbique per id quod Deus est, in cœlo per id quod homo. Atque in eadem epistola hoc discrimen habitationis his verbis Augustinus explicat. Quid ergo est? Hoccine interesse arbitramur inter caput & membra cætera, quod in quolibet quamuis præcipuo mébro,velut in aliquo magno prophera aut Apostolo,quamuis diuinitas habitet,non tamen sicut in capite,quod est Christus, omnis plenitudo diuinitatis. Nam & in nostro corpore inest sensus singulis membris, sed non tantus quantus in capite, vbi prorsus omnis est quinque partitus. Ibi enim & visus, & auditus, & olfactus, & gustus, & tactus. In cæteris autem solus est tactus. An etiam præter hoc quod tanquam in templo in illo corpore habitat omnis plenitudo diuinitatis, est aliud quod interfit inter illud caput & cuiuslibet membri excellentiam? Est plane, quod singulari quadam susceptione hominis illius vna facta est persona cum verbo.
units.tr: although by his essence he fills Peter as he fills the man Christ, yet he does not communicate to Peter all his properties, but only some. But the Son of man, assumed from the Virgin Mary, he adorns not with some gifts only, but with all his gifts, and communicates to him all his properties." Likewise elsewhere he says: "The man Christ is not called God because God is in him, but because in the assumption of the flesh he gave to this man all power in heaven and on earth, and communicated to him all the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The man Christ, on account of the immensity and infinity of the gifts, he says, has been made equal to God, etc." In this opinion we first object to this: that Christ is reduced to the order of the saints. For if the union is placed in the communication of gifts, the saints too will be God in their own way, to whom many and great gifts are conferred by God. Nor is this a sufficient distinction, that the saints have received measured gifts while Christ received immeasurable ones, for in that way they would nonetheless not differ in genus, but only in more and less; whereas that indwelling of God in the saints and in the assumed man differs in its whole genus. Jacob Andreae indeed tries to prove his opinion by these words of St. Augustine: "God, who is everywhere, does not dwell in all things; even in those in whom he dwells, he does not dwell equally. And whence in all the saints are some more holy than others, unless from God dwelling in them more abundantly? But that man is in God in one way, and God is in that man in another way." These words he adduces, but he omitted what is joined to them and completes the sentence, using a manifest fraud. Augustine's full sentence reads: "That man is in God in one way, and God is in that man in another way, by a certain proper and singular mode. For one person is God and man, and he is one Jesus, everywhere through what he is as God, in heaven through what he is as man." And in the same letter Augustine explains this difference of indwelling in these words: "What then is it? Do we think this is the only difference between the head and the other members, that in any member, however outstanding, as in some great prophet or apostle, the divinity dwells, yet not as in the head, which is Christ, in whom is all the fullness of the divinity? For in our body the sense is present in each member, but not as great as in the head, where all of it is fivefold: for there is sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. In the others, however, only touch is present. Is there also something beyond this, that in that body all the fullness of divinity dwells as in a temple, which distinguishes that head from the excellence of any member? There plainly is: that by a singular assumption of that man, one person was made with the Word."

units.la: De nullo enim sanctorum dici potuit, aut potest, aut poterit, Verbum caro factū est. Nullus sanctorum qualibet præstantia gratiæ, vnigeniti nomē accepit, vt quod est ipsum Dei Verbū ante secula, hoc simul cum assumpto homine diceretur. Singularis est ergo illa susceptio, nec cum hominibus aliquibus sanctis quantalibet sapientia & sanctitate præstantibus, vllo modo potest esse communis, vbi diuinæ gratię satis clarum perspicuumq; documentum est. His verbis si D. Augustinus dicit, quod Iacobus Andreæ asserit, hoc vnū esse ratione inhabitationis discrimen, quòd Deus sanctis distribuat sua dona dimensa, Christo homini sine mensura, hoc est immen sa: quòd sanctis dederit singulis suam potestatem, Christo homini autem omnem potestatem: si inquam hoc Augustinus dicit, vicerit sane Andreas: sin quod manifestum est, hoc ipsum negat, nonne impostor est qui truncato Augustini testimonio nobis fucum facere, & plane contrariam Augustino sententiam ex ipso probare conatus sit?
units.tr: For of none of the saints could it be said, or can it be said, or will it be said, "The Word was made flesh." No one of the saints, by any excellence of grace, has received the name of Only-begotten, so that what is the Word of God itself before the ages would be said at the same time of the assumed man. That assumption, then, is singular, and it cannot in any way be common with any men, however eminent in wisdom and holiness, and this is a clear enough and manifest proof of divine grace. If St. Augustine says in these words what Jacob Andreae asserts, that the only difference in respect of indwelling is that God distributes his gifts to the saints in measure, but to the man Christ without measure, that is, immeasurably; that he gave to each saint his own power, but to the man Christ all power: if Augustine indeed says this, Andreas will certainly have won. But if, as is plain, he denies this very thing, is he not an impostor, who, having mutilated the testimony of Augustine, has tried to deceive us and to prove from Augustine himself a sentiment entirely contrary to Augustine's?

units.la: Alterum etiam in hac personalis vnionis definitione viri doĉti dudum reprehenderūt, quod hæc vnio non sit vere personalis, hac ē nim ratione humanam naturam non personę ςπλοΥov sed toti Trinitati vnitam esse, propterea quod communicatio donorum commune opus sit totius Trinitatis, Respondet Andreas eandem quidem esse vt essentiam ita etiam potentiam Patris & Filij, aliam tamen ex ratione proprietatum personarum, quia alia est genita, alia ingenita: cum homine autem non esse personaliter vnitam potentiam & sapientiam ingenitam, quae est Pater, sed sapientiam & potentiam Filij quae est genita, non minus tamen infinita quam Patris aut Spiritus sancti. Verum hac ratione elabi non potest, nam definiens vnionem personalem per communicationem donorum, nullam donorum distinctione fecit iuxta personarum proprietates, imo nominatim mentionem fecit donorum Spiritus sancti, vnde apparet eum de essentiali & non personali vnione loqui. Deinde posuit eandem genere inhabitationem & communionem donorum in Christo & sanctis, dicens hoc vnum discrimen esse quod homini assumpto immensa dona data sint, sanctis dimensa. At de sanctis dicere non potest, illis haec communicata tantum per Filium, nisi velit statuere personalem operationem in Trinitate, & ita non tantum personas sed etiam naturas diuidere.
units.tr: Learned men have long criticised another point in this definition of personal union: that the union is not truly personal. On this reasoning the human nature would be united not to the person of the Word but to the whole Trinity, since the communication of gifts is the common work of the whole Trinity. Andreas replies that the power and wisdom of the Father and the Son are the same, as is their essence, yet there is a difference according to the properties of the persons, because one is begotten and the other unbegotten. So with the man, it is not the unbegotten power and wisdom, which is the Father, that is personally united, but the wisdom and power of the Son, which is begotten, though no less infinite than that of the Father or the Holy Spirit. But this reply cannot save him. In defining personal union through the communication of gifts, he made no distinction among the gifts according to the properties of the persons; indeed he expressly mentioned the gifts of the Holy Spirit. From this it is clear that he is speaking of an essential union and not a personal one. Next, he holds that the indwelling and the communion of gifts are of the same kind in Christ and in the saints, saying that the only difference is this: immeasurable gifts were given to the assumed man, measured gifts to the saints. But he cannot say that these gifts were communicated to the saints only through the Son, unless he wishes to posit a personal operation within the Trinity, and so to divide not only the persons but also the natures.

units.la: Tertio transfusio illa realis proprietatum diuinae naturae in humanam naturam, non tantum noua est scripturae & veteri ecclesiae incognita, quae nunquam ita loquuta est, sed revera nihil aliud est quam naturarum confusio. Proprietas enim (vt aduersarij definiunt) est quod
units.tr: Third, that real transfusion of the properties of the divine nature into the human nature is not only new and unknown to Scripture and to the ancient Church, which never spoke in this way, but is in truth nothing other than a confusion of natures. For a property (as our opponents define it) is that which

units.la: Confusio naturarum. Vwigadus de communic. Idiom. est quod naturam à natura secernit: item proprietas naturæ seu essentialis est id quod ipsam naturam constituit, & sine quo natura cuius est proprietas cōstare nō potest. Quod si proprietates diuinæ naturæ omnes realiter transfunduntur in humanam naturam quomodo discernuntur naturæ? quomodo autē salua manet differentia naturarū si proprietates quibus inter se discernuntur, ab vna natura realiter transfunduntur in aliam? Damascenus, Diuinitatem igitur dicentes, nō de illa nominamus ea quæ humanitatis sunt: nō enim dicimus Deitatem passibilem aut creatam. Neque de carne, id est humanitate prædicamus ea quæ deitatis sunt propria: nā neque dicimus carnem, id est humanitatem increatam. At vero de hypostasi, siue ex vtraque, siue ex vna naturarum eam nominamus vtriusque naturarum propria illi adijcimus. Sed si propria diuinæ naturæ in humanam transfunderentur, liceret etiam ea de humanitate dicere. Hieronymus quoque, Illorum, inquit, similiter execramur blasphemiā, qui nouo sensu afferere conantur, à tempore susceptŗ carnis, omnia quæ erant Deitatis in homine demigrasse, & rursum quæ erant humanitatis in Deum esse trâsfusa, vt quod nulla vnquam hæresis dicere ausa est, videatur hac confusione vtraque exinanita substātia. Deitatis scilicet & humanitatis, & à proprio
units.tr: Confusion of natures. Wigand, On the Communication of Idioms: is that which separates one nature from another. Likewise the property of a nature, or essential property, is that which constitutes the nature itself, and without which the nature whose property it is cannot exist. But if all the properties of the divine nature are really transfused into the human nature, how are the natures distinguished? And how is the difference of the natures preserved if the properties by which they are distinguished are really transferred from one nature into the other? Damascene: "Therefore, when we speak of the Deity, we do not name in it what belongs to humanity, for we do not say that the Deity is passible or created. Nor do we predicate of the flesh, that is of the humanity, what is proper to the Deity, for we do not say that the flesh, that is the humanity, is uncreated. But of the hypostasis, whether from both natures or from one of them, we name it, and we attach to it the properties of both natures." But if the properties of the divine nature were transfused into the human nature, it would be lawful to say these things also of the humanity. Jerome too: "We execrate in the same way the blasphemy of those who try to assert in a new sense that from the time of the assumption of the flesh all things that belonged to the Deity have passed over into the man, and again that what belonged to the humanity has been transfused into God, so that, what no heresy has ever dared to say, the substance of both appears emptied by this confusion: of the Deity and of the humanity, and from its own."

units.la: Lib.3. cap. 4.
units.tr: Book 3, chapter 4.

units.la: In symb. explan. ad Damasc. statu in aliud esse commutata. Iacobus Andreæ cum dudum illi duo hæc testimonia opposita fuissent, Damasceni dictum tanquam nihil ad se pertinens silentio præterit: Hieronymi sententiam se recipere inquit, se enim non afferere eo modo ea quæ deitatis sunt ita demigrasse in hominem vt confusio substantiarum sit facta, se enim docere permanentibus naturis & substantijs humanitatem summaiestate ornatam esse qua ad dexteram Dei sedet. At Hieronymus non tantum naturarum confusionem damnat, sed ipsam transfusionem proprietatum vnius naturæ in alteram, quod scilicet hanc sequatur confusio quæ naturæ abolentur: Neque hic peculiaris modi meminit Hieronymus, vt dicat ea quæ Deitatis non] ITA demigrasse, vt hac confusione vtraque substantia sit commutata, sed hoc ITA desuo apposuit Andreas, quasi innueret Hieronymus posse alio modo demigrare in humanitatem omnia quæ Deitatis sunt, vt tamen nulla sequatur confusio. Cæterum Lucas Osiander distinguit inter naturalem & realem communicationem idiomatum, & accusat Vuitebergenses qui realem & physicam Idiomatum communicationem sophistice coniungant. Vult autem physicam communionē esse quando diuina natura humanæ ita suas proprietates communicat, vt humana natura (etiamsi à diuina separari posset) in fe habeat huiusmodi proprietates, quasi naturales suas proprietates, amissis prioribus suis proprietatibus. Talem communicationem improbat: sed aliam ait realem communicationé esse, qua diuina natura humanitati Christi proprietates suas communicat, sic vt diuinitas omnipotentiam suam & omnia diuina opera operetur per assumptā humanitatem. Sed Brentius communicatio-nem talem statuit, vt Deus in homine, aut fi-lius Dei effuderit in filium hominis omnem suam maiestatē, omnipotentiam, omniscientiam, omnisapientiā, omnijustitiā, omniprasentiam, & omnifœlicitatem, humanā enim naturam huius infinitæ maiestatis Dei capacem esse, & hac capacitate perfici & ornari. Hanc communicationem plenitudinem deitatis nominat, & distinguit hanc deitatis plenitudinem & omnipotentiā communicatam à deitate & omnipotentia Filij Dei: hanc maiestatem ait humanā naturam reipsa vere posse sidere, & vna cum verbo omnia coram gubernare, vna cū ipso omnipotente esse. Cum autem talem statuant realem transfusionem in ipsam humanitatem, certe physicam statuūt communicationem, neque enim est verbalis communicatio: neq; tantū volunt ea quæ naturæ sunt propria personæ propria fieri, sed suā communicationem faciūt transfusione proprietatum ex vna natura in alteram. In eo autem
units.tr: In the Explanation of the Creed, on Damascene. Jacob Andreae, when these two testimonies had long been set against him, passed over the saying of Damascene in silence, as having nothing to do with him. He says he accepts Jerome's opinion, for he does not assert that the things of the Godhead have passed over into the man in such a way that a confusion of substances results. He teaches that, the natures and substances remaining, the humanity is adorned with the majesty by which it sits at the right hand of God. But Jerome condemns not only the confusion of natures but the very transfusion of the properties of one nature into the other, because a confusion of natures follows from it, by which the natures are abolished. Nor does Jerome here mention any peculiar mode by which the things of the Godhead passed over in such a way that both substances were changed by this confusion. Andreae added this "in such a way" himself, as if Jerome hinted that all the things of the Godhead could pass over into the humanity in some other way, so that no confusion would follow. Otherwise, Luke Osiander distinguishes between a natural and a real communication of idioms, and accuses the Wittenbergers who unite the real and physical communication of idioms in a sophistical way. He holds that the physical communication takes place when the divine nature so communicates its properties to the human nature that the human nature (even if it could be separated from the divine) has such properties in itself as its own natural properties, having lost its former properties. He rejects such a communication. But he says there is another, a real communication, by which the divine nature communicates its properties to the humanity of Christ, so that the divinity works its omnipotence and all its divine works through the assumed humanity. But Brenz posits a communication such that God, or the Son of God, has poured into the Son of man all his majesty, omnipotence, omniscience, all wisdom, all justice, omnipresence and all blessedness. For he holds that the human nature is capable of this infinite majesty of God and is perfected and adorned by this capacity. He calls this communication the fullness of the Godhead, and he distinguishes this communicated fullness of the Godhead and omnipotence from the Godhead and omnipotence of the Son of God. He says that the human nature can truly sit in this majesty in fact, and govern all things together with the Word, and be omnipotent together with him. Since they posit such a real transfusion into the humanity itself, they certainly posit a physical communication, for it is not a verbal communication. Nor do they want only the things that belong to the nature to become the proper possession of the person, but they make their communication by the transfusion of properties from one nature into the other. In this, however,

units.la: errant quod non distinguût communicationem donorû, à communicatione proprietatum, Deum varia & amplissima dona largiri hominibus manifestissimum est, humanitas tem etiâ Christi in se præ omnibus aliis creaturis excellentissimis donis ornatam esse non est controuersum, hæc autem dona sunt creata & finita: sed an etiam proprietates Deitatis infinitæ & æternæ, in humanam naturâ sint transfusæ vt eas in se habeat, de hoc est controversia. Quod autem aiunt posita tali communicatione non tamen ideo tolli humanæ naturæ proprietates, nec exæquari naturas, impudenter sane faciunt qui contradicentia de eodem subiecto simul & semel affirmata vera esse velint: humanæ naturæ proprietas est esse finitum & circumscriptum, Diuinæ infinitum & incircumscriptum, si hoc transfunditur in humanâ naturâ & tamen ea suam proprietatem feruet, eadem finita & infinita erit. Si autem dicunt infinitû & incorporeum & abs; principio esse non transfundi in humanâ naturam, tum illa omnium proprietatum transfusio non est fine exceptione, vt Brentius affirmat, & quidem ita constanter, vt affirmet non esse differentiam inter Christum & alios homines, nec verbum potuisse fieri carnem, nisi humana natura omnes Dei proprietates abs; exceptione acceperit. Præterea cum proprietates naturam constituant, & in Deo idem sint cum essentia, potentia sa‑pientia & reliqua propria, non potest in Chri‑sto statui alia proprietatum communicatio quam qualis statuitur essentiæ communica‑tio. Essentiarum autem realis transfusio absque earundem confusione non potest constitui. Mirum autem est istos homines in effusione donorum in humanam naturā quærere rationē vnionis personalis, & duntaxat de eo disputa‑re quomodo Homo sit Deus, sit omnipotens & omnipræsens factus, cum scripturæ alio or‑dine vtantur, & Verbū dicant carne factum: non carne verbū factum: Patres quoq; Cyril‑lus, Maxētius, & alij monēt scripturā tradere quod Deus homo factus sit, non quod homo Deus sit factus, quod Nestoriani docebāt. Cer‑te si quis bene expendat vniuersam doctrinā Brētij & suorū, vix poterit eos à crimine Ne‑storianæ hæreseos defendere. Cum aūt expli‑cāt communionē realē seu transfusionē pro‑prietatum diuinæ naturæ in humanam, eam nihil aliud esse quam quod Verbum assūm‑pta humana natura nihil operetur nisi cum illa & per illam, sicut anima omnia operatur per corpus, in eo ipsi peccant quod in nobis accusant: rem enim ambiguā pro confessa su‑munt, & argumento vtuntur æque incerto atque id quod in quæstione versatur, deniq; hoc concessō non tamen conficiunt quod vo‑lunt. Ac primum Verbum nihil nunc agerē fine carne assumpta libenter illis damus,operatur enim vt Deus incarnatus, neque quam semel in suâ hypostasim assumpsit humanam naturam à se deponit aut separat: an autè Verbum omnia suæ omnipotentiæ opera per suam humanitatem vt per instrumentū perficiat,id non facile absq; exceptione illis quis concesserit. Anima quidem nihil agit vllo in loco à quo corpus eius actu absit, sunt enim ambo finitæ naturæ, & anima quasi intra corpus concluditur: at non sic diuina natura infinita, humanitati finitæ iuncta est vt intra illam concludatur, sed multa operatur in illis locis in quibus humanitas eius essentialiter & reipsa non adest.Neque enim Centurionis puerum per corpus vt per instrumentum sanauit, neque Lazarum per corporeos oculos absentes,vt per instrumentum morientem aspexit: etsi enim vtrunque non sine corpore factum est, non tamen per hoc vt per instrumentum factum est. Multo minus dicendum est Christum à mortuis suscitasse corpus suum, & sustulisse supra omnes cœlos, per humanitatem suam tanquam per instrumentū. Deinde quod sumunt animam per corpus vt per instrumentum omnia sua opera exercere, controuersum est: nam non ignobiles Peripatetici docent animā per mentem intelligere vt corpore pro instrumento non vtatur: & tamē homo intelligere dicitur.
units.tr: they err in that they do not distinguish the communication of gifts from the communication of properties. It is perfectly plain that God bestows various and very great gifts on men, and it is not in dispute that the humanity of Christ too, in itself, is adorned with gifts that surpass all other most excellent creatures. But these gifts are created and finite. Whether the properties of the infinite and eternal Godhead have also been transfused into the human nature, so that it has them in itself, is the matter in dispute. As to their claim that, with such a communication posited, the properties of the human nature are nevertheless not therefore taken away, nor are the natures made equal, they certainly act shamelessly who wish contradictory statements about the same subject, affirmed together and at once, to be true. It is a property of the human nature to be finite and circumscribed, of the divine to be infinite and uncircumscribed. If this is transfused into the human nature and yet it keeps its own property, it will be both finite and infinite. But if they say that the infinite, the incorporeal and the unbounded is not transfused into the human nature from the beginning, then that transfusion of all properties is not without exception, as Brenz affirms, and that so firmly that he asserts there is no difference between Christ and other men, nor could the Word have become flesh unless the human nature had received all the properties of God without exception. Moreover, since properties constitute the nature, and in God they are the same as the essence, power, wisdom and the other proper attributes, no other communication of properties can be posited in Christ than the communication of the essence that is posited. But a real transfusion of essences cannot be established without a confusion of those same essences. It is strange, moreover, that these men look for a reason for personal union in the pouring out of gifts into the human nature, and dispute only how man is made God, omnipotent and omnipresent, when Scripture uses another order and says that the Word was made flesh, not that the Word was made flesh by the flesh. The Fathers too, Cyril, Maximus and others, warn that Scripture teaches that God was made man, not that man was made God, which the Nestorians taught. Certainly, if anyone carefully weighs the whole doctrine of Brenz and his followers, he will scarcely be able to defend them from the charge of Nestorian heresy. When they explain the real communion, or transfusion of the properties of the divine nature into the human, as nothing other than that the Word, having assumed the human nature, works nothing except with it and through it, as the soul works all things through the body, they sin in the very thing they accuse us of. For they take a doubtful matter as conceded, and use an argument as uncertain as the very point under dispute. And finally, even with this conceded, they do not achieve what they want. For first, we gladly grant them that the Word now does nothing without the flesh it has assumed, for it works as the incarnate God, and it does not lay aside or separate from itself the human nature which it once assumed into its own hypostasis. But whether the Word performs all the works of its omnipotence through its humanity, as through an instrument, that could not easily be granted to them without exception. The soul indeed does nothing in any place from which its body is actually absent, for both are of finite nature, and the soul is as it were enclosed within the body. But the infinite divine nature is not joined to the finite humanity so as to be enclosed within it; rather it works many things in those places where its humanity is not essentially and actually present. For neither did he heal the centurion's servant through the body as through an instrument, nor did he see Lazarus, dying, through bodily eyes that were absent. For although each of these things was not done without the body, yet they were not done through it as through an instrument. Much less must it be said that Christ raised his body from the dead and lifted it above all the heavens through his humanity as through an instrument. Next, that they assume the soul exercises all its works through the body as through an instrument is disputed. For not ignoble Peripatetics teach that the soul understands through the mind, so that it does not use the body as an instrument, and yet a man is said to understand.

units.la: Simili modo etiamsi Verbum operetur quædam non per assumptam humanitatem, nihilominus dicitur Christus hæc operari, Verbum enim nihil agit absq; humanitate postquam eam semel in vnitate personæ assumpsit, etsi non omnia per illud vt per instrumentum faciat. At concessò verbum per corpus vt per instrumentum omnia agere, tamen non erit hæc propria & specifica differentia vnionis personalis, neque enim per aliquem facere aliquid efficit vnam personam, nam Pater dicitur omnia fecisse per Filium, neque instrumentum esse alicuius efficit vnam esse personam.
units.tr: In the same way, even if the Word works certain things not through the assumed humanity, Christ is still said to do those things. For the Word does nothing apart from the humanity once it has assumed it in the unity of the person, although it does not do all things through it as through an instrument. But even if we grant that the Word works everything through the body as through an instrument, this will not be the proper and specific difference of the personal union. To do something through someone does not make one person, for the Father is said to have made all things through the Son, and being the instrument of something does not make two things one person.

units.la: An ex vnione personali statuatur omnium præsentia corporis Christi, & hac negata naturæ separentur, & vnio vera tollatur.
units.tr: Whether the omnipresence of Christ's body is established from the personal union, and whether, if this is denied, the natures are separated and the true union is destroyed.

units.la: Quæstio de vnione personali ab aduersariis ideo mota, est vt statuant omnipræsentiam corporis Christi, & ex illa probent realem & substantialem præsentiam corporis & sanguinis Domini in pane cœnæ Dominicę, vt autem hanc suam sententiam confirment, ita argumentantur. Verbum caro factum est, hoc est Deus & homo in Christo ita sunt conjuncta vt constituant vnam personam, nec possunt à se inuicem ne morte quidem separari. Vbicunque igitur est diuinitas Christi, ibi humanitas Christi sit necesse est. Diuinitas autem Christi est in pane coenæ dominicæ quia replet omnia ineffabili modo. Ergo necessarium est vt & humanitas Christi, hoc est, corpus & sanguis Christi, sint in pane coenæ dominicæ praesentia. Si enim (aiunt) ratio vnitatis personæ in Christo non eo se extendit, vt diuinitas Christi vbique habeat humanitatem quam assumpsit sibi coniunctam, & indissolubili nexu copulatam, sed humanitas eius in vno tantum certo loco est, siue in terra siue in coelo, sola autem diuinitas coelum & terrā implet, quid aliud sequeretur, quàm quòd Christus in vno tantum loco Deus esset & homo, in omnibus autem alijs solùmodo Deus? An non hoc est clare, aperte & manifeste facere duas personas? Ad hoc argumentum cum copiose à nostris responsum sit, illud tamen ante omnia repetendum est, etsi dicamus corpus Christi propter veri corporis rationem circumscriptum & in vno tantum loco simul & semel esse, non tamen nos negare diuinitate Christi vbique habere humanitatem quam assumpsit SIBI coniunctam & indissolubili nexu copulatam. Totus Christus vbicumque est, Deus & homo est, ideoque nusquam est sine humanitate, non tamen totum Christi est essentialiter vbique. Diuinitas enim Verbi quae vbique praesens est non localiter alicubi est, aut circumscriptiue, aut definitiue, sed vbique tota est essentialiter, cum autem adest
units.tr: The adversaries raised the question of the personal union so that they could establish the omnipresence of Christ's body, and from it prove the real and substantial presence of the body and blood of the Lord in the bread of the Lord's Supper. To confirm this opinion they argue as follows. The Word became flesh; that is, God and man in Christ are so joined that they constitute one person, and cannot be separated from each other, not even by death. Wherever the divinity of Christ is, the humanity of Christ must necessarily be there too. But the divinity of Christ is in the bread of the Lord's Supper, since it fills all things in an ineffable manner. Therefore the humanity of Christ, that is, the body and blood of Christ, must also be present in the bread of the Lord's Supper. For if (they say) the ground of the unity of person in Christ does not extend so far that the divinity of Christ has everywhere the humanity it assumed, joined to itself and bound by an indissoluble bond, but his humanity is in only one certain place, whether on earth or in heaven, while only the divinity fills heaven and earth, what else would follow than that Christ would be God and man in one place only, but in all others only God? Is this not clearly, openly and manifestly to make two persons? Although our side has answered this argument at length, it must above all be repeated that, even if we say the body of Christ, by the nature of a true body, is circumscribed and is in one place only at one time, we do not deny that by his divinity he has everywhere the humanity he assumed, joined to himself and bound by an indissoluble bond. Whole Christ, wherever he is, is God and man, and therefore he is nowhere without humanity; yet the whole of Christ is not essentially everywhere. For the divinity of the Word, which is present everywhere, is not locally anywhere, either circumscriptively or definitively, but is wholly everywhere essentially. When it is present

units.la: Recog. pag. 17 adest non adest vt Verbum absque carne sed Verbum incarnatum, & illa eadem diuinitas quæ præsens est in terris, humanitate suam quæ in cœlis est, sic sustentat, vt eam non deserat nec ea aliter quam in diuinitate sibi vnita subsistat, aȝtamen non ideo humanitas in terris præsens est: itaque hoc non est probandum aduersarijs diuinitatem Verbi habere vbique SIBI coniunctam humanitatem, neq; enim hoc negamus, sed negamus ꝓpterea sesqui. Cui rei diuinitas essentialiter præsens est, vt illi rei essentialiter præsens etiā sit humanitas diuinitati coniuncta, vt scilicet diuinitas eam sistat præsente in omnibus locis ad quæ ipsa quasi diffunditur. Nam alius modus est præsentiæ diuinitatis quæ infinita est, alius modus præsentiæ humani corporis quod finitum & circumscriptum localiter & circū scriptiue præsens est, vbi sua substantia præsens est. Exempli causa humana anima tota est in capite & in eodē præcipue vires suas exerit, & tamen eadem anima quæ tota est in capite, tota etiam est in pedibus, neque propterea caput est in pedibus, aut anima à capite ideo separatur, quia non simul existit in pedibus. Neque sequitur, anima mea vbicunque fuerit habet sibi vnitum caput meum in eadem hypostasi, ergo vbicunque est anima puta in manu vel pede ibi est caput. Fateor hoc exemplum non per omnia congruere, quoniam non caput solum cum anima facit vnam personā, sed totum corpus, sed nihilo minus hoc exēplo satis ostenditur vnionem inseparabilem permanere etiāsi rebus vnitis non tribuatur coexistentia. Neque debet hoc exemplum inconueniens videri, vbi de capite agitur parte tantum totius corporis hypostatice vniti cum anima, quando hic quoque potissimū quaeritur de corpore quod est pars humanae naturae cū verbo personaliter vnitę.
units.tr: Recog. pag. 17 It is present not as the Word without flesh but as the incarnate Word. The same divinity which is present on earth sustains its humanity, which is in heaven, in such a way that it does not forsake it, nor does that humanity subsist otherwise than united to the divinity. Yet the humanity is not therefore present on earth. So it is not to be proved to our adversaries that the divinity of the Word has everywhere the humanity joined to itself; for we do not deny this, but we deny that it is therefore present everywhere. The divinity is essentially present to a thing so that the humanity joined to the divinity is also essentially present to that thing, namely in such a way that the divinity makes it present in all the places into which it is, as it were, diffused. For there is one mode of presence of the divinity, which is infinite, and another mode of presence of a human body, which is finite and circumscribed, and is locally and circumscriptively present where its substance is present. For example, the human soul is wholly in the head, and especially exercises its powers there; yet the same soul, which is wholly in the head, is also wholly in the feet, and yet the head is not therefore in the feet, nor is the soul separated from the head because it does not exist at the same time in the feet. Nor does it follow that wherever my soul is, my head, united to it in the same hypostasis, is there; so wherever the soul is, say in the hand or foot, the head is there too. I admit that this example does not agree in every respect, since not the head alone but the whole body makes one person with the soul. Nevertheless, the example sufficiently shows that the inseparable union remains even when coexistence is not ascribed to the united things. Nor should this example seem unsuitable, since we are speaking of the head, a part of the whole body, hypostatically united with the soul, and here too the question is chiefly about the body, which is a part of the human nature personally united with the Word.

units.la: Ratio autem cur humana natura non sit vbique praesens vti diuina, haec est, quod diuina natura infinita est & incorporea, humana autē corporea, finita & certo loco circumscripta: diuina autē natura assumpsit humanam naturam saluis ipsius proprietatibus, alias confunderentur naturae, & vna mixta fieret.
