Atque proprietates humanae naturae salvas mansisse in vnione personali, Brentius quoque fatetur, sed tamē distinguit proprietates, quod aliquae sint substantiales, aliquae accidentariae & separabiles, & terrenae infirmitatis: substantiales autem mansisse saluas, caeteras non item: & inter accidentarias proprietates hanc vnam esse vt corpus sit in loco, itaque non repugnare proprietatibus substantialibus & ipsi essentiae humanae naturae, vt corpus Christi diuina potentia sit vbique. Verum longe aliter se res habet, nam circumscriptio adeo propria est naturae creatae, vt etiam beati angeli qui proprie non sunt in lo co, quod cum sint incorporei non habent cor pus ambiens, tamē quia habent substantiam limitatam quoad ordinem vniuersi etiam in loco aut certo Vbi sunt. Vbique vero præsen tem esse ita proprium est diuinæ naturæ vt hoc argumento firmissimo diuinitatē Filij & Spi ritus sancti veteres demonstrarint, quod cer te horum sententia prorsus conuellitur qui ybiquitatem humanæ naturæ tribuunt. Sunt autem proprietates essentiales consentiente Brentio quas definitione comprehendimus, sed ad humani corporis definitionem perti net vt sit organicum, vt singulæ partes pro priam habeant conformatione seu figuram, dimensionem & magnitudinem, ordine item inter se ac situm : vt autem singula organa vel partes corporis suam proportionem, quanti tatem, ordinem & situm habet: ita totū quo que corpus certam dimensione situm, ideoq; certum locum seu vbi habere oportet. Quin imo Brentiani ipsi hic aliquantulum à Bren tio suo recesserunt & fassi sunt proprietatem esse corporis certum Vbi, scribētes triplicem esse corporis Christi considerationem, phy sicam qua corpus Christi natura finitū simul & eodem tempore vnum tantū locum occu pauit, secundam esse considerationem corpo ris Christi in gloria, hac ratione pro natura & proprietate gloriosorum corporū, corpus
units.tr: The reason why the human nature is not everywhere present as the divine nature is, is this: the divine nature is infinite and incorporeal, while the human nature is corporeal, finite and circumscribed in a certain place. The divine nature assumed the human nature with its own properties preserved, otherwise the natures would be confused and one mixed nature would result. Brentius also admits that the properties of the human nature remain intact in the personal union, but he distinguishes the properties: some are substantial, others accidental and separable, belonging to earthly weakness. He holds that the substantial properties remain intact but the others do not; and among the accidental properties he counts this one, that a body is in a place. Thus, he says, it is not repugnant to the substantial properties and to the very essence of the human nature that the body of Christ should be everywhere by divine power. But the matter stands far otherwise. For circumscription is so proper to a created nature that even the blessed angels, who are not properly in a place (since, being incorporeal, they have no body enclosing them), nevertheless, because they have a substance limited with respect to the order of the universe, are in a place, or have a definite where. But to be present everywhere is so proper to the divine nature that the ancient writers demonstrated the divinity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit by this most firm argument; and therefore the opinion of those who ascribe ubiquity to the human nature is entirely overthrown. Now, according to Brentius, the essential properties are those we comprehend in the definition; but it belongs to the definition of a human body that it is organic, so that each part has its own conformation or figure, dimension and magnitude, and likewise order and position among themselves. Just as each organ or part of the body has its own proportion, quantity, order and position, so the whole body too must have a definite dimension and position, and therefore must have a definite place or where. Indeed the Brentians themselves here have somewhat departed from their Brentius, and have confessed that a definite where is a property of the body, writing that there is a threefold consideration of the body of Christ: the physical, by which the body of Christ, being finite by nature, occupied only one place at once and at the same time; the second is the consideration of the body of Christ in glory, by which, according to the nature and property of glorified bodies, the body

units.la: Christi proprietate substantiæ finiri vt non sit vbique, sed alicubi vbicunque sit. Tertiam esse rationem humanitatis Christi ad dexteram virtutis & maiestatis Dei collocatæ, iuxta hanc rationem Christum etiam secundum humanitatem vbique præsentem esse. Sed si hæc est naturalis & gloriosi corporis proprietas, vt non sit vbique, tale autem corpus a Christo assumptum est, aut hæc proprietas sublata est vnione personali, & falsum est proprietates salvas mansisse, falsum etiam corpus Christi in gloria substantiæ proprietate finiri & non esse vbique: aut non est sublata hæc proprietas naturalis & gloriosi corporis, & tamen sessione ad dexteram seu maiestatis modo humanitas Christi vbique præsens est: atq; tu hoc modo vel naturale & substantiale corpus Christi saluis suis proprietatibus naturaliter & substantialiter præsens est, & contradictoria de eodem corpore affirmantur, illud simul & semel eodem tempore & vno tantum in loco & vbique naturaliter & essentialiter præsens esse: aut non affirmatur essentialis & substantialis omnipræsentia qua substantia & essentia sua præsens sit corpus Christi, sed alia quædam, forte ἀνυπαρκτικὴ præsentia ab his intelligitur, & frustra de hac præsentia contenditur ad stabiliendam præsentiam corporis Christi in pane cœnæ Domini, hanc enim præsentiam hactenus corporalem, naturalem, talem, essentialem, substantialem esse docue- runt. Neque refert quod modos praesentiae distinguunt: hoc in quaestione versatur, an corpus Christi essentia & substantia sua actu & reipsa in uno aliquo loco sit (quod adversarii de corpore Christi naturali & glorioso nunc fatentur) & idem eodem tempore essentia & substantia sua actu reipsa ubique sit, hoc autem affirmare est plane contradictoria statuere, sive dicas sessione ad dexteram seu quocunque alio modo id fieri. Magis ergo consentaneè suae opinioni Brentius scripsit, qui in loco esse, negat esse proprietatem essentialem corporis, sed accidentariam & sublatam a corpore Christi, quam hi qui hanc proprietatem retinent, & tamen nihilominus Omnipraesentiam corpori Christi tribuunt.
units.tr: of Christ is limited by the property of its substance, so that it is not everywhere, but is somewhere wherever it is; and the third is the consideration of the humanity of Christ placed at the right hand of the power and majesty of God, according to which reason Christ is also present everywhere according to his humanity. But if this is the natural property of a glorified body, that it is not everywhere, and such a body was assumed by Christ, then either this property was removed by the personal union, and it is false that the properties remained intact, and false also that the body of Christ in glory is limited by the property of its substance and is not everywhere; or this natural property of a glorified body was not removed, and yet by the sitting at the right hand, or by the mode of majesty, the humanity of Christ is present everywhere. In this way either the natural and substantial body of Christ, with its properties preserved, is present naturally and substantially, and contradictory things are affirmed of the same body, namely that it is at the same time, at one and the same time, in only one place and everywhere, naturally and essentially present; or else the essential and substantial omnipresence, by which the body of Christ is present in its own substance and essence, is not affirmed, but some other, perhaps a non-existent [ἀνυπαρκτικὴ] presence is meant by them, and it is in vain that they contend about this presence in order to establish the presence of the body of Christ in the bread of the Lord's Supper. For up to now they have taught that this presence is bodily, natural, such, essential and substantial. Nor does it matter that they distinguish modes of presence. The question here is whether the body of Christ is in one place by its essence and substance actually and in fact (which the adversaries now confess of the natural and glorious body of Christ), and whether the same body, at the same time, is everywhere by its essence and substance actually and in fact. To affirm this is plainly to state contradictories, whether you say it happens by sitting at the right hand or in any other way. Brentius therefore wrote more consistently with his own opinion, for he denies that being in a place is an essential property of the body, and holds it to be accidental and removed from the body of Christ; whereas those who retain this property nevertheless ascribe omnipresence to the body of Christ.

units.la: Unio etiam personae non posita est in coexistentia unitarum naturarum ut una sit ubi cunque est altera, quamuis enim haec coexistentia in finitis naturis quae eiusdem sunt mensurae locum habeat, ut in anima & corpore sit tota hypostasim spectamus (quamuis etiam anima inseparabiliter tota sit in parte aliqua, quae tamen ut diximus non ubique est ubicunque anima est, nec ideo ab anima separatur) non tamen est propria ratio & specifica differentia unionis, alioqui quae simul exis- stunt & operatur, una persona essent. Neque etiam unio posita est in transfusione aut comunicatione donorum in naturis, cum naturae proprietates personae communicentur, illa autem transfusio in alteram fit confusio naturarum. At vero unio posita est in identitate hypostaseos, ut humana natura suam existentiam habeat habuerit habituraq; sit semper in Verbo, ut diximus, ad hoc autem non requiritur ut humanitas una cum divinitate ubique substantialiter adsit, nam nihilominus manet unum θεάνθρωπον, humanitas enim licet in coelo sit, divinitatem tamen in persona Verbi coniunctam habet, & in illa subsistit, neque vllam extra λόγον personalitatem habet: divinitas etiam sive λόγος licet ubique sit, eadem tamen est & non alia quam quae humanitas in sua persona sustentat, & nō minus integra est in minima vniuersi parte, quam in vniuerso toto: nec aliter hic aliter ibi, sed simul & semel intra, extra & supra singula & vniuersa, nō diffusione locali nec mole se extendens, sed praesentia substantiae omnia continens & gubernans. Quare vbicunque sit, quia humanitatem in hypostasim suam attum- pfit, sine ea esse non potest. Qnamuis non sit cut illa substantialiter vbique est, ita quoque humanitatem praesentem esse necesse fit, cum id naturae veri corporis & testimonijs sacrae Scripturae repugnet. Primum enim ante resurrectionem Christi a mortuis, corpus eius non fuisse vbique praesens sed certo in loco
units.tr: The union of the person is also not located in the coexistence of the natures, so that one is wherever the other is. For although this coexistence takes place in finite natures of the same measure, as with soul and body, where we regard the whole person (though the soul too is wholly and inseparably in some part, which nevertheless, as we have said, is not everywhere wherever the soul is, and is not for that reason separated from the soul), it is still not the proper ground and specific difference of the union. Otherwise, things that exist and act together would be one person. Nor is the union located in the transfusion or communication of gifts between the natures, since the properties of a nature are communicated to the person, whereas that transfusion into the other would produce a confusion of natures. Rather, the union is located in the identity of the hypostasis, so that the human nature has, has had, and will always have its existence in the Word, as we have said. For this, however, it is not required that the humanity be substantially present everywhere along with the divinity, for it remains one God-man [θεάνθρωπον] nonetheless. The humanity, though it is in heaven, has the divinity joined to it in the person of the Word, and subsists in it, and has no personality outside the Word [λόγον]. The divinity also, or the Word [λόγος], although it is everywhere, is nonetheless the same and no other than what the humanity sustains in its person, and it is no less whole in the smallest part of the universe than in the whole universe. It is not one thing here and another there, but at once and in a single act within, outside and above single things and all things together, not extending itself by local diffusion or bulk, but containing and governing all things by the presence of its substance. Therefore, wherever it is, since it has assumed the humanity into its hypostasis, it cannot be without the humanity. Yet it does not follow that, just as the divinity is everywhere substantially, the humanity must also be present everywhere, since that is contrary to the nature of a true body and to the testimonies of holy Scripture. For first, before the resurrection of Christ from the dead, his body was not present everywhere but was in a certain place.

units.la: Unio hypostatica in quo consistat.
units.tr: The hypostatic union: in what it consists.

units.la: Corpus Christi non est ubique.
units.tr: The body of Christ is not everywhere.

units.la: manifestū est ex scripturis, quç corpus Chri-sti visibile & palpabile,organicum suam for-mam figuram & circumscriptionem habuis-se ostendunt, & eidem motum de loco in lo-cum,& certum locum tribuunt,& Christum ita in loco vno fuisse tradunt ut alibi non es-set, veluti cum Lazaro mortuo se inquit gau-dere propter discipulos quòd illic non fuerit. Et mulieribus Christum in sepulchro quæ-rentibus Angelus respondit, eum surrexisse & non hic esse. Neque nos mouet quod Bren-tiani hæc quæ de Christo dicuntur per dis-pensationem exponunt: aut enim quod exi-nanitioni & dispensationi tribuunt vere & reipsa ita fuit & factū est vt Christus vere & reipsa corpore suo esset in certo aliquo & de-finito loco, & eodem substantialiter & reipsa alibi tum non esset, aut tantum visus est vno in loco esse,reuera autem ibi non fuit:hoc po-sterius si dicant,Martionitæ sunt:sin alterum concedunt, ruit eorum argumentum: quod enim actu & reipsa est ac sit vna cum perso-nali vnione duarum naturarum, hoc vnione non soluit:at humanitas Christi actu& reipsa essentia sua fuit vno in loco vt eodem alibi reipsa substātia & essentia sua non esset, diui-nitate interim cœlum terramque implente, Quare non soluitur vnio quando humana na-tura nunc quoque vno in loco est, diuinitas vbique.Nam hoc ipsum scriptura quoque de corpore Christi in gloria testatur: Christus mox à resurrectione corpus suum visibile & palpabile discipulis ostendit, ascensio eius in cœlos fuit corporalis & visibilis, denique Petrus ait Christum oportere cœlo capi ἀνχανὸν ... ἄχρι vsque ad tepora restitutionis omnium; quamuis enim Selneccerus cum suis multum se torqueat in huius loci interpretatione, tamen hic est manifestus verborum sensus, Christum in cœlis esse aut contineri (scilicet corpore suo) vsq; ad tempus illud quo venturus est adiudicandū orbem terrarū, & sic hunc locū tota antiquitas intellexit & interpretata est.
units.tr: It is manifest from the Scriptures that they show the body of Christ to have been visible and palpable, organic, and to have had its own form, shape and circumscription; they attribute to it motion from place to place and a definite place, and they relate that Christ was in one place in such a way that he was not elsewhere. So, for example, he says he rejoiced over Lazarus when dead because he had not been there. And when the women sought Christ in the sepulchre, the angel answered that he had risen and was not here. Nor are we moved by the fact that the Brentians explain these things said of Christ as belonging to the dispensation. For either what they attribute to the emptying and the dispensation was truly and actually so and happened so, that Christ truly and actually was in a certain and definite place with his body, and substantially and actually was not elsewhere at that time; or he only seemed to be in one place, but in truth was not there. If they say the latter, they are Marcionites; if they concede the former, their argument collapses. For what is actually and really so, and remains so, with the personal union of the two natures, is not dissolved by that union. But the humanity of Christ actually and really was in one place by its substance and essence, so that it was not elsewhere by its substance and essence, while the divinity filled heaven and earth. Therefore the union is not dissolved when the human nature is now also in one place while the divinity is everywhere. For Scripture itself testifies this of the body of Christ in glory: immediately after the resurrection Christ showed his visible and palpable body to the disciples; his ascension into heaven was bodily and visible; and finally Peter says that Christ must be received by heaven [δεῖ οὐρανὸν μὲν δέξασθαι ἄχρι χρόνων] until the times of the restoration of all things. Although Selnecker and his men wrestle greatly over the interpretation of this passage, the plain sense of the words is that Christ is in heaven, or contained there (namely in his body), until that time when he is to come to judge the world. This is how the whole of antiquity understood and interpreted the place.

units.la: Porro qui affirmant humanitatem Christi vbique esse vbi diuinitas eius praesens est, vtsicuti corpus hominis vbiq; praesens est vbi anima est, ita etiam humanitas praesens sit vbi λόγος, & ni hoc statuatur, naturas loco separari aiunt, quod vno in loco sit Christus Deus & homo, in altero Deus tantum, hi quod aliis obijciunt, nimis crassas de diuinitate imaginationes animo concipiunt, ac videntur exi-stimare Diuinitatem in humanitate inclusam quodammodo esse, & definitam terminis humanae naturae, sicuti anima in corpore est non quidem loco sed proprietate substantiae illic circumscripta aut definita. Nam si sequitur humanitatem vbique esse vbi diuinitas est, eandem omnino mensuram vtriusque statuere oportet, & vel diuinitatem humanitate tate cate circumscribere & definire, aut humanitatem cum diuinitate quasi coextendere & infinitam facere. Quam autem diuersa hic ratio sit Diuinitatis & humanitatis ad sumptae, ab anima humana cum corpore vnira Athanasius in lib. de humanitate Verbi eiusq; corporali aduentu ostendit, cuius verba non pigebit adscribere. Non enim (inquit) in corpore re circumclusus erat: neque quum in corpore aderat alibi deerat; neque quum illud moueat bat, alia eius vi a&tu & prouidentia destituta fuere: sed quod sum mae admirationis est, ea omnia ipse, vt ratio a nemine contentus continebat. Et sicuti praesens in omni rerum natura, extra tamen omnia subsistit, quantum attinet ad ipsius substantiam, ita quoque intra omnia habetur, quantum spectat ad ipsius potentiam omnia gubernans, & ad omnia in omnibus suam prouidentiam pandens: singulaque separatim, cunctaque in vniuersum simul viuificans: circumplectens omnia, a nullo circumplexus, sed per omnia quum sese extendat in solo Patre totus & integer permanet. Ita quoque cum esset in humano corpore, atque illud ipse viuificaret, eodem quoque momento viuificabat vniuersa, & in omnibus aderat, & extra vniuersa subsistebat, & quum per corpus operaq; sua innotesceret, ne tum quidem (quantum ad energiam actumq; rerum naturae omnium pertinet) obscuriter las tebat. Mentis haud dubie officium est, cogitationibus, quæ foris extraq; suū corpus comsistunt, contemplari, actum tamen vimquesuā extra corpus non porrigere, nec quæ longinqua sunt, ea sua præsentia mouere: Nuncquam enim homo longinqua cogitans, eaquæ cogitat statim mouet aut transfert. Neque præterea (si quis domi desidens de cœlocogitationes ineat) ideo continuo & solummouerit & cœlum circumuerterit, sed vt eacontuetur in motu & rerū natura existere, itavim suam explicare in ea non potest. Cæterum nequaquam eodem modo Dei Verbumin corpore humano versabatur, vt quod ibinon colligatum esset, sed potius corpus in secontineret, adeo vt & ibi esset, & in omnibusexisteret, & extra rerum essentias versaretur,& in solo Patre requiesceret. Hæc Athana-
units.tr: Moreover, those who affirm that the humanity of Christ is everywhere where his divinity is present, so that just as the body of a man is present wherever the soul is, so the humanity is present wherever the Word [λόγος] is, and unless this is maintained, they say, the natures are separated by place, because Christ is God and man in one place and God only in another. These people, in objecting this to others, conceive overly crude imaginations of the divinity, and seem to think that the divinity is in some way enclosed in the humanity and defined by the bounds of the human nature, just as the soul is in the body, not indeed by place but circumscribed or defined by the property of its substance there. For if it follows that the humanity is everywhere where the divinity is, one must set down exactly the same measure for each: either the divinity must be circumscribed and defined by the humanity, or the humanity must be extended together with the divinity and made infinite. How different the relation of the divinity to the assumed humanity is from that of the human soul to the body united with it, Athanasius shows in his book on the humanity of the Word and his bodily coming, whose words I will not be ashamed to quote. For (he says) he was not enclosed in a body, nor when he was in the body was he absent elsewhere, nor when he moved that body was he destitute of his other power, activity and providence. But, what is most wonderful, he himself contained all these things as the Reason, subject to no one. And just as he is present in the whole nature of things, yet subsists outside all things so far as his substance is concerned, so he is also held within all things so far as his power is concerned, governing all things and displaying his providence over all things in all; separately enlivening single things and together enlivening the universe, embracing all things and embraced by none, but while he extends through all things, he remains whole and entire in the Father alone. So too, when he was in the human body and quickened it, at the same moment he also quickened the universe, and was present in all things, and subsisted outside the universe; and when he made himself known through the body and his works, not even then was he obscurely absent (so far as the energy and activity of all the nature of things is concerned). Doubtless it is the office of the mind to contemplate thoughts which lie outside and beyond its body, yet not to extend its action and power outside the body, nor to move by its presence things that are far off. For a man who thinks of distant things never moves or transfers at once the things he thinks of. Nor, again, if someone sitting at home thinks about the heavens, does he therefore at once move them and turn the heavens around; but though he beholds them in motion and existing in the nature of things, he cannot extend his power into them. Otherwise, the Word of God was in no way in the human body in the same manner, as if it were not bound there, but rather it contained the body, so that it both was there and existed in all things, and dwelt outside the essences of things, and rested in the Father alone. Thus far Athanasius.

units.la: sius cuius verba ideo apposui vt appareat il-los abuti similitudine humanæ animæ & cor-poris, qui inde Vbiquitatem humanæ nātu-ræ in Christo probare volunt, atque vt refu-tarem illos qui ex Athanasio vbiquitatem corporis Christi probare conantur, quia Ora-tione contra Arianos scribit, Iam vero quum eius sit corpus, neq; Verbum sit exa-tra corpus, merito exaltato corpore ipse vt homo exaltatus esse memoratur. Neq; enim his verbis vel verbum corpore circumscribit, vel corpori vbiquitatem tribuit, sed corpus non ñon separatum fuisse à Verbo ait: erat proprium Verbi corpus quod exaltatum est. Sed non eum tribuere coexistentiam talem Verbo & corpori, vt vbi sit Verbum ibi sit corpus, satis eius verba commemorata redarguũt. Apparet autem ex Vigilio tales olim Eutychianorum cogitationes fuisse, vt existimarint vel mensura humanæ naturæ circumscribedam diuinam naturam, vel humanitatem cum illa per omnia diffundendam. Disserit autem hic auctor valde perspicue de tota hac controuersia, sed ex illo pauciora testimonia adfero, quod velim hunc integrum vna cum Theodoreto diligenter ad totius controuersiæ explicationem cognosci.
units.tr: I have quoted these words of Athanasius so that it may appear that those men abuse the likeness of the human soul and body, who from it wish to prove the ubiquity of the human nature in Christ. I have also quoted them to refute those who try to prove from Athanasius the ubiquity of the body of Christ, because in his Oration against the Arians he writes: "Now since it is his body, and the Word is not outside the body, the body having been exalted, he himself is said to have been exalted as man." For in these words he neither confines the Word within the body nor ascribes ubiquity to the body; he says only that the body was not separated from the Word, and that the body which was exalted was the proper body of the Word. That he does not attribute to the Word and the body such a coexistence that wherever the Word is, there the body is, is sufficiently refuted by the words I have cited. Moreover, it appears from Vigilius that such thoughts of the Eutychians existed long ago, namely that they judged either that the divine nature was to be circumscribed by the measure of the human nature, or that the humanity was to be spread through all things together with it. This author discusses the whole of this controversy very clearly, but I cite only a few of his testimonies from him. I would like him to be read in full, together with Theodoret, for a diligent explanation of the whole controversy.

units.la: De sessione ad dexteram Dei Patris.
units.tr: On the sitting at the right hand of God the Father.

units.la: Inter alia argumenta quibus Vbiquistæ vntur, hoc inter præcipua vnum est: Dextera Dei est vbique. Christus secundum humanitatem suam sedet ad dexteram Dei. Ergo Christus secundum humanitatem suam est vbique. Item Dextera Dei non est locus, ergo Christus qui humanitate sua ad dexteram Dei sedet, non est in loco. Si Christus per sessionem ad dexteram Dei, humanitate sua non est vbique sed in cœlo tantum, tum sequitur eum non ad totam dexteram Dei sed ad partem eius sedere. Staruerat hoc argumentum sæpe à nostris confutatum præterire, sed quia
units.tr: Among the arguments the Ubiquitists use, one of the chief is this: the right hand of God is everywhere; Christ according to his humanity sits at the right hand of God; therefore Christ according to his humanity is everywhere. Likewise, the right hand of God is not a place; therefore Christ, who sits at the right hand of God in his humanity, is not in a place. If Christ, by sitting at the right hand of God, is not everywhere in his humanity but only in heaven, it follows that he does not sit at the whole right hand of God but at a part of it. Our people have often refuted this argument, and it had been their practice to pass it over, but because

units.la: ascensionem in cœlos, & sessionem ad Dexteram Dei cum vnione personali confundut deea quoque aliquid dicendum existimatur. Quoniam vero hæc in symbolo fidei nostræ distinctè proponuntur, Qui conceptus est ex Spiritu sancto, natus ex Maria virgine, Ascen dit in cœlos, Sedet ad dexterā Dei patris omni potentis, feruemus nos hanc distinctionem neque hæc confundamus. Nam & idipsum scriptura testatur, Christum excitatū à mortuis, & dextera Dei euectum ascendisse in cœlum, & sedere ad dexteram Patris. Ita etiam sacra historia tradit Christum assumptum in cœlum consedisse à dexteris Dei. Christus ipse à resurrectione dicebat discipulis, Nonne hæc oportuit pati Christū, & introire in gloriam suam? Similiter in epistola ad Hebræos traditur Christum victimam se obtulisse pro peccatis, & cruce pertulisse, & in perpetuum ad dexteram throni Dei consedisse. Sed Vbi quitarij, qui sessionem ad dexterā nihil aliud esse definiunt, quàm Christum cum Deo Patre suo æquali esse maiestate & omnipotentia, aiunt hoc factum esse quando assumpsit humanitatem in Deum, atque ita ab ipsa incarnatione Christum collocatum ad dexteram Dei, sed post resurrectionem man feliciter & declaratam esse sessionem quàm semper habuerit. Non quæro iam de sessione ad dexteram quomodo hæc Christo secundum humanam naturam tribuatur, hoc primum arguo, quod confunduntur distincti articuli fidei, deinde quod sessio contra scripturam tribuitur humanitati Christi ab ipsa incarnatione. Scholastici quidem docent dexteram Dei trifariam accipi, & aliquando significare gloriam & honorem deitatis, sedere autem ad dexteram significare quandoque convenientiam, quod hic habeat gloriam deitatis cum quadam tamen distinctione, atque sic Christum secundum divinam naturam sedere ad dexteram Patris, quod eandem cum patre naturam & deitatem habeat, atque ita sit patri aequalis, quamvis sit alia persona: alio autem modo secundum gratiam unionis hominem Christum sedere ad dexteram Patris, secundum quod homo est Filius Dei: non quod haec humanae naturae conveniant, ut haec in se habeat, sed quod hoc secundum unitatem personae aut suppositi illi tribuatur, quod eodem honore veneramur filium Dei cum natura assumpta. Itaque si naturas in Christo spectamus, secundum divinam naturam, sessio ad dexteram significat aequalitatem patris; secundum humanam naturam beatitudinem maiorem caeteris creaturis & iudiciariam potestatem signi ficat: at ratione personae, Christum secundum quod homo est quoque priori modo ad dexteram patris sedere. Atque si ita de sessione loquerentur Brentiani ferri possent, nunc quae personæ sunt naturę tribuunt, & omnem gloriam & æqualitatem deitatis, seßione hac humanæ carni per transfusionem quandam communicatam volunt. Scripturæ ita dicūt Christum sedere ad dexteram Dei, vt sanƈti quoq; cum illo confideant ad dexteram Dei: Consedere nos fecit cum ipso in cœlestibus. Item Vincenti & seruanti opera mea vsq; in finem, dabo potestatem super gentes, & reget eas in virga ferrea, sicut & ego accepi à Patre meo. Apoc. 2. Rursus Ibidem 3 cap. Qui vi-cerit dabo ei sedere mecum in sede mea sicut & ego vici, & sedi cum Patre meo in sede ipsius. Hæc autem non possunt intelligi de æqualitate maiestatis quam humanæ naturæ tribuunt aduersarij ratione vnionis, nam vt vnio ita hæc quæ vnione accepit, genere toto differunt à præsentia & operatione Deitatis in sanƈtis.
units.tr: they think that the ascension into heaven and the sitting at the right hand of God are confused with the personal union, something must be said about these matters too. Since these articles are set out distinctly in our confession of faith, "He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty," we keep this distinction and do not confuse these things. Scripture itself testifies to this: that Christ, raised from the dead and carried up by the right hand of God, ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. Sacred history likewise relates that Christ, taken up into heaven, sat down at the right hand of God. Christ himself, after the resurrection, said to his disciples, "Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?" Similarly, the epistle to the Hebrews tells us that Christ offered himself as a sacrifice for sins, endured the cross, and sat down forever at the right hand of the throne of God. But the Ubiquitists, who define the sitting at the right hand as nothing other than Christ being equal in majesty and omnipotence with God his Father, say that this came about when he assumed humanity into God, and that thus from the incarnation itself Christ was placed at the right hand of God; but after the resurrection this sitting was openly declared and made manifest, though it had always been his. I am not now asking how this sitting at the right hand is ascribed to Christ according to his human nature. I argue first that distinct articles of faith are confused, and second that the sitting is ascribed to the humanity of Christ, against Scripture, from the incarnation itself. The Schoolmen indeed teach that the right hand of God is taken in three ways, and sometimes signifies the glory and honour of the deity; and that to sit at the right hand sometimes signifies a fellowship, namely that Christ, according to the divine nature, has the glory of the deity, yet with a certain distinction, and so sits at the right hand of the Father, because he has the same nature and deity as the Father and so is equal to him, although he is another person. In another way, however, the man Christ sits at the right hand of the Father by the grace of the union, insofar as he is the Son of God as man: not that these things belong to the human nature so that it possesses them in itself, but that they are ascribed to it on account of the unity of the person or supposit, because we venerate the Son of God with the same honour as the assumed nature. Thus, if we look at the natures in Christ: according to the divine nature the sitting at the right hand signifies equality with the Father; according to the human nature it signifies a greater blessedness than other creatures and judicial power; but by reason of the person, Christ, insofar as he is man, also sits at the right hand of the Father in the first way. And if the Brentians spoke of the sitting in this way, they could be tolerated; but now they assign to the nature what belongs to the person, and they want all the glory and equality of the deity to be communicated to the flesh by a certain transfusion through this sitting. The Scriptures say that Christ sits at the right hand of God in such a way that the saints also sit with him at the right hand of God: "He made us sit together with him in the heavenly places." Likewise: "To him who overcomes and keeps my works until the end, I will give power over the nations, and he shall rule them with an iron rod, as I also received from my Father" (Apoc. 2). Again, in the same book, chapter 3: "He who overcomes, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne." But these things cannot be understood of the equality of majesty that our adversaries attribute to the human nature by reason of the union. For, just as the union itself, so also what has been received by the union differs entirely in kind from the presence and operation of the Deity in the saints.

units.la: Porro argumentum hoc, Dexteram Dei esse vbique: Humanitatem esse ad dexteram Dei: ergo humanitatē esse vbique: est vitiosum & sophisticum: nàm vt firma esset conclusio oporteret sumere, Humanitatem esse dexteram: Filio autem Dei secundum diui-nam naturam non tantum tribuitur quòd sedeat ad dexteram Dei, sed etiam quòd sit dextera Patris, hoc vero de humana natura dici non potest. Quod si dicunt dexteram Dei significare maiestatem, imperium, gubernatio-nem nem omnium rerum,cum autemChriftus fe‑deat ad dexteram, hoc est cum Deo Patre re‑gnet, oportere humanam naturam quæ ad dexteram Patris sedet, vbique prefentem esse, quoniam Deus omnia vbique præfens regat: hæc erit eorû hypothesis, Id quod est ad dex‑tera Dei quia dextera infinita & vbique præ‑fens est,idipsum quoque vbique prefens esse. Sed his nostri recte responderunt verbis D. Augustini. Non est autem consequens vt quod in Deo est,ita fit vbique vt Deus. Nam & denobis verissima scriptura dicit, quod in illo viuimus mouemur & fumus, nec tamen sicut ille vbique fumus, sed aliter homo ille in Deo, quoniam aliter & Deus ille in homi‑ne proprio quodam & singulari modo. Vna enim persona Deus & homo est, & vtrunque est vnus Christus Iesus, vbique per id quod Deus est, in cœlo autem per id quod homo. Conantur aduersarij hanc sententiam elude‑re,quod Augustinus tantum comparatę neget omniprælentiam carnis Christi,quòd nó vt diuinitas hoc est eo modo quo diuinitas sed alio modo omniprælens fit:sed hoc est me‑rum sophisma:nam mox hęc inter fe opponit quod vt Deus vbique fit,&quod per id quod homo, hoc est fecundum humanam naturam in cœlo fit. Supra etiam : Secundum homi‑nem (inquit) in terra erat, non in cœlo vbi nunc est : item Christum ait iuxta humanam humilitatem per carnem fuisse in sepulchro, per animam in inferno, iuxta diuinam immutabilitatem, quia semper vbique est nunquam de paradiso receßit, ac subijcit, Noli itaque dubitare ibi nunc esse hominé Iesum Christum, vnde venturus est, memoriterque recole & fideliter tene Christianam confessionem, quoniam resurrexit à mortuis, ascendit in cœlum, sedet ad dexteram Patris, necnon inde venturus est ad viuos mortuos tuosque iudicandos. Et sic venturus est illa angelica voce testante, quemadmodum ire vidistis in cœlum, id est in eadem carnis forma atque substantia cui profecto immortalitatem dedit, naturam non abstulit. Secundum hanc formam non est putandus vbique diffusus. Cauendum est enim, ne ita diuinitatem adstruamus hominis, vt veritatem corporis auferamus. His subijcit ea verba quae nos ante adduximus: quae si bene expendantur facile apparebit vbiquitatem corporis Christi ne quaquam ab Augustino asseri. Neque licet hic vti vsitato sophismate quod Augustinus loquatur de humana natura in se considerata, non autem de modo maiestatis. Nam iubet ita diuinitatem hominis adstruere ne tollatur veritas humanae naturae: siue autem diuinitatem hominis intelligamus, maiestatem diuinam homini communicatâ qualem Adversarij fingunt; siue diuinitatem veram, quâ homo
units.tr: Moreover, this argument, "The right hand of God is everywhere; the humanity is at the right hand of God; therefore the humanity is everywhere," is faulty and sophistical. For to make the conclusion valid one would have to assume, "The humanity is the right hand." But to the Son of God according to the divine nature is ascribed not only that he sits at the right hand of God, but also that he is the right hand of the Father, and this cannot be said of the human nature. And if they say that the right hand of God signifies majesty, dominion, and the government of all things, and that since Christ sits at the right hand, that is, reigns together with God the Father, the human nature which sits at the right hand of the Father must be present everywhere, since God rules all things present everywhere: this will be their hypothesis, that what is at the right hand of God, because the right hand is infinite and present everywhere, is itself also present everywhere. But our people have answered this rightly in the words of St. Augustine: "It does not follow that what is in God is everywhere in the way God is everywhere. For Scripture says truly of us too, that in him we live, move, and are, and yet we are not everywhere as he is; rather that man is in God in a way peculiar to himself and singular, just as that God is in man in a peculiar and singular way. For God and man are one person, and both are one Christ Jesus, everywhere through that which is God, but in heaven through that which is man." The adversaries try to evade this opinion by saying that Augustine denies only the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ when compared with the divinity, namely that it is not made omnipresent as the divinity is, that is, in the same way as the divinity, but in another way. But this is mere sophistry, for he immediately sets over against this that he is everywhere as God, and that through that which is man, that is, according to the human nature, he is in heaven. Earlier too he says: "According to the man he was on earth, not in heaven where he now is"; likewise he says that Christ, according to the human lowliness, was in the sepulchre through the flesh and in hell through the soul, but according to the divine immutability he is always everywhere and never departed from paradise; and he adds: "Do not doubt that the man Jesus Christ is now there, whence he is to come, and hold in memory and faithfully keep the Christian confession, that he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and from there is to come to judge the living and the dead, and your dead. And thus he is to come, as that angelic voice testifies, just as you saw him go into heaven, that is, in the same form and substance of the flesh, to which indeed he gave immortality but did not take away its nature. According to this form he is not to be thought to be diffused everywhere. For we must take care lest we so affirm the divinity of the man that we take away the truth of the body." To these he adds the words we cited before, which, if they are weighed carefully, will easily show that the ubiquity of the body of Christ is by no means asserted by Augustine. Nor is it permissible here to use the common sophism that Augustine speaks of the human nature considered in itself, and not of the mode of majesty. For he bids us affirm the divinity of the man in such a way that the truth of the human nature is not removed; whether we understand the divinity of the man as the divine majesty communicated to the man, such as the adversaries imagine, or as the true divinity by which the man

units.la: Chapter catchword: homo hic est Deus, vna exi{s}tete persona Verbi & hominis, tamen monet vt hominis diuinitate, nec per vnionem seu assumptionem, nec per communicatione maiestatis, humanæ naturæ veritatem negemus, illam scilicet veritatem circumscriptæ formæ & substantiæ quam supra docuit.
units.tr: Chapter catchword: Here the one Person of the Word and the man is God, yet he warns that by the union or assumption, and by the communication of majesty, we must not deny the truth of the human nature, namely that truth of a circumscribed form and substance which he taught above.

units.la: Præterea si in ipsa incarnatione Christi caro collocata est ad dexteram Dei, aut si post resurrectionem carnem suam Christus eduxit ad dexteram patris, talem vtiq; carnem eduxit qualem assumpsit, & qualem à resurrectione habuit, hoc est finitam & humanæ naturæ proprietates seruantem, neque veritatem naturæ humanæ & proprietatum eius sessio ad dexteram aboleuit, nam vt Augustinus ait, Christus immortalitatem carni suæ dedit, naturam non abstulit: & Eutychianum est affirmare naturam sublatam, aut quod idem est proprietates naturæ sublatas, nam recte VI. synodus affirmat, naturarum proprietates tollentes, ipsas naturas tollere. Itaque sicut λόγος assumpsit humanam naturam seruata tamen proprietate humanæ naturæ, sic eandem in sua hypostasi vt assumpsit, ita quoque ad dexteram Patris collocauit, seruata veritate naturæ, quamuis eam supra omnes alias creaturas cœlestibus donis ornarit. Atque ita docuit vetus ecclesia, humanitate Christi in forma serui & nostræ naturæ proprietate sedere ad dexteram Dei, & inter corporalis absentiæ, & veri corporis argumenta ab illis ponitur sessio ad dexteram: atque huic præsentiam Maiestatis opponunt: id quod vno atque alte-ro testimonio ostendisse faterit. Theodore-tus Dialogo 2, Corpus Domini quod resur-rexit, à corruptione quidem & interitu alie-num & impassibile, & immortale & diuina gloria glorificatum, & sessione ad dexteram patris dignatum est, & à cœlestibus adoratur potestatibus, corpus tamé est, & habet quam prius habuit, formam, figuram, & circumscri-ptione. Augustinus etiā in his quæ supra ad-duximus dicit, Christum secundum formam & substantiam carnis qua in cœlos ascendit & sedet ad dexteră Dei, & inde venturus est ad iudicandum, non esse vbique diffusum. Et alibi ait, Secundum carnem quam verbū af-sumpsit, & corporis præsentiam, ascendit in cœlum, & non est hic (ibi enim sedet ad dex-teram Patris) & hic est, non enim recessit præ-sentia maiestatis. Forma serui leuata est in cœlum: in ipsa sedet ad dexteram Dei Patris, in ipsa venturus est ad iudicium. Fuit autem, vt ibi appareat, Arianorum sententia, Formam serui resurrectione consumptam, quod Augustinus negat, & eam manere docet, sed in me-lius commutatam, & propter serui formam dicere Christū, Ascendo ad Deum meum, & propter eandem formā post iudiciū subiectū fore ei qui subiecit illi omnia. Forma serui liberata est infirmitate, non tamen exæquata formæ Dei. Cyrillus. Nam etsi abest corporé Patri pro nobis apparens, ac à dexteris eius sedens, habitat tamen in sanctis per spiritum.
units.tr: Moreover, if the flesh was placed at the right hand of God in the very incarnation of Christ, or if after the resurrection Christ brought his flesh up to the right hand of the Father, then he certainly brought it up as he had assumed it and as he had it from the resurrection, that is, finite and preserving the properties of human nature. The session at the right hand has not abolished the truth of the human nature or its properties. For, as Augustine says, Christ gave immortality to his flesh but did not take away its nature. To affirm that the nature is taken away, or what is the same, that its properties are taken away, is Eutychian. For the Sixth Synod rightly affirms that those who take away the properties of the natures take away the natures themselves. Therefore, just as the Word assumed human nature while preserving its human properties, so he placed that same nature at the right hand of the Father in his own hypostasis, as he had assumed it, preserving the truth of the nature, although he adorned it with heavenly gifts above all other creatures. And so the ancient Church taught that the humanity of Christ, in the form of a servant and with the property of our nature, sits at the right hand of God. Among the proofs of bodily absence and of a true body, they set the session at the right hand, and they oppose to this the presence of majesty. Theodoret has shown this by one and another testimony. In Dialogue 2: The body of the Lord which rose, free from corruption and death, impassible and immortal, glorified with divine glory and honoured with the session at the right hand of the Father, and adored by the heavenly powers, is nonetheless a body, and has the form, figure and circumscription which it had before. Augustine also, in the passages we have quoted above, says that Christ according to the form and substance of the flesh in which he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God, and from whence he will come to judge, is not diffused everywhere. And elsewhere he says: According to the flesh which the Word assumed, and the presence of the body, he ascended into heaven and is not here (for there he sits at the right hand of the Father), and yet he is here, for the presence of his majesty has not withdrawn. The form of the servant was lifted up into heaven; in that form he sits at the right hand of God the Father, and in that form he will come to judgment. Now, so that it may appear there, this was the opinion of the Arians: that the form of the servant was consumed by the resurrection. Augustine denies this, and teaches that it remains, but changed for the better, and that Christ on account of the form of the servant says, I ascend to my God, and on account of the same form he will be made subject after judgment to him who subjected all things to him. The form of the servant was freed from infirmity, yet not made equal to the form of God. Cyril: For although the body that appeared for us is absent from the Father, and sits at his right hand, he nonetheless dwells in the saints through the Spirit.

units.la: Præterea grauissimā consolationem inde perfuntpiæ mentes, quod caro nostra in Christo sedet ad dexteram Dei, unde Tertullianus inquit eum à nobis arrhabonē carnis accepisse & in cœlos euexisse, pignus totius summæ illius quandoque redigendæ. Et Augustinus: Quod ex nobis suscepit in cœlum leuauit, & ad dexteram patris collocauit, & fidei nostræ certū pignus dedit, quod membra sunt ipsum secutura. De tanto igitur capite fideliter speràrent, ad ipsum se posse peruenire, quem iam credunt ad dexterâ Patris sedere. Regnat homo susceптus à Christo, ad dexteram Patris sedens, & vt sui regnum ab eo accipiant, vocat inuitat & hortatur. At si humana natura in Christo sedens ad dexteram Patris, humanæ naturæ proprietates exuit, & toto genere dissimilis est nostræ (talem autem aduersarij statuunt, vtcunque id verbis negent) quę nostra est communio cum carne Christi? Conci dit hac ratione spes nostra.
units.tr: Moreover, pious minds draw very great comfort from this, that our flesh sits at the right hand of God in Christ. Hence Tertullian says that he received from us the pledge of the flesh and carried it up into heaven, the guarantee of that whole sum which is one day to be restored. And Augustine: What he took from us he lifted up into heaven, and placed at the right hand of the Father, and gave a sure pledge of our faith, that the members will follow him. Therefore, from so great a head they might faithfully hope that they can come to him whom they now believe to sit at the right hand of the Father. The man taken up by Christ reigns, sitting at the right hand of the Father, and he calls, invites and exhorts us to receive his kingdom from him. But if the human nature in Christ, sitting at the right hand of the Father, has put off the properties of human nature, and is wholly unlike ours (and our opponents set this up, however much they deny it in words), what communion do we have with the flesh of Christ? By this reasoning our hope collapses.

units.la: Præterea præsentia corporis & sanguinis Christi in cœna Domini non statuitur sessio ne ad dexteram Dei, tale enim corpus nobis in cœna ad manducandum datur quale pro nobis est in mortem traditum. Nam vt Augustinus inquit, Sacramentum est illius corporis quod visibile, palpabile & mortale in cruce positum immolatum q; fuit. Et Christus ipse loquitur de corpore suo pro nobis tradito, & sanguine suo pro nobis effuso. Alius autem est modus corporis traditi pro nobis, alius modus maiestatis quem Brentiani statuunt ex sessione ad dexteram Dei.
units.tr: Moreover, the presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Lord's Supper is not placed in the session at the right hand of God. For such a body is given to us in the supper to eat as was given up for us to death. For, as Augustine says, it is a sacrament of that body which was visible, palpable and mortal, placed on the cross and sacrificed. And Christ himself speaks of his body given for us and his blood poured out for us. But the mode of the body given for us is one thing, and the mode of majesty, which the Brentians set up from the session at the right hand of God, is another.

units.la: Futile etiam est argumentum, Dextera Dei non est locus, Christus humana natura seu in carne sua sedet ad dexteram Dei, ergo humana natura Christi non est in loco. Si concludant sessionem Christi non esse localem situm, aut sessionem, non contenderemus cum illis: sed non ideo quia dextera Dei non est locus, corpori Christi circumscriptio & certum vbi seu locus debet adimi. Nam alioqui ita quoque argumentari liceret: Dextera Dei est infinita, Corpus Christi sedet ad dexteram Dei, Ergo est infinitum. Item Dextera Dei non est corpus, Caro Christi sedet ad dexteram Dei, Ergo caro Christi non est corpus. Item Dextera Dei non est visibilis aut palpabilis, ergo Christi corpus non est visibile aut palpabile. Ac forte aliquas harum consecutionum nonnulli probabunt, & nos ridebunt qui ra crasse sentiamus de corpore Christi: sed nos scripturis inhaerentes maiestatis eorum figmenta & dispensationes non curamus, cū sciamus veteres
units.tr: The argument is also futile: the right hand of God is not a place; Christ sits in his human nature, or in his flesh, at the right hand of God; therefore the human nature of Christ is not in a place. If they conclude that the session of Christ is not a local position, we would not contend with them on that. But it does not follow, because the right hand of God is not a place, that a circumscription and a definite where, or place, must be taken away from the body of Christ. For otherwise one could argue in this way too: The right hand of God is infinite; the body of Christ sits at the right hand of God; therefore it is infinite. Likewise: The right hand of God is not a body; the flesh of Christ sits at the right hand of God; therefore the flesh of Christ is not a body. Likewise: The right hand of God is not visible or palpable; therefore the body of Christ is not visible or palpable. Perhaps some will approve some of these consequences and laugh at us who think too crudely about the body of Christ. But we, adhering to the Scriptures, do not care about their fictions and distinctions of majesty, since we know that the ancients too understood plainly those Scriptures which ascribe to Christ a visible form and a palpable body.

units.la: De fide ad Petrum. veteres quoque simpliciter scripturas, quę visibilem formam, & palpabile corpus Christo tribuunt, intellexisse: unde Gelasius contra Eutychianos qui humanitatis in Deum transfusionem quandā fingebant sic scribit. Nam si & substantia & forma Christi, &c. Neque firmius est alterū. Si Christus sessione ad dexteram Dei non sit ubique humanitate sua, tum eum sedere ad partem dexterae. Dextera enim Dei loco non definitur, & tota est in mi nima quaque re, & tota etiam est in toto universo, tota est ubique. Nam dexteram Dei maiestate & potentia adversarii definiunt, huius autem eadem cum essentia ratio, cum non aliud sit in Deo potentia & essentia. Quod si Christus sedet in coelo ad partē dexterae Dei, pars duntaxat dexterae Dei in coelo est: si autem tota dextera Dei in coelo est, quid prohibet quo minus corpus Christi in coelo maneat & non ubique sit, atque nihilominus ad totam Dexteram Dei sedeat?
units.tr: On the Faith to Peter. The ancients too: Gelasius, against the Eutychians, who imagined a certain transfusion of humanity into God, writes thus: For if both the substance and the form of Christ, etc. Nor is the other alternative any firmer. If Christ, by his session at the right hand of God, is not everywhere in his humanity, then he sits at a part of the right hand. For the right hand of God is not bounded by place; it is whole in the smallest thing, and whole in the whole universe, whole everywhere. For our opponents define the right hand of God by majesty and power, but the reason for this is the same as for his essence, since in God power and essence are not different. But if Christ sits in heaven at a part of the right hand of God, then only a part of the right hand of God is in heaven. If, however, the whole right hand of God is in heaven, what prevents the body of Christ from remaining in heaven and not being everywhere, while nonetheless sitting at the whole right hand of God?

units.la: An Christi corpus propter conceptionem ex Spiritu sancto habeat praeter naturales proprietates, ita ut ubiq; praesens esse possit.
units.tr: Whether the body of Christ, because of its conception by the Holy Spirit, has properties beyond the natural ones, so that it can be present everywhere.

units.la: Sicut ex unione personali ita ex conceptione e Spiritu sancto quidam Omnipraesentiam corpori Christi tribuunt, atq; aiunt corpus hoc quod conceptum sit ex Spiritu sancto multas praeternaturales proprietates habere, ac dissimile esse nostris corporibus, itaq; non constare hanc rationem: Nostra corpora non possunt vbique esse, ergo corpus Christi non potest vbique esse: hoc enim corpus inquiut ex Virgine natum est non de viri femine, clau fis ingreditur ostijs & per lapidem sepulchri, earnalibus legibus nó est subditum, & omnia humana transcendit: formatio huius corpo† ris in vtero virginis ex Spiritu sancto, conue† nit vnitioni diuinae & humanae naturę, ac ati tulit prĵternaturalia idiomata, ita vt Christus fecundum vtranque naturam vbique fit præ• fens. Est autem hoc non nouum argumen• tum, sed eo Eutychiani quoque veritate hu• manæ naturæ abnegantes vsi sunt, & longe ante hos simili argumento, Origenes refurre• stione carnis negauit, vt refert Hieronymus ad Pammachiu, imo hoc argumento vsi sunt omnes quotquot humanae naturae veritatem in Christo seruatore nostro abnegarunt. Etsi vero ab his plurimum sibi differre videntur nostrae aetatis Vbiquitarij, tamen eadem fere ex eorum dogmatibus sequuntur, vt non mi rum fit eosdem paribus argumentis vti. Fa• tentur fe in Christo agnoscere humanam na• turam, itemproprietates substantiales, atta• men neque quae illae sunt explicant, & illas proprietates quæ veri & organici corporis propriæ sunt, feparabiles & accidentarias ef• fe volunt, quas Christus exuerit: & contra di• uinae
units.tr: Just as they ascribe omnipresence to the body of Christ on the basis of the personal union, so some also ascribe it on the basis of the conception by the Holy Spirit. They say that the body conceived by the Holy Spirit has many supernatural properties and is unlike our bodies. So, they argue, this inference does not hold: our bodies cannot be everywhere, therefore the body of Christ cannot be everywhere. For, they say, this body was born of the Virgin and not from a man's seed; it enters through closed doors and passes through the stone of the sepulchre; it is not subject to the laws of nature and surpasses all human things. The formation of this body in the Virgin's womb by the Holy Spirit, they say, fits the union of the divine and human natures, and so it has carried supernatural attributes, so that Christ is present everywhere according to both natures. This is not a new argument, however. The Eutychians also used it when they denied the truth of human nature, and long before them Origen, as Jerome reports in his letter to Pammachius, denied the resurrection of the flesh by a similar argument. Indeed, all who have denied the truth of human nature in Christ our Saviour have used this argument. Although the Ubiquitarians of our own age seem to differ greatly from these, nevertheless almost the same consequences follow from their doctrines, so it is no wonder that they use similar arguments. They confess that they recognise in Christ a human nature and its substantial properties, but they neither explain what these are, nor do they want those properties that belong to a true and organic body to be separable and accidental, which Christ has put off. And, on the contrary, the divine

units.la: Veteres haeretici eodem argum. vsi sunt. uīnæ naturæ idiomata,ac proprietates quasi-dam supernaturales corpori Christi tribuūr, quæ tam sunt alienæ à humana natura, vt nunquam humana natura hæc habere possit saluis suis essentialibus & naturalibus pro-prietatibus,nisi contradictoria simul vera ef-se possint: quod quidam eorū contra omnem rationem & cōtra scripturas affirmare audēt, solo argumento omnipotentiæ id euincere volentes.Longe autem aliter ex scripturis do-cuit vetus ecclesia cum de alijs dogmatibus, tum de hac ipsa Conceptione ex Spiritu san-ćto: Sed quid ad hos vetus ecclesia, quos non pudet loca scripturæ plurima, & articulos fi-dei apertissimos noua ratione interpretari, & allegorias, tropos, figuras nouas & inauditas fingere, tantummodo ne cogantur tropum admittere in verbis cœnæ Domini?Cęterum quod ad proprietates supernaturales corpo-ris Christi attinet, fatemur præter naturam qua reliqui homines nascimur & concipi-mur, multa diuinitus data corpori Christi: nos in peccatis nascimur & cōcipimur,Chri-sti humana natura ab omni peccato pura & vacua fuit, Christi corpus ex Spiritu sanćto conceptum ex virgine natum est, longe ali-ter nostra corpora generantur & nascuntur: corpus Christi est proprium corpus pora nostra esi à Deo accepimus & ab eo su-stentantur & conseruantur, tamen non sunt corpus filij Dei, nec ab eo ideo facta sunt vt sua ipsius separatim sint, nec illi vnita & proprium Verbi indumentum & quasi instrumentum sunt vt illud corpus quod ex Virgine assumpsit.
units.tr: The ancient heretics used the same argument: the attributes and properties of the divine nature, certain supernatural properties, are ascribed to the body of Christ, and these are so foreign to human nature that human nature could never have them while keeping its essential and natural properties, unless contradictories could be true at once. Some of them dare to affirm this against all reason and against the Scriptures, wanting to prove it by the argument of omnipotence alone. But the ancient Church taught quite differently from Scripture, both about other doctrines and about this very conception by the Holy Spirit. But what has the ancient Church to do with these men, who are not ashamed to interpret very many passages of Scripture and the most plain articles of faith in a new way, and to invent new and unheard-of allegories, tropes and figures, only so that they need not admit a trope in the words of the Lord's Supper? Moreover, as far as the supernatural properties of the body of Christ are concerned, we confess that, beyond the nature by which the rest of mankind are born and conceived, many gifts were divinely given to the body of Christ. We are born and conceived in sins; Christ's human nature was pure and free from all sin; the body of Christ, conceived by the Holy Spirit, was born of a virgin. Our bodies are generated and born in a far different way. The body of Christ is the proper body of the Son of God. Our bodies, indeed, we have received from God, and are sustained and preserved by him, yet they are not the body of the Son of God, nor were they made by him so that they might be separately their own, nor are they united to him and are his proper garment and, as it were, instrument, as the body that he assumed from the Virgin is.

units.la: Interea nihilominus ipsum Christi corpus quoad omnes naturales humani corporis proprietates nostris corporibus per omnia simile factum est vno peccato excepto. Quare non debent tribui corpori Christi huiusmodi proprietates supranaturales quae veri & naturalis corporis proprietates tollant: etsi enim origine differt a nostris, non tamen nascendi varietas naturâ corporis mutauit. Itaque
units.tr: Meanwhile, nonetheless, the body of Christ itself, in all the natural properties of the human body, has been made in every way like our bodies, with the single exception of sin. Therefore such supernatural properties, which abolish the true and natural properties of a body, ought not to be ascribed to the body of Christ. For although its origin differs from ours, the difference in the manner of birth has not changed the nature of the body. Therefore:

units.la: » D. Hieronymus. Vis (inquit) & quantum hu-manae generationis genus audire? Spiritus sanctus superueniet in te, & virtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi. Propterea quod nascetur ex te sanctum, vocabitur filius Dei. Aliter Adam, aliter Eua, aliter Abel, aliter homo Iesus Christus. Et in omnibus diuersis exordijs vna hominis natura no differt. Athanasius de humanitate Christi & corporali eius aduentu,
units.tr: Jerome: "Do you want, he says, to hear the kind and the extent of human generation? The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Because that which is born of you will be holy, it will be called the Son of God. Adam was made one way, Eve another, Abel another, and the man Jesus Christ another. Yet in all these different beginnings the nature of man does not differ." Athanasius, on the humanity of Christ and his bodily coming:

units.la: » Corpus Christi inquit, quod miraculo ex vir-gine coaluerat, communem tamen habebat naturam. Leo, Noua autem natiuitate gene-ratus, quia inuiolata virginitas concupiscentiam nescuit, carnis materiam ministrauit.
units.tr: "The body of Christ, he says, which had been formed by a miracle from the virgin, nevertheless had a common nature." Leo: "But born by a new birth, because the inviolate virginity knew no lust, he supplied the matter of the flesh."

units.la: » Adsumpta est igitur de matre Domini natu-ra non culpa, nec in Domino Iesu Christo, exvtero virginis genito, quia natiuitas est mira bilis, ideo nostræ est naturæ dissimilis. Item, An forte ideo putauit Dominum nostrū Ie sum Christum, non nostræ esse naturæ, quia missus ad beatam Mariam angelus ait:Spiri tus sanctus superueniet in te, & virtus altissi mi obumbrabit tibi. Ideoque & quod nasce tur ex te sanctū, vocabitur Filius Dei, vt quia conceptus virginis diuini fuit operis, non de natura concipientis fieret caro concepti? Sed ita non est intelligenda illa generatio singu lariter mirabilis & mirabiliter singularis, vt per nouitatem creationis, proprietas remota sit generis. Fœcunditatem enim virgini Spi ritus sanctus dedit, veritas autè corporis sum pta de corpore est, & ædificante sibi sapientia domum, Verbum caro factum est, & habita uit in nobis, hoc est in ea carne, quam sum psit ex homine, & quam spiritus vitæ ratio nalis animauit.
units.tr: "Therefore the nature taken from the Lord's mother was without fault, and in the Lord Jesus Christ, born from the virgin's womb, because the birth is wonderful, it is for that reason unlike our nature." Likewise: "Or perhaps he thought that our Lord Jesus Christ was not of our nature, because the angel sent to the blessed Mary said: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and therefore that which is born of you will be called the Son of God, so that, since the virgin's conception was a work of God, the flesh of the one conceived would not come from the nature of the one conceiving? But that generation is not to be understood in such a way, singularly wonderful and wonderfully unique, that through the novelty of the creation the property of the kind is removed. For the Holy Spirit gave fruitfulness to the virgin, but the truth of the body was taken from the body, and 'wisdom building for herself a house', 'the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us', that is, in that flesh which he took from man, and which a rational spirit of life animated."

units.la: Porro exempla quæ afferunt non probant carnem Christi ex conceptione supranatu rales proprietates accepisse, Ambulauit super aquas. Sed Petrus etiam super aquas ambula uit, graui & solido corpore (inquit Hieronÿ mus) mollis vnda non cedit, paululum fides dubitat, & statim naturam suam corpus intel ligit, vt sciamus super aquas non corpus am bulasse sed fidem. Et Euphemius vt in sexta synodo habetur, de ambulatione super aquas scribit ex ambulatione quæ pedum naturalis est operatio, proprietatem humanæ naturæ apparere, qua conseruata in natura humana vltra naturam operatum esse Christū Deum super fluctus ambulando:greßum quidem es se corporalem & sensibilem:ambulare autem super mare Deitatis fuisse per humanā carne operāris. Aiunt corpus hoc Clausis ostijs ingredi,& per lapide sepulchri trásire.Non quę to iam an ita factum fit vt aduersarij asserūt, quādo clausis ostijs potuit ita ingredi sicut Petrus clausis ostijs è carcere egressus est, illis prius apertis:neq; quæro an lapis sepulchri aut te resurrectione corporis Christi à sepulchro remotus fuerit, neq; hæc miracula in dubiū reuoco. Sed inde non inferri posse contendo corpus Christi nō seruasse naturales proprietates,hæc enim non proprietate prætematu- rali corporis Christi euenerunt, sed hæc virtus Dei fuit (vt rursus Hieronymi verbis vtar) & creatura cessit creatori. Ex miraculo vno extraordinario non est statuendū de proprietate rei : alioqui dicemus Mosen nō opus habuisse cibo quia quadraginta diebus absque cibo in monte vixit : & dicemus corpora sociorum Danielis fuisse ἀοβισα, quia ab igne illæsa fuerunt quando in fornacem ardentem iussu regis coniecti sunt, & per miraculum a Deo seruati.
units.tr: Moreover, the examples they bring forward do not prove that the flesh of Christ received supernatural properties from its conception. "He walked upon the waters." But Peter also walked upon the waters. "A heavy and solid body" (says Jerome) "is not yielded to by a soft wave; faith wavers a little, and at once the body understands its own nature. Let us know that it was not the body but faith that walked upon the waters." And Euphemius, as recorded in the Sixth Synod, writes about walking upon the sea: from the walking, which is a natural operation of the feet, the property of human nature appears; while that nature was preserved in the human nature, Christ, being God, acted beyond nature in walking upon the waves. To go was indeed bodily and sensible, but to walk upon the sea was an act of the Deity performed through the human flesh. They say that this body enters with the doors shut and passes through the stone of the sepulchre. I do not now ask whether it happened as our opponents assert, when he could enter with the doors shut just as Peter went out of prison with the doors shut, after they had first been opened. Nor do I ask whether the stone of the sepulchre was removed by the resurrection of Christ's body from the tomb, nor do I call these miracles into doubt. But I contend that it cannot be inferred from them that the body of Christ did not keep its natural properties, for these things happened not through a supernatural property of the body of Christ but through the power of God (to use Jerome's words again), and "the creature yielded to the Creator." One extraordinary miracle must not be used to establish the property of a thing. Otherwise we would say that Moses had no need of food because he lived for forty days without food on the mountain; and we would say that the bodies of Daniel's companions were ἄφλεκτα [incombustible], because they were unharmed by fire when they were thrown into the blazing furnace by the king's command and were preserved by God through a miracle.

units.la: Legibus naturæ Christum non fuisse subiectum
units.tr: That Christ was not subject to the laws of nature.

units.la: An corpus Christi natura legibus subiectum fuerit. sectum agnoscimus, nisi quia volens se subiecit, est Dominus naturæ, sed assumpta carne, sponte in ea naturalibus proprietatibus subiectus fuit: & de eo nobis ita statuendum est prout se in verbo suo patefecit, ac nobis de proprietatibus corporis Christi ex scripturis iudicandum est. Nam vt Gelasius docet, ita magnificauit naturam suam sicut voluit, sicut per prophetas suos ante prædixit: sicut per Apostolos suos, per Euangelistas ecclesiæ suæ voluit intimari. Remittit autem nos Gelasius ad historiam euangelicam, & ita nos vult de Christo sentire, de eius conceptione, partu, de resurrectione & post hanc conuersatione cum discipulis, ascensione in cœlos, patefactione sui de cœlis, aduentu ad iudican dum, sicut scripturæ attestantur. Neque hic vllius dispensationis meminit, sed vult nos ve te post resurrectionem Christum secundum corpus visibilem & palpabilem agnoscere.
units.tr: Whether the body of Christ was by nature subject to the laws of nature. We acknowledge that he was subject to them, except that, being willing, he subjected himself. He is the Lord of nature, but having assumed flesh, he voluntarily became subject to its natural properties in it. We must therefore hold concerning him as he has revealed himself in his Word, and judge concerning the properties of Christ's body from the Scriptures. For, as Gelasius teaches, he magnified his nature as he willed, as he had foretold through his prophets, and as he willed to be made known through his Apostles and Evangelists to his Church. Gelasius refers us to the gospel history, and wants us to think of Christ thus: concerning his conception, birth, resurrection, and his conversation with the disciples after the resurrection, his ascension into heaven, his self-manifestation from heaven, and his coming to judge, as the Scriptures attest. Here he makes no mention of any dispensation, but wants us to acknowledge Christ after the resurrection as visible and palpable according to the body.

units.la: Si enim inquit forma & substantia hominis Iesu Christi hac transfusione consumpta est, quis est quem vidit ad dexteram virtutis stantem S. Stephanus? Quis hominis filius venturus est ad iudicãdos viuos & mortuos? Quis erit quem videbunt in quem compunxerunt? Abolitum est omne mysterium, vacuatum est atque resolutum, vt dictum est, quod absit, omne sacramætum, falsumq; erit, quod ait ipse Saluator: Palpate & videte quia
units.tr: For he says: "If the form and substance of the man Jesus Christ has been consumed by this transfusion, who is it whom St Stephen saw standing at the right hand of power? Who is the Son of Man who is to come to judge the living and the dead? Who will be the one whom they will see, whom they pierced? All mystery has been abolished, emptied and dissolved, and, which God forbid, every sacrament has been destroyed; and the Saviour's own words will be false: 'Handle me and see, because

units.la: „ Spiritus carnem & offa non habet, sicut me „ videtis habentem. Et certe hoc post refurre- „ ftionem dixit, talis iam dixit qualis cum di- „ fcipulis conuersatus est, conuescens & cohaa „ bitans cum eis. Talis dixit qualis ascendit in „ coelos: talis dixit qualis promissus est inde ef- „ fe venturus. Aut legant ipsi vbi, posteaquam „ defe illa professus est,fuerit immutatus: & a- „ liter quàm fe discipulis patefecit afcederit le- „ uatus in coelum. Aut nos rectius ea sequi- „ mur, quae diuinis voluminibus astruuntur, „ non delirantium somnia,& phantasmata va- „ na sectamur.
units.tr: a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having.'" And certainly he said this after the resurrection; he spoke as he was when he conversed with his disciples, eating and dwelling with them. He spoke as he ascended into heaven; he spoke as he was promised to come from there. Or let them read where, after he professed that, he was changed, and ascended into heaven lifted up in a manner other than he had shown himself to the disciples. Rather, let us follow those things which are asserted in the divine books, and not pursue the dreams and empty phantasms of madmen.

units.la: Aiunt formationem corporis Christi in vtero virginis ex Spiritu sancto conuenire v- nitioni diuinae & humanae naturae, atq; ideo attulisse praeternaturalia idiomata, ita vt Christus fecundum vtranq; naturam fit praefens. Nos respondemus cum Cyrillo: Filium Dei genitum esse ex virgine θεικῶς & ἀνθρωπίνως diuinè & digne Deo, simul & humanè, hoc est, carnaliter. Ac est quidem diuina natiuitas Verbi aeterna eius generatio qua ex fubftan- tia Patris genitum est: sed etiam aflumpta car ne generatio illa diuine facta dicitur. Deus enim existens fecundum naturam Verbum caro factum, processit vt decet eum qui fecun dum veritatem est Deus: solus enim habuit matrem nuptias non expertam, & seruauit virginem eam quae ipsum peperit fecundum carnem, neque communis homo ex virgine natus est, sed ipsum Dei verbu caro factum. Attamen admirabilis haec natiuitas & spiritus sancti operatio, qua in utero formauit partum, non tollunt carnalem natiuitatem: Quoniam enim quod natum ex carne caro est, genuit virgo vt caro existens carnaliter. Sed si caro Christi vbique praesens facta est per conceptionem ex Spiritu sancto, non nata est vere carnaliter: secundum carnem enim & carnaliter nasci, significat Cyrillo veritatem humanae carnis, quae manere non poterat si substantiales carnis proprietates per contraria idiomata super naturalia sublatae sunt, alioquin si verba fiant de praerogatiuis humanae carnis in Christo, eas libenter agnoscimus, salua tamen vtriusque naturae proprietate.
units.tr: They say that the formation of Christ's body in the womb of the virgin by the Holy Spirit agreed with the union of the divine and human nature, and therefore brought in supernatural properties, so that Christ is present according to both natures. We answer with Cyril: that the Son of God was born of the virgin divinely [θεικῶς] and humanly [ἀνθρωπίνως], divinely and worthily of God, and at the same time humanly, that is, carnally. Indeed the divine birth is the eternal generation of the Word, by which he was begotten of the substance of the Father; but that generation is also said to have been made divine in the assumed flesh. For being God by nature, the Word was made flesh, and proceeded as befits him who is God in truth. For he alone had a mother not experienced in marriage, and he preserved the virgin who bore him according to the flesh; nor was he born from the virgin as an ordinary man, but the Word of God himself was made flesh. Yet this wonderful birth and the operation of the Holy Spirit, by which he formed the offspring in the womb, do not take away the carnal birth. For since what is born of flesh is flesh, the virgin bore him so that he, being flesh, was born carnally. But if the flesh of Christ was made present everywhere through conception by the Holy Spirit, it was not truly born carnally; for to be born according to the flesh and carnally signifies, for Cyril, the truth of human flesh, which could not remain if the substantial properties of flesh were removed by contrary properties beyond nature. Otherwise, if the words are about the prerogatives of human flesh in Christ, we gladly acknowledge them, the property of each nature remaining safe.

units.la: De vera praesentia Christi in his terris secundum humanitatem.
units.tr: On the true presence of Christ on these earths according to the humanity.

units.la: Aduersarij nostri quotiescunque negamus realem & corporalem praesentiā carnis Christi in coena Domini, aut etiam eiusdem vbiquitatem, mox nos accusant quod Christum secundum humanitatem suam omnimodo a coena sua & ab Ecclesia excludamus. Itaque ne hic propter varios modos praesentiae cal-lumniae eorum locus aliquis pateat, dicam di lucide quam praesentiam Christi secundum humanam naturā concedamus aut negemus.
units.tr: Whenever we deny the real and corporal presence of Christ's flesh in the Lord's Supper, or even its ubiquity, our opponents at once accuse us of excluding Christ altogether from his supper and from the Church according to his humanity. So that no room be left here for their slanders because of the various modes of presence, I will state clearly which presence of Christ according to the human nature we concede or deny.

units.la: ” Spiritus carnem & offa non habet, sicut me ” videtis habentem. Et certe hoc post refurre… ” ftionem dixit, talis iam dixit qualis cum di… ” fcipulis conuersatus est, conuescens & cohaa ” bitans cum eis. Talis dixit qualis ascendit in ” cœlos: talis dixit qualis promissus est inde ef… ” fe venturus. Aut legant ipsi vbi, posteaquam ” de fe illa professus est,fuerit immutatus:& a… ” liter quàm fe discipulis patefecit afcéderit le… ” uatus in cœlum. Aut nos reftius ea sequi… ” mur, quæ diuinis voluminibus astruuntur, ” non delirantium somnia,& phantasmata va… ” na feftamur.
units.tr: "A spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having." And certainly he said this after the resurrection; he spoke as he was when he conversed with his disciples, eating and dwelling with them. He spoke as he ascended into heaven; he spoke as he was promised to come from there. Or let them read where, after he professed that, he was changed, and ascended into heaven lifted up in a manner other than he had shown himself to the disciples. Rather, let us follow those things which are asserted in the divine books, and not pursue the dreams and empty phantasms of madmen.

units.la: Aiunt formationem corporis Christi in vtero virginis ex Spiritu sancto conuenire v… nitioni diuinæ & humanæ naturæ, atq; ideo attulisse præternaturalia idiomata, ita vt Christus fecundum vtranq; naturam fit præ… fens. Nos respondemus cum Cyrillo: Filium Dei genitum esse ex virgine θεικῶς & ἀνθρωπίνως diuinè & digne Deo, simul & humane, hoc est, carnaliter.
