Ac est quidem diuina natiuitas Verbi æterna eius generatio qua ex fubftan… tia Patris genitum est: sed etiam aflumpta car ne generatio illa diuine facta dicitur. Deus enim existens fecundum naturam Verbum caro factum, processit vt decet eum qui fecun dum veritatem est Deus: solus enim habuit matrem nuptias non expertam, & seruauit virginem eam quæ ipsum peperit fecundum carnem, neque communis homo ex virgine natus est, sed ipsum Dei verbū caro factum. Attamen admirabilis haec natiuitas & spiritus sancti operatio, qua in vtero formauit patrum, non tollunt carnalem natiuitatē: Quoniam enim quod natum ex carne caro est, genuit virgo vt caro existens carnaliter. Sed si caro Christi vbique praesens facta est per conceptionem ex Spiritu sancto, non nata est vere carnaliter: secundum carnem enim & carnaliter nasci, significat Cyrillo veritatem humanae carnis, quae manere non poterit si substantiales carnis proprietates per contrarias idiomata super naturalia sublatae sunt, alioquin si verba fiant de praerogatiuis humanae carnis in Christo, eas libenter agnoscimus, salua tamen vtriusque naturae proprietate.
units.tr: They say that the formation of Christ's body in the womb of the virgin by the Holy Spirit agreed with the union of the divine and human nature, and therefore brought in supernatural properties, so that Christ is present according to both natures. We answer with Cyril: that the Son of God was born of the virgin divinely [θεικῶς] and humanly [ἀνθρωπίνως], divinely and worthily of God, and at the same time humanly, that is, carnally. Indeed the divine birth is the eternal generation of the Word, by which he was begotten of the substance of the Father; but that generation is also said to have been made divine in the assumed flesh. For being God by nature, the Word was made flesh, and proceeded as befits him who is God in truth. For he alone had a mother not experienced in marriage, and he preserved the virgin who bore him according to the flesh; nor was he born from the virgin as an ordinary man, but the Word of God himself was made flesh. Yet this wonderful birth and the operation of the Holy Spirit, by which he formed the offspring in the womb, do not take away the carnal birth. For since what is born of flesh is flesh, the virgin bore him so that he, being flesh, was born carnally. But if the flesh of Christ was made present everywhere through conception by the Holy Spirit, it was not truly born carnally; for to be born according to the flesh and carnally signifies, for Cyril, the truth of human flesh, which could not remain if the substantial properties of flesh were removed by contrary properties beyond nature. Otherwise, if the words are about the prerogatives of human flesh in Christ, we gladly acknowledge them, the property of each nature remaining safe.

units.la: De vera praesentia Christi in his terris secundum humanitatem.
units.tr: On the true presence of Christ on these earth according to his humanity.

units.la: Aduersarij nostri quotiescunque negamus realem & corporalem praesentiā carnis Christi in coena Domini, aut etiam eiusdem vbiquitatem, mox nos accusant quod Christum secundum humanitatem suam omnimodo a coena sua & ab Ecclesia excludamus. Itaque ne hic propter varios modos praesentiae calumniae eorum locus aliquis pateat, dicam di lucide quam praesentiam Christi secundum humanam naturā concedamus aut negemus.
units.tr: Our opponents, whenever we deny a real and bodily presence of Christ's flesh in the Lord's Supper, or even his ubiquity, at once accuse us of shutting Christ off altogether from his Supper and from the Church according to his humanity. So that their calumny may find no opening here because of the various modes of presence, I will state clearly which presence of Christ according to his human nature we grant and which we deny.

units.la: Præsertim cum totam hanc tractationem de præsentia Christi secundum carnem inscripserimus: nam & in controversia de Cœna hoc potissimum controvertitur, & Vbiquitas inventa est ad præsentiam realem & carnalem in cœna stabiliendam: & noua doctrina de vnione personali, quæ per energiam & realem transfusionem proprietatum diuinæ naturæ in humanam definitur, Vbiquitatis confirmandæ causa in ecclesiam nuper introducta est.
units.tr: This is especially so since we have given this whole treatment the title "On the presence of Christ according to the flesh." For in the controversy over the Supper this is the chief point in dispute, and ubiquity was devised to establish a real and fleshly presence in the Supper. And the new doctrine of the personal union, which is defined as an energy and real transfusion of the properties of the divine nature into the human, has lately been introduced into the Church to confirm ubiquity.

units.la: Primus igitur præsentiæ modus est substantialis, quo corporata substantia qualis est humanitas Christi, præsens dicitur, quando substantia sua corporaliter, localiter & naturaliter præsens est: hoc modo Christus antequam in cœlos ascenderet corpore suo in his terris præsens fuit. Et similiter iuxta Sacras literas veturus esse creditur. Nunc autem post ascensionem suam corpore suo non ita in his terris præsens est, sed veram corporis sui substantiam in cœlos euexit, & ideo ea in cœlis manente usque ad extremum diem, neque in cœna, neque usquam alibi in terra corpore suo realiter & substantialiter præsens est. Atque ita Veteres semper senserunt, qui ascensionem Christi corporali eius præsentiæ oppositum, ac docuere Christum secundum humanam naturam qua ascendit in cœlos, iam non esse in terris, nec etiam fore ante secundi eius aduentum.
units.tr: The first mode of presence, then, is substantial: a embodied substance, such as the humanity of Christ is, is said to be present when its substance is present bodily, locally and naturally. In this way Christ was present on earth in his body before he ascended into heaven, and according to the Holy Scriptures he is believed to return in the same way. But now, after his ascension, he is not present on earth in his body in this way. He has carried the true substance of his body up into heaven, and since it remains there until the last day, he is not present in his body, really and substantially, either in the Supper or anywhere else on earth. The ancients always thought so, those who set Christ's ascension against a bodily presence, and taught that Christ according to the human nature in which he ascended into heaven is no longer on earth, nor will he be until his second coming.

units.la: Ac Fulgentius ad Thrasimundum regē mulſtis ostendit,veram Christi humanitatem esse localem,ideoque unum eundemq; secundum humanam substantiam absentem cœlo fuisse cum esset in terra,& dereliquisse terram cum in cœlum ascendit: secundum diuinam vero immensamque substantiam nec cœlum dimiſse cum cœlo descendit, nec terram deseruisſe cum ad cœlum ascendit. Et ideo Dominum vt humanitate localem ostenderet dixisse discipulis: Ascendo ad Patrem meum &ad Patrem vestrum: immensitatem vero diuinitatis suæ ostendisse discipulis dicēdo: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus vsque ad conſummationem seculi. Non autē potuisse deſcendere nisi fuisset verus & localis homo. Probat deinde Apostoli testimonio qui iuſbet expectare filium Dei de cœlis,monstrans corporaliter de cœlo venturum. Item memiſnit ascensionis qua corporaliter in cœlū ascenſderit,& in eadem veritate corporis de cœlo venturus sit:&ex eo quod corpora nostra coſformia erūt corpori Christi,conficit, corpus Christi loco contineri: ac tandem ita concluſdit:Est itaque filius in cœlo,&habitat in noſbis in terra,scilicet illa su v immensitatis præ-sentia qua in nobis Pater Spirituſque sanſtushabitat. D. quoque Augustinus Epistola 57.asserit Christum secundum hominem ante ascensionem eius non fuisse in cœlo, vbi nūc est, quâuis secúdum id quod filius Dei erat, ef set in cœlo, Itaq; nô dubitandû ibi nûc esse ho mine Christû, vnde venturus est secundum Christiana confessione, in eadé videlicet carnis forma, cui immortalitatem dedit, naturâ nó abstulit. Similiter illa loca scripturę, in quibus Christo modo praesentia modo absentia à terris tribuitur, Veteres interpretatur de corporali absentia, quod corpore non sit hic, atq; ita Augustinus verba Domini: Me autem non semper habebitis interpretatur Traft. 50. super Ioan. Accipiat & hoc boni, sed nô sint soliciti: loquebatur enim de praesentia corporis sui: nam secundû maiestatem suâ, secundum prouidentiam, secundum ineffabilem & inuisibilem gratiam, impletur quod ab eo dictum est: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus vsque ad consummationem seculi. Secundum carnem vero quam Verbû assumpsit, secundum id quod de virgine natus est, secundum id quod à Iudæis comprehensus est, quod ligno confixus, quod de cruce depositus, quod linteis inuolutus, quod in sepulchro conditus, quod in resurrectione manifestatus, non semper habebitis me vobiscum. Quare? Quoniam conuersatus est secundû corporis praesentiam quadraginta diebus cum discipulis suis, & eis deducentibus videndo, non sequendo, ascedit in coelum, & non est hic: ibi enim sed et ad dexteram patris: & hic est, non enim recessit præsentia maiestatis. Aliter secundum præsentiam maiestatis semper habemus Christum: secundum præsentia carnis, recte dictū est discipulis, me aut non semper habebitis. Habuit enim illū Ecclesia secundū præsentia carnis paucis diebus: modo fide tenet, oculis non videt. Idem cum D. Augustino sentit Cyrillus lib.9.in Ioannem cap.11. Credere autem oportet fideles quamuis a nobis corpore absit, virtute tamen sua omnia & nos gubernare, adesseq; semper ipsum omnibus qui eum diligunt, propterea dicebat: Amen amen dico vobis, vbicunq; sunt duo aut tres congregati in nomine meo, ibi sum in medio eorum. Nam quemadmodum, quando vt ho mo in terra conuersabatur, tunc etiam cœlos implebat, & angelorum consortia non relinquebat: eodem nunc modo quum sit in cœlis cum carne, terram tamen replet, & cum eis est, qui eum diligunt. Obseruandū autem est, quia quamuis secundum carnem solummodo abiturus erat (adest enim semper virtu te deitatis, vt diximus) modico tamen tempo re cum discipulis se futurum dicebat: aperte seipsum nominans, ne quis in duos filios diuidere Christum audeat: sed vt vnum omnino esse credat Dei patris & virginis filium: non quia vna natura sit, sed quia post incarnationem pia hæc diuisio non est. Vnus enim in vtraque natura Christus est. Porro cum
units.tr: Fulgentius, in his letter to King Thrasamund, shows at length that the true humanity of Christ is local, and that therefore the same one, according to his human substance, was absent from heaven while he was on earth, and left the earth when he ascended into heaven; but according to his divine and immense substance he did not leave heaven when he came down from heaven, nor forsake the earth when he ascended to heaven. Therefore the Lord, to show that his humanity was local, said to the disciples: "I ascend to my Father and to your Father" (John 20:17); but to show the immensity of his divinity he said to the disciples: "Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the world" (Matt. 28:20). Yet he could not have come down unless he were a true and local man. Fulgentius then proves it by the testimony of the Apostle, who bids us wait for the Son of God from heaven (1 Thess. 1:10), showing that he will come bodily from heaven. Likewise he recalls that Christ ascended bodily into heaven and will come from heaven in the same truth of his body; and from the fact that our bodies will be conformed to the body of Christ, he concludes that the body of Christ is contained in a place. At last he concludes thus: "The Son is therefore in heaven, and dwells in us on earth," namely by that presence of his immensity by which the Father and the Holy Spirit dwell in us. Augustine too, in Epistle 57, affirms that Christ according to the man was not in heaven before his ascension, where he now is, although according to what he was as the Son of God he was in heaven. Therefore we must not doubt that the man Christ is now there, whence he will come, according to the Christian confession, in the same form of flesh, to which he gave immortality and did not take away its nature. Similarly, those passages of Scripture in which Christ is attributed now presence, now absence, from the earth, the Fathers interpret of a bodily absence, namely that he is not here in his body. So Augustine interprets the words of the Lord, "You will not always have me" (John 12:8), in his Tractate 50 on John: "Let this also be taken as a good thing, but let them not be anxious. For he was speaking of the presence of his body. For according to his majesty, according to his providence, according to his ineffable and invisible grace, what he said is fulfilled: 'Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the world.' But according to the flesh which the Word assumed, according to what was born of the virgin, according to what was seized by the Jews, what was fixed to the wood, what was taken down from the cross, what was wrapped in linen, what was laid in the tomb, what was manifested in the resurrection, you will not always have me with you. Why? Because he conversed with them according to the presence of his body for forty days with his disciples, and while they escorted him they saw him but did not follow him; he ascended into heaven and is not here. For there he is also at the right hand of the Father; and he is here, for the presence of his majesty has not departed. Otherwise, according to the presence of his majesty we always have Christ; according to the presence of the flesh it was rightly said to the disciples: 'You will not always have me.' For the Church had him according to the presence of the flesh for a few days; now she holds him by faith, and does not see him with her eyes." Cyril, in book 9 on John, chapter 11, thinks the same as Augustine: "The faithful must believe that, although he is absent from us in body, he nevertheless by his power governs all things and is always present to all who love him. Therefore he said: 'Verily, verily I say unto you, where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them' (Matt. 18:20). For just as, when he lived on earth as a man, he then also filled the heavens and did not leave the company of the angels, so now, though he is in heaven with his flesh, he nevertheless fills the earth and is with those who love him. But we must observe that, although he was going to depart only according to the flesh (for the power of the Godhead is always present, as we have said), yet he said that he would be with the disciples for a short time, plainly naming himself, lest anyone dare to divide Christ into two sons, but that we should believe that he is altogether one, the Son of God the Father and of the Virgin: not because there is one nature, but because after the incarnation this pious division does not exist. For Christ is one in both natures." Moreover, since

units.la: Christum maiestate sua praesentem adesse seruri hunc patres, eamq; praesentia maiestatis corporali praesentia opponant, maiestatis nomine non intelligunt quandam communicatam maiestatem aliam a maiestate Verbi, qua corpus Christi realiter & substantialiter vbique praesens fiat, sed hoc nomine ipsam diuinitatem intelligunt quae essentialiter praesens vbique adest, id autem non obscure conficitur, cum ex his locis quae adscripsi, tum etiam ex Vigilij, Fulgentij & aliorum patrum scriptis, vbi humanitas, & diuinitas, caro, & deitas, corpus, & maiestas inter se opponuntur quoties de praesentia Christi agitur, vt secundum aliud praesens, secundum aliud absens dicatur.
units.tr: the fathers hold that Christ is present by his majesty, and they set this presence of majesty against bodily presence, they do not by the name of majesty understand some communicated majesty, distinct from the majesty of the Word, by which the body of Christ becomes present everywhere really and substantially; rather by this name they understand the very divinity, which is present everywhere essentially. This is not obscure, as is shown both from the passages I have cited and from the writings of Vigilius, Fulgentius and other Fathers, where humanity and divinity, flesh and deity, body and majesty are set against each other whenever the presence of Christ is discussed, so that he is said to be present in one respect and absent in another.

units.la: Cur autem Christus humanitatis suae praesentiam mundo subtraxerit, ipse seruator explicat Ioannis 16. Et ego (inquit) veritatem dico vobis, expedit vobis vt ego abeam, nisi enim abiero consolator ille non veniet ad vos: sin autem profectus fuero, mittam eum ad vos. Christus venit in hunc mundum ac verbum carnem assumpsit, vt in carne obiret munus Messiae, & pro nobis pateretur ac moreretur, atque ita mortem destrueret: sed non tantum hoc Messiae munus fuit, sed vt nos in ipsos coelos reduceret, & coram ipso Patre collocaret. Noster enim Pontifex non in manufacta sanctuaria ingressus est, nec in exemplaria verorum sed in ipsum coelum, vt appareat vultui
units.tr: Why Christ withdrew the presence of his humanity from the world the Saviour himself explains in John 16: "And I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Comforter will not come to you; but if I depart, I will send him to you." Christ came into this world and the Word took on flesh, so that in the flesh he might carry out the office of the Messiah, suffer and die for us, and so destroy death. But this was not the whole of the Messiah's office: he was also to lead us back into heaven itself and place us before the Father himself. For "our High Priest has entered not into sanctuaries made with hands, nor into copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, that he may appear before the face of God for us" (Heb. 9:24).

units.la: Dei pro nobis, Iraque quum fit primitiæ generis nostri, in cœlum cum carne ascendit, & nos coram patre constituit, atque ad perfectam dispensationem carnis affumptæ pertinebat, vt per actis omnibus quæ in his terris facienda fuerat ad patrem ascenderet, & carnem quasi pignus & arrhabone nostræ resurrectionis in cœlis deponeret, vt Tertullianus scribit. Ascendens autem in altum ablata carne sua, dona misit ecclesiæ, spiritum consolatorem quem hic promisit. Poterat quidem etiam in his terris manens Spiritum sanctum largiri, neque deitate cœlo aberat cum corpore nondum illuc conscendisset, sed fideles nimiu carnali præsentiæ addicti minus apti fuissent ad accipiendum Spiritum sanctum: atque hoc testatur Augustinus qui sic scribit, Semper quidem nobiscum est diuinitate sua, sed nisi corporaliter abiret a nobis, semper eius corpus carnaliter videremus, & nunquam spiritualiter crederemus. Cyrillus in Ioanne lib. 11. cap. 21. Putabant discipuli absentiam Christi, vt hominis dico (Deus enim vbiq; adest) multorum eis incommodorum causam futuram: cum non adesset, qui ab omnibus eos posset malis eruere. Sed oportebat (Dicã enim etiam si luminaria orbis postea facti sunt,) non solum in carnem Christi, verum etiam in Deitatem respicere: quæ quamuis oculis non cernatur, adest tamen semper summa cum potestate. Nec quicquam est quod prohibere possit, quin omnia repleat, & quod velit, peragat: Non enim loco aut dimensionibus circumscriptibilis natura diuina est. Quare cum Deus & homo Christus verè sit, oportuit eos intellexisse, ineffabili Deitatis potestate vna cum eis semper futurum, etiamsi carne absent. Idcirco enim ipse quoque in superioribus dicebat: Pater sancte serua eos in nomine tuo quos dedisti mihi. Aperte significans Deitatis ratione, non carnis præsentia eos posse seruari, &c. Item alibi, Nihil ergo mali vobis accidere potest ait, si carne absuero: quùm Deitatis meæ potestas, quæ vos hucusque seruauit, in posterum etiam seruatura sit. Hæc non ideo dicimus, quia Domini corpus non magni æstimemus: sed quia mirabiles hos effectus, gloriæ Dei attribuendos putamus. D. item Augustinus Tract. 94. super Ioannem: Quid est ergo, Si nō abiero? Paracletus non veniet ad vos? nisi non potestis capere spiritum, quam diu secundum carnem persistitis nosse Christum. Scholastici etiam Theologi complures rationes afferunt, cur vtile fuerit Christum secundum carnem à terris discedere, quas ego nunc commemorare nolo. Hoc tantum rogo vt considerent singuli primum quot superstitiones pepererit falsa opinio carnalis præsentiæ, & quam horrēdæ artolatriæ causa fuerit: deinde quod ipsi Scholastici scri- bunt
units.tr: And since he is the firstfruits of our race, he ascended into heaven with his flesh and presents us before the Father. It belonged to the complete administration of the flesh he had assumed that, once all that was to be done on earth had been accomplished, he should ascend to the Father and lay his flesh up in heaven as a pledge and earnest of our resurrection, as Tertullian writes. But when he ascended on high, having taken his flesh with him, he sent gifts to the Church, the Comforter Spirit whom he had promised here. He could indeed have bestowed the Holy Spirit while still remaining on earth, and his deity was not absent from heaven even before his body had gone up there; but the faithful, being too much given over to a carnal presence, would have been less fit to receive the Holy Spirit. Augustine bears witness to this, writing thus: "He is indeed always with us by his divinity, but unless he had departed from us bodily, we would always see his body in the flesh and never believe in the Spirit." Cyril, on John, book 11, chapter 21: "The disciples thought that the absence of Christ, I mean as man (for God is everywhere present), would be the cause of many troubles for them, since he was not there who could rescue them from all evils. But it was necessary (for I will say it even though the lights of the world came into being afterwards) to look not only to the flesh of Christ but also to his Deity, which, though it is not seen by the eyes, is nevertheless always present with the greatest power. Nothing can prevent it from filling all things and accomplishing what it wills, for the divine nature is not confined by place or dimensions. Therefore, since Christ is truly both God and man, they ought to have understood that by his ineffable divine power he would always be with them, even though absent in the flesh. For this reason he also said above: 'Holy Father, keep those whom you have given me in your name,' clearly signifying that they could be kept by the presence of his Deity, not of his flesh, and so on." Likewise elsewhere: "Nothing evil, he says, can happen to you if I am absent in the flesh, since the power of my Deity, which has kept you until now, will keep you also in time to come." We do not say this because we think lightly of the Lord's body, but because we think these wonderful effects are to be ascribed to the glory of God. Augustine likewise, in tractate 94 on John: "What then is the meaning of 'If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you'? Unless you can not grasp the Spirit so long as you continue to know Christ according to the flesh." Many of the Scholastic theologians also give reasons why it was useful for Christ to depart from the earth according to the flesh, which I do not wish to recount here. I ask only that each person consider, first, how many superstitions the false opinion of a carnal presence has produced, and what a horrible cause of idolatry it has been; and second, that the Scholastics themselves write that the bodily absence of Christ serves to increase our faith and, moreover, to confirm our hope: namely, since our head reigns in heaven, we too will be received there, according to Christ's promise: "In my Father's house there are many mansions; otherwise I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you, and when I have gone and prepared a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you may be too." Those who make the carnal presence of Christ, taken alone, somehow the anchor of our faith and hope differ greatly from this. I know indeed that everyone desires the bodily presence of Christ, which Paul even placed before his own life, as Cyril writes: "desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ." But what we most eagerly long for is not immediately the most useful thing for us. Therefore we must here acquiesce in the divine will, and so determine concerning the presence of Christ as he has taught it in his word.

units.la: Christum deitatis praesentia falsat. bunt absentiam corporalem Christi seruire augmento fidei nostræ,& præterea ípem nos- stram confirmare, népe cum caput nostrum in cœlis regnet, fore vt nos quoque illuc reci- piamur, iuxta Christi promissionem : In do- mo patris mei mansiones multæ sunt, alio- quin dixissem vobis, abeo autem paraturus vobis locum, & cum profectus fuero & para uero vobis locum, rursus veniâ & assumam vos ad meipsum, vt vbi sum ego & vos sitis. Ab his multum dissentiunt qui carnalé Chri sti præsentiam vnicam quodammodo fidei & spei nostræ anchoram faciunt. Scio equi- dem desiderari ab omnibus corporalem Chri sti præsentiam, quam Paulus etiam vitæ suæ præponebat, vt Cyrillus scribit: cupiens dis- solui & esse cum Christo. Sed non statim idi- psum nobis vtilissimum est quod auidissime appetimus. Itaque diuinæ voluntati hic ac- quiescendum est,& ita statuendum de Christi præsentia prout in verbo suo docuit.
units.tr: The presence of Christ's deity falsifies the carnal presence. They say that the bodily absence of Christ serves to increase our faith, and further confirms our hope. Since our head reigns in heaven, we too shall be received there, according to Christ's promise. Those who make the carnal presence of Christ the one anchor of our faith and hope in some way differ greatly from these. I indeed know that everyone desires the bodily presence of Christ, which Paul even placed before his own life, as Cyril writes: "desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ." But what we most eagerly long for is not at once the most useful thing for us. Therefore we must here acquiesce in the divine will, and so hold concerning the presence of Christ as he has taught it in his word.

units.la: Alter præsentiæ modus est, quo corpus Christi seu humanitas eius præsens nobis est virtute, gloria & maiestate operationeque, quamuis interea essentia ipsius vno dunta- xat loco reipsa & actu contineatur. Christus enim caput est Ecclesiæ, rex, Dominus, me- diator & iudex noster secundum vtranq; na- tura. Itaq; sua ὑπόστασις qua gubernat Ecclesiam totus præsens nobis est, adeoque cogitationes cordium nostrorum sit & iudicat, & hac ratione ad dexteram patris consedisse in cœlis dicitur. Ad hanc autem præsentiam ἀνθρωπίνην non requiritur realis & essentialis & corporalis & localis præsentia humanitatis Christi,
units.tr: There is another mode of presence, by which the body of Christ, or his humanity, is present to us by virtue, glory, majesty and operation, although meanwhile his essence is really and actually contained in one place only. For Christ is the head of the Church, our king, Lord, mediator and judge according to both natures. Therefore his hypostasis [ὑπόστασις], by which he governs the Church, is wholly present to us, and so he knows and judges the thoughts of our hearts, and in this way is said to have sat down at the right hand of the Father in heaven. For this presence [ἀνθρωπίνην, human], however, there is not required a real, essential, corporal and local presence of the humanity of Christ,

units.la: id quod etiam Cyrillus affirmat, qui inquit, Credere oportet fideles, quàuis corpore suo absit Christus, virtute tamen sua omnia & nos gubernare, adesseque semper ipsum omnibus qui eum diligunt, propterea dicebat, Amen dico vobis, vbicunque sunt duo vel tres congregati in nomine meo, ibi sum in medio ipsorum. Nam quemadmodum quando vt homo in terra conuersabatur, tunc etiam cœlos implebat, & angelorum consortia non relinquebat: eodem nunc modo quum sit in cœlis cum carne, terram tamen replet & cum ijs est qui eum diligunt. Obseruandum est autem, quia quamuis secundum carnem tàtum abiturus erat (adest enim semper virtute Dei tatis vt diximus) modico tamen tempore se cum discipulis futurũ docebat, aperte seipsum nominans, ne quis in duos filios Christũ diuidere auderet, sed vt vnum omnino esse quis què credat, non quod vna sit natura, sed quia vnus in vtraque natura est Christus. In his verbis Cyrillus aperte docet gubernationem Christi non fieri carnis eius præsentia, sed eum carne absentem Deitatis virtute adesse. Adest autem Deitatis virtute non vt verbum absque carne, sed vt Deus verbum incarna-tum,itaque hæc gubernatio ad humanitatem eius quoque pertinet, quatenus Christus di-uinitate sua essentialiter vbiq; præsens, Chri-stus inquam, hoc est, Deus & homo, omnia sciente & volente mente humana gubernat & administrat. Quoniam vero Christus ita gubernat omnia, vt omnia etiã etiam illi sint præsentia, dicitur per anastrophen omnibus rebus etiam secũdum humanitatem præsens esse. Animæ enim Christi quæ Verbo vnita est omnia præsentia sunt, non quod ipsa hu-manitas singulis rebus substătialiter præsens sit,sed quod illi propter lumē diuinitatis om-nia sint in verbo prẹsentia,cui vnita,cũsta cer-nat vt in Deo sunt,& illi sunt præsentia. Atq; de hac præsentia multa acute à Scholasticis disputantur, qui tamen communiter omnes concludũt, humanam naturam nihilominus finitam manere,neque vbique esse, neq; omnipotentem esse.
units.tr: as Cyril also affirms, who says: "The faithful must believe that, although Christ is absent in his body, he nevertheless governs all things and us by his power, and that he is always present to all who love him. For this reason he said: 'Amen, I say to you, wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.'" For just as, when he lived on earth as a man, he then also filled the heavens and did not leave the company of the angels, so now, although he is in heaven with his flesh, he nevertheless fills the earth and is with those who love him. It should be observed that although he was going to depart only according to the flesh (for he is always present by the power of the Deity, as we have said), he nevertheless taught that he would be with the disciples for a short time, plainly naming himself, lest anyone dare to divide Christ into two sons; rather, one should believe him to be wholly one, not because the nature is one, but because Christ is one in both natures. In these words Cyril clearly teaches that the government of Christ is not effected by the presence of his flesh, but that, though absent in the flesh, he is present by the power of the Deity. He is present, however, by the power of the Deity not as the Word without flesh, but as God the Word made flesh; so this government pertains also to his humanity, inasmuch as Christ, present everywhere essentially by his divinity, that is, Christ God and man, governs and administers all things with a human mind that knows and wills them. Since Christ governs all things in such a way that all things are present to him, it is said, by anastrophe [ἀναστροφήν], that he is present even to all things according to his humanity. For the soul of Christ, which is united to the Word, is present to all things, not because the humanity itself is substantially present to each thing, but because all things are present to it through the light of the divinity, to which it is united; it sees all things as they are in God, and they are present to it. Many subtle points about this presence are disputed by the Scholastics, who nevertheless commonly conclude that the human nature remains finite, and is neither everywhere nor omnipotent.

units.la: Ea etiam est coniunctio Christi capitis no bilcum,vt nos simus caro ex carnibus eius & & os ex ossibus eius. Hæc autem coniunctio non constat cōtaćtu aut præsentia aliqua cor-porali,aut aliqua locorum coniunctione, sed caro Christi reddimur dum in eum credimus & mortem illius in pretium pro nobis perso-lutam fide comprehendimus, ita enim carnes nostræ postquam sumus regenerati,eiusdem sunt naturæ cum carnibus Christi earundem proprietatum, & ab eo vera vita donantur,& motu & gratia & spiritu. Donum autem hoc vitæ & sustentationis ad nos fluit & defertur per carnem Christi nostra causa in crucem & mortem traditam, atq; ita caro fumus de carne Christi, non solum quo ad animum nostrum, verum etiam quo ad corpus, quoniam istud capax fit beatæ resurrectionis & æternæ vitæ, atque instauratur ad inferiora. Jam spiritui, per gratiam & vim quæ à divinitate Christi per eius corpus ad nos derivatur: vim enim istâ qua renascimur ut fiamus caro ex carne Christi, à Deo per Christi carnem habemus ut pro nobis in pretium & mortem data est. Porro quia in Baptismo Christum induimus, Chrysostomus scripsit eandem illam communicationem carnis Christi etiam in Baptismo fieri, ac Pauli verba exponit ad hunc modum : Et quomodo? Iterum au-
units.tr: Such also is the union of Christ the head with us, that we are flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones. This union, however, does not consist in any contact or bodily presence, or in any joining of places, but we become the flesh of Christ when we believe in him and grasp by faith his death paid for us as a price. For our flesh, once we are regenerated, is of the same nature, with the same properties, as the flesh of Christ, and is given true life by him, both in motion and in grace and in the Spirit. This gift of life and sustenance flows and is conveyed to us through the flesh of Christ, which was delivered to the cross and death for our sake; and thus we are flesh of the flesh of Christ, not only as to our soul but also as to our body, since this is made capable of blessed resurrection and eternal life, and is restored for the things above. Now, the power which we have from the Deity of Christ, through his body, by grace, is conveyed to the spirit: for we have from God, through the flesh of Christ, that power by which we are reborn so as to become flesh of the flesh of Christ, a power given for us as a price and in his death. Moreover, because in Baptism we put on Christ, Chrysostom wrote that this same communion of the flesh of Christ also takes place in Baptism, and he explains Paul's words in this way: "And how? Again, listen"

units.la: di quid beatus ille dicat ad Hebr. 2. Quoniam pueri commercium habuerunt cum car-ne & sanguine & ipse similiter particeps fa-ctus est eorundem: sed hic ipse nobiscum commercium traxit, non nos cum illo. Quomodo ergo ex carne eius & ex ossibus eius sumus? Sunt qui per sanguinē dicat & aquam. Verum nihil est. Sed quemadmodum ille fit ne virili cogressu natus est ex Spiritu sancto, ita & nos illud efficimur in lavacro : Vide quanta exempla adducat vt generationi illi fidem faciat. Ex hac interpretatione Chrysostomi conficitur carnem Christi credentibus communicari spiritualiter, & energia sua praesentem esse, absque reali & substantiali ipsius praesentia: nisi forte velit quis carnem & sanguinem atque ossa Christi, realiter cum aqua in Baptismo coniungere.
units.tr: Let us hear what that blessed man says on Hebrews 2: "Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise became a partaker of the same." But here he himself has taken on fellowship with us, not we with him. How then are we of his flesh and of his bones? Some say it is through blood and water. But that is nothing. Rather, just as he was born of the Holy Spirit without male intercourse, so we are made so in the bath. See what examples he adduces to make that generation credible. From this interpretation of Chrysostom it follows that the flesh of Christ is communicated to believers spiritually, and is present through its power, without any real and substantial presence of it; unless perhaps someone wishes to join the flesh, blood and bones of Christ really to the water in Baptism.

units.la: Adest etiam Christus praesens humanitate sua per gratiam, vt tamé corpore interim absens fit, vnde Emissenus in sermone de corpore & sanguine Domini scribit: Christū quia corpus assumptum ablaturus, erat ab oculis nostris & syderibus illaturus, sacramentum corporis & sanguinis sui confecrasse, vt colerentur iugiter per mysterium quod semel offerebatur in pretium, vt quia quotidiana & indefessa currebat pro hominis salute redemptio, perpetua esset eius redemptionis obligatio, & perennis illa victima viueret in memoria, & semper praesens esset in gratia.
units.tr: Christ is also present with his humanity through grace, although meanwhile he is absent in body. Hence Emissenus writes in his sermon on the body and blood of the Lord: "Since Christ, who was about to take up the body he had assumed out of our sight and carry it to the stars, consecrated the sacrament of his body and blood, so that they might be honoured continually through the mystery of that which was once offered as the price; so that, since the redemption for human salvation runs on daily and without ceasing, the obligation of that redemption might be perpetual, and that everlasting sacrifice might live in memory and always be present in grace."

units.la: Praeterea est etiam fidei praesentia qua nostri dicunt Christum in coena nobis corpore suo praesentem esse. Fides enim vera tantae est efficaciae vt res praesentes constituat non quidem realiter sed spiritualiter, eas enim per fidem ita complectimur ac si essent ante oculos. Etenim si ea vis est sensuum nostrorum vt oculi caelum & solem & astra, quoties illa cernimus praesentia nobis efficiat: & cogitatio quoque res praeteritas aut remotas præ-sentes quodam modo statuat, cur non concederemus eandem vim & efficaciam fidei datam esse, vt etiam ea quæ longe absunt constituat præsentia, non quidem substantialiter sed spiritualiter? Præsertim cum fides omnem humanam noticiam longe superet, vtpote cuius efficacia potestas est divini spiritus, quæ efficit vt ea quæ credimus potentius atque evidentius adsint animis nostris, quam quæ mentis tantum vi & acumine revocantur sub aspectum. Neque hic fides rerum veritatem immutat, vt ea quæ futura aut præterita sunt, neget esse talia, aut quæ realiter absentia sunt, realiter præsentia faciat, sed eadem fide, qua persuasum est res, quoad substantiam abesse, res ipsæ per spiritum, dum fides in illarum meditatione versatur, præsentes nobis fiunt. Si enim quæ cogitatione complectimur velocius cernimus, nobis sunt præsentia, multo magis ea præsentia sunt quæ fide cernuntur, cum fidei efficacia sensus omnes longe superet: Atque ita res eadem & absens est & præsens, alio atque alio modo. Hoc modo Christus ait Abrahamum vidisse diem suum, & itaque Prophetæ Christum viderunt: etsi enim Christus quod ad carnem attinet venturus erat, tamen illis tum per fidem quodammodo erat præsens, neque enim quicquam videri potest quod non aliquo modo adsit videnti præsens.
units.tr: There is also a presence of faith, by which our people say that Christ is present to us in the Supper with his body. For true faith is of such efficacy that it makes present things present, not indeed really but spiritually; for through faith we embrace them as if they were before our eyes. And if the power of our senses is such that the eyes, when they see heaven and the sun and the stars, make them present to us, and thought too in some way makes past or distant things present, why should we not grant that faith has been given the same power and efficacy, so that it makes present even things that are far away, not substantially but spiritually? Especially since faith far surpasses all human knowledge, being an efficacy that is the power of the divine Spirit, which brings it about that the things we believe are present to our minds more powerfully and more evidently than those recalled to view by the mere force and keenness of the mind. Nor does faith here alter the truth of things, so as to deny that things future or past are such, or to make things that are really absent really present; but by the same faith by which we are persuaded that the things are absent in substance, the things themselves become present to us through the Spirit, while faith is occupied in meditating on them. For if we see more quickly those things we embrace in thought as present to us, much more are those present which are discerned by faith, since the efficacy of faith far surpasses all the senses. And so the same thing is both absent and present, in different ways. In this way Christ says that Abraham saw his day, and so the prophets saw Christ; for although Christ was to come as regards the flesh, yet to them he was in some way present through faith, for nothing can be seen which in some way is not present to the one who sees it.

units.la: {*} (no further marginal notes on this page) præsens. Tanta autem erat prophetarum fides certitudo, ut res futuras quodammodo haberent præsentes, & sic in conspectu, ut sæpe nō loquuti sint verbis futuri temporis, quam-uis alioquin de rebus futuris, sed pro illis vt surparint aut præsens tempus aut etiam præteritum. Et sane quamuis Abrahamus & corpore & tempore longe abesset ab illis rebus, quæ postea gerendæ erant per Christum, eas tamen haud dubie præsentes habuit per spiritum. Similiter alij patres in veteri Testamento fide sua Christum in carne vere appreherunt, unde etiam Apostolus illis tribuit præsentiā earū rerum quas nos hodie percipimus in mysterijs, ait enim eos comedisse eandem escam, & bibisse eundem potū spiritualem. Neue dubites eos comedisse eandem escam & bibisse potum eundem nobiscum, addit: Bibebant autē de spirituali consequente eos petra, Petra autem erat Christus. De Galatis scribit Paulus: Christum ante oculos eorum fuisse crucifixum. Prædicatione enim Euangelij quam fide amplexi fuerant, Christus ita animis illorum impressus fuerat, vt hac noticia, quam fide compatatam habebat, Christum quodammodo præsentem & ob ocu los mentis propositū habere t. Sic idem Apostolus scribit: Nos iam sedere ad dexteram Dei in cœlestibus, & nos iam spe saluos esse. Nam vt Chrysostomus scribit in vndecimū caput ad Hebraeos: Ea quae sunt in spe sine substantia esse putantur, sed fides eis tribuit substantiam, magis autem eis non tribuit, sed ipsa est substantia eorum vt puta, nec dum resurrectio facta est, & nec dum est in substantia, sed spes facit eam subsistere in anima nostra, hoc est quod dixit substantia. Quod si fides aut spes, quae hoc loco pro eadem re sumuntur, potest rebus quae nondum sint, dare substantiam, quanto probabilius est eam posse efficere, vt corpus Christi quod iam existit & habet substantiam, spiritualiter subsistat in anima nostra? Dicuntur autem res quae fide nobis praesentes sunt, spiritualiter praesentes esse: quoniam fides charisma est spirituale, & animus noster quo res illas complectimur, est spiritus: res autem quae alicubi suscipitur, modum suum habet ab eo, a quo suscipitur. Sic quae sensu recipiuntur dicimus adesse sensibiliter, & quae recipiuntur, animo & spiritu, dicimus adesse spiritualiter. Itaque cum Christum dicimus spiritualiter praesentem esse, non dicimus carnem Christi conversam in spiritum, aut solum spiritum intelligimus, aut carnem Christi hac voce excludimus, sed ostendimus Christum fide & spiritu a nobis apprehendi & percipi.
units.tr: {*} (no further marginal notes on this page) present. The faith of the prophets was so great and certain that they had future things in a way present, and so before their eyes that they often did not speak in the future tense, although they were speaking of future things, but used either the present tense or even the past, as if the things had already happened. And indeed, although Abraham was far away both in body and in time from those things which were afterwards to be done through Christ, nevertheless he undoubtedly had them present through the Spirit. Likewise the other fathers in the Old Testament truly laid hold of Christ in the flesh by their faith; hence the Apostle also attributes to them the presence of those things which we today receive in the mysteries, for he says that they ate the same food and drank the same spiritual drink. And lest you doubt that they ate the same food and drank the same drink as we do, he adds: "And they drank of the spiritual Rock that followed them; and the Rock was Christ." Paul writes of the Galatians that Christ was crucified before their eyes; for by the preaching of the gospel, which they had embraced by faith, Christ had been so impressed on their minds that by this knowledge, which they had acquired by faith, they had Christ in some way present and set before the eyes of the mind. So the same Apostle writes: "We already sit at the right hand of God in the heavenly places, and we are already saved in hope." For as Chrysostom writes on the eleventh chapter of Hebrews: "Things that are in hope are thought to be without substance, but faith gives them substance; or rather, it does not give it to them, but it is their substance, as it were; since the resurrection has not yet happened, and they are not yet in substance, but hope makes it subsist in our soul; this is what he meant by substance." If faith or hope, which are taken here for the same thing, can give substance to things that do not yet exist, how much more probable is it that it can bring it about that the body of Christ, which already exists and has substance, subsists spiritually in our soul? Things are said to be spiritually present when they are present to us by faith, because faith is a spiritual gift, and our mind by which we embrace those things is spirit; and a thing received anywhere has its mode from that by which it is received. Thus we say that things received by the senses are present sensibly, and things received by the mind and spirit we say are present spiritually. Therefore when we say that Christ is spiritually present, we do not mean that the flesh of Christ has been changed into spirit, or that we understand only the Spirit, or that we exclude the flesh of Christ by this word; but we show that Christ is laid hold of and perceived by us through faith and the Spirit.

units.la: Praeterea praesens est Christus in verbo & sacramentis, Verbum enim Dei Christum nobis proponit, docet & offert, & ideo etiam dicitur
units.tr: Furthermore, Christ is present in the Word and in the sacraments. For the Word of God sets Christ before us, teaches him and offers him, and therefore it is also called

units.la: Praesens Christus in Verbo. dicitur prædicatio Euangelij esse sermo salu-tis, quod in se Christum qui vita & salus nostra est, contineat, non quidem essentiali & corporea præsentia, sed significatione, quam cum Spiritus sanctus reddit efficacem in animis auditorum, affertur illis certa salus. Simili modo sacramenta Christum nobis offerunt, nam sunt visibile verbum Dei, & Christus ipse est corpus & substantia sacramentorum omnium, ideoque etiam symbola corpus Christi continere dicitur, quod illud denotent, often dant, significent. Et modum hunc præsentiæ aliquando spiritualem esse dicimus, respicientes ad modum supra expositum, aliquando per mysterium, typum, symbolum, signum, figuram, significationem, sacramentalem hanc præsentiam explicamus, respicientes coniunctionem signi cum re signata. Cæterum aliam esse rei ipsius præsentiam, & aliud esse in sacramento tantum præsens esse, hinc apparet, quod fideles qui in Christo sunt & in quibus Christus est, in cœna Domini verum corpus & sanguinem Christi manducant, spiritualiter tamen per fidem. Hypocritæ autem fide in Christum carentes, tantum ipsum sacramentum seu sacramentotenus Christum edere & bibere dicuntur, qua distinctione alii quoties D. Augustinus vtitur, & in celebri illa Berengarij confessione dicitur corpus & sanguine Domini nostri Iesu Christi sensua liter manducari in veritate, non solum sacra⁠mentum seu in sacramento. Citantur etiam in Decretis aliquae huius generis sententiae, veluti Augustini in Sermone de verbis Euan⁠gelij: Quid est Christum manducare? Non hoc solum est in sacramento corpus eius accipere, multi enim indigne accipiunt, de qui⁠bus ait Apostolus: qui manducat & bibit calicem Domini indigne, iudicium sibi mandu⁠cat & bibit. Sed quomodo manducandus est Christus? Quomodo ipse dixit: Qui enim manducat carnem meam & bibit sanguinem meum, manet in me, & ego in illo. Item alibi: Caro eius est quam sub forma panis opertam in Sacramento accipimus. Aberrant autem a sententia Veterum qui existimant idem esse in mysterio aut in sacramento praesens esse & sumi corpus Christi, atque realiter & substantialiter cum pane & vino idem praesens esse. Veteres enim sumi in sacramento ad symbo⁠la retulerunt, vbi symbolu seu sacramentum sumitur, non autem res ipsa sacramenti quod est corpus Christi. Sic Augustinus Tract. 26. super Ioannem inquit: Participatione filij quod est per vnitatem corporis & sanguinis Christi, homo manducans viuit, non sumens tantu in Sacramento quod mali faciunt, sed vsque ad spiritus participationem, vt in corpore Domini tanquam membrum maneat & eius spiritu vegetetur. Hic dicit impios in sacramento manducare corpus & sanguinem Christi. Alibi negat impios hæc manducare, sed tantū sacramentum, non rem sacramenti, quod est corpus Christi, percipere. Itaque in Sacramento edere corpus Christi,idem est atque signum corporis Christi sumere. Sic cum inquit, Quod in Sacramento visibiliter sumi tur, in ipsa veritate spiritualiter manducatur & bibitur. In Sacramēto sumere est rei ipsius sacramentū accipere, id enim visibiliter sumi tur. Eodem modo Christus præsens est in Sa-cramento, quod ea symbola & signa Christū nobis significant, neque tamen nuda & inanis est horum significatio, sed diutni spiritus efficacia res ipsæ significatæ fidei nostræ præ-sentes statuuntur. Neque præsentia ὑπ‌ρστικὴ a sacramentali separanda est, sed distinguenda. Postremò dicitur corpus Christi persona-liter ubique esse: et si autem hæc loquendi forma non ex scripturis, neque ex Veteris Eccle-siæ consuetudine, sed ex Scholastica Theolo-gia deprompta est, & admodum est impropria, ut humana natura quæ non est persona, personaliter adesse dicatur, tamen hunc quoque præsentiæ modum sano intellectu nō re-ijcimus. Quod scilicet humanitas ubique est, quia persona Christi, cuius humana natura est pars quædam, ubique est: Vel humana natura ubique est personaliter, quia humana natura non in se subsistit, sed in verbo: illa autem persona, à qua sustentatur, vbique præ‐sens est. Christus enim qui diuinitate sua vbi‐que præsens est, cum aliquid agit, vbi corpo‐re præsens non adest, veluti cum curauit ser‐uum Centurionis, non solum vt Deus, sed vt persona Deus & homo existens præsens ægro to fuit eumque sanauit. Itaque corpus Chri‐sti re ipsa & essentia sua absens ab eo loco vbi æger decumbebat, personaliter præsens ægro fuit, hoc est, persona cuius corpus hoc erat, præsens ei fuit, non secundum essentiam quidé corporis sed essentiæ diuinæ. Sic etiam Lazaro morienti Bethaniæ personaliter ad‐fuit corpore suo Christus, quanquam reuera corpore Bethaniæ non esset: ait enim gaude‐re se propter discipulos quod ibi non fuerit, dicit etiam Euangelista eum adhuc biduum in eodem loco trans Iordanem videlicet com‐moratū fuisse, postquā Lazari sorores, ægro‐tare frātrem ei nunciassent: cognouit autem mortuum esse, & morienti procul dubio ad‐fuit, eidem rursus non adfuit. Adfuit diuini‐tate sua, non adfuit corpore seu humanitate. Eadem autem adfuisse personaliter dici po‐test, quia non ita morienti adfuit ac si vnige‐nitus Dei filius tantum esset: sed vt Christus, vt qui non Deus tantum sed homo etiam es‐set. Neque quia humanitate sua abfuit ideo homo non adfuisse dicetur, humanitas enim Christi (vt sæpe dictum est) nusquam per se & in se sed in verbi persona subsistit. Itaque illa per se homo non nominatur, sed hoc nomen personæ est quæ etiam Deus in una eademq; indiuisa persona est. Quemadmodum autem Deus dicitur personaliter crucifixus, mortuus & sepultus, quia persona quæ passa hoc fuit, non vt homo tantum sed vt homo & Deus passa fuit, licet secundum humanam naturam tantum, cum diuinitas per se & in se & secundum essentiam suā pati non possit: sic etiam dicimus hominem Christum esse omnipræsentem personaliter, quamuis hoc humanæ naturæ per se & secundum essentiam minime congruat, sed quia persona Christus vbique est præsens, quæ non Deus tantum, sed simul etiam homo est. Quamuis enim vbique sit secundum alteram solum naturam, nempe diuinam, de toto id Christo atque etiam de humana natura dicitur: nam diuina natura quæ vbique est, non vt natura diuina tantummodo, sed vt persona ex hac & humana constans natura, vbique est. Etsi autem hoc modo tolerabiliter dici potest, corpus Christi aut humanitatem eius personaliter vbique esse, phrasis tamen hæc est inusitata & impropria. Natura enim humana etsi non minus perfecta est in Christo quam in nobis, tamen in ipso non est persona sed natura, propterea quod antequam suscipieretur à diuina non fuit, nec se ipsa vnquam subsistit, & ne hodie quia dem subsistit sed à diuina sustentatur, rectius autem dicitur hominem Christum persona liter esse vbique, cum hominis nomen in coĝ creto totam personam significet.
units.tr: Christ is present in the Word. The preaching of the Gospel is called the word of salvation because it contains in itself Christ, who is our life and salvation. He is not present there in an essential and bodily way, but by signification: when the Holy Spirit makes that signification effective in the minds of the hearers, certain salvation is brought to them. In a similar way the sacraments offer Christ to us, for they are the visible Word of God, and Christ himself is the body and substance of all the sacraments. For this reason the symbols too are said to contain the body of Christ, because they denote, offer and signify it. We sometimes call this mode of presence spiritual, looking to the mode explained above, and sometimes we explain this sacramental presence by the terms mystery, type, symbol, sign, figure and signification, looking to the joining of the sign with the thing signified. That the presence of the thing itself is one thing, and being present only in the sacrament is another, is clear from this: the faithful, who are in Christ and in whom Christ is, eat the true body and drink the true blood of Christ at the Lord's Supper, but they do so spiritually, through faith. The hypocrites, however, who lack faith in Christ, are said to eat and drink Christ only in the sacrament, or sacramentally. Augustine often uses this distinction, and in the well-known confession of Berengar it is said that the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ are handled sensually and truly, not only sacramentally or in the sacrament. Some sayings of this kind are also cited in the Decretum, for example from Augustine's sermon on the words of the Gospel: "What is it to eat Christ? It is not only to receive his body in the sacrament, for many receive it unworthily, of whom the Apostle says: he who eats and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself. But how is Christ to be eaten? As he himself said: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him." Likewise elsewhere: "This is his flesh, which we receive in the sacrament, hidden under the form of bread." But those who think that to be present in the mystery or in the sacrament and to be received are the same thing, and that the body of Christ is really and substantially present in the same way as bread and wine, depart from the view of the ancients. For the ancients referred the reception in the sacrament to the symbols, where the symbol or sacrament is received, not the thing of the sacrament itself, which is the body of Christ. So Augustine in Tractate 26 on John says: "By the participation of the Son, which is through the unity of the body and blood of Christ, a man who eats lives, not only by receiving in the sacrament what evil men do, but by reaching to the participation of the Spirit, so that he remains in the body of the Lord as a member and is quickened by his Spirit." Here he says that the wicked eat the body and blood of Christ in the sacrament. Elsewhere he denies that the wicked eat these things, but says that they receive only the sacrament, not the reality of the sacrament, which is the body of Christ. Therefore to eat the body of Christ in the sacrament is the same as to take the sign of the body of Christ. So when he says: "What is taken visibly in the sacrament is in truth itself eaten and drunk spiritually," and: "To take in the sacrament is to receive the sacrament of the thing itself, for that is what is taken visibly." In the same way Christ is present in the sacrament, in that these symbols and signs signify him to us; yet the signification of these is not bare and empty, but through the efficacy of the divine Spirit the things signified themselves are set before our faith as present. Nor is the essential presence to be separated from the sacramental, but distinguished from it. Lastly, it is said that the body of Christ is present personally everywhere. Although this form of speech is derived not from the Scriptures or the custom of the ancient Church but from Scholastic theology, and is quite improper (since a human nature, which is not a person, is said to be present personally), nevertheless we do not reject this mode of presence either, if it is understood soundly. That is, either the humanity is everywhere because the person of Christ, of which the human nature is a certain part, is everywhere; or the human nature is everywhere personally, because the human nature does not subsist in itself but in the Word, and that person by whom it is sustained is present everywhere. For Christ, who is present everywhere by his divinity, when he does something where his body is not present, as when he healed the centurion's servant, was present to the sick man not only as God but as the person who is God and man, and he healed him. So the body of Christ, really absent in its substance from the place where the sick man lay, was personally present to the sick man; that is, the person of whom this body was a part was present to him, not indeed according to the essence of the body but according to the divine essence. So too Christ was personally present in his body to Lazarus dying at Bethany, although in truth he was not in body at Bethany. For he said that he rejoiced because of the disciples that he was not there, and the Evangelist also says that he remained for two more days in the same place beyond the Jordan, after Lazarus's sisters had told him that their brother was sick. He knew that he was dead, and undoubtedly was present to him as he died, yet again was not present to him. He was present by his divinity, not present by his body or humanity. And he can be said to have been present personally, because he was present to the dying man not merely as the only-begotten Son of God, but as Christ, who was not only God but also man. Nor because he was absent in his humanity is he therefore said not to have been present as man, for the humanity of Christ (as has often been said) does not subsist anywhere in itself and by itself, but in the person of the Word. Therefore that humanity is not named man by itself, but this name belongs to the person, who is also God, in one and the same undivided person. Just as God is said to have been crucified, to have died and to have been buried in person, because the person who suffered this suffered not only as man but as man and God, although only according to the human nature, since the divinity cannot suffer by itself and in its own essence: so we also say that Christ as man is omnipresent personally, although this scarcely befits the human nature by itself and according to its essence, but because the person of Christ is present everywhere, who is not only God but at the same time also man. For although he is everywhere according to the one nature only, namely the divine, this is said of the whole Christ and also of the human nature: for the divine nature, which is everywhere, is everywhere not as the divine nature alone, but as the person made up of this and the human nature. Although this way of speaking can be tolerated, the phrase that the body of Christ or his humanity is personally everywhere is nevertheless unusual and improper. For the human nature, although in Christ it is no less perfect than in us, is not a person in him but a nature, because before it was assumed by the divine it did not exist, and it never subsisted by itself, nor does it even today subsist by itself, but is sustained by the divine. It is more correct to say that Christ as man is personally everywhere, since the name man, taken concretely, signifies the whole person.

units.la: Porro hanc præsentiæ rationé nostri cum Veteribus interpretantur per cômunicatio̅ nem proprietatum, ita enim cum Christus lo quereturin terra, dixit Filium hominis esse in cœlo, & id tribuit humanitati suæ quod proprie coueniebat diuinitati. Falsum autem est quod quidam obijciunt, Petrum aut Pau̅ lum aut quemuis alium sanctorum simili mo do posse nobis præsentem dici, propterea quod diuinitas quæ in illis inhabitat nobis præsens fit. Nam vt supra ostendimus, longe alia ratione diuinitas in assumpta carne habi tat, vbi vna est persona verbi & carnis, atque in cæteris sanctis hominibus, in quibus cum diuinitas & humanitas non conuenerint in vnam ὑπόστασιν, non potest diuinitate præsente, per communionem idiomatum aut synech̅ dochen de illis dici quod ipsi præsentes sint. Neque vero existimandum est rem nihili es̅ se & inane tantum nomen tribui Christo, quando dicimus Christum hominem siue etiam eius humanitatem personaliter seu per communicationem idiomatum præsente es̅ se. Nam hæc communicatio idiomatum nobis vnitatem personæ indicat seu identitatem ὑποστάσεως. Ex hac autem oritur illa præsentia saluti̅ fera & viuifica ὑπερούσιος qua totus Christus nobis maiestate, virtute, operatione, gratia & spiritu suo adest, nos gubernat, regit, fouet & viuificat.
units.tr: Our side explains this manner of presence, with the Fathers, by the communication of properties. So when Christ was speaking on earth, he said that the Son of Man is in heaven, and he attributed to his humanity what properly belongs to his divinity. The objection that Peter, Paul, or any other saint could likewise be called present to us, because the divinity that dwells in them is present to us, is false. As we showed above, divinity dwells in the assumed flesh in a very different way, since there is one person of the Word and the flesh. In the other holy men, however, divinity and humanity have not come together into one hypostasis, so with divinity present, it cannot be said of them, by the communication of idioms or by synecdoche [συνεκδοχή], that they themselves are present. Nor should it be thought that we attribute a thing of no account, or an empty name, to Christ when we say that Christ, or even his humanity, is present personally or by the communication of idioms. For this communication of idioms signifies to us the unity of the person, or the identity of the hypostasis [ὑποστάσεως]. From it arises that saving and life-giving presence, supersubstantial [ὑπερούσιος], by which the whole Christ is with us in his majesty, power, working, grace and Spirit, governing, ruling, cherishing and quickening us.

units.la: Sed aduersarij nostri personalis praesentiae nomine aliter vtuntur, nā personali hac praesentia contendunt corpus Christi essentialiter praesens fieri, ita vt in coena vere, reipsa & naturaliter ore corporeo recipiatur, atq; effusione quadam donorum Spiritus sancti volunt humanitati Christi eam diuinitatem & maiestatem communicatam esse, vt vbique non minus quam diuinitas praesens sit. Atque cum multa olim crasse admodum de Vbiquitate corporis Christi scripserint & disputarint, existimant multi ipsos, vt mederentur absurditati, quae omnibus iam manifesta erat, ad latebras has personalis praesentiae & duplicis essentiae essentialis & personalis confugere voluisse. Atque cum hactenus semper nostris obiecerint ipsos vti philosophicis rationib. ipsi nunc tota quodammodo Philosophiam ne dicam sophisticen Theologiae miscent, & in ecclesiam inuehunt inusitatum loquendi genus. Alia illis est essentia corporis Christi naturalis aut gloriosi, alia est eiusdem essentiae personalis. Et Christus praesens est humanitate sua essentialiter, sed non naturaliter, aut corporaliter, aut localiter, sed personaliter, quasi per accidens. Christus item illis est omnis.
units.tr: But our opponents use the name of personal presence differently. By this personal presence they contend that the body of Christ is made essentially present, so that in the Supper it is truly, really and naturally received with the bodily mouth. They want the divinity and majesty to have been communicated to the humanity of Christ by a certain outpouring of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that it is present everywhere no less than the divinity is. Since they once wrote and disputed very crudely about the ubiquity of Christ's body, many think that, to remedy the absurdity, which by then was obvious to everyone, they wished to take refuge in these hiding-places of personal presence and of a double essence, essential and personal. And although they have always accused us of using philosophical arguments, they now mix, in a way, the whole of philosophy, not to say sophistry, into theology, and introduce into the Church an unusual way of speaking. For them the essence of Christ's body is one thing, natural or glorious, and the personal essence of the same body is another. Christ is present in his humanity essentially, but not naturally, or corporeally, or locally, but personally, as it were by accident. Likewise, to them Christ is omnipresent, omnipotent, omniscient, not consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] nor co-essential, but ... (the rest of their formula is obscure).

units.la: nipraesens, omnipotens, omniscius non ὁμοούσιος φωτὶ nec ὁμοούμενος sed ἀφ' ὧν τῆς ἐν. Etsi autem haec & multa alia huius generis hactenus inu sitata fuerūt in purioribus Theologorū scholis, ferri tamen poslent si in scholis disceptationi causa tantum propositā fuissent, si nō absurdas etiam interpretationes alicubi adhibe-rent dissentientes à Scholasticorum sententia, à quibus pleraque mutuari sunt, si non etiam omnes qui aliter sentiunt & loquuntur, è numero Christianorum eijcerent. Nunc vero quando nos cū veteri Ecclesia negamus substantialem omniprsesentiam corporis Christi, sed dicimus Christum substantia corporis sui nunc à terris absentem cœlo contineri, divinitate autem sua vbique praesentem esse: Fatemur autem Christū ἀνθρωπινῶς praesentia quāuis corpore absentem, nobis tamen nihilominus secundum vtranq; naturam praesentem esse, quòd ipse sit caput ecclesiæ, summus pontifex, mediator, intercessor, rex & iudex quoque totius orbis, ideoque perpetuò adest Ecclesiæ suæ, eam colligit, docet, sustentat, viuificat sua membra, potenter protegit & liberat, suaque gratia consolatur & fouet, adhæc agnoscimus illi omnia præsentia esse & ideo per anastrophen ipsum posse dici vbiq; præsentē. Fide præterea ipsum spiritualiter nobis præsentē esse docemus: postremo assentimur Christū homine personaliter, sed nō naturaliter liter aut corporaliter vbique praesentem esse, hoc est vt ipsi Scholastici interpretatur, quod homo Christus vbique est sed non iuxta hu-manam verum iuxta diuinam naturam. Ta-men haec omnia non sufficiunt aduersarijs. Accusamur nihilominus quod omnem praesentiam Christi secundum humanam natu-ram negemus: quod eum omnimodo a coena absentem statuamus: quod ecclesiae caput suum praesens esse negemus: pios Mediatore suo spoliemus: Christū dicamus humanitate sua nullo modo nobis adesse neq; quicquam nobiscum agere. Atqui haec est manifesta & atrox calumnia, cū diserte toties testati simus, nos tantum negare carnis eius substantialē & corporale praesentiam, quae etiam non potest non localis esse, quam aduersarij ipsi improbant, & pugnat cum ascensione Christi & vericate humanae naturae.
units.tr: Even if these and many other things of this kind have hitherto been unheard of in the purer schools of the theologians, they could still be tolerated if they had been proposed in the schools merely as matters for debate, and if they did not, here and there, employ absurd interpretations that differ from the opinion of the Schoolmen, from whom most of them have been borrowed, and if they did not also cast out of the number of Christians all who think and speak otherwise. But now, when we deny with the ancient Church the substantial omnipresence of Christ's body, and say that Christ, who is absent from earth in the substance of his body, is contained in heaven, while by his divinity he is present everywhere, we confess that Christ, though absent in body, is nevertheless present to us according to both natures, humanly [ἀνθρωπίνως]. He is the head of the Church, the supreme high priest, mediator, intercessor, king and also judge of the whole world, and therefore he is always present to his Church. He gathers it, teaches it, sustains it, quickens his members, powerfully protects and frees them, and comforts and cherishes them by his grace. Besides, we acknowledge that all things are present to him, and therefore he can be said, by anastrophe [ἀναστροφή], to be present everywhere. Moreover, we teach that he is present to us spiritually by faith. Lastly, we agree that Christ as man is personally, but not naturally or corporeally, present everywhere, that is, as the Schoolmen themselves explain it, that the man Christ is everywhere, not according to his human nature but according to his divine nature. Yet all this is not enough for our opponents. We are accused nonetheless of denying every presence of Christ according to his human nature, of holding that he is wholly absent from the Supper, of denying that he is present as head of his Church, of robbing the faithful of their Mediator, and of saying that Christ by his humanity is in no way with us and does nothing with us. But this is a manifest and savage calumny, since we have so often clearly testified that we deny only the substantial and bodily presence of his flesh, which cannot but be local, which our opponents themselves reject, and which conflicts with the ascension of Christ and the truth of human nature.

units.la: Falsò nos accusari quod Christum spoliare conemur sua diuinitate & potentia, & nihil amplius quā Machumetani illi tribuamus.
units.tr: It is a false accusation that we try to strip Christ of his divinity and power, and that we ascribe to him nothing more than the Mohammedans do.

units.la: Initio tristis illius controuersiae Sacramen-tarie cum quidam Vbiquitate corporis Christi afferere iam tum inciperent, Zuinglius ma-gno iudicio & singulari gratia discernendo-rum spirituum praeditus, cepit monere Eccle-siam vt sibi ab hoc dogmate caueat, quod id resipiat errorem Martionis, & spectet ad aboiendam veritatem humanæ naturæ in Christo seruatore nostro. Postea verò cum Brentius & Andreas Vbiquitatem hanc nouis coloribus fucatam denuò Ecclesiæ obtrudere conati sunt, ibi rursus viri complures doctissimi, atque inter hos præcipui, Martyr, Bullingerus & Beza, ostenderunt ab ipsis veteres errores renouari. Nam quod ad conuentum & vnionem naturarum attinet, ad Nestorianam hærefin ipsos accedere, quantum verò ad realem communicationem & transfusionem proprietatum, & exequationem humanitatis cū diuinitate, in eo prorsus Eutychianos esse. Has accusationes vt grauissimas, ita etiam verissimas cum illi ferre non possent, vt sese horum criminum suspicione liberarent, eadem nostris impingere cœperunt, non dissimiles hac in re furi cuidam nundinario, qui cū rebus alterius furto ablatis in magna hominum turba fuga se subduceret, altero insequente & clamante, tenete furem: ipse quoque clamabat furem tenendum esse, quasi insons à crimine alterum furti arceret: Simili modo nouæ huius Vbiquitatis authores vt se ipsos crimine liberent, omnium pene αὐθέντων suspicione nostras Ecclesias grauare conantur. Porro cum de incarnatione Domini & Seruatoris nostri Iesu Christi, nō aliam doctrinam proponamus in Ecclesijs nostris ab illa quam quæ ex Sacris literis deprompta & in Veteri Ecclesia perpetuo consensu tradita est, in qua & caeteri praeter Vbiquistas Augustanae confessionis sectatores, & praeterea etiam Papistae absque vlla controuersia inter se haftenus consenserunt, tamen illis omissis nos praecipue inuadunt: quia enim perpetuis calumniis Zuinglianorum nomen apud vulgus exosum reddiderunt, existimant sibi libe rum esse quiduis de illis fingere, praesertim cum diligenter ante cauerint vt omnis defensionis locus illis praecludatur. Etsi autem la-cobo Andreae non incognita est doctrina Ec-clesiarum nostrarum, tamen non veretur etiam contra suam ipsius conscientiam huiusmodi putidissima mendacia de nobis spargere. Itaque cum nullae quantumuis iustae defensiones apud huiusmodi homines locum habere possint, apud reliquos vero qui moderato ingenio praediti absque praeiudicio nostrorum scripta legunt, non longa defensione opus sit, ego quoq; non diu in hoc loco immorabor, sed tantum quasi praetereundo falsitatem huiusmodi criminationum notabo.
units.tr: At the start of that sad Sacramentarian controversy, when some men began to assert the ubiquity of Christ's body, Zwingli, endowed with great judgment and a singular gift of discerning spirits, began to warn the Church to beware of this doctrine, since it savoured of the error of Marcion and tended to abolish the truth of human nature in Christ our Saviour. Later, when Brenz and Andreae tried again to force this ubiquity on the Church, decked out in new colours, several very learned men, and among them above all Martyr, Bullinger and Beza, showed that the old errors were being revived by them. For as far as the union and conjunction of the natures is concerned, they approach the Nestorian heresy; but as far as the real communication and transfusion of properties and the equalising of the humanity with the divinity is concerned, they are wholly Eutychian. Unable to bear these accusations, which were as grievous as they were true, and wishing to free themselves from suspicion of these crimes, they began to hurl the same charges at us, not unlike a certain market thief who, having stolen goods from another, slipped away into a great crowd while the owner pursued him shouting, "Stop the thief!" The thief himself also shouted that the thief had to be stopped, as if the innocent man could ward off the charge of theft from himself by accusing another. In the same way the authors of this new ubiquity, to clear themselves of the crime, try to burden our Churches with the suspicion of almost every author of heresy [αὐθέντων]. Moreover, since in our Churches we set forth on the incarnation of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ no other doctrine than that which is drawn from the Holy Scriptures and has been handed down with constant agreement in the ancient Church, a doctrine in which the other churches, apart from the Ubiquists and the followers of the Augsburg Confession, and besides them even the Papists, have hitherto agreed without any controversy among themselves, yet they pass over all these and attack us in particular. For since by their constant slanders they have made the name of the Zwinglians hateful among the common people, they think it lawful to invent whatever they like about them, especially since they have carefully taken precautions that no place for defence is left open to them. Although the doctrine of our Churches is not unknown to Jacob Andreae, he does not hesitate to spread such filthy lies about us, even against his own conscience. Therefore, since no defences, however just, can have any effect with men of this kind, while with the others, who are of a moderate disposition and read our writings without prejudice, a long defence is not needed, I too will not linger long on this point, but will only, as it were in passing, point out the falsehood of these accusations.

units.la: Est igitur haec ipsius accusatio: Negare nos Christum hominem omnipotentem esse, ideoq; etiam eiusdem diuinitate, omnesq; simul articulos fidei negare, atque nihil plus Christo tribuere quam illi Machumetus in suo Alcorano tribuat. Grauis mehercule accusatio & omnium atrocissima quae nobis intendi potest. fit, quæ si vera esset, merito ab omni societate Christianorum hominum excludendi & arcendi essemus: quod si falsa est, vri facile nos demonstraturos speramus, quid sentiendum est de his, qui huiusmodi calumniis & horrendis criminationibus insontes Ecclesias oppri mere conātur? Sed quia nos Christū hominē omnipotentē esse & Deum esse negare aiūt, de eo primum agamus quomodo Deus sit, neq; enim aliter omnipotens, aliter Deus est. Hominis autē nomine si ipsam personam intelligimus, fatemur ex animo & syncerè credimus, Iesum Christum ex Maria virgine natum, ab æterno verè & essentia Deum esse & vnigenitum Dei filium. Si autem loquuntur de humanitate assumpta à Deo Verbo, dicimus eam creaturam nostræ naturæ consubstantialem esse, non autem essentia aut diuinitatis communicatione in se Deum esse, non magis quàm humanitas est diuinitas. Et quomodo humanitas in se esset Deus, cum ipsa in se non habeat propriam subsistentiam? Et quod homo est, hoc est rationabilis indiuidua & incommunicabilis substantia, hoc in Deo Verbo habet, in cuius persona subsistit & à qua sustentatur. Itaque cum dicitur homo esse Deus, subiecto de quo dicitur Deus, est ipsa Filij persona in qua Christus homo subsistit. Quod si qui hominis nomine intelligunt ipsam humanitatem, & quærunt quomodo
units.tr: The accusation, then, is this: that we deny that Christ is an almighty man, and therefore also deny his divinity, and that we deny all the articles of faith at once, and attribute to Christ no more than Muhammad attributes to him in his Koran. By God, a grave accusation, and the most atrocious that can be brought against us. If it were true, we would rightly be excluded and kept out of all fellowship of Christians; but since it is false, we hope to show easily what ought to be thought of those who try to overwhelm innocent Churches with such calumnies and dreadful charges. But since they say that we deny that Christ is an almighty man and God, let us first consider how he is God, for he is not omnipotent in one way and God in another. If by the name of man we understand the person itself, we confess from our heart and sincerely believe that Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, is truly God from eternity in essence and the only-begotten Son of God. But if they speak of the humanity assumed by God the Word, we say that this humanity is a creature consubstantial with our nature, and that it is not God in itself by any communication of essence or divinity, any more than humanity is divinity. And how could humanity be God in itself, since it does not have a subsistence of its own? What it is to be man, namely a rational, individual and incommunicable substance, this it has in God the Word, in whose person it subsists and by whom it is sustained. Therefore, when it is said that man is God, the subject of which God is predicated is the very person of the Son in whom Christ as man subsists. But if those who understand by man the humanity itself ask how

units.la: Quomodo homo Deus. modo homo ille fit Deus, non vnione sed in se communicata Deitate, hi humanæ naturæ aliam à Verbo personam tribuunt, & Christum diuidunt.
