Similiter qui Christum seruatorem duplici diuinitate Deum faciūt, vna naturali per essentiam, altera communicata per gratiam, qua humanitas Christi peculiari quadam participatione Deitatis Deus fit, hi omnino cum Nestorio Christū in duas personas diuidunt: alia enim erit diuinæ naturæ persona, quæ natura Deus est: alia hominis persona, quæ fit communicatione & participatione gratiæ Deus, atqui ita etiam erunt duo filij, alter secundum diuinitatem & naturam, alter deificata humanitate per gratiam, & item Maria Dei genitrix dicetur, quod hominem pepererit, qui secundum communicatas diuinæ naturæ proprietates Deus dicatur.
units.tr: How man is God. In what way that man becomes God, not by union but by a divinity communicated into himself, these attribute to the human nature a person other than the Word and divide Christ. Likewise those who make Christ the Saviour God by a double divinity, one natural by essence, the other communicated by grace, by which the humanity of Christ becomes God through a certain peculiar participation in the Godhead, these altogether divide Christ into two persons together with Nestorius. For there will be one person of the divine nature, which is God by nature, and another person of the man, who becomes God by communication and participation of grace. And so there will also be two sons, one according to the divinity and nature, the other the humanity deified by grace. And likewise Mary will be called the Mother of God because she bore the man, who is called God according to the properties of the divine nature communicated to him.

units.la: At longe aliter Cyrillus & reliqui Veterum qui Nestorianum errorem confutarunt, docuere, qui ideo sanctam Virginem Dei genitricem nominarunt, quod Deus Verbum, qui ante secula ex patre natus est, in vltimis diebus ex ipsa incarnatus & natus est, Verbum enim cum secundum naturam Deus esset, sensim Abrahæ assumpsit & caro factū est, nulla quidem essentiæ suæ conuersione, alteratione aut commixtione, confusione & temperatura cum carne, sed ita vnitum est carni animam rationalem habenti, vt vnus sit Dei ac patris filius Dominus noster Iesus Christus.Sicut igitur Dei genitrix dicitur propter Deum verbû assumpta carne natû, sic etiam Christus homo vere Deus est Verbi Deitate, sicut Augustinus inquit:In assumptione formæ serui à forma & persona Dei vtrunqué Deus est,sed per assumentem Deum: sicut vtrunq; homo est, sed per acceptû hominem.
units.tr: But Cyril and the other ancients who refuted the Nestorian error taught quite otherwise. They called the holy Virgin the Mother of God because God the Word, who was born of the Father before the ages, was in the last days incarnate and born of her. For the Word, though God by nature, took the seed of Abraham and became flesh, not by any conversion, alteration or mixture, confusion or blending of his essence with the flesh, but was so united to flesh having a rational soul that there is one Son of God and Father, our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, just as the Mother of God is so called because the Word of God was born in the assumed flesh, so also Christ as man is truly God by the Godhead of the Word, as Augustine says: "In the assumption of the form of a servant, both are God by the form and person of God, but through the God who assumes; just as both are man, but through the man who is assumed."

units.la: Atque in hanc sententiam Veteres omnes Christum hominem Deum esse docuerunt, atque inter alios Cassianus(quem Vbiquistæ & Schuencfeldiani falso sibi patrocinari arbitrantur) septem libris de incarnatione Domini aduersus Nestorii scriptis, vbi hoc vnice contendit, Iesum conceptû ex Spiritu sancto & natum ex Maria virgine, quem videre discipuli & palpauerẹ,verum Deum esse, neque tamen vsquam meminit vllius communicatæ deitatis, qua hic homo Deus sit, sed hoc vbique vrget,Christum antequam in carne nasceretur Deum fuisse & Dei filium, & carne assumpta vnum esse Dei filium ,ideoq; hominem Deum esse, per ipsum cui vnitus erat,Dei Verbum.Vndelib.5. Ergo (inquit) euidentissimum est quod ambo Dominum Iesum Christum & hominem manifestarunt & Deum,quia eundem postea homine quem semper Deum , ac per hoc homine & Deum, quia homine ipsum Deum. Iesum Christum (inquit) manifestatum esse à prophetis Euangelistis hominem, quem scilicet viderint & palparint, & qui homo etiam nomine tur aperte in scripturis. Item Deum qui in principio semper fuerit, & Deus excelsus ab illis nominatur: ideo autem eundem hominem & Deum esse, quia qui semper fuit Deus Verbum, postea homo factus est, & per hoc homo & Deus, vt scilicet iam incarnatione facta verbum assumpta carne homo fit, & ita vnus & idem Christus, homo fit & Deus: idque quia homo ipse Deus, hoc est, non alius est homo, alius Deus, sed vnus & idem vtrumque. Homo enim ipse ex Virgine natus ita vnitus est Deo Verbo, vt in illo subsistar, quare paulo post Cassianus hanc vnitatē adhuc clarius exprimit, Idem (inquit) Iesus heri & hodie, id est: idem ante exordium mundi, qui in carne: idem in præterito, qui in præsenti: idem quoque etiam in secula: quia idem per omnia qui ante omnia. Et hoc totum Domi-nus Iesus Christus. Et quomodo idem ante mundi ortum, qui nuper ortus? scilicet quia idem in homine nuper ortus, qui ante ortum omnium Deus. Et ideo Christus totum nominatur quod Deus: quia tanta est Christi & Dei vnitas, vt nemo vtique iam omnino possit vel Christum dicens, non Deum in Christi nomine dicere: vel Deum dicens, non Christum in Dei nomine nuncupare. Ac sic vnito sibi penitus per maiestatem sacræ natiui
units.tr: In this sense all the ancients taught that Christ as man is God, and among others Cassian (whom the Ubiquists and the Schwenckfeldians falsely think defends them), in seven books on the incarnation of the Lord against the writings of Nestorius, where he contends above all that Jesus, conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, whom the disciples saw and touched, is the true God. Yet he nowhere mentions any communicated deity by which this man is God, but everywhere he insists that Christ, before he was born in the flesh, was God and the Son of God, and that after the flesh was assumed he is the one Son of God, and therefore the man is God through the Word of God to which he was united. Lib. 5. "Therefore," he says, "it is most evident that both the prophets and the Evangelists have shown the Lord Jesus Christ to be both man and God: because he who was always God was afterwards made man, and so is man and God, because the man himself is God." Jesus Christ, he says, was revealed by the prophets and Evangelists as man, that is, the one whom they saw and touched, and who is plainly called man in the Scriptures. Likewise, the one who was God from the beginning and is called the high God by them. He is therefore both man and God, because he who always was God the Word was afterwards made man, and so is man and God, namely that, the flesh having been assumed and the incarnation accomplished, the Word becomes man, and so the one and the same Christ becomes man and God. And this is because the man himself is God; that is, the man is not one and God another, but the one and the same is both. For the man himself, born of the Virgin, is so united to God the Word that he subsists in him. Shortly after, Cassian expresses this union still more clearly: "The same Jesus," he says, "yesterday and today, that is, the same before the beginning of the world as in the flesh, the same in the past as in the present, and the same also for ever, because the same in all things as before all things." And all this is the Lord Jesus Christ. And how is he the same before the beginning of the world who has recently begun? Surely because he who recently began in man is the same who was God before all things began. And therefore Christ is named by the whole of what he is, God; because the unity of Christ and God is so great that no one, when he speaks of Christ, can fail to name God in the name of Christ, or, when he speaks of God, fail to name Christ in the name of God. And thus, the two substances having been completely joined through the majesty of the sacred nativity, what was each, namely man and God, has become wholly God.

units.la: M tatis vtriusque substantiæ Sacramento, quica quid erat, scilicet homo & Deus, factum est totum Deus. Item alibi Dei & Christi insepa- rabilem inquit esse substantiam, quòd scilicet vna sit persona inseparabilis, inter Deum & Christum nullam esse distantiam: item per- vnitatem ineffabilem nullam esse distantiam inter Christum & verbum: item Dei filium vnû veré & semper omnia gessisse quæ sunt hominis, & quæ sunt Dei: item quicquid est homo & Deus, totû penitus nominatur Deus indiscreta vnius nominis maiestate, quia vnitus est cum homine Deus: multæque huius generis locutiones apud hunc authorem occurrunt, quibus explicat inseparabilem persona vnitatem, cuius ratione homo Deus dicitur. Loca etiam scripturæ, in quibus quæ vnius naturæ sunt alteri in concreto tribuuntur, aut vbi vnius naturæ nomine tota persona significatur, docet interpretanda esse per synechdochen. Postremo in fine 7. libri, Veterum testimonia quàm plura adducit, in quibus etiam hominem Christum Deum esse asseritur, sed non alia ratione, quam quod vnus & idem sit Dominus noster Iesus Christus, Deus verus ex Deo vero & ante secula natus & postea homo genitus.
units.tr: ...of both substances, the sacrament of his nativity. Because what he was, namely man and God, was made entirely God. Elsewhere too he says that the substance of God and Christ is inseparable, since it is one inseparable person, and that there is no distinction between God and Christ. Likewise, through an ineffable unity, there is no distinction between Christ and the Word. Again, he says that the Son of God, being one, truly and always did all the things that belong to man and all that belong to God. Again, whatever Christ is, both man and God, is wholly and entirely called God by the undivided majesty of the one name, because God is united with man. Many expressions of this kind occur in this author, by which he explains the inseparable unity of person, on the ground of which man is called God. He also teaches that passages of Scripture in which things belonging to one nature are attributed to the other in the concrete, or in which the whole person is signified by the name of one nature, are to be interpreted by synecdoche. Finally, at the end of the seventh book, he adduces very many testimonies of the Fathers, in which it is also asserted that the man Christ is God, but for no other reason than that our Lord Jesus Christ is one and the same, true God from true God, born before the ages and afterwards born as man.

units.la: Nos quoque non aliam fidem habemus de Domino & seruatore nostro Iesu Christo, sed cum D. Petro eum qui est hominis filius aperte confitemur esse filiu Dei viui: & cum D. Paulo hunc qui ex femine Dauid natus est secundum carnem, credimus esse Deum, & quidem Deum super omnia benedictum: Et cum D. Thoma eum qui vulneratus, crucifixus & mortuus, vera palpabili & aspectabili forma a mortuis resurrexit, Dominum & Deum nostrum esse clamamus: agnoscimus enim in eo qui crucifixus est, omne plenitudine Deitatis inhabitare σωματικῶς, & vnū atq; eundem esse, qui in forma Dei, hoc est verus Deus existēs, assumpsit formā serui, Verbum enim quod caro factum est, erat apud Deum & erat Deus.
units.tr: We too hold no other faith concerning our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. With St. Peter we openly confess that he who is the Son of man is the Son of the living God. With St. Paul we believe that he who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh is God, indeed God blessed above all things. With St. Thomas we cry out that he who was wounded, crucified and dead, rose from the dead in a true, palpable and visible form, is our Lord and our God. For we acknowledge that in him who was crucified, all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily [σωματικῶς], and that he who, existing in the form of God, that is, being true God, took the form of a servant, is one and the same. For the Word which was made flesh was with God and was God.

units.la: Quod si aliqui hac simplici confessione Apostolica non contenti, existimant in ipsa carne Christi quandam communicatā Deitatem, aliam à Deitate Verbi qua illud Patri & Spiritui sancto consubstantiale est, quaerendam esse, caueant ne, quod maximum pia culum est & Antichristi opus, Iesum Christum soluant, & nobis pro vero Deo hominem diuinum aut deificatū adorandum proponant. Nam æternæ & infinitæ Deitatis ea est ratio, vt non possit transfundi in creaturam sic vt illa fiat Deus: effusio enim donorū non efficit vt ea creatura cui dona Dei communicata sunt, Deus sit: Erit quidem diuina, ornata donis diuinitatis, sed non propterea Deus. Ideoque etiam non adoranda, manet
units.tr: But if some, not content with this simple Apostolic confession, think that in the very flesh of Christ there is a certain communicated Godhead, other than the Godhead of the Word by which he is consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit, they should take care lest, which is the greatest impiety and a work of Antichrist, they dissolve Jesus Christ and set before us a divine or deified man to be worshipped as the true God. For the nature of eternal and infinite Godhead is such that it cannot be poured into a creature so that the creature becomes God. The outpouring of gifts does not make the creature to whom the gifts of God are communicated God. It will indeed be divine, adorned with the gifts of divinity, but for that reason it is not God. Therefore it is not to be worshipped either,

units.la: enim fixum illud: Iehouam Deum tuum adorabis. Quę quidem adorationis ratio in Christo nobis optimè cóstat, quando eundem qui homo est, scimus verè & natura Deum esse, ideoque omnipotentem & inspectorem cordium nostrorum, neque alibi vsquam hominem à Deo separamus: & vt humanitati quæ à diuinitate suscepta est, non tribuimus peccatum: ita etiam non illi in se tribuimus quod sit adoranda, quod sit omnipotes, quod præsentissimè adsit & corda scrutetur. Si enim hæc humanæ naturæ in sese tribuantur vt transfusa à diuinitate in humanam naturam in ipsa tanquam in suo subiecto inhæreant, simul quoque (vt supra diximus) tribuitur sua hypostasis separata humanitate, & Christus soluitur & duo fiunt Dij & filij, naturæ alter, alter gratia: & sequitur vel hominem hunc nō adorandū esse, vel aliquē adorandū esse qui natura non sit Deus. Qui igitur diuinitatis & adorationis & omnipotentię rationem in ipsa humana Christi natura quærunt, & hominem hunc per naturam humanitatis suæ Deum omnipotentem & adorandum esse volunt, non intelligūt quomodo Christus verè sit homo: Christus enim, quod sæpe dictum est, nō per se aut seorsim, sed in ipsa omnipotentis Verbi persona est homo. Humanitas enim in Christo non est homo, etiamsi integra sit vt in cæteris hominibus, sed persona Verbi na Verbi vnitam in fe habet & subsistentem humanitatem, cui mysterio nihil simile in alijs hominibus cogitari potest.
units.tr: for that statement stands fixed: "Thou shalt worship Jehovah thy God." This rule of worship is best observed in Christ for us, when we know that he who is man is truly and by nature God, and therefore almighty and the searcher of our hearts, and we nowhere separate the man from God. And just as we do not attribute sin to the humanity which was assumed by the divinity, so we do not attribute to it in itself that it is to be worshipped, that it is almighty, that it is present everywhere and searches the hearts. For if these attributes of human nature were ascribed to it in itself, as if they were transfused from the divinity into the human nature and inhered in it as in their own subject, then at the same time (as we said above) its hypostasis would be attributed separately from the humanity, and Christ would be dissolved, and there would be two Gods and sons, one by nature and the other by grace. It would follow either that this man is not to be worshipped, or that someone is to be worshipped who is not God by nature. Therefore those who seek the reason of divinity, of worship and of omnipotence in the human nature of Christ itself, and want this man to be almighty and to be worshipped as God through the nature of his humanity, do not understand how Christ is truly man. For Christ, as has often been said, is man not by himself or apart, but in the very person of the almighty Word. For the humanity in Christ is not a man, even though it is whole as it is in other men; rather, the Word of God has in its person a humanity united and subsisting, and nothing like this mystery can be conceived in other men.

units.la: Porro quod aduersarij quærunt: An humanitas Christi cum omnipotentia diuina nullam reipsa communionem habeat, <bl>Ob die menschlich natur mit der Allmechtige Gottheit nichts mit der thaat gmein habe</bl> / Ambi guum est: Nam per communionē intelligi potest comunio personalis, quod scilicet humana natura ab ea persona assumpta est & in illa sustentatur, quæ Deus est & omnipotens, atque hæc communio dici forte potest realis, quoniam vnio naturarum vera est & ineffabilis, & ea quæ naturarum sunt propria, reipsa sunt huic personæ communia, sed quę diuina sunt in natura Dei Verbi, & quę humana, in ipsa humanitate. Atque ita dicimus humanam naturā communionem habere omnipotentiæ, sicut & Deitatis: sicut enim humana natura non in se est Deus vel diuinitas, sed homo est Deus: sic etiā in se non est omnipotēs, sed pars personæ omnipotentis: Liceat enim nobis exemplo Veterum naturas in Christo partes personæ illius nominare. Rursus quæ de reali communicatione omnipotentiæ proposita sunt ab aduersarijs, intelligi possunt de reali transfusione, quasi diuina natura suam omnipotentiam transfuderit in humanā, sic vt Christus homo, quatenus homo seu secundum humanam naturā, sit omnipotens dono & communicatione factus: hanc communionem nos negamus. Quoniā vt supra ostendimus, realis illa transfusio proprietatum propter sus Eutychiana est, & veritatem humanæ naturæ in Christo abolet. Neque tamen propterea accusandi sumus quod Christū impotentem hominē faciamus, nam quod nos docemus, docent Sacrae literæ, & has eodem modo quo & nos Lutherus interpretatus est, cuius authoritas ab aduersarijs reijci non potest, quando omnium patrū authoritati a ple risque eorū præponitur: Is autē in 7. cap. Danielis ita scribit: Ab eo momento quo diuini & humanitas in vnā persona vnitæ sunt, homo Mariæ filius est, ac nominatur omnipotens, æternus Deus, qui æternam potestatem habet, omniaq; creauit & conseruat, per communicationē idiomatum: propterea quod vna est cum diuinitate persona & verus etiam Deus: & de hoc loquitur Matth. 11. Omnia mihi data sunt à patre: & Matth. vlt. Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra. Lo-qui autem hic Lutherū eodem modo de communione idiomatum, quo nos docemus, non de reali illa communione nuper confista, in-de apparet, quod hac comunicatione Christo homini æternam potestatē & omniū rerum creationem tribuit. Longe autē clarius alibi inquit: Intempestiuam narrationem quidam hic af
units.tr: Furthermore, as to what our opponents ask: whether the humanity of Christ has no real communion with the almighty divinity, <bl>whether the human nature has nothing in common in fact with the almighty Godhead</bl>. The question is ambiguous. For communion can be understood as personal communion, namely that the human nature was assumed by that person who is God and almighty and is sustained in him. This communion may perhaps also be called real, since the union of the natures is true and ineffable, and what belongs to the natures is in fact common to this one person: what is divine in the nature of God the Word, and what is human in the humanity itself. And so we say that the human nature has communion with almighty power, just as with the Godhead. For just as the human nature is not God or divinity in itself, but man is God, so it is not almighty in itself but is a part of the almighty person. For with the example of the ancients let us be allowed to call the natures in Christ parts of that person. Again, what our opponents have put forward about a real communication of omnipotence can be understood as a real transfusion, as if the divine nature had poured its omnipotence into the human nature, so that Christ as man, in so far as he is man or according to the human nature, has been made almighty by gift and communication. This communion we deny. For, as we have shown above, that real transfusion of properties is Eutychian and abolishes the truth of the human nature in Christ. Nor, however, are we to be accused of making Christ an impotent man, for what we teach the Sacred Letters teach, and Luther has interpreted them in the same way as we do. His authority cannot be rejected by our opponents, since it is placed before the authority of all the Fathers by most of them. In chapter 7 of Daniel he writes thus: "From the moment when the divine and the human were united in one person, the man, son of Mary, is also called almighty, eternal God, who has eternal power, and created and preserves all things, by the communication of idioms, because the person is one with the divinity and is also true God." He speaks of this in Matth. 11: "All things are given to me by the Father," and Matth. last: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth." That Luther here speaks of the communion of idioms in the same way as we teach, and not of that real communion just now mentioned, is clear from this: by this communication he ascribes to the man Christ eternal power and the creation of all things. Yet he says even more clearly elsewhere:

units.la: Lutherus negat Christi quoad humanam naturam omnipotentem nisi per communicationem idiomatum. hic afferunt, dicentes, Filius nescit, id est, nolu-it scire. Quid enim opus istis commentis? Christus verus homo fuit, quare vt alius pu-rus, sed sanctus homo, non quolibet tempore cogitauit, dixit, voluit, intellexit omnia, sicut imperiti quidam omnipotentem in eo homi-nem faciunt, permiscetes duas naturas, atque opera earum parum prudenter. Sicut enim non quolibet tempore omnia vidit, audiuit, atque sensit, ita etiam corde non omnia sem-per agnouit, sed quantum illum duxit ac do-cuit Dominus. Scholastici etiam de omnipotentia humanae naturae in Christo sic scribunt: Homini Christo attribuitur omnipotentia per communicationem idiomatum, sicut caeterae proprietates diuinae: sed de humana natu-ra in Christo quae est creatura, respondetur breuiter, quod omnipotentia nulli creaturae communicari potest. Si igitur Turcae sunt qui humanitatem Christi seu humanam naturam omnipotentem esse negant, age Lutherum primum damnet, deinde Scholasticos scripto-res, ad quos tamen cum ipsi libet, Iacobus Andreae prouocat, & multa ab illis de mysterio Trinitatis & vnionis personalis pie & erudi-te scripta, asseritis.
units.tr: Luther denies that Christ is almighty as regards his human nature, except through the communication of idioms. "Some here bring up an untimely story, saying, 'The Son does not know,' that is, 'he was unwilling to know.' For why do we need such inventions? Christ was a true man, and therefore, like any other pure but holy man, he did not at every time think, say, will and understand all things, as some unskilled persons make him an almighty man, mixing the two natures and their works rather unwisely. For just as he did not see, hear and feel everything at every time, so also in his heart he did not always know everything, but as much as the Lord led him and taught him." The Scholastics also write about the omnipotence of the human nature in Christ as follows: "Omnipotence is attributed to the man Christ through the communication of idioms, as are the other divine properties; but concerning the human nature in Christ, which is a creature, it is briefly answered that omnipotence cannot be communicated to any creature." If therefore it is the Turks who deny that the humanity of Christ or the human nature is almighty, then let them first condemn Luther, and then the Scholastic writers, to whom Jacob Andreae appeals whenever it pleases him, and whom you assert to have written piously and learnedly, and with much from them, about the mystery of the Trinity and the personal union.

units.la: At inquit: Zuingliani non plus tribuunt filio Mariae quam Turcae. Alcoranus enim Turcicus huic tribuit quod Deus illi animā suam dederit, eumque omnibus prophetis excellentiorem fecerit, negat tamen eum omnipotentem esse: non plus autè (inquit) Andreas Zuingliani Christo tribuunt. Hoc vero salsissimum est: ac mirum profecto est hominem Theologum adeo omnem pudorem exuisse, vt non dubitet publice ea de nobis afirmare, de quibus mendacij & calumniae eum arguunt non tantum nostrorum scripta & conciones, sed propria ipsius quoque absque dubio conscientia: neque enim ignorat quae sit nostra fides & confessio de Iesu Christo Dei & Mariae filio, & quâ haec nihil habeat commune cum Alcorano. Num enim Alcoranus docet Iesum esse Deum & seruatorem nostrum Dei filium? Vbi vero Alcoranus meminit illius ineffabilis mysterij, quod Verbum caro factum est & Deus homo natus seu Deus manifestatus in carne? Sed quid ego hanc comparationem ingredior, cum totum genus doctrinae diuersum sit? Neque enim vllu caput nostrae doctrinae Iacobus Andreae proferre potest, in quo à Catholica Ecclesia dissentientes cum Alcorano congruamus. At (inquit) Alcoranum adimere Christo homini omnipotentiam, idem autem nos quoque facere. Sed pe iam dixi nos nunquam negasse neque etiam negare Christum hominem esse omnipotentem, nisi hominis nomen pro abstracto potentia, tum enim cum Veteribus Christū hominem hoc est, quatenus homo est, seu humanam nam eius naturā in se & reipsa non esse omnipotentem afferimus. Sed hoc illud est quod ante dixi & deinceps repetendum erit, illi ipsi qui nobis Machumetanismi crimen impingunt, verè Nestoriani sunt, quorum error primus ad Machumetanissimum gradus est: humanam nanque naturam in Christo ut per se subsistentē considerant, ideoque ut propriam personam illi tribuunt, non autem tantum a Verbo eam sustentari agnoscunt, ita quoque propriam illi omnipotentiam & Deitatem affingunt: atque ut illis non satis est hominem hunc in verbo subsistere; ita illis etiam non satis est hominem hunc in verbi natura omnipotentem esse. Nam si non extra Verbi personam hominem hunc considerarent, sicut etiam Machumetani faciunt, faciunt le viderent nos hoc ipso quòd aliā quàm Machumetani subsistendi rationem huic homini tribuimus, prorsus ab illis discrepare. Etsi enim illi Iesum Mariae filium nominant, quia tamen hunc non agnoscunt Dei filium, & vnum atque eundem in eadem persona hominem & Deum, non magis eundem Christum nobiscū profitentur, quàm eundē Deum creatorem coeli & terrae, qui illis neque pater neq; filius neq; Spiritus sanctus est, sed est figmentum cordis eorū, vnde etiam veteres anathema dixerunt Deo Machometis holosphyro.
units.tr: But they say: the Zwinglians attribute no more to the Son of Mary than the Turks do. The Turkish Koran grants that God gave him his soul and made him more excellent than all the prophets, yet it denies that he is almighty; and yet (they say) Andreas holds that the Zwinglians attribute no more to Christ than that. This is most absurd. It is truly astonishing that a theologian has so cast off all shame that he publicly asserts about us things which not only the writings and sermons of our people, but his own conscience beyond doubt, prove to be lies and slander. For he is not ignorant of what our faith and confession about Jesus Christ, God and son of Mary, is, and how little it has in common with the Koran. Does the Koran teach that Jesus is God and our Saviour, the Son of God? Where does the Koran mention that ineffable mystery, that the Word was made flesh, and that God was born a man, or God was manifested in the flesh? But why do I enter into this comparison, since the whole kind of doctrine is different? Indeed Andreas cannot point to any article of our doctrine in which we, who dissent from the Catholic Church, agree with the Koran. But (he says) the Koran takes away from Christ as man the power to be almighty, and we do the same. But I have already said that we have never denied, nor do we now deny, that Christ as man is almighty, unless by "man" one means the abstract power; for when we with the ancients affirm that Christ as man, that is, insofar as he is man, or his human nature in itself and in reality, is not almighty, we are not denying anything. But this is what I said before and must repeat from now on: those very men who charge us with the crime of Mohammedanism are truly Nestorians, and their error is the first step toward the most Mohammedan extreme. For they regard the human nature in Christ as subsisting in itself, and therefore ascribe to it a proper person, and do not merely acknowledge that it is sustained by the Word; so they also attribute to it its own omnipotence and deity. And just as it is not enough for them that this man subsists in the Word, so it is not enough for them that this man is almighty in the nature of the Word. For if they did not consider this man outside the person of the Word, as the Mohammedans also do, they would see that by the very fact that we ascribe to this man a mode of subsisting different from that of the Mohammedans, we differ from them entirely. For although they call Jesus the son of Mary, because they do not acknowledge him as the Son of God, and as one and the same man and God in one and the same person, they profess the same Christ with us no more than they profess the same God, creator of heaven and earth, who for them is neither Father, nor Son, nor Holy Spirit, but is a figment of their heart; whence also the ancients pronounced anathema on the God of Mahomet, the holosphyrus.

units.la: Quod autem obijciunt nobis improbos tarij. nebulones qui vel prorsus ad Turcas defece‑runt, vel Samosatenicos furores Turcicis assi‑nes in Polonia & Transyluania fpargut, hos dicentes a nobis egressos esse, atque inde con‑stare nos alere femina Turcicae doctrinae: ar‑gumentu est admodum futile. An non enim primi illi haeretici ex Apostolica Ecclesia e‑gressi sunt? de quibus Apostolus inquit: E‑gressi sunt ex nobis, sed non fuerunt ex nobis. Possem multos nominatim commemorare qui ab aduersarijs nostris ad Papistas defecerunt, num vero inde conficere licet ipsorum doctri‑nam esse Papiftica? praesertim cum non pau‑ca proferri possint in quibus cum Papistis consentiunt. Certum est Antitrinitarios, & qui blasphemas opiniones de Christo in Po‑lonia, Transyluania & alibi diffeminarunt, omnes ex Serueti schola prodijfe, Seruetus autem nunquam fuit membrum nostrarum Ecclesiarum, sed ab initio cum sua impia dog‑mata in lucem proferre conaretur, nostrarum Ecclesiarum ministri constantissime seilli op‑posuerunt, & quae postea fuerint cum magi‑stratuum politicorum, tum etiam ministrorum Ecclesiae de Serueta doctrina iudicia, ex ho‑rum libris et illorum rebus gestis vniuerso orbi notu est. Vtinam vero illi, qui nobis iniuste imputant Antitrinitariorum furores, non ipsi eosdem suis nouis figmentis, & inusitatis in‑terpretationibus locorum scripturae confir‑marent. marent. Nam in Transyluania de Christi hominis diuinitate & quomodo Deus sit, ita docent: Deum censeri paternæ diuinitatis inhabitatione, participationeque, communicata illi virtute, diuinitate, & miraculorum potestate: itaque enim scribunt in libello de Mediatoris Iesu Christi hominis diuinitate æqualitateque, edito Albæ Iuliæ, 1568. & ibidem has rationes afferūt, cur homo Christus sit Deus: Primò quod sit proprius Dei filius conceptus de spiritu Dei in vtero virginis. Deinde quia dedit illi Deus nomen quod est super omne nomen. Quod omnis plenitudo diuinitatis in illo corporaliter inhabitat. Item, Quia illi data fuit omnis potestas in cælo & in terra, &c. Hisadmodum affinia sunt, quæ Iacobus Andreæ scribit, qui enumeratis locis scripturæ quibus dicitur Christo data omnis potestas, & collocatum ad dexteram patris, & omnia subiecta pedibus eius, & in ipso habitare omnem plenitudinē, subijcit: Hæc sunt testimonia illustria, quæ docent, cur homo Christus dicatur Deus, nō quia Deus sit in ipso (qui in omnibus creaturis est non modo natura, sed etiam secundum subsistentias, sicut supra demonstratum est) sed quia in assumptione car nis dedit huic homini omnem potestatem in cælo & in terra, ornauit eum omniscientia & sapientia, communicauit ei omnia dona Spiritus sancti, collocauit cum super omnē principatum, dedit ei nomen super omne nomen, quod nomen est Dei nomen. Et hoc est homi-nem quoque esse Deum. Rursus Franciscus Dauidis in opere contra Petri Carolini librū locū Pauli ad Philippenses: In ipso inhabitat plenitudo deitatis corporaliter, sic interpre-tatur. Vocabulum corpus opponitur umbris veteris Testamenti, in quibus ex parte ac sub umbris virtus deitatis splenduit & emicuit, & explicatur ad Heb.10. quod significet, non in parabolis vel exemplis, sed reipsa, Plenitudo deitatis accipitur pro donis diuinis quibus Christus exædificatus est fine defectu, vt omnes nos ex ipsius sapientia participaremus & impleremur: significat plenaria Dei dona quę ex parte etiam fidelibus dantur. Conferatur cum hac interpretatione Vbiquitaria huius loci interpretatio, expendantur etiam alia loca scripturarum quæ de Deitate Christi loquuntur, inueniemus Vbiquistas cum Antitrinitarijs vbique fere consentire, quod hæc de humana natura Christi & illi communicata Deitate interpretantur. Etsi autem Vbiquistæ in eo ab Antitrinitarijs dissentiunt quod λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο agnoscunt qui carnem humanā assumpserit, facile tamen apparet quantum eorum causam iuuent, quando hæc fundamenta illorum confirmant, nempe scripturam hic non loqui de æterna & vera Deitate, sed quadam communicata, item Deitatem esse communicabile homini. Equidem me-lius de illis spero quàm vt existimem ipsos tam horrendis furoribus Seruetanorum pa-trocinari velle, interim cum immerito nos il-lis coniungant, non potui nec debui præteri-re quin ostenderem ipsos Seruetanorum fun-damenta ex parte substruere: neque in hanc tantum partem peccant, sed dum nimio con-tendendi studio doctrinam de incarnatione filij Dei suo arbitratu fingunt atque refingūt, quàm plurimos errores Veterum dudū dam-natos renouant, sicut deinceps ostendemus.
units.tr: As for their objection that we are supported by wicked tricksters and scoundrels, who either have completely deserted to the Turks or in Poland and Transylvania scatter the Samosatene frenzies, like asses to the Turks, saying that these men went out from us, and that from this it is established that we nourish the seed of Turkish doctrine: this is a very trifling argument. For did not those first heretics go out from the apostolic Church? Of them the Apostle says: "They went out from us, but they were not of us." I could name many who have deserted from our opponents to the Papists; but can one therefore conclude that their doctrine is Papist, especially since many things could be cited in which they agree with the Papists? It is certain that the Antitrinitarians, and those who spread blasphemous opinions about Christ in Poland, Transylvania and elsewhere, all came out of the school of Servetus; but Servetus was never a member of our Churches, and from the beginning, when he tried to bring his impious dogmas to light, the ministers of our Churches most steadfastly opposed him. What judgments on Servetus's doctrine were later pronounced both by the political magistrates and by the ministers of the Church is known to the whole world from their books and deeds. Would that those who unjustly impute to us the frenzies of the Antitrinitarians did not themselves confirm the same by their new fictions and unusual interpretations of passages of Scripture. For in Transylvania they teach thus about the divinity of Christ the man, and how God is: that God is reckoned by the indwelling and participation of the Father's divinity, with power, divinity and the faculty of miracles communicated to him. For so they write in a little book on the divinity and equality of the Mediator Jesus Christ the man, published at Alba Iulia in 1568, and there they give these reasons why the man Christ is God: first, because he is the proper Son of God, conceived of the Spirit of God in the virgin's womb; second, because God gave him the name which is above every name; third, because all the fullness of the divinity dwells in him bodily; likewise, because all power in heaven and on earth was given to him, and so on. Very similar to these are the things Andreas writes, who, after listing the passages of Scripture which say that all power was given to Christ, that he was seated at the right hand of the Father, that all things were subjected under his feet, and that all fullness dwells in him, adds: these are the striking testimonies which teach why the man Christ is called God, not because God is in him (who is in all creatures not only by nature but also according to subsistences, as has been shown above), but because in the assumption of flesh he gave to this man all power in heaven and on earth, adorned him with omniscience and wisdom, communicated to him all the gifts of the Holy Spirit, set him above every principality, and gave him a name above every name, which name is the name of God. And this is also to say that the man is God. Again, Franciscus Davidis, in his work against Peter Carolus's book, interprets the passage of Paul to the Philippians, "In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily," thus: the word "body" is set against the shadows of the Old Testament, in which the power of the Godhead shone and gleamed partly and under shadows, and it is explained in Hebrews 10, that it signifies not in parables or examples but in reality. "Fullness of the Godhead" is taken to mean the divine gifts by which Christ was built up without defect, so that we all might share in his wisdom and be filled; it signifies the full gifts of God which are given in part also to the faithful. If the Ubiquitarian interpretation of this passage is compared with this interpretation, and other passages of Scripture which speak of the Deity of Christ are weighed, we will find that the Ubiquitarians agree almost everywhere with the Antitrinitarians in interpreting these things of the human nature of Christ and of the deity communicated to it. Although the Ubiquitarians differ from the Antitrinitarians in acknowledging that the Word [λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο] took on human flesh, it nevertheless easily appears how greatly they help their cause when they confirm these foundations of theirs, namely that Scripture here does not speak of the eternal and true Deity, but of a certain communicated one, and also that Deity can be communicated to a man. Indeed I hope better of them than to think that they wish to defend so horrible the frenzies of the Servetians; yet since they unjustly join us with them, I could not and ought not to pass over without showing that they in part lay the foundations of the Servetians. Nor do they err only in this part; but while through an excessive zeal for contending they feign and refashion the doctrine of the incarnation of the Son of God at their own pleasure, they renew very many errors of the ancients long since condemned, as we shall show below.

units.la: Vbiquistæ suis dogmatibus Nestorianam & Eutychianam atq; alias his cognatas hæreses renouant.
units.tr: The Ubiquitists renew the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies, and others akin to them, through their doctrines.

units.la: Etsi sæpe antea nostri copiose & perspicue demonstrarunt, quæ sit cognatio nouæ huius doctrinæ Vbiquisticæ cum Veteribus dudum damnatis hæresibus, tamen arbitror non molestum fore lectori si quod in aliis partibus huius tractationis feci, breuem summam eorum quæ ab aliis susius tradita sunt hic re-petam. Nam cum ipsos non pudeat eosdem errores repetere & renouare, nos quoq; non pigere nec pudere debet Ecclesiam subinde de his erroribus admonere, & indicare instàs periculum, ne incauti aliqui & simplices se-ducantur.
units.tr: Although our people have often already shown, fully and clearly, how closely this new Ubiquitarian doctrine is related to the heresies condemned long ago, I think the reader will not mind if, in this part of my treatment, I briefly repeat a summary of what others have set out at greater length. Since they are not ashamed to repeat and revive the same errors, we ought not to be reluctant or ashamed to warn the Church from time to time about these errors and to point out the danger that some unwary and simple people may be led astray.

units.la: Initio igitur doctrinam eorum de vnione personali, quam per transfusionem aut communicationem realem omnium donorum & proprietatum diuinæ naturæ definiunt, dici-mus ad Sabellianam & Patripassianorum hæ-resin accedere. Comunicatio enim donorum ex æquo ad omnes personas Trinitatis perti-net: ac quod Andreas dicit aliam esse ingenitam patris, aliam genitam filij, aliam procedentè Spiritus sancti sapientiâ & potentiâ, agnoscimus quidè personas ita distingui inter se, at vbi de comunicatione agitur, comunis est operatio trium personarū. Itaq; sequitur vt communicatio hæc communis est tribus personis, ita etiam vnionem seu assumptionem carnis commune illis esse, & sic passionem & mortem non tantū ad filij, sed etiam ad Patris & Spiritus sancti personas pertinere.
units.tr: To begin, we say that their doctrine of the personal union, which they define as a transfusion or real communication of all the gifts and properties of the divine nature, comes close to the heresy of the Sabellians and Patripassians. For the communication of gifts pertains equally to all the persons of the Trinity. And although Andreas says that the unbegotten nature belongs to the Father, the begotten to the Son, and that which proceeds to the wisdom and power of the Holy Spirit, we grant that the persons are distinguished from one another in this way. But when the discussion turns to communication, the operation of the three persons is common. It follows, therefore, that since this communication is common to the three persons, the union or assumption of the flesh is also common to them, and so the passion and death pertain not only to the person of the Son but also to the persons of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Deinde vnio illa quod eadem inhabitatio sit filij Dei in filio hominis quæ & in cæteris sanctis, sed solum hoc differat, quod aliis certa tantum & finita dona, huic autem omnem suam potentiam communicet, prorsus Nestoriana est, & nominatim damnatur à B. Cyrillo Anathematismo 5. In quo constanter asserit Deum Verbum aliter habitare in assumpta carne atque in cæteris sanctis. Nam cum reprehensores Cyrilli Christū dixissent Deum ferum hominem, sed qui non particularem quandam gratiā acceperit sed omnem vnitatem habeat filij deitatem, reijcit id Cyrillus, & docet loncet longe aliud esse Verbū factum esse hominem quàm habitare in homine. Idem etiā sensisse D. Augustinum supra docuimus. Iamquod Brentius scribit de Petri miraculis : Etedidit hæc miracula potentia diuina eaque non longe absenti, sed omnino intime præ-senti, non igitur ne hac quidem ratione di-scrimen est inter Christum & Petrum. Item quod de resurrectione addit: Sicut Christus excitatus est diuina virtute, ita resurget etiā Petrus diuina virtute, eaque non absenti sed omnino præsenti, nec minus ipsi quàm Chri sto intime præsenti, eaque tota præsenti, quod vbicunque est diuinitas, ibi sit tota, cum Ver-bum seu ὁ λόγος non minus sua essentia, poten-tia & præsentia habitet in Petro quam in ho-mine Christo. Hæc inquam omnia Nestoria-na sunt, & cum septimo & nono Anathema-tismo Cyrilli pugnant. Petrus & alij sanctíin spiritu sancto miracula operati sunt, qui tamen alij ab ipso fuerunt, quod si Christus & Petrus eodem modo miracula operati sunt, oportet in Christo quoque virtutem spiritus operantem aliam ab ipso fuisse, quod vt Ne-storianum damnat Cyrillus, ac inter alia in-quit : Itaq; vnus & solus Christus Iesus, quasi per organa corporis sui operatus est diuina signa, & non operandi virtute habuisse eum dicimus secundum similitudinem sanctorum. Præterea ita loquuntur Vbiquiste vt vix ipse
units.tr: Next, their claim that this union is the same indwelling of the Son of God in the Son of man as in the other saints, differing only in that he gives to the others certain and limited gifts but communicates to this man his whole power, is altogether Nestorian. It is expressly condemned by Saint Cyril in his fifth Anathematism, where he firmly asserts that the Word of God dwells in the assumed flesh in a different way from the other saints. For when the critics of Cyril had said that Christ was a God-bearing man, but one who had received not some particular grace but had the deity of the Son in its entire unity, Cyril rejects this and teaches that it is far different for the Word to have become man than for it to dwell in a man. We have shown above that Saint Augustine also held the same view. Again, when Brenz writes about the miracles of Peter: "This power of God wrought these miracles, and it was not far absent but wholly and intimately present," therefore there is no difference between Christ and Peter even in this respect. Likewise, when he adds about the resurrection: "Just as Christ was raised by divine power, so Peter also will rise by divine power, and that not absent but wholly present, and no less intimately present to him than to Christ, and wholly present, because wherever the divinity is, there it is whole," since the Word, or ὁ λόγος, dwells in Peter no less by its essence, power and presence than in the man Christ. I say all these things are Nestorian, and they conflict with the seventh and ninth Anathematisms of Cyril. Peter and the other saints worked miracles in the Holy Spirit, yet they were distinct from him. But if Christ and Peter worked miracles in the same way, it must follow that in Christ also the power working through the Spirit was other than himself. Cyril condemns this as Nestorian, and among other things he says: "So the one and only Christ Jesus worked divine signs, as it were through the organs of his body, and we do not say that he had the power of working as the saints do, by likeness." Moreover, the Ubiquitarians speak in such a way that Nestorius himself, [3 continued] scarcely...

units.la: Nestorius alijs locutionibus quæ apertiùs personas separarent, vsus fuerit (si modo dè illo iudicium faciendum est ex fragmentis concionum eius & epistolis, quæ Ephesino concilio coniuncta habentur, veluti cum dicunt, Aeternum Dei filium habitare in filio hominis quem ex Maria virgine assumpsit. Item , filium Dei implere sua essentia filium hominis quem assumpsit : item Christum hominem æquè ac Christum Deum vbique præsentem esse : Christum hominem omnia facere velle ac posse quæ Christus Deus vult facit ac potest : quasi scilicet alius sit filius Dei, alius filius hominis, alius Christus Deus,alius Christus homo : & nō potius vnus & idem Dei & hominis filius, Deus & homo.
units.tr: ...Nestorius scarcely used other expressions that separated the persons more plainly (if indeed we are to judge him from the fragments of his sermons and letters, which are preserved in the records of the Council of Ephesus), as when they say: "The eternal Son of God dwells in the Son of man whom he assumed from the Virgin Mary"; likewise, "the Son of God fills with his essence the Son of man whom he assumed"; likewise, "Christ the man is present everywhere just as Christ God is"; "Christ the man wills and is able to do all the things that Christ God wills and does and is able to do." As if, forsooth, the Son of God were one and the Son of man another, Christ God one and Christ man another, and not rather one and the same Son of God and man, God and man.

units.la: Atque etiam apertius quasi de duobus filijs loquuntur, dicentes: Hominē Christum vnam personam factum cum filio Dei participatione proprietatum filij Dei.Item hominem Christum parem maiestatem cum filio Dei habere.Nam in huiusmodi locutionibus conumeratione videtur indicari personarum multitudo & separatio. Ac præpositio Cum à Patribus in abstracto quidem vsurpatur,sed eodem modo in concreto adhibita, duas personas coniungere videtur. Huiusmodi autem locutionibus pleni sunt Vbiquitarum libri, qui nescio quo consilio absque vllo discrimine vocibus abstractis & concretis eodē modo vtun{a}vtuntur. Item quod scribunt diuinitatem realiter communicare humanitati personā, prior sus Nestorianū est. Sicut enim suæ communicationis realis ratione aliam statuunt diuinitatem hominis Christi, communicatā illi ab essentiali & æterna diuinitate verbi: ita etiam eiusdem ratione illos statuere oportet aliam communicatam personam hominis Christi a persona verbi, atque ita duæ erunt personæ Christus homo, & Christus Deus, quæ est impia Nestorij hæresis. Neque refert quod deinde communicatione proprietatum & hæ rum exæquatione vnam personam faciunt; namq; etiam Nestorius idem faciebat, docens hac adunationis ratione, qd' homini huic dō nata esset a Deo æqualitas dignitatis siue authoritatis; & vt similili appellatione Christus & filius dicatur & Dominus, sicut Cyrillus scribit cap. 27. lib. de Incarnatione. Præterea pro Trinitate quaternitatem in diuinitate statuunt, si enim humana natura in Christo communicata diuinitate & transfusione donorum Deus facta est, atq; alia hæc est communicata diuinitas ab æterna deitate verbi, oportet vt quartam personā faciant Christum hominē Deum secundum humanam naturam. Simul etiam duplicem deitatem faciunt eamq; inæqualem. Et tale quid innuit Marpachius, qui proprietates & opera diuinitatis, & nomen atque honorem Iehouæ, inquit nemini com-
units.tr: Even more openly they speak as if of two sons, saying: "Christ the man has been made one person with the Son of God by the participation of the properties of the Son of God." Likewise: "Christ the man has equal majesty with the Son of God." For in such expressions a counting-together seems to indicate a plurality and separation of persons. The preposition "with" (cum) is used by the Fathers in the abstract sense, but when applied in the same way in the concrete it seems to join two persons. Yet the books of the Ubiquitarians are full of such expressions, which for some reason they use without any distinction, employing abstract and concrete terms in the same way. Likewise, their statement that the divinity communicates its person to the humanity really is more Nestorian than before. For just as by their theory of real communication they posit another divinity of the man Christ, communicated to him from the essential and eternal divinity of the Word, so by the same reasoning they must posit another person of the man Christ communicated from the person of the Word; and so there will be two persons, Christ the man and Christ God, which is the impious heresy of Nestorius. Nor does it matter that they afterwards make one person by the communication of properties and the equalization of them; for Nestorius also did the same, teaching by this manner of union that equality of dignity or authority was given by God to this man, so that he is called by a similar title Christ and Son and Lord, as Cyril writes in chapter 27 of his book On the Incarnation. Furthermore, in place of the Trinity they posit a quaternity in the Godhead. For if the human nature in Christ has become God by the communication of the divinity and by the transfusion of gifts, and if this communicated divinity is other than the eternal Godhead of the Word, they must make a fourth person, Christ the man, God according to the human nature. At the same time they make a double Godhead, and an unequal one. Something of this sort is hinted at by Marbach, who says that the properties and works of the divinity, and the name and honour of Jehovah, belong to no one except the Trinity, or to him who is substantially joined to the Trinity and contained in it.

units.la: N uenire nisi trinitati,aut huic qui Trinitati per fonaliter coniunctus sit, & in ea contineatur. Atq; haec disiunctiua propositio fundamentum est omnium illius argumentorum, quibus nos crasso volumine dudū edito profiterı voluit, & tamē nusquā hanc probat,sed quasi pro confesso sumit. Vbi ego hoc quaero a Domino Superintendente, vtrum de persona,an de natura loquatur?Si enim loquitur de natura,proprietates & opera,nomen & honor sant Trinitatis soli diuinae naturae conueniūt, quod si vult haec ad creatitiā naturam transferri posse,ostendat id,vt omnes videant eum Arrianorum & Seruetanorum nostrae aetatis su-roribus viam sternere. Quod si de persona loquitur, rursus etiam hac disiunctione nō erat opus,nam si aliam personam Trinitati connumerare vult, quaternitatem facit, si de aeterna verbi persona loquitur, non opus erat disiunctione,cū Christus non sit coniunctus Trinitati,sed vnus ex Trinitate.Neq; nos Christum hominē trinitate excludimus,nam illa persona quę est Christus homo, nō est creata aut finita persona,sed aeterna persona Dei verbi, haec assumptione carnis non est mutata, neq; nostra aliqua persona Trinitati accessit. Videtur autem opinione sua Marpachius inclinare ad eorum errore qui stulto metu ne statueretur quaternitas propter carnis assumptionē, docuerunt carnem verbo consubstantiale fuisse, quorum quorū erroré grauiter cófutauit Athanafius, Præterea veram Christi adorationem euer tunt,nam cū sit immota regula: Nemini ado‑ratione deberi,nisi qui sit natura Deus,ideoq; ecclesia Christum,vt verum Deum & consub‑stantialem patri filium inuocarit, naturas in eo non separans, sed ad ipsam personam eius æternam adoratione dirigens, isti noua ado‑rationis rationem instituunt, docentes huma‑nitatem Christi illa transfusione proprietatū diuinitatis accepisse, vt Deus sit & adoretur. Et cum dicunt Christum homine adorandū esse, non loquuntur veterum more, vt homi‑nis nomine totum Christum intelligant, sed hominis nomē pro humana natura accipiūt, ostendunt autem se cum Nestorio esse ἀνθρωπον ἀνθρωπον, humana enim natura nulla transfusio‑ne mutatur in diuinam, & homo communi‑catione donorum nō fit Deus sed homo diui‑nus. Nos verò sicut Ephesina synodus do‑cuit, vna adoratione Emanuelé honoramus, sicut & in vnū Christū baptizati sumus,& in vnū Christū credimus,& adoramus incarna‑tū Dei verbū cū sua carne,quemadmodū etiā anima cū suo corpore honoratur: qui verò se paratim in humana natura adorationis cau‑sas quæruut,illi omnino duos Christos faciūt.
units.tr: This disjunctive proposition is the foundation of all those arguments which he wished to profess in his thick volume published some time ago, and yet he nowhere proves it, but takes it as conceded. Here I ask the Superintendent: does he speak of the person or of the nature? If he speaks of the nature, then the properties and works, the name and honour of the Trinity, belong only to the divine nature. But if he wishes to show that these can be transferred to a created nature, let him demonstrate it, so that all may see that he is paving the way for the furies of the Arians and Servetians of our age. But if he speaks of the person, then again there was no need for this disjunction; for if he wishes to count another person along with the Trinity, he makes a quaternity; and if he speaks of the eternal person of the Word, there was no need for the disjunction, since Christ is not joined to the Trinity but is one of the Trinity. Nor do we exclude Christ the man from the Trinity, for that person who is Christ the man is not a created or finite person but the eternal person of the Word of God; this was not changed by the assumption of flesh, nor did some other person join the Trinity. Marbach seems in his opinion to lean toward the error of those who, from a foolish fear that a quaternity would be posited because of the assumption of flesh, taught that the flesh was consubstantial with the Word; and Athanasius refuted this error severely. Moreover, they overturn the true adoration of Christ. For since the rule is fixed that adoration is due to no one except him who is God by nature, therefore the Church invokes Christ as the true God and as the Son consubstantial with the Father, not separating the natures in him but directing adoration to his eternal person itself. These men introduce a new manner of adoration, teaching that the humanity of Christ received by that transfusion of the properties of the divinity, so that it is God and is to be adored. And when they say that Christ is to be adored in his man-hood, they do not speak in the manner of the ancients, who understood the whole Christ by the name of man, but they take the name man for the human nature; and they show that they agree with Nestorius in speaking of "man" as man [ἄνθρωπον ἀνθρωπον]. For the human nature is not changed by any transfusion into the divine, and a man by communication of gifts does not become God but a divine man. But we, as the Council of Ephesus taught, honour Emmanuel with one adoration, just as we were baptized into one Christ and believe in one Christ, and we adore the Word of God incarnate with his flesh, just as the soul is also honoured with its body. But those who seek separately the grounds of adoration in the human nature make two Christs altogether.

units.la: Atq; hactenus quidem Vbiquitaria doctri na Nestorianæ hæresi suffragatur,cæteris in re bus Eutycheo errori affinis est. Quāuis enim hæreses iste contrariæ fuerint, tamen si partes inter se conferantur, est quædam consensio. Nam & Nestoriani cum Eutychianis vnam in Christo voluntatem & operationem statuerunt vt in sexta synodo scribitur, sed tamen connexione affectus vnam. Et rursus Gelasius Eutychianos accusat quod in quibusdam Nestorianizent. Et Seuerus a Iustiniano vtriusque erroris causa damnatus fuit. Itaque no debet cuiquam mirum videri, quod nos quoq; Vbi quistas contrariarum hæresum reos peragimus. Porrò inter Eutychiana dogmata hoc vnum est: diuinam naturā quæ alioquin per se impassibilis est, in Christo factam passibilem. Etsi enim Iacobus Andreæ nusquam se dicat inuenisse hunc errorem attributum Eutychetî, tamen certum est hæc de Eutychianis scribere Theodoretum & Vigilium. Et Cedrenus item historicus illorum dogmata recensens inquit: Τῆς θεότητος πάθος ἀπονέμουσι. De ipso quoque Eutychete Leo Papa refert, eum tertium dogma Apollinaris amplexum fuisse, deitatem conuersam in carnem animamq;. Quam autem huic Eutychiano errori affinia sint hæc Vbi quistarum dicta: Christum secundum vtramque naturam pro nobis passum esse: diuinam naturā in Christo passionis & mortis suo modo participem factam esse: humanæ naturæ passionem in ipsam diuinitatem redundasse, moderato & pio lectori expendendum relinquis.
units.tr: So far, indeed, the Ubiquitarian doctrine lends support to the Nestorian heresy, while in other respects it is akin to the error of Eutyches. For although these heresies were opposed to each other, if their parts are compared there is a certain agreement. The Nestorians and the Eutychians both asserted one will and one operation in Christ, as is written in the sixth synod, though one by a connection of affection. Again, Gelasius accuses the Eutychians of Nestorianizing in certain points, and Severus was condemned by Justinian as guilty of both errors. So no one should think it strange that we too charge the Ubiquitarians with being guilty of contrary heresies. Moreover, among the dogmas of Eutyches this one stands out: the divine nature, which is otherwise impassible in itself, was made passible in Christ. For although James Andreae nowhere says that he found this error attributed to Eutyches, it is certain that Theodoret and Vigilius write this about the Eutychians. Cedrenus the historian likewise, in listing their dogmas, says: [Τῆς θεότητος πάθος ἀπονέμουσι] they ascribe suffering to the Godhead. Pope Leo also reports of Eutyches himself that he embraced the third dogma of Apollinaris, that the deity was changed into flesh and soul. How closely related to this Eutychian error are these assertions of the Ubiquitarians, that Christ suffered for us according to both natures, that the divine nature in Christ was made a partaker of suffering and death in its own way, and that the suffering of the human nature overflowed into the divinity itself? I leave it to the moderate and pious reader to weigh.

units.la: Actione 18.
units.tr: Action 18.

units.la: quimus. Deinde Eutychiani nō tantū damnati sunt quod humanitatem in Christo abolerent: cum enim non ita crasse loquerentur, verum confiterentur Christum humanū corpus habere, sed eius proprietates abiecisse, vt molem corporis, colorem &c. nihilominus hoc ipso nomine dānati sunt in posteriorib. synodis quę Chalcedonią sequuntę sunt. Rectę enim censuit sexta synodus, eos naturas tollere qui proprietates naturarū tollunt, neq; dubitauit Euphemius Antiochenus Episcopus palam in eo conuentu dicere, peius & detegerius esse docere Christi carnem diminutam in suis proprietatibus & imperfectā, quàm eandem penitus non existere. Vt autem appareat quæ fuerit Eutychianorum sententia, appo-nam huc Theodori Pharanitani Episcopi verba damnata in eadem synodo actione 13. Nos-tra quidem anima non habet infitū talis esse virtutis, vt & naturales corporis proprietates ab ea & à semet expellat: sed neque dominari in tantum apparuit rationalis anima ipsius proprij corporis, vt etiam quę circa hoc sunt, huicque sunt insita, id est, molem, fluxumque; & colorem continet, atque citra hoc vnquam constituat. Quę omnia in dispensatione Christi saluatoris nostri, & conscripta, & facta sunt in illo diuino & viuifico corpore. Etenim absq; mole, & (vt ita dicatur) incorporabiliter absq; direptione de vulua processit, & sepulchro etiā, vt &, tanquā super pauimentū, supra mare ambularet. Quid verò Vbiquistæ sentiunt? Aliquando quidè profitentur fere« tinere in Christo saluas proprietates humanæ naturæ, sed proprietatū nomine ipsam natu« ræ substantiā intelligunt, ita vt relicta tantum prima essentia proprietas naturæ videatur mansisse, interea humanæ Christi naturæ omnes proprietates diuinitatis tribuunt, quas illa saluis suis proprietatibus habere non po« test, vt supra ostendimus. Deinde ē numero creaturarum humanitate Christi eximunt, ita enim argumentatur Parsimonius: Extra creaturas nihil est nisi Deus, Humanitas Christi est extra creaturas. Exiuit enim è mundo, hoc est, extra oēs creaturas in regno suo, in quo fuit antequā esset vlla creatura. Ergo necesse est humanitatem Christi esse quod Deus est. Alij etiam scribunt corpus Christi alia habe« re priuilegia, exemptum fuisse carnalibus le« gibus & omnia humana transcendisse: itē pro prietates humanæ naturæ, quales sunt videri, tangi, loco circumscribi, per resurrectionē suā depositi. Atq; vt ostendant humani corpo« ris proprietates non conuenire corpori Christi obijciunt, corpus hoc super mare ambulasse, & clausis ostijs ingressum esse, & alia huius generis, quę etiā veteres Eutychiani in argumentū afferebant. Et si autē supra ad hæc re« sponderimus, tamē nō pigebit hoc loco etiam
units.tr: ...we say. Next, the Eutychians were condemned not merely because they abolished the humanity in Christ. For although they did not speak so crudely, but confessed that Christ had a human body, and only said that he had cast off its properties, such as the bulk of the body, its colour and so on, they were nonetheless condemned under this very name in the later synods that followed Chalcedon. The sixth synod rightly judged that those who take away the properties of the natures take away the natures themselves. Euphemius, bishop of Antioch, did not hesitate to say openly in that assembly that it was worse and more detestable to teach that Christ's flesh was diminished and imperfect in its properties than to teach that it did not exist at all. To make plain what the Eutychian view was, let me set down here the words of Theodore, bishop of Pharan, condemned in the same synod, action 13: "Our soul does not have it in its nature to possess such power that it expels from itself the natural properties of the body; nor did the rational soul appear to rule its own body so far that it contained the things that surround the body and are inherent in it, namely its bulk, its flow and its colour, and never established them apart from it. All these things, both written and done in the dispensation of Christ our Saviour, were in that divine and life-giving body. For without bulk, and (so to speak) incorporeally, without violation, he came forth from the womb; and even from the sepulchre, and as if upon a pavement, he walked over the sea." What, then, do the Ubiquitarians hold? At some times they profess that the properties of the human nature remain safe in Christ, but by "properties" they understand the very substance of the nature, so that, with only the primary essence left, the property of the nature seems to have remained. Meanwhile they attribute to the human nature of Christ all the properties of the divinity, which the human nature cannot have while its own properties remain safe, as we have shown above. Then they remove the humanity of Christ from the number of creatures. For Parsimonius argues thus: outside the creatures there is nothing but God; the humanity of Christ is outside the creatures. For it went out of the world, that is, outside all creatures, into his kingdom, in which he was before any creature existed. Therefore the humanity of Christ must be what God is. Others also write that the body of Christ had other privileges: that it was exempt from the laws of flesh and had surpassed all human things; and likewise that the properties of human nature, such as being seen, being touched, and being confined to a place, were laid aside through his resurrection. And to show that the properties of a human body do not belong to the body of Christ, they object that this body walked upon the sea, entered with the doors shut, and other things of this kind, which the ancient Eutychians also brought forward as arguments. And although we have answered these things above, it will not be tedious to add here also

units.la: Euphemij refponfionem è sexta synodo sub‐ijcere: Dicito inquit nobis ō tu ab omni ad‐ uerfitate sinceram custodiens mentem tuam. Erat aliquando tépus ab incarnatione,quan‐ do incarnatus verbum Deus non habuit per‐ festam suam animatam carnem,aut quia pe‐ defter ibat super fluctus maris, non conferua‐ bant pedes proprietatem humanæ naturæ? sed optimè in natura humana vltra naturam operabatur Christus Deus noster, & nō per‐ empta vel extincta humana propria fui car‐ ne, saltem ipsius operationis effigies suadeat tibi cófiteri,quod caro in propria natura per‐ mâfit. Nam ambulare & pedibus super mare nisi fecundum phantasiâ fiebat, liquet quod pedum est operatio ipsius naturæ nostræ, & vtiq; ipsa species operationis, exclamat in pri ftinis mensuris carnè fuisse seruatam, & hu‐ iufmodi gressum omnes corporalem & sen‐ sibile dicunt: ambulare autè super mare hoc deitatis erat per humanâ carnem operantis.
units.tr: the reply of Euphemius from the sixth synod. He says: "Tell us, you who keep your mind pure from all contrariety. Was there ever a time after the incarnation when the Word of God, made flesh, did not have his flesh perfectly animated; or, because he walked upon the waves of the sea, did his feet not preserve the property of human nature? But Christ our God operated most excellently in human nature beyond nature, and his own human flesh was not destroyed or extinguished. At least the very form of the operation should persuade you to confess that the flesh remained in its own nature. For walking and walking upon the sea with feet happened only in a phantasy, if it is clear that walking with feet is an operation of our own nature; and certainly the very appearance of the operation cries out that the flesh was preserved in its original measures, and all men call such a step bodily and sensible. But to walk upon the sea was an operation of the deity working through the human flesh."

units.la: Postremò inter damnata Eutychianorum dogmata hoc quoq; numeratur,vnam esse in Christo voluntatem & actionem. Iacobus au tem Andreæ scribit, Ratione vnionis perfo‐nalis vnam esse actionem λόγου & hominis af‐ sumpti, vt λόγος fine homine aífumpto nihil nobifcû agat,sed omnia cû ipso & per ipsum. Neq; vero ipsum ab errore Monothelitarû li‐berat quod ratione vnionis personalis vnâ astione ponit,nam & ratione vnionis personꝝ lis vnam tantũ voluntate hi asserebat. Vnam voluntate affirmantes (vt Paulus Constantinopolitanus Monothelita scribit) ne aduersitate vel differentiam voluntatũ introducerent, & ita duos volentes; neq; enim se hac ratione voluisse vel naturas confundere, vel alteram abolere, sed dicto hoc insinuantes inquit, quod eius rationaliter ac intellectualiter animata caro ex ipsa principali vnitione ineffabiliter queq; dicta una sunt locupletata eam sibi vniente secundum subsistentiam verbo, ipsam diuinā possidet bar, & non differente voluntate. Porro quod addit λόγος sine assumpta humanitate nihil nobiscum agere sed omnia cum ipsa, non impro-bamus, quoniam vtraq; natura operatur cum alterius communione hoc quod propriū habuit: sed qd addit per humanitatē assumptā omnia facere λόγος, nescio an cum veteris ecclesiæ doctrina consentiat. Cyrillus scribit λόγῳ vsum tanquā instrumento propria carne ad operā carnis & infirmitates naturales quæq; a vitio longe sunt: anima vero sua ad humanas & inuperabiles ægrimonias. Anastasius autem Antiochenus ita de Christi energijs statuit, vnam quidem esse diuinam miraculorū effectricem, eorum præsertim qu̓g absq; sacrosanctæ illius carnis contactu edita fuerunt, vt sa-natio filiæ Chananeæ, & filij Centurionis, tabernaculi disruptio, solis defectus, petrarum diffisio.
units.tr: Finally, among the condemned dogmas of the Eutychians this too is counted: that there is one will and one action in Christ. James Andreae, moreover, writes that by reason of the personal union there is one action of the Word [λόγου] and of the assumed man, so that the Word does nothing with us without the assumed man, but all things with him and through him. Yet he does not free himself from the error of the Monothelites by positing one action by reason of the personal union, for those men also asserted, by reason of the personal union, only one will. They affirmed one will (as Paul the Constantinopolitan Monothelite writes), lest they introduce contrariety or difference of wills, and so two willing subjects. For they did not, by this reasoning, wish either to confuse the natures or to abolish one of them; but, hinting at it by this saying, he says that the flesh, rationally and intellectually animated, by that very first union, is enriched by the things that are ineffably said in common, since the Word unites it to himself in subsistence, and it possesses the divine itself, and not with a differing will. Further, that he adds that the Word does nothing with us without the assumed humanity, but all things with it, we do not disapprove, since each nature operates in communion with the other what it has as its own. But what he adds, that the Word does all things through the assumed humanity, I do not know whether it agrees with the doctrine of the ancient Church. Cyril writes that the Word used the proper flesh as an instrument for the works of the flesh and its natural weaknesses, which are far from vice; but used his own soul for human and unconquerable sufferings. Anastasius of Antioch, moreover, thus set down the energies of Christ: that one is divine, the effecter of miracles, especially of those that were done without contact with that most holy flesh, such as the healing of the Canaanite's daughter and of the centurion's son, the rending of the veil, the eclipse of the sun, the splitting of the rocks,

units.la: Synodo 6. Act. 13. diffifio, mortuorum resurrectio, quæ omnia sacrosancto Christi corpore mortuo in cruce pendente, neq; horum quicquam attingente, sola Dei verbi energia diuina operata est. Altera esse humana energia, pura, sancta, incorta minatâ à Deo creatâ atq; datâ, eandemq; viui sicam. Tertio esse communem vtriq; naturæ energiam eam, quæ vtriq; naturæ conuenien ter congruenterq;, seu communi vtriusq; naturæ opera formatur: cuiusmodi illa fuit, vi- sus per sputum restitutio, filiæ principis synagogæ à mortuis excitatio, quæ sanctæ ipsius manus contactu facta est, &c. Similia scribunt alij è veteribus, neque absolutè vsquam affirmant λόγῳ OMNIA per humanitatem assumptam operatum esse. Quod si dicant sessione ad dexteram in hanc maiestatem euectum λόγῳ, ea tamen nihilominus illi tribuenda erit mox ab ipsa Incarnatione seu vnione personali (quâ ipsi non distinguunt à sessione ad dexterâ) qd' tamen nusquâ veteres docuerūt.
units.tr: Synod 6, Act 13. the splitting, the resurrection of the dead, all of which the divine energy of the Word alone effected, without the most holy body of Christ, which hung dead on the cross, touching any of these things. Another is the human energy, pure, holy, uncorrupted, created and given by God, and likewise life-giving. A third is the energy common to both natures, which is formed congruently and fittingly in both natures, or through the common operation of both natures; of this kind was the restoration of sight through spittle, and the raising of the ruler of the synagogue's daughter from the dead, which was done by the touch of his holy hands, and so on. Others among the ancients write similarly, and nowhere do they absolutely affirm that the Word did ALL things through the assumed humanity. But if they say that the Word was raised to this majesty by sitting at the right hand, that too must nonetheless be attributed to him immediately from the Incarnation itself or from the personal union (which they do not distinguish from the session at the right hand), a thing the ancients nowhere taught.

units.la: Postremo doctrina hæc realis communi-cationis veterem Martionis & Manichæorū errorem, per cuniculos in ecclesiam introdu-cere conatur, qui negarunt Christum verum & naturale hominis corpus habuisse, atq; ea quæ hominum more fecerit & passus sit, solum phantasma quoddam fuisse. Nam si hu-mana natura statim ab ipsa vnione personali ipsa omnes diuinitatis proprietates accepit neq; amplius eiusdē nobiscū naturę mansit, sequitur Christum non fuisse verè aspectabi-lem & palpabilem, neq; etiam verè, vel de loco in locum ambulasse, vel comedisse aut dor-miuisse, esurijsse, lassum fuisse, passum deniq;, crucifixum & mortuum esse, sed hæc omnia tantum fuisse quædam sensuum & oculorum ludibria. Neq; aduersarios excusat, quod aiût corpus Christi semper habuisse huiusmodi diuinas proprietates, sed non semper exeruisse. Etenim dispensatio quam hic fingunt, pa-rum admodum à Manichaico phantasmate differt. Si enim humana Christi natura tem-pore exinanitionis reipsa prędita fuit diuinis proprietatibus, gloria et maiestate, oportet vt humanas infirmitates non vere & reipsa in se habuerit & senserit. Itaque omnes humanas actiones & passiones tantum hominum opi-nione sustinuit. Aut si verè & reipsa hæc su-stinuit, tum vna & eadem natura eodem tem-pore verè & reipsa infirmitati obnoxia fuit, & simul non fuit: fuit visibilis & inuisibilis, mortalis & immortalis, circumscripta in vte-ro virginis, sed simul implens vniuersum or-bem, eodem tempore mortua iacebat in sepul-chro, & simul viua, atq; vbique præsens gu-bernabat vniuersum orbē. Hæc & alia huius generis quę aperte sibi contradicunt, quantū-uis aduersarij conciliare conentur, nunquam tamē illo modo maiestatis efficient vt hæc de humahumana Christi natura eiusq; substantia simul vere & reipsa dici possint, sed omnino statuitur phantasticū quoddam corpus, nō vera forma & figuram habens neq; vere ea faciens quae facere videtur, sed tantum extranea et apparente forma pro nostro captu sese in hac humilitate ostendens. Atque haec portentosa & horribilia auditu sunt pijs mentibus, sed cū plæraq; ipsi Vbiquistæ afferere non dubitēt, cætera vero ex eorum doctrina manifesta & necessaria consecutione conficiantur, necesse est ut de his pios homines admoneamus. Val de enim metuendū est nisi serio his malis occurratur, fore tandem vt hæc Martionitica, Nestoriana & Eutychiana dogmata in Machumetanismū desinant, præsertim cum Vbi quistæ Seruetanis, Machumeto viam sternen tibus, tot argumenta suppeditent. Atque hæc nostra querela longe iustior est quam illorū qua salsissimè de nobis spargunt, Zuinglianos homini Christo non plus tribuere quàm illi Machumetus in suo Alcorano tribuat. Vereor etiam ne plures quoque articuli fidei nostræ breui ab ijsdem hominibus in contro uersiam vocentur, & nominatim resurrectio carnis nostræ, quam in symbolo Apostolico nos credere profitemur. Nisi enim nobis maneat veritas carnis humanæ salua in Christo seruatore nostro, resurrectio quoque carnis nostræ integra nobis constare nō poterit. Extant etiam quorundam de hac re scripta, quæ propendere videntur in Origenis opinionem dudum à veteribus damnatam. Sed ego hæc lubens prætereo, neq; enim velim nos uas cótrouersias temere mouere, tantũ volui monere eos qui huiusmodi audiunt, vt non statim talia dicta, quæ in quodã contentionis feruore forte temere illis exciderunt, arripiat, & plura adhuc noua dogmata hinc extruant.
units.tr: Lastly, this doctrine of real communication tries to smuggle into the Church the old error of Marcion and the Manichaeans, who denied that Christ had a true and natural human body and held that what he did and suffered in the manner of men was only a kind of phantasm. For if the human nature, from the very moment of the personal union, received all the properties of the divinity and no longer remained of the same nature as ours, it follows that Christ was not truly visible and palpable, nor truly walked from place to place, ate, slept, hungered, grew weary, suffered, was crucified and died, but that all these things were only deceptions of the senses and the eyes. Nor does it excuse our opponents that they say the body of Christ always had such divine properties but did not always exercise them. For the dispensation they devise here differs very little from the Manichaean phantasm. If the human nature of Christ in the time of his humiliation was really endowed with divine properties, glory and majesty, then it must not have truly and really had and felt human weaknesses. Thus he would have undergone all human actions and sufferings only in the opinion of men. Or, if he truly and really underwent these things, then one and the same nature was at the same time truly and really subject to weakness, and at the same time was not: it was visible and invisible, mortal and immortal, confined within the womb of the virgin, yet at the same time filling the whole world; at the same time it lay dead in the tomb, and at the same time it was alive and everywhere present, governing the whole world. These and other things of this kind, which plainly contradict one another, however much our opponents try to reconcile them, will never by that sort of majesty bring it about that these statements can be said truly and really of the human nature of Christ and its substance at the same time. Instead, a kind of phantastic body is posited, which does not have a true form and shape, nor truly does the things it seems to do, but only shows itself in this humiliation in an external and apparent form suited to our comprehension. And these monstrous and horrible things are to be heard by pious minds; but since the Ubiquists themselves do not hesitate to assert many of them, and the rest follow from their doctrine by clear and necessary consequence, we must warn pious people about these matters.
