Indeed we must fear that, unless these evils are seriously resisted, these Marcionite, Nestorian and Eutychian dogmas will at last end in Mahometanism, especially since the Ubiquists supply so many arguments to the Servetians, who are paving the way for Mahomet. And this complaint of ours is far more just than the complaint of those who spread the most spiteful slander about us, that the Zwinglians attribute to the man Christ no more than Mahomet attributes to him in his Alcoran. I fear also that many more articles of our faith will shortly be called into controversy by these same men, and especially the resurrection of our flesh, which we profess to believe in the Apostles' Creed. For unless the truth of human flesh is kept safe in Christ our Saviour, the resurrection of our flesh also cannot stand whole for us. There are also writings by certain men on this matter which seem to lean toward the opinion of Origen, long since condemned by the ancients. But I gladly pass these over; for I would not wish to stir up controversies rashly. I have only wished to warn those who hear such things that they should not seize upon such statements, which perhaps have slipped from them rashly in the heat of some dispute, and build upon them still more new dogmas.

units.la: Vbiquitarios cum à Lutbero, tum etiam ipsos inter se mutuò dissentire.
units.tr: That the Ubiquitarians dissent both from Luther and from one another.

units.la: Posteaquam haftenus ostendi Vbiquitariam doctrinam à veteris ecclesiæ doctrina diuersam, renouare quàm plurimos veterum hereticorum errores, deinceps expendendum nobis est, quomodo cum Lutheri doctrina atq; ipsa Augustana confessione consentiat, & quis sit inter ipsos Vbiquistas consensus. Neque tamen hic singula minutatim persequar, id enim si quis facere velit, & non tantum vetera eorum scripta, sed solum prima quæ in hac controuersia edita sunt cum postremis conferat, magnam congeriem contra distionum colligere poterit, nos hic tantum summa capita controuersiæ huius attingere volumus.
units.tr: Having so far shown that the Ubiquitarian doctrine differs from the doctrine of the ancient Church, and that it revives the errors of very many ancient heretics, we must next consider how it agrees with the doctrine of Luther and with the Augsburg Confession itself, and what agreement there is among the Ubiquists themselves. I shall not, however, pursue the individual points here in detail. Anyone who wished to do so, and who compared not only their older writings but also the first works published in this controversy with the latest, could collect a great heap of contradictions. We wish here only to touch on the main heads of this controversy.

units.la: Primum igitur vniuersa hæc doctrina realis communicationis, cum Augustana confessione, & doctrina Lutheri pugnat. Etenim quod articulum de Trinitate attinet, & de natura in Christo, nulla vnquam fuit controuersia inter Pontificios, & illos qui Augusta ftanæ confessioni fubfcripferūt, agnoscebant enim hi veteris ecclesiæ doctrinam de his dogmatibus ex sacris literis desumptam, & veterum Synodorum authoritate confirmatam, in Papatu retentam fuisse. Itaque sæpe in Comitijs asseruerunt de his nullam controuersiam esse. Idem quoque Lutherus in scriptis suis testatus est, veluti in eo libello quo complexus est capita fidei Christianæ, contra Papam & portas inferorum constanter afferenda: nam in prima parte proponens sublimia capita de diuina maiestate, nempe de Vnitate essentiæ, & personarum distinctione in sacro sancta Trinitate, & incarnatione filij, subijcit: De his articulis nulla controuersia aut contentio est, cum vtrosque utrinque confiteamur. Quare superuacaneum erit de his prolixius agere. Porrò certum est Vbiquitatiorum doctrinam de reali communicatione idiomatum damnari à Papistis. Nam non tantum in Germania publico scripto hanc damnarunt, sed in celeberrima quoq; Gallia rum Academia Parifina aperte asseruerunt hoc dogma hæreticum esse: neque difficulter ostendi potest plurimum hanc opinionem à Scholasticorum sententia differre, à quibus etiam plæraque Vbiquitariorum argumenta acutè refutantur. Itaq; dissentiunt à confessiͤne Augustana & nouas controuersias mouét Vbiquitarij hac sua nova & veteri ecclesiæ in audita doctrina de reali communicatione. Aliter etiam Lutherum sensisse scripta eius ostē dunt, & quamuis Vbiquitarij eum secum sen tire afferant, diuersum tamen ex scriptis eius ostendunt non tantum Zuingliani quos vo-cant, sed ipsius Lutheri discipuli, qui eius doc-trina constanter retinent, neq; vllo modo cū Zuinglianis colludunt: imò hoc ipsum quidā nō extremi nominis ex his qui nunc Vbiqui tatem probant, olim assernerūt. De Philippo etiam Melanchtone, quem hi ingrati discipu-li mortuū mordent ac lacerant, non est dubiū eum cōstanter asseruisse realem hāc communi-cationem esse transfusionē physicā proprieta-tum qua naturæ cōfunduntur, aut altera abo-letur. Reliquos doctores ecclesiarū Augustanæ confessionis non necesse est commemora-re, qui inter se consentientes nunquam agno-uerunt hanc realem communicationem.
units.tr: First, then, this whole doctrine of real communication conflicts with the Augsburg Confession and with the doctrine of Luther. For as far as the article on the Trinity and on the natures in Christ is concerned, there was never any controversy between the Papists and those who subscribed to the Augsburg Confession; for these recognised that the doctrine of the ancient Church on these dogmas, drawn from the holy writings and confirmed by the authority of the ancient Synods, had been retained in the Papacy. Accordingly they often declared at the Diets that there was no controversy about these matters. Luther himself also testified in his writings to the same effect, as in that little book in which he gathered together the heads of the Christian faith, to be firmly maintained against the Pope and the gates of hell. For in the first part, setting out the lofty heads concerning the divine majesty, namely the unity of the essence and the distinction of persons in the most holy Trinity, and the incarnation of the Son, he adds: "There is no controversy or contention about these articles, since we both confess them on both sides." Therefore it would be superfluous to treat of these at greater length. Moreover, it is certain that the Ubiquitarian doctrine of the real communication of properties is condemned by the Papists. For they have not only condemned it in a public writing in Germany, but the famous Academy of Paris in Gaul has also openly declared this doctrine to be heretical. And it can easily be shown that this opinion differs very much from the opinion of the Schoolmen, by whom also most of the Ubiquitarian arguments are skilfully refuted. Thus the Ubiquitarians dissent from the Augsburg Confession, and by their new doctrine of real communication, which is new and unknown to the ancient Church, they raise new controversies. Their writings show that Luther also thought otherwise, and although the Ubiquitarians assert that he agreed with them, his writings show the contrary; and not only those called Zwinglians but also Luther's own disciples, who steadfastly hold to his doctrine, show this, and in no way collude with the Zwinglians. Indeed some men of no small name among those who now approve of Ubiquity once asserted this very thing. As for Philip Melanchthon, whom these ungrateful disciples bite and tear after his death, there is no doubt that he constantly maintained that this real communication is a physical transfusion of properties by which the natures are confounded, or one of them is abolished. There is no need to mention the remaining teachers of the churches of the Augsburg Confession, who, agreeing among themselves, never acknowledged this real communication.

units.la: Porrò de ipsa comunicatione reali diuersi- s Vbiquitariorū sunt opiniones: aliqui eni vo-lunt humanam naturam suas quoq; proprie-tates diuinæ naturæ communicare: alij contra censent tantū diuinarum proprietatū transfu-sionē in humanā naturā fieri. Atq; rursus has spriet ates omnes absq; exceptione humanæ naturæ communicari Brentius asserit: alij contra distinā
units.tr: Moreover, concerning the real communication itself, the opinions of the Ubiquitarians differ. For some want the human nature to communicate its own properties also to the divine nature; others, on the contrary, think that only a transfusion of the divine properties into the human nature takes place. And again, Brenz asserts that all these properties are communicated to the human nature without exception; others, on the other hand, make a distinction

units.la: Diuersæ opiniones de communi. distinctione faciunt, & quasdã incomunicabiles, quasdé comunicabiles esse aiunt: quę tamen sint comunicabiles, nondū prorsus inter ipsos conuenit, sicuti neq; de comunicationis tepore, quando alij hãc maiestaté humanitati Christi ab ipsa conceptione tribuūt, alij demū postquã à mortuis resurrexit et clarificata est. Similiter de ᵱprietatibus humani corporis diuersa sunt eorū iudicia, nã circūscribi & in loco esse Brentius inter accidétales proprietates corporis numerat: et quidã scribit corpꝯ Christi has ᵱprietates vt tãgatur & in loco sit, post resurrectionē abiecisse. At verò Iacobus Andreæ & nonnulli alij circumscriptionem veram & essentialé humani corporis proprietatem esse agnoscunt: ita vt etiã corpus Christi gloriosum in cœlo circūscriptū esse fateatur.
units.tr: Their opinions differ concerning the distinction of communicable properties: they say some are incommunicable and some communicable; but which of them are communicable has not yet been fully agreed among them, nor has the time of the communication, when some attribute this majesty to the humanity of Christ from the very conception, others only after he rose from the dead and was glorified. Their judgments also differ concerning the properties of the human body. For Brenz counts being circumscribed and being in a place among the accidental properties of the body, and some write that the body of Christ laid aside these properties, of being touched and being in a place, after the resurrection. But Jacob Andreae and several others acknowledge circumscription as a true and essential property of the human body, so that he even confesses that the glorified body of Christ is circumscribed in heaven.

units.la: Deinde quod ad alterum caput huius controuersię pertinet, de præsentia corporis Christi in cœna sacrosanctaꝯ, ne hic quidé cum Luthero consentiūt. Luthervs enim asseruit corpus Christi gloriosum, saluo pane sic esse in Sacramento, sicut ignis est in ferro, salua ferri substantia, sic enim scribit in libro contra regem Angliæ: Cur non posset Christus corpus suum intra panis substantiam continere, sicut in accidentibus? Ecce ignis & ferrū sunt duę substantię, sic miscétur in ferro ignito, vt quilibet pars sit ferrū & ignis. Cur nō multo magis corpus Christi gloriosum, sic in omni parte substantiæ panis esse posset? His verbis vult Christum ratione gloriosi corporis in cœna præsentem esse. Hanc autem præsentiam ita explicat, quod definitiue & corporaliter adsit: nam in Cófessione parua edita anno 1544. sic ait: Hoc autem modo docent Papistæ (imò non Papistæ sed ecclesia, non enim Papa sacramentū instituit) & nos cum ijs, quod corpus Christi non sit localiter in Sacramento, sed definitiue, hoc est, certò est ibi corporaliter & verè. Sæpe etiam scribit, Christi corpus in cœna cum pane corporaliter manducari ore nostro. Sed contra Iacobus Andreæ tres constituēns rationes corporis Christi, physicam, gloriosam & maiestatis, ne gat Christum ratione gloriosi corporis in cœna præsentem esse. Idem scribit corpus Christi non manducari carnaliter & corporaliter, neque carnaliter, aut corporaliter, aut naturaliter in Sacramento præsens esse. Præterea Lutherus realem & corporalem præsentiam corporis Christi in cœna, docuit nouam quandam esse existentiā substantiæ corporis Christi quæ ante in pane non fuerit, sed facta sit verborū Domini, vnde etiā hanc præsentiam huiusmodi locutionib⁹ explicat, corpus Christi corporaliter esse in pane, inuadere & per verbū aduehi in pane, latere in pane, intra panis substantiā contineri, in omnibus sub Sacramento locis esse. Contra vero Vbiquistæ docent
units.tr: Next, as to the second point of this controversy, the presence of Christ's body in the holy Supper, they do not agree with Luther here either. Luther asserted that the glorified body of Christ is present in the sacrament while the bread remains, just as fire is in iron while the substance of the iron remains. He writes this in his book against the king of England: "Why could Christ not contain his body within the substance of the bread, just as he does in the accidents? Look, fire and iron are two substances, and they are so mixed in red-hot iron that every part is both iron and fire. Why could the glorified body of Christ not be present in the same way in every part of the substance of the bread, and much more so?" By these words he means that Christ is present in the Supper by reason of his glorified body. He explains this presence in the following way: that he is present definitively and corporally. For in the Small Confession published in 1544 he says: "Indeed the Papists teach this way (or rather not the Papists but the Church, for the Pope did not institute the sacrament), and we with them, that the body of Christ is not locally in the sacrament but definitively, that is, it is there certainly, corporally and truly." He also often writes that the body of Christ is corporally eaten with the bread by our mouth. But Jacob Andreae, who posits three kinds of Christ's body, physical, glorious and of majesty, denies that Christ is present in the Supper by reason of his glorified body. He likewise writes that the body of Christ is not eaten carnally and corporally, and is not present in the sacrament carnally, corporally or naturally. Moreover, Luther taught a real and corporal presence of Christ's body in the Supper, namely a certain new existence of the substance of Christ's body, which was not in the bread before but comes about through the words of the Lord. Hence he explains this presence by such expressions as: the body of Christ is corporally in the bread; it enters the bread and is carried into it through the word; it lies hidden in the bread; it is contained within the substance of the bread; it is in all places under the sacrament. The Ubiquitists, on the other hand, teach that the substance of Christ's body, on account of the personal union and the session at the right hand of God, has received that majesty and power by which it is present in all places and in all creatures; yet in the bread of the Lord's Supper it is dispensed in a certain definite manner and given to be eaten.

units.la: Contra Be ꝑ.90. Andreæ tres ... ént substantiam corporis Christi propter vnionem personalem & sessionem ad dexteram Dei, eam maiestatem & potentiam accepisse, vt in omnibus locis, atque in omnibus creaturis praesens sit: attamen in pane coenae dominicae certa quadam ratione dispensari & manducandam dari.
units.tr: Against Brenz, p. 90. Andreae's three ... (they say) that the substance of Christ's body, on account of the personal union and the session at the right hand of God, has received that majesty and power by which it is present in all places and in all creatures; yet in the bread of the Lord's Supper it is dispensed in a certain definite manner and given to be eaten.

units.la: Rursus quod ad interpretationem verborum coenae domini pertinet, Lutherus ita interpretatur: Hoc est corpus meum, id est, hic panis est corpus meum. Nam textus sic habet: Accepit panem, benedixit, fregit et dixit: Hoc est corpus meum &c. Vides hic, vt omnia illa verba, accepit, benedixit, fregit, de pane dicantur? Et eundem demonstrat pronomen HOC, quia illud ipsum, quod accepit, benedixit, fregit, hoc (inquam) acceptum & benedictum, & fractum significatur, cum dicitur: Hoc est corpus meum, non praedicatum, sed subiectum demonstratur. Non enim corpus suum accepit, benedixit, & fregit, sed panem, ideo non demonstrat corpus, sed panem. Contra vero Vbiquistae in colloquio Mulbrunensi pertinaciter negarunt propositionem hanc: Hoc est corpus meum; idem esse atq; Hic panis est corpus meum: atq; in scriptis suis contendunt esse propositionem identicam, aut demonstrationem, HOC, panem simul & corpus Christi demonstrare. Rursus aliqui Vbiquistarum praesentiam corporis Christi in sacramento cramento voluit definiri his verbis, Hoc est corpus meum quod pro vobis traditur: ac aiunt somniare eos qui volunt corpus absolutum de pane praedicari, cum id intelligendum sit ratione abditi praedicati Quod pro vobis traditur. Contra vero sententiant alij verbis: Hoc est corpus meum, ipsam absolutam substantiam sacramenti describi, addita autem praedicatione, Quod pro vobis traditur, vsum eiusdem indicari. Iam sunt nonnulli eorum, qui nullum prorsus tropum in verbis coenae domini admittendum putant: contra alij censent esse in his verbis synechdochen. Saepe etiam dicunt solam fidem sufficere ad manducandum corpus domini: rursus aiunt oportere omnino vt oraliter quoq; illud manducemus. Iam vero illa quis non iudicet contradictoria esse: Christi verum, naturale & substantiale corpus adesse realiter & substantialiter, non tamen corporaliter aut localiter: aut vt alij dicunt adesse naturaliter, sed modo non naturali: esse in loco sed non localiter: non adesse localiter, & tamen ore manducari & manu ministri porrigi: non esse physicam carnalem & corporalem praesentiam, & tamen physice & corporaliter manducari, & quidem ita vt Lutherus scribat: Os & stomachum Christi corpus manducantem in aeternum viuere, & corpora nostra physice percipientia Euchatistiam corporis Christi etiā incorruptibilia & æterna fore? Multa præterea alia huiusmodi ex ipsorum scriptis proferri possent, quæ nunc libens prætereo. Scio enim aduersarios habere plenas thecas distinctionum, quibus omnia hæc conciliare possunt, sed ego hoc vt ium peto à moderatis lectoribus, vt sepositò omni affectu res ipsas diligenter expendant, considerent quid simplici scriptturarum sensu consentaneum sit, quid cum purioris eccle siæ doctrina consentiat aut discrepet, id enim si sedulo faciant, de tota hac controuersia facile iudicare poterunt.
units.tr: Again, as to the interpretation of the words of the Lord's Supper, Luther interprets them thus: "This is my body," that is, "This bread is my body." For the text reads: "He took bread, blessed it, broke it and said: This is my body," etc. Do you see how all those words, "took," "blessed," "broke," are said of the bread? And the pronoun THIS points to the same thing, because what he took, blessed and broke, this (I say) taken, blessed and broken, is what is signified. When it is said, "This is my body," the subject, not the predicate, is pointed out. For he did not take, bless and break his body, but the bread; therefore THIS does not point to the body but to the bread. On the other hand, the Ubiquitists at the Colloquy of Mulbronn stubbornly denied that this proposition, "This is my body," is the same as "This bread is my body," and in their writings they contend that it is an identical proposition, or that the demonstrative THIS points to the bread and the body of Christ at the same time. Again, some of the Ubiquitists wanted the presence of Christ's body in the sacrament to be defined by these words: "This is my body which is given for you." They say that those who want the body to be predicated absolutely of the bread are dreaming, since it must be understood by reason of the added predicate, "which is given for you." Others, on the contrary, hold that the words "This is my body" describe the absolute substance of the sacrament, while the added predicate, "which is given for you," indicates its use. Further, some of them think that no trope at all is to be admitted in the words of the Lord's Supper, while others judge that there is a synecdoche in these words. They also often say that faith alone is sufficient for eating the body of the Lord, yet again they say that we must altogether eat it orally too. Now who would not judge these statements to be contradictory: that the true, natural and substantial body of Christ is present really and substantially, yet not corporally or locally; or, as others say, is present naturally but in a non-natural mode; is in a place but not locally; is not present locally, and yet is eaten by the mouth and offered by the hand of the minister; that there is no physical, carnal and corporal presence, and yet it is eaten physically and corporally, and indeed in such a way that Luther writes: the mouth and stomach of Christ, eating the body of Christ, live forever, and our bodies, physically receiving the Eucharist of the body of Christ, will also be incorruptible and eternal? Many other things of this kind could be brought forward from their writings, which I now gladly pass over. For I know that our opponents have full cabinets of distinctions by which they can reconcile all these things. But I ask this of moderate readers, that setting aside all partisanship they weigh the matters themselves diligently, and consider what agrees with the plain sense of the Scriptures, and what agrees or disagrees with the doctrine of the purer Church. If they do this carefully, they will be able to judge the whole of this controversy easily.

units.la: Quoniam vero duæ sunt res, quibus quasi præiudicijs quibusdam aduersarij nos oppri mere conantur, necessario mihi quoq; de his dicendum existimaui. Primum iactant se asse rere gloriam & maiestatem domini & seruatoris nostri Iesu Christi, ideoq; vbiquitatem seu omnipræsentiam corporis eius, nunc no- uo maiestatis nomine ornant. At quis vellet impugnare maiestatem Christi, & glorię eius aliquid detrahere? Verum hic admonendus est simplex harum controuersiarum lector, longe aliud esse vbiquitatem corporis, aut fa- ctam & communicatam Deitatem quam hu- manæ naturæ tribuunt, aliud maiestatem ve- ram & cœlestę Christi seruatoris nostri. Vbi- quitatem corporis eius negamus, propterea quod illa cum sacrarum literarum doctrina & articulis fidei, veritatęq; humanæ naturæ pugnat. Christus equidem non est ⸗ purus aut merus homo, sed Deus homo, & quamuis non sit homo merus, est tamen homo verus, integram enim humanā naturam nobis per omnia similem excepto peccato assumpsit, cuius naturae veritatem nos tueri & retinere oportet. Neque enim Christus homo verus est, nisi naturae suae proprietate subsistan tialiter praeditus sit. Interea veram eius maiestatem, non minus quam aduersarij nostri affer-imus, aeternā, infinitamq; diuinitatis maiestatem afferentes in Christo seruatore nostro. Quae enim quaeso maior esse potest carnis maiestas & gloria, quam quod aeternus Dei filius eam ita in vnitatem personae suae assumpsit, vt vere dicatur, verbum caro factū, ita vt iam Deus ab homine separari non possit, nec alterutrum nominari, quin alterum simul intelligatur, cum vnus & idem sit Deus & homo, Dei filius & hominis filius? Sed fuit haec antiquitus multorum errorum occasio, quod humanae naturae infirmitatem spectantes, existimarunt no conuenire huius assumptionem infinitae maiestati, inde variae opiniones Docitarum exortae sunt, quorum alij coelestē aut aereum corpus seruatori nostro tribuerunt, & tantum in phantasmate ipsum apparuisse dixerunt: alij vero initio retinentes humanae substantiae veritatem, postea tamē eam vel in diuinitatem conuersam, vel ab eadem absorptam voluerunt. Etsi au⁠tem nostri Vbiquitarij fe longe ab horum o⁠pinionibus abelTe afferunt, nihilominus ta⁠men res ipsa indicat,& nos supra monuimus, quàm parum distent ab his veterum hæresi⁠bus. Quare nomine maiestatis non pariatur lector sibi fucum fieri,ita enim maiestas Chri⁠sti fecundum carnem afferenda est,vt ipsa ca⁠ro cum suis proprietatibus salua maneat, eiuf⁠dem enim periculi est in Christo humanæ na⁠turæ veritatem tollere, atq; diuinitatem eius abnegare. Si enim non est verus homo, non etiam est mediator noster, mediatoreautem amisso,quid spei nobis restat?
units.tr: Since there are two matters by which our opponents try to overwhelm us, as if by certain prejudices, I have thought I must speak about them too. First, they boast that they assert the glory and majesty of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, and therefore they now adorn the ubiquity, or omnipresence, of his body with the new name of majesty. But who would wish to attack the majesty of Christ or take anything away from his glory? Yet here the simple reader of these controversies must be warned that the ubiquity of the body, or the Deity made and communicated, which they attribute to human nature, is one thing, and the true and heavenly majesty of Christ our Saviour is another. We deny the ubiquity of his body, because it conflicts with the doctrine of the Holy Scriptures, with the articles of faith, and with the truth of human nature. Christ is indeed not a pure or mere man, but God-man; and although he is not a mere man, he is nevertheless a true man, for he assumed our whole human nature, like ours in all things except sin, and we must maintain and hold fast the truth of that nature. For Christ is not a true man unless he is endowed with the properties of his nature and subsists in them. Meanwhile we assert his true majesty no less than our opponents do, ascribing eternal and infinite divine majesty to Christ our Saviour. For what greater majesty and glory of the flesh can there be, I ask, than that the eternal Son of God assumed it into the unity of his person in such a way that it is truly said, "The Word became flesh," so that God cannot now be separated from the man, nor either be named without the other being understood at the same time, since God and man, the Son of God and the Son of man, are one and the same? But from ancient times it has been the occasion of many errors that, looking to the weakness of human nature, men thought this assumption did not fit with infinite majesty. Hence the various opinions of the Docetists arose. Some of them attributed a heavenly or aerial body to our Saviour and said that he appeared only in appearance; others, at first retaining the truth of the human substance, afterwards wanted it either turned into the divinity or absorbed by it. Although our Ubiquitists affirm that they are far removed from these opinions, the matter itself nevertheless shows, as we have said above, how little they differ from these ancient heresies. So let the reader not allow himself to be deceived by the name of majesty. The majesty of Christ according to the flesh must be asserted in such a way that the flesh itself remains with its own properties intact. For it is equally dangerous to abolish the truth of human nature in Christ and to deny his divinity. If he is not a true man, he is not our mediator either; and once the mediator is lost, what hope remains for us?

units.la: Alterum deinde est quod omnes qui ab il⁠lis diuersum sentiunt,Zuinglianorum nomi⁠ne exosos vulgo faciunt. Nam sicut quódam solum Christianum nomen addamnandum fatis erat, ita vt fi quis diceretur Christianus, mox clamaretur ad ignem, ad gladium,ad be⁠ftias: Ita nostra ætate Theologi quidam per Germaniam Zuinglij nomen assiduis crimi⁠nationibus ita exosum reddiderûr, vt vulgus hominum quibus ignota est Zuinglij doctri⁠na (studiosé enim cauent isti Theologi, ne Zuinglianorum libri à quoquam legantur) Zuinglianos omniû hæreticorum pefsimos esse existiment. Ac vtile quidem effet,& decebat hoc Christianam simplicitate, omnia fa⁠ctionum nomina tam Lutheranorum quàm Zuinglianorū ē medio sublata esse, sed quando id in hac temporum miseria sperari non potest,& quia nomen Zuinglianorum, quod nunquam nobis sumpsimus, neq; adhuc vsurpamus, Christo enim non Zuinglio nomen dedimus,attamen ab aduersarijs nobis impositum reijcere non possumus, dicam breuiter quod sit caput illud Zuinglianæ doctrinæ, cuius nomine tantopere exosi sumus. Illud autem vnicum est de modo præsentiæ corporis Christi in cœna domini.
units.tr: Next, there is another matter: all who think differently from those people make the name of the Zwinglians hateful to the common folk. For just as in former times the mere name of Christian was enough for condemnation, so that if anyone was called a Christian he was at once cried out to the fire, the sword, and the beasts, so in our own day certain theologians throughout Germany have made the name of Zwingli so hateful by constant accusations that the common people, who are ignorant of Zwingli's teaching (for those theologians take care that the books of the Zwinglians are not read by anyone), think the Zwinglians are the worst of all heretics. It would indeed be useful, and it would befit Christian simplicity, if all the names of factions, both of the Lutherans and of the Zwinglians, were removed from the midst; but since this cannot be hoped for in this wretched age, and since we have never taken the name of Zwinglians, nor do we even now use it (for we have given our name to Christ, not to Zwingli), yet cannot reject a name imposed on us by our adversaries, I shall state briefly what is the chief point of that Zwinglian doctrine by whose name we are so hated. It is this one point alone: the manner of the presence of Christ's body in the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Etenim cum anno Domini 1529. Zuinglius atq; Lutherus euocati ab illustrissimo Hessorum principe Philippo Marpurgū conuenissent,de cæteris quidem partibus doctrinæ Christianæ inter se consenserunt, tantum de modo præsentiæ non potuerunt conuenire:verūtamen amicè discessum est,vtrisq; assentientibus, quandoquidem in præcipuis dogmatibus idem sentirent, abstinendū esse deinceps ab omni contentione, & Deum orandum,vt in hac etiam controuersia lumen accendat,& concordiæ viam ostendat. Neq; ab eo tempore nos vllum caput doctrinæ in nostris ecclesijs mutauimus, vt obijcere forte possint,tum quidem nostram doctrinam probatam fuisse Luthero,aut nos nunc aliter docere, quàm olim consuetum fuerit in ecclesijs nostris.Quanta autem hæc sit iudiciorum iniquitas,æquus lector iudicet. Primum omnia
units.tr: For in the year of the Lord 1529, when Zwingli and Luther had been summoned by the most illustrious prince of the Hessians, Philip, and had met at Marburg, they agreed with one another on the other parts of Christian doctrine, but they could not come to agreement on the manner of the presence. Nevertheless they parted on friendly terms, and both assented that, since they held the same view on the chief doctrines, they ought thenceforth to abstain from all contention, and to pray God to kindle light also in this controversy and to show the way to concord. Nor from that time have we changed any article of doctrine in our churches, so that they could perhaps object that our doctrine was approved by Luther at that time, or that we now teach otherwise than was customary in our churches formerly. Let the fair reader judge how great the iniquity of these judgments is. First of all,

units.la: Zuinglius ipse optimè de ecclesia Dei meri-tus, & ecclesiæ ab illo institutæ pro pessimis hæreticis damnantur, tantum quia de modo præsentiæ corporis Christi in Eucharistia, de quo plerique aduersariorum nihil in S. literis definitum esse fatentur, à Papistis & à Luthe-ro dissentiunt. Damnantur deinde ob hanc controuersiā, quam olim Lutherus Marpur-gi, & postea etiā in negotio concordiæ, non tanti esse putauit, vt propter hanc concordiā ecclesiarum dissoluenda sit, & si postea vel quadam ingenij vehementia, vel factiosorum hominum sermonibus instigatus, aliter scri-psit & fecit. Postremò pro hæreticis pessimis proclamantur, cum tamen nunquā causa le-gitimè cognita damnati sint. Etenim si nobis obijciunt suorum Theologorum conuentus, in quibus nonnunquam nostri damnati sunt, nō possumus hos pro legitimis iudicijs agno scere, cum nostros nunquam audiuerint, nul-lum illis locum defendendi doctrinam suam dederint, libris quoq; eorum omnem aditum præcluserint. Si hæc esset legitima damnatio, non minus legitimè aduersarij nostri damna-ti essent à concilio Tridentino, in quo tot vi-ri docti ex diuersis admodum prouincijs con-uenientes, authoritate summorum regum & principum, ipsos damnarunt. Possumus etiā ipsorum conuentibus alios contrarios con-uentus opponere, in quibus cum nonnulli hoc potisimum agerent,vt Zuingliani nomi natim damnarentur,non potuerunt id efficere,quoniam plaeriq; illustrisimorum principum, & saniores etiam Theologorum pars ab huiusmodi illegitima, & iniqua damnatione abhorrebat. Quod si vnius Lutheri authoritate nos premere voluntquasi ea satis sit ad nos omnes condemnandos, cur non liceat nobis Luthero, magno quidem viro & eximio Dei seruo, sed tamen homini, vicisim alios homines opponere, vel veteris ecclesiae patres orthodoxos, ad quorum iudicia provocare nunquam dubitauimus, vel quem tantopere oderunt Zuinglium ipsum & Oecolampadium? Hi enim ambo (quod absq; inuidia dictu sit) Luthero neq; doctrina, neq; pietate, neq; studio propagandi Euangelij, neq; laboribus & periculis afflictionibusq; Christi causa perse rendis, vlla ex parte inferiores fuerunt. Quaedam autem iniqua sint Germanorum quorundam de optimis atq; sanctissimis hominibus iudicia, tamen alibi, vbi praeiudicia haec non regnant, scio longe honorificentius homines de illis scribere & loqui, quando Dei beneficio plurimi sunt in Gallia, Italia, Anglia, Polonia, aliisq; regionibus, qui ingenue fatentur sese horum doctrina, & scriptis non parum adiutos fuisse, vt ad veras religionis agnitionem peruenirent. Spero etiam multos esse in ipsa Germania, & quotidie plures fore, qui sepositi sita omni hominum authoritate, causam atq; rem ipsam diligentius expendentes nos non ita pro desperatis & a vera ecclesia alienis habituri sint. Nam si maxime in hac de modo praesentiae controuersia nostri a vero aberrafsent, tamen cum de reliquis doctrinae partibus pie & orthodoxe scripserint, atq; S. literas optime & doctissime interpretati sint, non erant certe tam atrociter ex ecclesia eijciendi, & omnia eorum scripta una exceptione damnanda. Quis enim ignorat, quot neguos & nõ leues errores Patribus condonare, & ad eos conniuere oporteat? Quoniam vero nondum constat nos errare, ne patiantur quaesto pij homines sibi imponi hac responsione, qua plaerasq; nostrorum rationes reijciunt, dicentes: Argumentum hoc Zuinglianum esse & dudum confutatum, ideoque nulla responsione opus habere. Verum cum Apostolus nos spiritus & prophetias dijudicare velit, cognoscant ipsi argumenta, & responsiones utrinq; allatas bene expendant, atq; ita causa bene cognita seposito omni affectu de re ipsa iudicet. Hoc si a bonis & moderatis viris impetrare poterimus, est sane quod gaudeamus, nā spes esset paulatim hac ratione diu exoptata concordia ecclesiae restitui posse. Sin autem contra omnis spes legitimae cognitionis, omnisque ratio ineundae concordiae nobis praecidi-tur, nos quidem propter ecclesiarū quae huic metuenda est, dissipationem plurimum dolebimus: sed videant hi pacis & concordiae hostes, quomodo Christo qui tantopere pacem & concordiam Ecclesiae suae commendavit, rationem reddituri sint nouorum & inutilium certaminum quae quotidie commouent. Ac siquidem meliora ab illis impetrare non possumus, te Domine Iesu Christe precamur, ut horum furores compescere velis, & Ecclesiae tuae largiri, ut in vera tui agnitione, sublatis tandem tristibus controuersiis, ut tua membra decet, sancte ac concorditer viuat, ut vere dicere possimus, omnium in te credentium esse cor vnum & animam vnam, Amen.
units.tr: Zwingli himself, who deserved very well of the Church of God, and the churches founded by him, are condemned as the worst of heretics merely because they dissent from the Papists and from Luther on the manner of the presence of Christ's body in the Eucharist, a point which most of our adversaries confess is not defined in the Holy Scriptures. They are then condemned on account of this controversy, which Luther once at Marburg, and afterwards also in the business of concord, did not think was so important that for its sake the agreement of the churches should be dissolved; and if he afterwards, either from a certain vehemence of temper or stirred by the talk of factious men, wrote and acted otherwise. Lastly, they are proclaimed the worst of heretics, although they were never condemned after a legitimate hearing of the cause. For if our adversaries object to us the gatherings of their theologians, in which some of ours have sometimes been condemned, we cannot acknowledge these as lawful judgments, since they never heard our men, never gave them any place to defend their doctrine, and have also closed every access to their books. If this were a lawful condemnation, our adversaries would not have been condemned any less lawfully by the Council of Trent, where so many learned men gathered from very diverse provinces condemned them by the authority of the highest kings and princes. We can also set against their assemblies other opposing assemblies, in which, although some were especially intent on this, that the Zwinglians should be condemned by name, they could not bring it about, because most of the most illustrious princes and the more sensible part of the theologians shrank from such an illegitimate and unjust condemnation. But if they wish to press us with the authority of Luther alone, as if that were enough to condemn us all, why should it not be permitted us to set against Luther, a great man and an excellent servant of God, yet still a man, other men in turn: either the orthodox fathers of the ancient Church, to whose judgment we have never hesitated to appeal, or Zwingli himself and Oecolampadius, whom they hate so bitterly? For these two (to speak without ill will) were in no way inferior to Luther in learning, in piety, in zeal for propagating the Gospel, or in labours, dangers and afflictions endured for the sake of Christ. Although some Germans' judgments on these best and most holy men are unfair, I know that elsewhere, where such prejudices do not reign, men speak and write of them far more honourably; since by God's benefit there are very many in France, Italy, England, Poland and other regions who freely confess that they were not a little helped by the teaching and writings of these men to come to a true knowledge of religion. I hope too that there are many in Germany itself, and that every day there will be more, who, setting aside all human authority and weighing the cause and the matter itself more carefully, will not regard us as so desperate and alien from the true Church. For even if our men had gone astray from the truth in this controversy about the manner of the presence, yet since they have written piously and orthodoxly on the other parts of doctrine, and have interpreted the Holy Scriptures very well and very learnedly, they certainly were not to be cast out of the Church so savagely, and all their writings condemned on a single exception. For who does not know how many, and not slight, errors must be pardoned to the Fathers, and how far one must connive at them? But since it is not yet established that we are in error, let the pious not allow themselves to be imposed upon by that answer with which most of our arguments are rejected, saying: this argument is Zwinglian and was refuted long ago, and therefore needs no reply. Rather, since the Apostle wills us to test spirits and prophecies, let them themselves know the arguments and carefully weigh the answers brought on both sides, and so, the cause being well understood and all feeling set aside, judge the matter itself. If we can obtain this from good and moderate men, there is indeed cause for rejoicing, for there would be hope that by this method the concord of the Church, long desired, could be restored. But if on the contrary every hope of lawful examination and every means of entering into concord is cut off from us, we indeed shall grieve greatly over the dispersion of the churches, which is to be feared; but let these enemies of peace and concord see how they will give account to Christ, who so earnestly commended peace and concord to His Church, for the new and useless quarrels which they stir up every day. And since we cannot obtain better things from them, we pray you, Lord Jesus Christ, that you would be pleased to restrain their furies, and grant to your Church that, in the true knowledge of you, with sad controversies at last laid aside, it may live holily and in harmony, as becomes your members, so that we may truly say that all who believe in you have one heart and one soul. Amen.

units.la: PROPOSITIONES DE VERA REALI ET SVBSTANTIALI PRAESENTIA corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi in Sacramento Altaris, auctore Andrea Musculo, S. Theologiæ doctore, & professore Academiæ Frankfordianæ.
units.tr: PROPOSITIONS CONCERNING THE TRUE, REAL AND SUBSTANTIAL PRESENCE of the body and blood of Jesus Christ in the Sacrament of the Altar, by Andreas Musculus, Doctor of Sacred Theology and professor at the Academy of Frankfurt.

units.la: VT effet publicum testimonium nos in Ecclesia nostra retinere formam sanorum verborum, quibus Christus vsus est in cœnæ institutione: atque vt bonis & pijs doctrinæ sanæ ministris: & de præsentia Christi in sacra Synaxi recte sentientibus planum fiat, nos idem cum ipsis sentire, & ex animo abhorre-re à Sacramentariorum & Caluinistarum ve-rum & recentiorum prauis atq; blasphemis dogmatibus, suscepimus in hac disputatione & examine publico doctorum virorum, li-centiam accipiendi gradum Doctorum in Theologia à nobis petentium, defensionem verae realis & substantialis præsentiæ corpo-ris & sanguinis Dei & Mariæ filij in Sacra-mento altaris.
units.tr: So that there may be a public testimony that we in our Church keep the form of sound words that Christ used in instituting the Supper, and so that it may be plain to good and godly ministers of sound doctrine, who think rightly about the presence of Christ in the holy Synaxis, that we think the same as they do and utterly abhor the perverse and blasphemous dogmas of the Sacramentarians and Calvinists, both old and new, we have undertaken, in this disputation and public examination of learned men, at the request of those seeking licence to take the degree of Doctor in Theology, the defence of the true, real and substantial presence of the body and blood of God and of Mary's son in the sacrament of the altar.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Ac primum omnium improbamus sini-stram ac vanam, Caluinistis non parum pa-trocinantem opinionem quorundam, qui vt Ecclesiæ tranquillitati & concordiæ consule-re velle
units.tr: And first of all we reject the mistaken and empty opinion of certain men, which lends no little support to the Calvinists, men who want to seem to be looking after the tranquillity and concord of the Church

units.la: PROPOSITIONES DE VERA KOINΩNIA CORPORIS ET SANGVINIS DOMINI nostri Iesu Christi, à Iosia Simlero oppositæ propositionibus Andreæ Musculi, quibus crassam illam realem & vbiquisticam præsentiam corporis Christi asserere conatus est.
units.tr: ON THE TRUE COMMUNION [κοινωνία] OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST: Propositions by Josias Simler, set against the propositions of Andreas Musculus, in which he tries to assert that crude real and ubiquitous presence of the body of Christ.

units.la: IN tanta varietate opinionum de modo præsentiæ Christi in sacra Eucharistia, nos quoque publice fidem nostram consentaneam sacris literis & doctrinæ veteris Ecclesiæ exponere voluimus, vt ostenderemus nos ex animo abhorrere ab Vbiquistica doctrina, & crassa eorū opinione, qui corpus & sanguinem Christi realiter & corporaliter in pane & vino includunt. Et ad præmonendos simplices & incautos, de vera & viuifica communione corporis & sanguinis Christi, quæ spiritualiter fit per fidem, ne præstigijs & sophismatibus Vbiquitariorū sibi hanc eripi patiantur, substituta in eius locum communione Vbiquistici corporis incogniti scripturis.
units.tr: In such a variety of opinions about the mode of Christ's presence in the holy Eucharist, we too have wished to set out publicly our faith, which agrees with the Holy Scriptures and the teaching of the ancient Church. We wanted to show that we utterly abhor the Ubiquitarian doctrine and the crude opinion of those who enclose the body and blood of Christ really and corporeally in the bread and wine. We also wished to warn the simple and the unwary about the true and life-giving communion of the body and blood of Christ, which takes place spiritually through faith. They should not allow the tricks and sophistries of the Ubiquitarians to snatch this from them, nor let the communion of an unknown ubiquitous body be substituted in its place, a communion that has no support in the Scriptures.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Ac primum eorum sententiam vt piam & modestam non improbamus, qui existimant hanc controuersiam de modo præsentiæ, exclusis nouis Vbiquistarum dogmatibus, non debere concordiæ re velle videantur, humana adducti sapientia plausibiliter quidem, sed non sine periculo amittendae veritatis institutionis coenae sacrae arbitrantur, & affirmant controversiam hanc sacramentariam nihil articulis fidei aut Ecclesiae symbolis derogare: & idcirco censent ma le eos facere, qui contradicendi studio diversum sentientibus sese opponunt, & lites in Ecclesia movent de rebus non adeo necessariis, & in quibus debeant esse sententiae liberae, & quemq; posse abfq; fidei & salutis periculo, quam velit pro arbitratu suo amplecti atque sequi sententiam & opinionem.
units.tr: First, we do not disapprove of the view of those who think, as a pious and moderate judgment, that this controversy about the mode of presence should not be pursued beyond the new dogmas of the Ubiquitarians. They are led by human wisdom, plausibly but not without danger of losing the truth of the institution of the Lord's Supper, and they affirm that this sacramentarian controversy takes nothing away from the articles of faith or the creeds of the Church. For this reason they judge that those act wrongly who, out of a desire to contradict, set themselves against those who think otherwise, and stir up quarrels in the Church over matters that are not so necessary, matters on which opinions ought to be free, and in which each person may, without danger to faith and salvation, embrace and follow whatever opinion he chooses at his own discretion.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Nos vero non rationis iudicio neq; nudis opinionibus, sed verbi Dei authoritate in contrariam sententiam vocati, statuimus hanc ipsam controversiam de coena Dominica omnino pertinere ad articulum fidei nostrae, & symboli secundam partem, quae est de incarnatione filii Dei, deq; ea pie & sobrie differendum esse. Nam destructo sublatoq; vero et sano intellectu verborum Christi κατὰ τὴν ῥητὴν, & alio eoq; peregrino simplicibus significantibusque verbis quibus Dominus in coenae institutione usus fuit, affecto & assumpto, euertitur sim ultorum hoc mysterium fide adorandum.
units.tr: We, however, are not moved to the contrary view by the judgment of reason or by bare opinions, but by the authority of the Word of God. We hold that this very controversy about the Lord's Supper pertains entirely to an article of our faith and to the second part of the creed, which concerns the incarnation of the Son of God, and that it must be discussed piously and soberly. For when the true and sound sense of Christ's words is destroyed and removed, and another, foreign sense is imposed and substituted for the plain sense [κατὰ τὴν ῥητήν] of the simple and meaningful words with which the Lord used in instituting the Supper, this mystery, which must be adored by faith, is overturned.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Qui ergo pio secundum scientiam Zelo sefuroribus Caluinistarum acriter opponunt, ij nobis Ecclesiarum obstare. Neque enim modus hic praesentiæ vnquam inter articulos fidei reputatus fuit, nisi quando Papistæ suam doctrinam de transsubstantiatione in concilio Lateranensi sanciuerunt. Neque sacramento quicquam derogatur, quando veram κοινωνίαν corporis & sanguinis Christi utraque pars profitetur. Ac idem sensisse videtur Lutherus, qui & Marpurgi cum Zuinglio, & Vuittenbergæ cum Bucero & aliis Ecclesiarum superioris Germaniæ ministris concordiam iniit.
units.tr: Those, then, who with pious zeal according to knowledge oppose the furious ravings of the Calvinists, these men stand in the way of the Churches. For this mode of presence was never reckoned among the articles of faith, except when the Papists sanctioned their doctrine of transubstantiation at the Lateran Council. Nor is anything taken from the sacrament when both sides profess the true communion of the body and blood of Christ. Luther also seems to have held this view, for he made concord both at Marburg with Zwingli and at Wittenberg with Bucer and other ministers of the Churches of upper Germany.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Itaque lites in Ecclesia non necessarias movent, qui viros bonos ac pios propterea damnant, quod carnalem & corporalem inclusionem corporis & sanguinis Christi in pane & vino cœnæ Dominicæ non agnoscunt. Graviús autem peccant qui articulum de Incarnatione Domini, controversiæ de cœna Dominica immiscent, & novam atque à scripturis alienam doctrinam de Vbiquitate corporis Christi, & reali communicatione, Ecclesiæ obtrudunt, atque ita totum mysterium salutis nostræ evertunt.
units.tr: Therefore those who condemn good and pious men for this reason, because they do not acknowledge a carnal and corporeal enclosing of the body and blood of Christ in the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper, stir up quarrels in the Church that are not necessary. But those sin more gravely who mix the article on the incarnation of the Lord into the controversy about the Lord's Supper, and who impose on the Church a new doctrine about the ubiquity of Christ's body and a real communication that is alien to the Scriptures, and so overturn the whole mystery of our salvation.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Hi autem verè sunt illi qui totam Germaniam turbant, & pacem Ecclesiarum impediunt, atque
units.tr: Those, however, are truly the men who disturb all Germany and impede the peace of the Churches, and

units.la: ij nobis bene recteq; facere, & bonam in Ecclesia Dei mereri laudem, neq; vllu dare scandalum, neque Israelem conturbare videntur, sed reipsa testatum facere se foederis eorum societatem fugere, neq; horrendos errores tacendo connivendoq; approbare velle.
units.tr: those who do good and right by us, and deserve a good reputation in the Church of God, do not seem to give any offence or to trouble Israel. Rather, they show in fact that they shun fellowship with those men, and they do not wish to approve dreadful errors by keeping silent and conniving at them.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Non enim ij leues & tollerabiles errores sed ipsissimas haereses Nestorij & Eutychis multis seculis ante damnatas, & ex Ecclesijs eiectas atque explosas denuo renouatas in eadem reuocant & introducunt.
units.tr: For these men do not revive and introduce light and tolerable errors, but the very heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches, condemned many centuries ago, and cast out and driven away from the Churches, which they now bring back and restore.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Nam dum pratia & impia imaginatione fascinati docent Christum secundum humanam naturam certo loco in coelo circumscriptum & alligatum, in eoq; vsque ad tempora restitutionis omnium mansurum esse, sit vt veram realem & substantialem Dei & Mariae filij praesentiam in coena pernegent, separent atque diuellant duarum naturarum vnionem ab ipso conceptionis exordio, nullo vnquam seculo separabilem.
units.tr: For while, bewitched by a foolish and impious imagination, they teach that Christ, according to his human nature, is circumscribed and bound to a certain place in heaven, and will remain there until the times of the restoration of all things, it follows that they deny the true, real and substantial presence of God and of Mary's Son in the Supper. They also separate and tear apart the union of the two natures from the very beginning of the conception, a union that was never separable at any age.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Quin & de errore in errorem prolapsi, Trinitate in vnitate substantiae Dei sublata, quaternitatem constituunt.
units.tr: Indeed, having fallen from error into error, they remove the Trinity in the unity of God's substance and so make a quaternity.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Nam Christus Deus & homo, Dei & Mariae filius in vna hypostasi, non in duabus subsistens, veteres errores Martionis, Eutychetis, Nestorij & Patripassianorum renouant, & in Ecclesiam denuo introducunt.
units.tr: For Christ, God and man, the Son of God and of Mary, subsisting in one hypostasis and not in two, revives the old errors of Marcion, Eutyches, Nestorius and the Patripassians, and introduces them afresh into the Church.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IIII.

units.la: Ac non pudet eos prauam & impiam imaginationem nominare, id quod scriptura apertis verbis docet: Christum secundum humanam naturam certo loco circunscriptum esse, ac coelo oportere contineri, vt Petrus dicit Acto. 3. vsque ad temporarestitutionis omnium.
units.tr: Nor are they ashamed to call this a wicked and impious fancy, when Scripture plainly teaches that Christ, according to his human nature, is circumscribed in a certain place and must be contained in heaven, as Peter says in Acts 3, until the times of the restoration of all things.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Existimant enim seruata in Christo humanae naturae veritate, vnionem personalem quae vere inseparabilis est, diuelli: & quod magis metuunt, tolli realem & substantialem praesentiam carnis Christi in Eucharistia. Itaque ipsi contra fingunt humanam naturam diuinae exaequatam, & cum ea vbique praesentem esse.
units.tr: For they suppose that, if the truth of the human nature in Christ is preserved, the personal union, which is truly inseparable, is torn apart, and, what they fear even more, the real and substantial presence of Christ's flesh in the Eucharist is taken away. So they invent for themselves a human nature made equal to the divine and present everywhere with it.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Vnde etiam alius eorum error oritur, quod e Trinitate quaternitatem faciunt, Christum hominem non in persona Verbi, sed communicata quadam deitate in se Deum facientes.
units.tr: Hence also arises another of their errors: they make a quaternity out of the Trinity, making Christ as man God in himself, not in the person of the Word, by some communicated deity.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Christus vero, Deus & homo & idem Dei ac hominis filius in vna hypostasi, non in duabus subsistens, vbicunque est, est Deus & homo, totus & in o
units.tr: But Christ, God and man, and the same Son of God and of man, subsisting in one hypostasis and not in two, wherever he is, is God and man, whole and entire,

units.la: e sistens, vbicunq; est, ibi quoq; est Deus & homo, totus & integer Christus.
units.tr: subsisting, wherever he is, there also he is God and man, whole and entire Christ.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Dato enim vno loco in quo Deus esse, homo autem nō esse dicatur, diu sa est irrefragabiliter persona, quæ vbicunq; est, inseparabilis est, constans tota & integra ex vnitione humanæ & diuinæ naturæ.
units.tr: For even if one place is named where God is said to be and man is not, the person is undoubtedly divided; but the person, wherever it is, is inseparable, consisting wholly and entire from the union of the human and divine natures.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Orthodoxa itaq; & Catholica fide edocti, retinemus vnionem hanc adorandam, ab vtero matris inseparabilem: & credimus inconcussa & indubitata fide totum Christum esse in vtero virginis, in horto, in cruce, in sepulchro, in cælo & in terris, & sic consequenter in cœna sacra.
units.tr: Therefore, taught by the orthodox and catholic faith, we hold to this union, which is to be adored and is inseparable from the mother's womb. And we believe, with unshaken and undoubting faith, that the whole Christ was in the virgin's womb, in the garden, on the cross, in the sepulchre, in heaven and on earth, and so consequently in the Lord's Supper.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Et ea pietate constanter negamus filiū hominis cœlo capi, eiq; inclusum & certo loco alligatum teneri, quia impietate cœnæ Dominicæ hostes hoc ipsum affirmant: & indubitanter asserimus Christum filium Dei & Mariæ simul & semel, & quidem in momento oculi in diuersis & singulis locis, vbicunq; voluerit esse, præsentem esse totum & integrum secundum vtranq; naturam in vna hypostasi subsistentem.
units.tr: And out of the same reverence we steadfastly deny that the Son of man is held by heaven, or kept enclosed and bound to a certain place, because his enemies affirm this very thing in their impiety towards the Lord's Supper. And we assert without doubt that Christ, the Son of God and of Mary, is present, whole and entire according to both natures, subsisting in one hypostasis, at once and together, and indeed in the twinkling of an eye, in various and separate places, wherever he is pleased to be.

units.la: XI. teger Christus, iuxta communionem idiomaton: seu vt in scholis dicitur, totus Christus vbiq; est, sed nō totum Christi.
units.tr: XI. entire Christ, according to the communication of properties; or, as it is said in the schools, the whole Christ is everywhere, but not the whole of Christ.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Nam vbicunq; est Christus, non adest vt Deus solum abfq; assumpta humanitate, sed vt Deus verbum Caro factum: neq; tamen propterea humana natura cum Verbo vbiq; est: Verbum enim quod vbiq; est, humanam naturam infua persona nihilo minus sustentat inseparabiliter, etiamsi eam non vna secū omnibus locis substantia sua praesentem statuat.
units.tr: For wherever Christ is, he is present not only as God apart from the assumed humanity, but as God the Word made flesh. Yet the human nature is not therefore everywhere with the Word; for the Word, which is everywhere, nonetheless sustains the human nature inseparably in his own person, even though he does not establish it as present by its own substance together with him in all places.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Itaq; quod ex Augustino adducitur, Christum to tum esse in vtero Virginis, in horto, in cruce, in sepulchro, in coelo & in terris, libenter admittimus, nempe quod haec persona diuina est, & ideo vbiq; tota & integra. Unde Augustinus ibidem praemittit: Hoc est Deum esse, quod vbiq; totum est. Cateterum quo ad naturas iuxta eundem Augustinum homo Christus secundum carnem fuit in sepulchro, secundum animam in inferno, Deus vero Christus vbiq; semper. Nec tamen (inquit) cum filium Dei Christum dicimus, hominem seperamus, aut cum eundem filium hominis dicimus, seperamus Deum: secundum hominem nanq; in terra erat non in coelo, vbi nunc est, quando dicebat: Nemo ascendit in coelum, nisi qui de coelo descendit filius hominis, qui est in coelo, quamuis secundum id quod filius Dei erat, esset in coelo: secundū id vero quod filius hominis erat, adhuc esset in terra nondum ascendisset in coelum.
units.tr: So, when it is quoted from Augustine that Christ is whole in the virgin's womb, in the garden, on the cross, in the sepulchre, in heaven and on earth, we gladly admit it, namely because this person is divine and therefore everywhere whole and entire. Hence Augustine in the same place prefaces: "To be God is to be wholly everywhere." But as for the natures, according to the same Augustine, Christ as man was in the sepulchre according to the flesh, and in hell according to the soul, while Christ as God was always everywhere. Nor, he says, when we call Christ the Son of God, do we separate the man; nor, when we call him the Son of man, do we separate God. For according to the man he was on earth and not in heaven, where he now is, when he said: "No one ascends into heaven, but he who came down from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven"; although, according to what he was as Son of God, he was in heaven; but according to what he was as Son of man, he was still on earth and had not yet ascended into heaven.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Itaq; recte cum scripturis & D. Augustino assen-
units.tr: Therefore we rightly agree with the Scriptures and with the holy Augustine,

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: In hac Orthodoxa confessione firmi consistentes & verbo Dei edocti, non veremur affirmare cum Idiomata humanae naturae nostrae angustiora sint, quam ut mirabili & ratione incomprehensibili unioni duarum naturarum respondeant & conveniant per omnia, Filium Dei in utero Virginis, in unione personali, praeter proprietates naturae humanae alias quoque praeternaturales in eam assumptisse, ut sit unus Christus, unus mediator & salvator, in una persona Deus & homo secundum utramque naturam, totus & integer Christus, Dei & Mariae filius, praesens suae ecclesiae, praesens in Coena, praesens ubique suis in regno sibi a Patre traditi.
units.tr: Standing firm in this orthodox confession and taught by the Word of God, we do not hesitate to affirm that, since the properties of our human nature are too narrow to correspond and agree in all respects with the wonderful and incomprehensible union of the two natures, the Son of God, in the personal union, in the virgin's womb assumed into it, beyond the properties of human nature, also other supernatural ones, so that there is one Christ, one mediator and saviour, one person, God and man according to both natures, the whole and entire Christ, Son of God and of Mary, present to his Church, present in the Supper, present everywhere in his kingdom, which has been given to him by the Father.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Ex hoc fundamento non est obscurum, quam misere caecutiant ignari spiritualium, qui eo quod Filius Dei factus sit homo, & humanae naturae proprietates habeat, harum considerationem ipsum certo in loco recte collocari, & caelo capi, concludique ut homine docent atque contendunt, cum scientes nesciant quod Filius Dei non tantum dicatur in scriptura conceptus & natus ex Maria virgine, sed de Spiritu sancto conceptus, virtute altissimi obumbrante Mariae. In qua sane conceptione et obumbratione virtutis altissimi nihil aliud ostendit & docet scriptura, quam supra commune rimum,filium hominis corpore suo cælo contineri, & certo loco circumscriptum esse, cum tamē diuinitate sua vbiq; præsens sit. Et impiā illorum sententiam detestamur, qui naturas confundentes, ea quæ diuinitatis sunt, vt vbiq; essentialiter præsentem esse, humanitati tribuunt.
units.tr: From this foundation it is not hard to see how wretchedly they grope in the dark, those who do not understand spiritual things. Because the Son of God became man and has the properties of human nature, they teach and contend that the consideration of these properties rightly places him in a certain location, and that he is held and enclosed in heaven as a man. They know nothing of what Scripture says: that the Son of God was not only conceived and born of the Virgin Mary, but was conceived of the Holy Spirit, by the power of the Most High overshadowing Mary. In that conception and overshadowing by the power of the Most High, Scripture shows and teaches nothing other than that the Son of man, according to his body, is contained in heaven and circumscribed in a certain place, although by his divinity he is present everywhere. We detest the impious opinion of those who, confusing the natures, attribute to the humanity what belongs to the divinity, namely to be essentially present everywhere.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Cum autem verbum Dei doceat duas naturas in Christo ita convenisse, vt non inde tertia quædam noua essentia facta fit, sed vt ambæ in suis proprietatibus salvæ permaneant: frustra quidam imaginantur humanæ naturæ datas esse quasdam præter naturales proprietates, vbiquitatem & similes, vt ita incomprehensibili vnioni idiomata hæc respondeant. Nam si talem velimus analogiam statuere inter vnita, humanam naturam infinitam facere oporteret, ita enim responderet naturæ diuinæ, cuius vnita est: sed nō & infinitum & æternus humanitatem temporalem & finitam integram manentibus suis proprietatibus sibi coniunxit. Etsi enim humana natura in Christo ineffabilibus donis ante & magis post glorificationem ornata est, nunquam tamen humanæ naturæ proprietates amisit.
units.tr: Since the Word of God teaches that the two natures came together in Christ in such a way that no third new essence arises from them, but that both remain intact in their own properties, it is vain for some to imagine that certain properties beyond the natural ones, such as ubiquity and the like, have been given to human nature, so that these attributes correspond to the incomprehensible union. For if we wished to set up such an analogy between the things united, we would have to make the human nature infinite, for so it would correspond to the divine nature with which it is united. But the eternal and infinite God did not join to himself a temporal and finite humanity while it kept its whole properties. For although human nature in Christ has been adorned with ineffable gifts, both before and more so after the glorification, it has never lost the properties of human nature.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Itaque recte concludunt, qui ex eo quod filius Dei homo factus humanæ naturæ proprietates habet, cum secundum humanam naturam certo in loco esse, & loco contineri afferunt. Etsi enim conceptus est ex spiritu sancto, tamen vt Leo inquit: munem formationem hominis, factam formationem in utero virginis ex Spiritu & virtute obumbrante conuenienter vnitioni inseparabili humanae & diuinae naturae, adiectis praeternaturalibus Idiomatibus, vt Deus & homo sit vnus Christus, Deus & homo in vna persona naturis non diuulsis aut separatis, in suo regno secundum suam naturam vbiq; praesens.
units.tr: Therefore those conclude rightly who, because the Son of God became man and has the properties of human nature, assert that he is, according to his human nature, certainly in a place and contained by a place. For although he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, as Leo says, the formation of the man, made in the womb of the Virgin by the Spirit and the overshadowing power, is fitting to the inseparable union of the human and divine natures, with the supernatural attributes added, so that Christ is one, God and man in one person, the natures not torn apart or separated, present in his kingdom everywhere according to his nature.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Sic ipsi assertione Physica proprietatum humanae naturae fascinati gloriantur, de victoria nondum parta, & pijs recte de conceptione & vnione naturarum Christi sententibus illudunt, & mysterium hoc de conceptione ex spiritu S. facta, & virtute altissimi obumbrante, quasi in eo nihil omnino momenti sit, tacite callideq; praetereunt.
units.tr: Thus the Papists, dazzled by the physical assertion of the properties of human nature, boast of a victory not yet won, and mock the godly who rightly think about the conception and union of the natures of Christ; and they silently and cunningly pass over this mystery of the conception made by the Holy Spirit and the overshadowing power of the Most High, as if there were nothing at all of importance in it.

units.la: XIIII.
units.tr: XIIII.

units.la: Nos vero non duce ratione humana q; sapientia, sed coelesti lumine illustrati, & verbo Dei edocti, fide adoramus hanc mirabilem, coelestem, & rationi atq; creaturae rationali abscondituram conceptionem, formationem & vnionem duarum naturarum diuinae & humanae, & vbiq; scimus, vbique agnoscimus totum & integrum Christum, neq; eum in loco diuisum, neque altera natura ab altera sepa-rata quaerimus.
units.tr: We, however, are not led by human reason or wisdom, but are illumined by the heavenly light and taught by the Word of God. We adore by faith this wonderful, heavenly conception, formation and union of the two natures, divine and human, which is hidden from reason and from the rational creature. We know, and everywhere acknowledge, the whole and entire Christ, and we do not seek him divided in place, nor one nature separated from the other.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Hoc fundamento firmo & immoto, fide certa Novitas creationis proprietatem generis non remouit. Natus quidem est ex Virgine & peccati omnis expers fuit, caeterum per omnia excepto peccato nobis simulis factus est.
units.tr: On this firm and immovable foundation, by sure faith, the newness of creation did not remove the property of the kind. Indeed he was born of a Virgin and was free of all sin; yet in all things, apart from sin, he was made like us.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Abutuntur itaque mysterio hoc conceptionis ex spiritu sancto factae, qui ex eo conficere volunt Corpus Christi supranaturales proprietates, & non minatim Vbiquitatem accepisse.
units.tr: Therefore they abuse this mystery of the conception made by the Holy Spirit, when from it they want to conclude that the body of Christ received supernatural properties, and indeed ubiquity without measure.

units.la: XIIII.
units.tr: XIIII.

units.la: Oportet enim nos ita hanc mirabilem & coelestem conceptionem & formationem sanctissimi partus in utero virginis, ut scripturis edocti sumus, credere: ut simul etiam humanae naturae suae proprietates non auferamus. Nam ut naturae non sunt separandae, ita etiam non sunt confundendae.
units.tr: For we must believe this wonderful and heavenly conception and formation of the most holy birth in the womb of the Virgin as we have been taught by the Scriptures, and at the same time we must not take away the properties of his human nature. For just as the natures are not to be separated, so also they are not to be confused.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Quare cum certa & indubitata fide credamus & confiteamur, Christum verum corpus & loco circumscriptum habere, eoque terris absentem coelo contineri, non possumus eorum opinioni assentiri, qui corpus ipsius realiter, substantialiter, & naturaliter praesens in pane coenae dominicae exhiberi aiunt.
units.tr: Therefore, since we believe and confess with certain and undoubted faith that Christ has a true body circumscribed in place, and that, being absent from the earth, he is contained in heaven, we cannot assent to the opinion of those who say that his body is exhibited really, substantially and naturally present in the bread of the Lord's Supper.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Sed sicut in prima coena, ubi tamen corporaliter & visibiliter aderat, discipuli ipsius corpus non manducarunt corporaliter, quod adhuc passibile erat, sed spiritualiter per fidem, ita nunc quoque vult suum corpus & sanguinem a credentibus certa indubitataque credimus, credentes lo❦ quimur & testamur in cœna facratissima, à Dei & Mariæ filio instituta & celebrata, & quæ celebratur & celebrabitur in sancta Ecclesia vsq; ad consummationem sęculi, verum corpus & sanguinem verum Iesu Christi, vere & substantialiter adesse, & exhiberi sumentibus, cum illis rebus quæ videntur panę & vino.
units.tr: But just as at the first supper, where he was indeed present bodily and visibly, his disciples did not eat his body bodily, since it was still passible, but spiritually, through faith, so now too he wills that his body and blood be received by believers. Holding this with certain and undoubted faith, we speak and testify, believing, that in the most sacred supper, instituted and celebrated by the Son of God and Mary, which is and will be celebrated in the holy Church until the consummation of the age, the true body and true blood of Jesus Christ are truly and substantially present and are exhibited to those who partake, together with those things which are seen, namely bread and wine.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Et credimus ipsum sicut in cœna prima, ita nunc quoq; suum corpus & suum sanguinem extra omnem rationis conieCturam, mę diante manu ministri, omnibus & singulis ad sacram synaxin accedentibus, dignis & indignis, licet sorte inæquali sumentibus, vt canit Ecclesia, porrigere.
units.tr: And we believe that he now gives his body and blood to all and each who come to the holy synaxis, worthy and unworthy, though receiving in unequal measure, just as he gave them at the first supper, beyond every conjecture of reason, through the hand of the minister, as the Church sings.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Confitemur quoq; nitentes firmissima pedtra verbi, in hac cœna non aliam nos carnem, quàm quæ nata est ex Maria virgine, & passa in cruce, & resurrexit à mortuis, fide & ore percipere atque manducare.
units.tr: We also confess, relying on the firmest rock of the Word, that in this supper we receive and eat, by faith and with the mouth, no other flesh than that which was born of the Virgin Mary, suffered on the cross, and rose from the dead.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Atque vt certam ex præmissis ponamus definitionem cœnæ Dominicæ, dicimus sacram synaxin esse actionem sacram, aut culrtum diuinum à Christo institutum, in quo Christus ipse totus & integer secundum vtrã que naturam, præsens in terris præbet suum corpus spiritualiter manducari per fidem, huic autem manducationi locorum distantia non obstat.
units.tr: To set down a sure definition of the Lord's Supper from what has been said: we say that the holy synaxis is a sacred action, or divine rite, instituted by Christ, in which Christ himself, whole and entire according to both natures, present on earth, offers his body to be eaten spiritually through faith. Distance of place does not hinder this eating.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Porro non aliam carnem quam quae nata est ex Maria virgine, & passa in cruce, & resurrxit a mortuis, manducari afferimus. Neq; enim Christo duo corpora affingimus, aut spirituale eius corpus facimus, sed modum manducationis spiritualem esse novimus, quae non fiat ore, sed fide.
units.tr: Furthermore, we affirm that no other flesh is eaten than that which was born of the Virgin Mary, suffered on the cross, and rose from the dead. For we do not attribute two bodies to Christ, nor do we make his body spiritual. Rather, we know the manner of eating to be spiritual, because it is done not with the mouth but by faith.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Recte autem Coena Domini describitur, quod sit Actio sacra a Christo instituta, ut a nobis in recenti memoria retineatur, et in nobis etiam obsignetur, maximum generi mortalium praestitum beneficium, quod corpus suum pro nobis tradidit, & sanguinem suum in remissionem peccatorum nostrorum effudit, & nos sua carne pascit, & suo sanguine potat, quae vera fide spiritualiter percepta nos alunt ad vitam aeternam. Et haec quidem visibiliter foris hoc sacramento repraesentantur, & oculis subiiciuntur, intus autem in animo invisibiliter per ipsum spiritum sanctum praestantur. Sicut enim fideles a ministro Domini, panem Domini accipiunt & edunt, ac bibunt de poculo Domini, ita intus per spiritum sanctum percipiunt carnem & sanguinem Domini, & pascuntur his in vitam aeternam.
units.tr: The Lord's Supper is rightly described as a sacred action instituted by Christ, so that the greatest benefit ever bestowed on the human race may be kept in fresh memory by us and also sealed in us: that he gave his body for us, poured out his blood for the remission of our sins, feeds us with his flesh and gives us his blood to drink. Received spiritually by true faith, these nourish us to eternal life. Indeed, these things are represented outwardly by this sacrament and set before the eyes visibly, but inwardly in the mind they are bestowed invisibly by the Holy Spirit himself. For just as the faithful receive and eat the bread of the Lord from the Lord's minister, and drink from the cup of the Lord, so inwardly, through the Holy Spirit, they receive the flesh and blood of the Lord and are fed by them unto eternal life.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Non existimandum est physicas & philosophicas imaginationes esse, quibus circumscriptio & certus locus, & reliquae proprietates humani corcorpus præsens non absens, non remotum non certo loco affixum in cœlo, verum, substantiale & naturale, & sanguinem suum verum in pane & vino sumentibus tam dignis, quam indignis, his quidem in iudicium, illis vero in testimonium applicationis remissionis peccatorum, & alios salutares vsus & fructus.
units.tr: It is not to be thought that the circumscription, a fixed place, and the other properties of a human body, by which the body of Christ is said to be present and not absent, not remote, not fixed to a certain place in heaven, but true, substantial and natural, and his true blood in the bread and wine for those who receive it, both worthy and unworthy (for the former to judgment, the latter to witness the application of the remission of sins, and other saving uses and fruits), are physical and philosophical fancies.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Execramur quoque deprauatorum cœnæ philosophicas coniecturas, & imaginationes de physica tantum conceptione, & formatione Christi in vtero virginis, & alias vanas ratiocinationes & dubitationes, quomodo Christus etiam secundum humanam naturam in tam paruo corpore panis & vini esse possit: sed nos duce scriptura sacra scimus nihil esse tam magnum, quin Deus sit maior, nihil tam paruum, quin Deus sit minor, nihil tam longum, quin Deus sit longior, nihil tam breue, quin Deus sit breuior, Iesus Christus verus Deus & homo in vna persona inseparabiliter existens.
units.tr: We also execrate the philosophical conjectures of the depraved about the Supper, and the imaginings about a merely physical conception and formation of Christ in the Virgin's womb, and other vain arguments and doubts about how Christ, even according to his human nature, could be in so small a body of bread and wine. But we, with holy Scripture as our guide, know that nothing is so great that God is not greater, nothing so small that God is not smaller, nothing so long that God is not longer, nothing so short that God is not shorter: Jesus Christ, true God and man, existing inseparably in one person.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Et negligentes illorum philosophicas speculationes non veremur affirmare, etsi fortasis parum Physice, attamen Theologice totum Christum & integrum in vna persona esse posse in loco, secundum omnem modum philosophicum, circumscriptiue, & definitiue, & repletiue.
units.tr: And disregarding their philosophical speculations, we do not hesitate to affirm that the whole and entire Christ, in one person, can be in a place, although perhaps not physically, yet theologically, in every philosophical mode: circumscriptively, definitively, and repletively.

units.la: XXI. pori Christi tribuuntur, quoniam scriptura hæc illi tribuit, & semper sic docuit vetus Ecclesia. Est autem absurda opinio, corpus Christi propter vnionem personalem esse vbiq;. Etsi enim de Deo dicitur nihil esse tam magnum, quin Deus sit maior, nihil tam paruum, quin Deus sit minor, nihil tam longum, quin Deus sit longior, nihil tam breue, quin Deus sit breuior: tamen id de humanitate Christi quæ circumscripta est dicere non licet, nisi exist[i]memus eam in diuinitatem mutatam.
