Ac sicuti non licet concludere: Deus est æternus, absq; principio, incorporeus, incircumscriptus. Christus Iesus est Deus. Ergo secundum humanam naturam æternus, absq; principio, incorporeus est. Ita etiā vbiquitatem corporis Christi ex vbiquitate diuinæ naturæ non licet conficere. XX.
units.tr: XXI. are attributed to the body of Christ, since Scripture ascribes these to him and the ancient Church has always so taught. But it is an absurd opinion that the body of Christ is everywhere because of the personal union. For although of God it is said that nothing is so great that God is not greater, nothing so small that God is not smaller, nothing so long that God is not longer, nothing so short that God is not shorter, yet this may not be said of the humanity of Christ, which is circumscribed, unless we suppose it changed into the divinity. Just as one may not conclude: God is eternal, without beginning, incorporeal, uncircumscribed; Christ Jesus is God; therefore according to human nature he is eternal, without beginning, and incorporeal, so too one may not infer the ubiquity of Christ's body from the ubiquity of the divine nature. XX.

units.la: Non reijcimus eorū speculationē, qui Christo in cruce mortuo, corpus eius circūscriptiue in cruce, et postea in sepulchro fuisse aiunt, animā definitiue apud inferos, diuinitatē repletiue vbiq; præsentem fuisse. Verum quia Christum secundū vtranq; naturā aiunt posse in loco esse circumscriptiue, definitiue, repletiue, prorsus non loquuntur Theologicè. Neq; enim Theologorū est absurda & contradictoria affirmare. Et circumscriptiue in loco esse, tam nō convenit diuinæ naturæ, quàm humanæ nō quadrat repletiue vbiq; esse, quod est solius diuinitatis, vt testatur Augusti. Epist. 57. Et magister sententiarum lib. 1. distinct. 37. XXI.
units.tr: We do not reject the speculation of those who say that Christ, dead on the cross, had his body circumscriptively on the cross and afterwards in the sepulchre, his soul definitively among the dead, and his divinity repletively present everywhere. But because they say that Christ according to both natures can be in a place circumscriptively, definitively, and repletively, they do not speak theologically at all. For it is not the part of theologians to affirm things that are absurd and contradictory. To be in a place circumscriptively belongs no more to the divine nature than to be repletively everywhere, which belongs to deity alone, fits the human nature, as Augustine testifies (Ep. 57) and the Master of the Sentences (book 1, distinction 37). XXI.

units.la: Ex eo autem quod corpus Christi clausis ianuis
units.tr: But from the fact that the body of Christ, with the doors shut,

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Ac sicut credimus, Christum non dissolua-ta vnione, neque confusis naturarum proprie-tatibus fuisse in lapide & ianua clausa: sic te-nemus quoque Catholica fide, eius carnem & sanguinem esse in pane & vino.
units.tr: And just as we believe that Christ, without the union being dissolved and without the properties of the natures being confused, was in the stone and with the door shut, so we likewise hold by the Catholic faith that his flesh and blood are in the bread and wine.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: In hac simplici & vera fide acquiescimus, & eam reuerentiam, potentiam & efficaciam, simplicibus & claris Christi verbis, pro vt so-nant, tribuimus, & fide oreque indubitanter corpus & sanguinem eius percipimus.
units.tr: In this simple and true faith we rest content, and we ascribe to the simple and plain words of Christ, as they sound, that reverence, power and efficacy; and with faith and mouth we receive without doubt his body and blood.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Cum ergo ille qui omnia potest, cui omnia cedunt, & extra cuius potentiam nihil est, di-xerit in sua sacratissima cœna, Hoc est corpus meum, Hic est sanguis meus, nō patimur ne-que patiemur vnquam nos vllis verborum præstigiis hostium cœnæ à simplici verbo-rum sensu de vera & reali præsentia Christi abduci, auertique.
units.tr: Since therefore he who can do all things, to whom all things yield, and outside whose power nothing exists, has said in his most sacred supper, "This is my body," "This is my blood," we do not allow, nor will we ever allow, ourselves to be drawn away and turned aside from the plain sense of the words, concerning the true and real presence of Christ, by any verbal sleight of hand of the enemies of the Supper.

units.la: XXIIII.
units.tr: XXIIII.

units.la: Ideoq; hæc verba Christi secundum genui-num, verum & grammaticum sensum accipi-mus: neq; eis symbolicum, denominatiuum, metonymicum, aut quemuis alium sensum à Sacramentariis & Caluinistis excogitatum & confictum, affingimus, & affingi patiemur.
units.tr: Therefore we accept these words of Christ in their genuine, true and grammatical sense; and we neither attach to them, nor will we ever allow to be attached to them, any symbolic, denominative, metonymical or other sense devised and invented by the Sacramentarians and the Calvinists.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Curiosa autē ingenia modum & ordinem quærent intrasse, & per lapidem sepulchri transiisse dici= tur, non tollitur veritas corporis. Nam vt patres aiunt: Creatura cessit creatori. At idem corpus rea= liter & substantialiter multis in locis aut vbique præsens esse, cū veritate humani corporis pugnat.
units.tr: Curious minds will ask about the manner and order: that he entered, and is said to have passed through the stone of the sepulchre, does not take away the truth of the body. For, as the Fathers say, the creature yielded to the Creator. But that the same body should be really and substantially present in many places at once, or everywhere, is contrary to the truth of a human body.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Quare à vero sensu verborum Christi aberrāt, qui afferunt corpus eius in cœna realiter & sub= stantialiter & corporaliter simul in multis locis præsens esse.
units.tr: Therefore those err from the true sense of Christ's words who maintain that his body is in the Supper really, substantially and corporeally present in many places at the same time.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Cum autem hæc sint verba Christi: Hoc est cor= pus meū, quod pro vobis traditur, Hoc est sanguis noui Testamenti, rectè faciunt, qui se ab his verbis & vero eorū sensu abduci non patiuntur.
units.tr: Since, however, these are the words of Christ, "This is my body, which is given for you," and "This is the blood of the new covenant," those do right who refuse to be drawn away from these words and their true sense.

units.la: XXIIII.
units.tr: XXIIII.

units.la: Sed neque genuinum & Grammaticum verborum sensum retinent, neque veram διάνοιαν asse= runt, qui excluso omni tropo realem & corpora= lem præsentiam corporis Christi in pane, aut cum vel sub pane ex illis verbis statuunt.
units.tr: But those who, with every trope excluded, affirm from those words a real and bodily presence of the body of Christ in the bread, or with or under the bread, neither keep the genuine and grammatical sense of the words nor assert the true meaning [διάνοια].

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Qui igitur veram διάνοιαν reuerenter in scriptu= ris quærunt, & secundum has explicant modum & ordinem verborum Christi, nequaquam curiosi aut blasphemi iudicari debent. quærentia, cum nemo sit qui verbis ea explicare, ac ne cogitatione quidem assequi possit, suæ relinquimus impietati & blasphemiæ curiositati, salutisque periculo non dubio.
units.tr: Therefore those who reverently seek the true meaning [διάνοια] in the Scriptures, and explain the manner and order of Christ's words according to these, ought by no means to be judged curious or blasphemous. As for things which no one can explain in words, or even grasp in thought, we leave them to their own impiety and blasphemous curiosity, with no doubt danger to salvation.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Nam hoc magnum pietatis mysterium non est subiectum communi naturæ ordini: sed ratio eius in virtute Christi est, scientia in fide, causa in potestate, & effectus in voluntate eiusdem.
units.tr: For this great mystery of piety is not subject to the common order of nature; its reason lies in the power of Christ, its knowledge in faith, its cause in power, and its effect in his will.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Sic vnio quoq; ipsa panis & corporis Christi est incomprehensibilis: quia non est personalis, neq; naturalis, neq; formalis, sed sacramentalis & supernaturalis.
units.tr: So the union itself of the bread and the body of Christ is incomprehensible, because it is not personal, nor natural, nor formal, but sacramental and supernatural.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Non enim includitur corpus Christi in panem localiter, neque modo naturali, sed præsens est realiter & substantialiter.
units.tr: For the body of Christ is not enclosed in the bread locally, nor in a natural manner, but is present really and substantially.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Neque etiam verborum sono corpus Christi de cælo detrahitur, neque nouum corpus fingitur, sed verum ac viuum corpus Christi statuitur in cœna præsens realiter, substantialiter & naturaliter.
units.tr: Nor is the body of Christ brought down from heaven by the sound of the words, nor is a new body invented; rather, the true and living body of Christ is affirmed to be present in the Supper really, substantially and naturally.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Communicantes ergo firmissima fide percipimus, & ore manducamus verum corpus & verum sanguinem Christi, admirando & adorando tantummodo.
units.tr: Therefore, communicating with the firmest faith, we receive and eat with the mouth the true body and the true blood of Christ, only with wonder and adoration.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Nam cum scriptura generaliter ita definiat nobis corpus Christi, quod illud pluribus in locis simul esse non possit ab hac eius definitione in cœna nobis non est recedendum, nisi perspicuo Dei verbo patefactum fuerit, Deum voluisse hic quicquam secus fieri. Vbi enim de voluntate Dei constat, ibi demum tota facti ratio consistit in potentia facientis.
units.tr: For since Scripture generally defines the body of Christ for us as something that cannot be in several places at once, we must not depart from this definition in the case of the Supper, unless it has been made plain by the clear Word of God that God has willed something different to happen here. For where the will of God is established, there the whole reason of the deed rests in the power of the one who does it.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Sic de vnione panis & corporis Christi (quamuis scripturæ non ita loquantur) non simpliciter ex potétia Dei argumentandum est, sed de voluntate eius quærendum. Recte autem dicitur vnione hanc non esse personalem, naturalem aut formalem, sed sacramentalem & supernaturalem.
units.tr: So concerning the union of the bread and the body of Christ (although the Scriptures do not speak in this way), we must not argue simply from the power of God, but must inquire into his will. It is rightly said that this union is not personal, natural or formal, but sacramental and supernatural.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Atq; vt corpus Christi non in panem includitur localiter, neq; verborum sono de cœlo detrahitur, neq; modo naturali præsens est: ita etiam non est coniunctu pani, & in cœna præsens realiter & substantialiter, quocunque tandem modo id fieri dicatur.
units.tr: And just as the body of Christ is not enclosed locally in the bread, nor brought down from heaven by the sound of the words, nor present in a natural manner, so it is not joined to the bread and present in the Supper really and substantially, however it may be said to happen.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Sed sacramentalis vnio est, vbi signum & res signata coniunguntur per relationem, qua signum rem ipsam efficaciter significat & repræsentat. Est autem hæc vnio supernaturalis, quoniam non naturaliter, neque ex hominum instituto, sed ex Dei ordinatione hæc externa symbola cœlestium rerum signa facta sunt.
units.tr: But the sacramental union is where a sign and the thing signified are joined through a relation by which the sign effectively signifies and represents the thing itself. This union is supernatural, since these external symbols were made signs of heavenly things not naturally, nor by human institution, but by the ordinance of God.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Multo minus imaginamur vllam corporis distractionem: neq; dicimus hac arcana præternaturali & corporali manducatione carnem Christi alterari in nobis vel etiam coinquinari.
units.tr: We by no means imagine any distraction of the body, nor do we say that by this secret, supernatural and bodily eating the flesh of Christ is altered in us or even defiled.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Ita pernegamus quoque Capernaiticam illam lanienam corporis Christi, & Scythicam quoq; cruoris Domini ingurgitationem.
units.tr: Likewise we utterly reject that Capernaitic butchering of the body of Christ, and the Scythian gulping down of the blood of the Lord.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Similiter etiam non intelligimus præsentiam Physicam, Geometricam aut Mathematicam, de paruitate aut magnitudine: sed sentimus in cœna verum corpus & verum sanguinem Christi adesse supernaturali & cœlesti modo.
units.tr: Similarly we do not understand a physical, geometrical or mathematical presence, concerning smallness or largeness. Rather, we hold that in the Supper the true body and true blood of Christ are present in a supernatural and heavenly manner.

units.la: XXXIIII.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Ideoq; asserimus corpus Christi accipi & manducari non visibiliter, neque sensibiliter: fatemur quidem ambas res vere & substantialiter in cœna adesse, panem & vinum sensibiliter & visibiliter, corpus vero & sanguinem Christi inuisibiliter & incomprehensibiliter.
units.tr: Therefore we assert that the body of Christ is received and eaten not visibly or sensibly. We do confess that both things are truly and substantially present in the Supper: the bread and wine sensibly and visibly, but the body and blood of Christ invisibly and incomprehensibly.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Nec manducari communem panem, sed illum, cum quo vere & substantialiter adest & exhibetur vescentibus corpus Christi.
units.tr: Nor is the common bread eaten, but that bread with which the body of Christ is truly and substantially present and offered to those who eat.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Communicantes ergo ore quidem externa fi-gna sumimus, rem autem ipsam fide percipimus spiritualiter.
units.tr: Therefore, communicating with the mouth, we indeed take the external signs, but we perceive the thing itself spiritually by faith.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Neq; hic imaginanda est vlla corporalis præsen-tia aut manducatio.
units.tr: Nor is any bodily presence or eating to be imagined here.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Illa enim si corporalis & carnalis est, Caper-naitica erit, quantumuis aliis coloribus ornetur.
units.tr: For if that presence is bodily and carnal, it will be Capernaitic, however much it is adorned with other colours.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Similiter physica & localis erit præsentia, si ve-rum & naturale corpus substantialiter præsens ad est. Modus enim cœlestis non efficit vt verum cor-pus non localiter adsit, si illud substantia sua præ-sens est.
units.tr: Likewise the presence will be physical and local if the true and natural body is substantially present. For the heavenly mode does not make it that the true body is not locally present, if it is present in its substance.

units.la: XXXIIII.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Ideoq; sibijpsis contradicunt, qui afferut corpus Christi vere & substantialiter in cœna adesse, ac ore manducari, & tamen manducationem eius su-pernaturalem esse volunt, quæ ore & fide fiat.
units.tr: Therefore they contradict themselves who affirm that the body of Christ is truly and substantially present in the Supper and is eaten with the mouth, and yet want its eating to be supernatural, taking place by mouth and by faith.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Panis autem cœnæ Domini non propterea com-munis est, si cum illo corpus Christi non substan-tialiter coniunctum est, sed est sacer & diuinus pa-nis non mutatione substantiæ, sed mysterij ratione.
units.tr: The bread of the Lord's Supper is not on that account common, if the body of Christ is not substantially joined with it. It is holy and divine bread, not by a change of substance but by reason of the mystery.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Captiua ergo teneatur ratio humana, & omnis intellectus sub fide & obedientia verbo rum Christi, & κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν Christi, vt sonant ac cipiantur, imo taceat omnino mulier in eccle sia et digito compescat labellum philosophia, quiescant Plato & Aristoteles in hisce sacris mysterijs.
units.tr: Let therefore human reason be held captive, and every understanding be subject to faith and to obedience to the words of Christ, taken according to the letter [κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν] as they sound and are understood. Indeed, let the woman keep entirely silent in the Church, and let philosophy put a finger to her lips; let Plato and Aristotle be quiet about these sacred mysteries.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Reuerenter quoq; cum timore & tremore sentiamus de hoc mysterio: & dicamus cum ecclesiæ hymno ad firmandum cor syncerum, sola fides sufficit: præstet fides supplementum sensuum defectui.
units.tr: Let us also think about this mystery with reverence, with fear and trembling, and let us say with the hymn of the Church, to strengthen the sincere heart: faith alone suffices; let faith supply what the senses lack.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Digna veneratione & hæc verba hymni amplectamur contra Sacramentariorū blasphemos furores. Quod non capis, quod non vides, animosa firmat fides præter rerum ordinem: Sub diuersis speciebus signis tantum, & non rebus latent res eximiæ. Caro, cibus, sanguis, potus, manet tamen Christus totus sub vtraq; specie. A sumente non concisus, non confractus, nec diuisus integer accipitur. Sumit vnus, sumunt mille, tantum ille, quàtum ille, nec sumptus absumitur. Sumunt boni, sumunt mali, sorte tamen inæquali vitæ vel interitus.
units.tr: Let us also embrace with due veneration these verses of the hymn against the blasphemous frenzies of the Sacramentarians: "What you do not grasp, what you do not see, a bold faith affirms, beyond the order of things. Under different species, signs only, and not the things, the great realities lie hidden. Flesh, food, blood, drink; yet Christ remains whole under either kind. He is received by the one who eats, not cut, not broken, not divided, but whole. One eats, a thousand eat; he is as much as that one, and when eaten he is not used up. The good eat, the bad eat; yet with unequal lot, of life or of death."

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Grata itaque mente cum Ecclesia sanctaab
units.tr: With a grateful mind, then, together with the holy Church

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Hoc mysterium non ratione humana, sed fide æ-stimandum est, & tenenda vera sententia verborum Christi, quæ cum reliquis locis scripturæ, & analogia fidei consentiat. Atq; hic seponatur Lutheri & omnis aliorum hominum authoritas.
units.tr: This mystery is to be judged not by human reasoning but by faith, and the true sense of Christ's words is to be held, which agrees with the other passages of Scripture and with the analogy of faith. And here the authority of Luther and of all other men is to be set aside.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Recipimus etiam sano sensu dictum hoc ex Ecclesiæ hymno: Sola fides sufficit, præstet fides supplementum sensuum defectui. Sed fidei nomine nō intelligimus falsam persuasionem de corporali præsentia, verum eam fidem qua credimus filium Dei pro nobis traditum, & ita traditū & affixum cruci, ut sit cibus noster & potus spiritualis, quo ad æternam vitam sustentemur, sicut Christus testatus est Ioan. 6. capite. Et cum institueret sacramentum Eucharistiæ repetijt.
units.tr: We also accept, in a sound sense, the saying from the Church's hymn: "Faith alone suffices; let faith supply what the senses lack." But by faith we do not mean a false persuasion about a bodily presence; we mean that faith by which we believe that the Son of God was given up for us, and given up and fastened to the cross in such a way that He is our spiritual food and drink, by which we are sustained unto eternal life, as Christ testified in John, chapter 6. And when He instituted the sacrament of the Eucharist, He repeated this.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Veruntamen hymnum hunc non multum moramur, etsi enim quædam commodam interpretationem admittant, tamen cum non sit veteris Ecclesiæ hymnus, sed à Thoma Aquinate compositus, idq; ad firmandam transsubstantiationem Papisticam & panis adorationem, eius auctoritas nulla est nisi apud Papistas, ad quorum castra vos transfitis.
units.tr: However, we do not dwell long on this hymn. Even if some of its phrases admit a convenient interpretation, it is not a hymn of the ancient Church but was composed by Thomas Aquinas, and it was written to confirm the Papist transubstantiation and the adoration of the bread. Its authority is therefore nothing except among the Papists, to whose camp you are defecting.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Nos verò cum veteri Ecclesia pia mente agnoscimus ac prædicamus immensum beneficium Filij Dei, quod nos fecit membra corporis sui,
units.tr: But we, with the ancient Church, acknowledge and proclaim with a devout mind the immense benefit of the Son of God, who has made us members of his body.

units.la: sta ab isto institutionis exordio agnoscamus ac celebremus hanc immensam bonitatem fi-lij Dei, quod sanctissimum suum corpus, & purifsimū suum sanguinem cum nostris cor-poribus multis modis pollutis, & horrendis infirmitatibus contaminatis coniungere non dedignatur.
units.tr: From this beginning of the institution, let us acknowledge and celebrate this immense goodness of the Son of God, who does not disdain to join his most holy body and his most pure blood to our bodies, which are polluted in many ways and contaminated by dreadful infirmities.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Detestemur simul & veterum & nouorum Sacramentariorū varias & multiplices glo-sas & interpretationes de signo, typo, figura & symbolo.
units.tr: We likewise condemn the various and manifold glosses and interpretations, both of the old and the new Sacramentarians, concerning the sign, type, figure and symbol.

units.la: XLI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: Non enim potest inueniri locus vllus in scriptura, qui testetur Christum non adesse in cœna, vt necesse sit ad allegorias tropos & fi-guras confugere.
units.tr: For no passage can be found in Scripture that testifies that Christ is not present at the supper, so that it would be necessary to take refuge in allegories, tropes and figures.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Proprijssime namq; Christus in cœna lo-qui, neq; vlla figurata loquutione hunc sacro sanctum thesaurum ecclesiæ suæ inuoluere voluit.
units.tr: For Christ speaks in the supper most properly, and he did not wish to wrap this most holy treasure of his Church in any figurative speech.

units.la: XLIII.
units.tr: XLIII.

units.la: Firmissima ergo & indubitata fide appre-hendamus hęc clara & genuina Christi verba in genuino sensu, quem natura, vsitata Gram-matica, & certa ipsorum significatio reddit.
units.tr: Let us therefore grasp these clear and genuine words of Christ with the firmest and most undoubting faith, in the genuine sense that natural, ordinary grammar and the certain meaning of the words themselves give.

units.la: XLIIII. carnem de carne sua, & os de ossibus suis. Sicut autem illa coniunctio cum Christo nostro capite non requirit realem & substantialem carnis Christi praesentiam, ita etiam ad veram κοινωνίαν corporis Christi, quam in coena Domini habemus, non necesse est id realiter & substantialiter praesens esse, ut ita nobis Christus physico cotactu iungatur.
units.tr: XLIIII. flesh of his flesh, and bones of his bones. Just as that union with Christ our head does not require a real and substantial presence of Christ's flesh, so too for the true communion [κοινωνία] with the body of Christ, which we have in the Lord's Supper, it is not necessary that he be present really and substantially, so that Christ would be joined to us by physical contact.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Fides enim nostra manducat veram carnem spiritualiter, quae ore animi sumitur, interim ore corporis signum, typum, figuram & symbolum accipimus: neq; hanc nostram interpretationem quisquam damnare potest, quin simul damnet veteres omnes, a quibus hanc desumpsimus.
units.tr: For our faith eats the true flesh spiritually, which is received by the mouth of the mind, while by the mouth of the body we receive the sign, type, figure and symbol. Nor can anyone condemn this our interpretation without at the same time condemning all the ancients, from whom we have taken it.

units.la: XLI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: Nam cum omnino sit eadem huius sacramenti ratio, quae & aliorum sacramentorum, in quibus res & signum distinguuntur, & signo nomen rei per Metonymiam tribuitur, necesse est quoq; eundem tropum hic retineri.
units.tr: For since the reasoning of this sacrament is entirely the same as that of the other sacraments, in which the thing and the sign are distinguished, and the name of the thing is given to the sign by metonymy, it is necessary that the same trope be retained here as well.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Neq; enim vllus scripturae locus profertur, qui cogat nos verba Domini aliter accipere quam vsitato sacramentorum more. Nam Christus in coena tropum in omnibus sacramentis vsitatum retinuit, neque propterea hunc Thesaurum imuoluit, cum haec loquendi ratio Ecclesiae nota sit.
units.tr: For no passage of Scripture is brought forward that compels us to understand the words of the Lord otherwise than in the customary manner of the sacraments. For Christ in the supper retained the trope that is in use in all the sacraments, and he did not therefore wrap up this treasure, since this manner of speaking is well known to the Church.

units.la: XLIII.
units.tr: XLIII.

units.la: Ergo veram & simplicem sententiam verborum Christi, desumptam ex omnium sacramentorum
units.tr: Therefore the true and simple sense of the words of Christ, taken from the usage of all the sacraments,

units.la: XLIIII.
units.tr: XLIIII.

units.la: Nec verba Christi falsa esse possunt, qui est ipsa veritas, sensus vero noster & intellectus quem non afferimus ex verbo, sed inferimus & affingimus potius, potest nos fallere vt sane fallit.
units.tr: Nor can the words of Christ be false, since he is truth itself; but our own sense and understanding, which we do not draw from the word but rather infer and attach to it, can deceive us, and indeed it does deceive us.

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Id testantur tot sensus & diuersissimæ opiniones, quæ sunt capita Sacramentariorum. Non enim de his vnum, qui cum altero sentiat, & non potius diuersam opinionem tueatur, inuenias.
units.tr: So many opinions and very diverse views testify to this, which are the chief positions of the Sacramentarians. For among them you will not find one who agrees with another, and who does not rather defend a different opinion.

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Vnde facile iudicari potest ipsos agitari malo spiritu, & iusto Dei iudicio confundi in sua sapientia, qua ipsi coelestem sapientiam iudicant.
units.tr: Hence it can easily be judged that they are driven by an evil spirit, and by the just judgment of God are confounded in their own wisdom, by which they judge heavenly wisdom.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Propterea damnandus & fugiendus est quoque prauus nouorum Caluinistarum intellectus, qui contra clara & perspicua Christi verba non verentur afferere Christum quidem vere & substantialiter in coena præsentem distribuere suum corpus & sanguinem suis mentibus, sed illud tamen ita longe absens, vt sceq communi ratione, & congruentem cum analogia fidei, firma & indubitata fide retineamus.
units.tr: Therefore the perverse understanding of the new Calvinists is also to be condemned and shunned, who, against the clear and plain words of Christ, do not hesitate to assert that Christ indeed truly and substantially distributes in the supper his body and blood to their minds, but that it is nonetheless so far away that we should hold, by common reason and in agreement with the analogy of faith, with firm and undoubting faith.

units.la: XLIIII.
units.tr: XLIIII.

units.la: Sicut autem verba Christi vera sunt, ita hic est verus ipsorum sensus, qui nos fallere non potest, quae ex analogia fidei & usitata scripturae loquendi ratione deprompsimus.
units.tr: Just as the words of Christ are true, so this is the true sense of them, which cannot deceive us, and which we have drawn from the analogy of faith and the usual manner of speaking in Scripture.

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Quod autem aliqui panem aiunt signum aut figuram esse corporis Christi, alij significare corpus Christi, in eo nulla est contradictio, cum eadem sit sententia diversis verbis expositá.
units.tr: As for some saying that the bread is a sign or figure of the body of Christ, and others that it signifies the body of Christ, there is no contradiction in this, since the meaning is the same, expressed in different words.

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Qui autem realem praesentiam fingunt, et hanc modo corporalem nominant, ac rursus corporalem esse negant: & modo in pane includunt, modo cum pane coniungunt corpus Christi: & de Vbiquitate & praesentia corporis Christi quotidie novas et diversas opiniones proferunt, hi ostendunt se nihil solidi habere, ac dum odio simplicis doctrinae sese in haec absurda immergunt, merito iusto Dei iudicio confunduntur.
units.tr: But those who imagine a real presence, and at one moment call it bodily, and at another deny that it is bodily; who at one moment enclose the body of Christ in the bread, and at another join it with the bread; and who every day put forward new and diverse opinions about the Ubiquity and presence of Christ's body, these show that they have nothing solid, and while out of hatred for simple doctrine they plunge themselves into these absurdities, they are rightly confounded by the just judgment of God.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Interea tamen non damnamus eos qui dicunt Christum vere & substantialiter in caelis contineri, atque nos nihilominus substantiam corporis et sanguinis eius in coena spiritualiter per fidem sumere aiunt. Corpus enim Christi pro nobis traditum, quod fide apprehendimus, quodque in caelis manet, vere est corpus et substantia, attamen non ita dicendum est subvt cœlum a terra distat: sicq; gratia & saluisi-ca potentia in ecclesia sparsa animo & fide substantiam corporis & sanguinis absentis percipi, sed a corporali manducatione remo-tissimam.
units.tr: Meanwhile, however, we do not condemn those who say that Christ is truly and substantially contained in the heavens, and who nevertheless say that we spiritually receive by faith the substance of his body and blood in the supper. For the body of Christ given for us, which we apprehend by faith, and which remains in heaven, is truly a body and a substance, yet it must not be said to be as far from us as heaven is from earth; and thus the substance of the absent body and blood is perceived in the Church, scattered through the soul and faith by the saving power of grace, yet is most remote from corporeal eating.

units.la: XLVIII.
units.tr: XLVIII.

units.la: Hic est vltimus in sacrosanctâ filij Dei cœ-nam blasphemus spiritus ex tenebris suis egressus, & in angelum lucis speciosius reli-quis Sacramētiḣostibus transformatus. Ideo timendum ne maiori quoque applausu eccle-sias Christi suis sordibus contaminet. Sed Dei & Mariæ filius autor preciosissimi thesauri ecclesiæ reprimat horum & aliorum furores, & hunc ecclesiæ thesaurum nobis & posteris nostris integrum incorruptumq; benigniter conseruet & tueatur.
units.tr: This is the last blasphemous spirit to come out of his darkness against the most holy Supper of the Son of God, transformed into an angel of light more strikingly than all the other enemies of the Sacrament. For this reason we must fear lest he defile the churches of Christ with his filth, even with greater applause. But may the Son of God and Mary, the author of the most precious treasure of the Church, restrain the rage of these men and of others, and kindly preserve and keep this treasure of the Church whole and uncorrupted for us and for our posterity.

units.la: QVÆSTIONES.
units.tr: QUESTIONS.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: An ascensio Christi ad cœlos quidquâ de-roget præsentiæ ipsius substantiali in cœna?
units.tr: Does Christ's ascension into heaven in any way detract from his substantial presence in the Supper?

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: An recte dicatur Christum in cœna verè & substantialiter adesse per communicatio-nem Idiomatum, hoc est, secundum diuinita-tem? stantia eius a nobis percipi fide, quasi corpus Christi vel in sacramento, vel in animis nostris ita praesens adsit, ut ibi substantiam suam & corpulentam materiam habeat. Sic enim in coelo tantum est, & certo aliquo loco continetur propter modum veri corporis.
units.tr: Is it right to say that Christ is present in the Supper truly and substantially through the communication of attributes, that is, according to his divinity? His substance is perceived by us through faith, as if the body of Christ were present either in the sacrament or in our souls in such a way that it has its substance and bodily matter there. For in that way he is only in heaven and is contained in a certain place, because of the manner of a true body.

units.la: XLVIII.
units.tr: XLVIII.

units.la: Vsi sunt autem boni viri hac phrasi, si forte illa controversiam de modo praesentiae tollere possent: sed quoniam ita contentionis spiritus plerosque agitat, ut ad stabiliendam cras-sam suam opinionem etiam bene dictis abutantur, & praeterea non dubitent novas & portentosas opiniones de Vbiquitate in Ecclesiam introducere, nos illos suo iudicio relinquamus, et in explicando hoc mysterio phrasibus & verbis simplicibus ac minime ambiguis deinceps vtamur. Interim Christum vnicum caput et gubernatorem ecclesiae suae precamur, ut hos pacis & tranquillitatis hostes compescat, & nos in vera sui agnitione quotidie augeat & conserUet.
units.tr: Good men have used this phrase, in case it might perhaps settle the controversy about the manner of the presence. But since the spirit of contention drives so many people that they abuse even well-chosen words to prop up their gross opinion, and moreover do not hesitate to introduce into the Church new and monstrous opinions about ubiquity, we shall leave them to their own judgement. In explaining this mystery we shall from now on use plain words and phrases that are in no way ambiguous. Meanwhile we pray that Christ, the one head and governor of his Church, will restrain these enemies of peace and tranquillity, and will daily increase and preserve us in the true knowledge of himself.

units.la: RESPONSIONES.
units.tr: REPLIES.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Articulum de ascensione veteres semper intelle-xerunt de corporali & physica locatione in coelo, & corporali praesentia Christi in his terris oppo-suerunt, unde recte asseritur substantialem in coena praesentiam cum ascensione Christi pugnare.
units.tr: The ancient writers always understood the article on the ascension as a bodily and physical location in heaven, and they set against it a bodily presence of Christ on these earth. Hence it is rightly argued that a substantial presence in the Supper conflicts with the ascension of Christ.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Cum essentialiter vbique praesentem esse solius divinae naturae proprium sit, Christus homo non po-test dici in coena praesens esse aliter quam per com cem, non autem secundum humanam naturam assumptam.
units.tr: Since being essentially present everywhere belongs only to the divine nature, Christ as man cannot be said to be present in the Supper in any other way than by communication, and not according to the human nature he assumed.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: An corpus Christi exhibeatur in cœna corporaliter, an verò tantum efficaciter secundū virtutem & efficaciam, non secundum substantiam.
units.tr: Whether the body of Christ is exhibited in the Supper bodily, or only efficaciously, according to its power and efficacy and not according to its substance.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IIII.

units.la: An corporalis manducatio sine spirituali prosit vel obsit magis.
units.tr: Whether bodily eating without spiritual eating profits or rather harms.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: An sextum caput Ioannis rectè referri possit ad corporalem manducationem in cœna.
units.tr: Whether the sixth chapter of John can rightly be referred to bodily eating in the Supper.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: An κοινωνία apud Paulum 1.Cor.10. sit intelligenda non tantum de fructu & efficacia, sed potius de substantia corporis Christi.
units.tr: Whether fellowship [κοινωνία] in Paul, 1 Cor. 10, is to be understood not only of the fruit and efficacy, but rather of the substance of the body of Christ.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: An etiam mali & impij corpus Christi verum, & sanguinem eius verum percipiant.
units.tr: Whether also the wicked and the impious receive the true body of Christ and his true blood.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: An fides dantium vel accipientium faciat sacramentum, vel potius sola institutio & verba Christi.
units.tr: Whether the faith of those who give or receive makes the sacrament, or rather the bare institution and words of Christ.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: An adoratio Christi præsentis in cœna sit approbanda.
units.tr: Whether the adoration of Christ present in the Supper is to be approved.

units.la: AD municatione idiomatu, non aut secundu humanitatis subfantiam. III.
units.tr: On the communication of properties, not according to the substance of the humanity. III.

units.la: Si quaerimus quomodo Christus fidei nostrae offeratur, efficacia corporis eius & virtus ab ipso corpore non est seiungenda, non tamè est statuenda substantialis praefentia corporis eius, vel in animis nostris, vel etiam in externis symbolis cum quibus nobis offertur. IIII.
units.tr: If we ask how Christ is offered to our faith, his bodily efficacy and power must not be separated from the body itself; yet a substantial presence of his body must not be posited, either in our souls or even in the external symbols by which he is offered to us. IV.

units.la: Si corporalis manducatio aliquid prodesset, non de illa dixisset Christus: Caro, hoc est, carnalis manducatio, quale Capernaitae coceperat, nihil pdest. V.
units.tr: If bodily eating profited anything, Christ would not have said of it: "The flesh, that is, carnal eating, profits nothing," as it was understood by the Capernaites. V.

units.la: Si corporalis manducationis nomine in coena, ipsa symbolorum manducatio intelligitur, de ea non loquitur Christus Ioan. 6. At res ipsa, hoc est, corpus Christi non aliter manducari potest, quam illo modo què Christus docuit Ioan. 6. spiritualiter per fidem. VI.
units.tr: If by bodily eating in the Supper is understood the eating of the symbols themselves, Christ does not speak of that in John 6. But the thing itself, that is, the body of Christ, cannot be eaten otherwise than in the way Christ taught in John 6: spiritually, through faith. VI.

units.la: Koinonia, de qua Paul. loquitur, non tantu beneficiu Christi, sed ipsius Christi koinonia est: ius et societas. VII.
units.tr: The fellowship [κοινωνία] of which Paul speaks is not only the benefit of Christ, but the fellowship of Christ himself: a right and a partnership. VII.

units.la: Impios abusu sacramenti reos fieri corporis & sanguinis Dni Paul. docet. Impios aut corpus et sanguinè Christi percipere, neq; ex script. neq; ex Patribus ostendi potest. VIII.
units.tr: Paul teaches that the impious are made guilty of the body and blood of the Lord by abusing the sacrament. That the impious receive the body and blood of Christ can be shown neither from Scripture nor from the Fathers. VIII.

units.la: Fides non facit sacramentu, sed recipit Christu non bis in sacramento oblatum.
units.tr: Faith does not make the sacrament; it receives Christ, who is offered in the sacrament, and not twice.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Qui adorationè Papisticam sacramenti et crassam illam artolatriam probat, facile adduci potest, ut reliquas etiam abominationes Papatus probet.
units.tr: Whoever approves the Papistic adoration of the sacrament and that gross idolatry of the bread will easily be led to approve the remaining abominations of the Papacy.

units.la: AD SECVNDAM DISPVTATIONEM DOCT. Andreæ Musculi Responsio.
units.tr: To the Second Disputation of Doctor Andreas Musculus: A Reply.

units.la: CVM meas propositiones Andreæ Musculi propositionibus nuper editis, oppositas, prelo subiecturus essem, cómodú ad me mittitur ab amico secunda eiusdem Disputatio, perlecta igitur illa huic quoq; respondere statui, attamen nõ existimaui, id quod in prio ri feceram, necesse esse, vt singulas propositio nes ordine oppositis contrarijs propositioni-bus refutarem, propterea quod propositio-nes quidem multæ sunt, sed res quæ in his tra stantur paucæ, verum satis fore iudicaui, si ca pita tantum controuersię attingerem: plenam enim disputationem de singulis nemo vt ar-bitror à me requirit, cum dudum omnia co-piose & erudite à multis exposita sint. Appa-ret autem Musculum hunc non tam suæ sen-tentiæ tuendæ, quam alienæ infestandæ stu-dio & cupiditate quadam hæc in lucem edi-disse. Atq; in vtraq; disputatione ostendit se vnum ex eorum numero esse, qui pacem & concordiam ecclesiæ ferre non possunt, & ni-hil magis metuunt, quam ne tandem tristis & lustuosa controuersia Sacramentaria, quę mi-rifice hastenus ecclesias Germaniæ turbauit, piorum & doctorum virorum opera compo-natur, natur, ne perpetuo tanta cum offensione infir morum, qui Euangelium profitemur ipsi inter nos mutuo decertemus. Initio quidem po sterioris disputationis aliquam de se moderas tæ & sanæ sententiæ spem præbet, nam regulam quæ ad illustrandam doctrinam de sacramentis vtilis & necessaria est, probat. Quod nihil habeat rationem Sacramenti veri extra vsum diuinitus institutum: & pontificiâ ido lomaniam, adorationem panis, eiusdem inclusionem, circumgestationem, applicationé ad pellendos dæmones, arcendas tempestates, restinguenda incendia, oblatione in Missa pro viuis & mortuis, & matrem omnium harū superstitionum Transubstantiatione damnat. Verum mox à recto tramite recedit, & tota disputatione nihil potius habet quam vt Regulæ ab initio à se positæ verum & simplicé sensum ab alijs optime expositum & illustratum, obscuret: deinde vt loco Transubstantiationis consubstantiatione, aut impanatione introducat, & nouam ἀρτολάτρειαν in ecclesia confirmet.
units.tr: When I was about to send to the press my propositions opposing those of Andreas Musculus, recently published, a friend sent me his second Disputation. Having read it through, I decided to answer this one too. Still, I did not think it necessary, as I had done with the first, to refute each proposition in order by setting against it contrary propositions. There are many propositions, but the matters they treat are few, so I judged it enough to take up the main heads of the controversy. Nobody, I think, requires a full disputation of each point from me, since all these things have long been set out at length and learnedly by many writers. It is clear that Musculus published these works less from a desire to defend his own opinion than from a certain eagerness and craving to attack another's. In both disputations he shows himself to be one of those who cannot bear the peace and concord of the Church, and who fear nothing more than that the sad and mournful Sacramentary controversy, which has so wonderfully troubled the churches of Germany until now, should be settled by the work of pious and learned men. He fears that we who profess the Gospel will forever contend among ourselves, to the great offence of the weak. At the start of the second disputation he does offer some hope of a moderate and sound opinion, for he approves a rule that is useful and necessary for clarifying the doctrine of the sacraments: that there is no true sacrament apart from the use divinely instituted. He also condemns the Papist idolatry: the adoration of the bread, its enclosure, its carrying about in procession, its application to drive out demons, to ward off storms and to quench fires, the offering in the Mass for the living and the dead, and, the mother of all these superstitions, Transubstantiation. But soon he departs from the straight path, and in the whole disputation he is intent above all on obscuring the true and simple sense of the rule he laid down at the start, a sense that others have expounded and illustrated very well. Then he introduces, in place of Transubstantiation, Consubstantiation or Impanation, and sets up a new artolatry [ἀρτολατρεία] in the Church.

units.la: Ac primũ affirmat panem esse ipsum Christi corpus, quod tamen non eo modo ab ipso dicitur quo veteres panem corpus Christi nominant, quia corporis eius signum & sacramentum est: nam inquit etiam pané esse corpus Christi, non tantum in pane esse corpus Christi, Cur autem hoc modo nûc loquatur, cum in priori disputatione tantum posuerit vnionem sacramentalem panis cum corpore Christi, non aliam causam video quam vt sibi aditum paret ad partis adorationem defen- dendam. Si enim panis vere & identice est corpus Christi, vtriq; adorari debet: sed quam ab- surdum hoc sit, & à vera fide alienum pij omnes vident.
units.tr: First, he affirms that the bread is the very body of Christ. Yet he does not say this in the way the ancients called the bread the body of Christ, namely because it is a sign and sacrament of his body. For he says that the bread is the body of Christ, not merely that the body of Christ is in the bread. Why he now speaks in this way, when in the earlier disputation he had only posited a sacramental union of the bread with the body of Christ, I see no other cause than that he might gain an opening for defending the adoration of the bread. For if the bread truly and identically is the body of Christ, it ought to be adored. But how absurd this is, and how foreign to the true faith, all the pious see.

units.la: Præuaricari deinde paululum videtur, dicens digne accedentibus et manducantibus, non tantum fructum & efficaciâ, sed ipsam essentiâ corporis Christi exhiberi: perinde enim videtur loqui, atq; si affirmaret tantū digne accedentes corpus Christi manducare, quod nos quoque affirmamus: sed postea asserit etiam indigne & sine fide accedentes, cum pijs verum corpus & sanguinem percipere.
units.tr: Next he seems to act somewhat dishonestly when he says that to those who come worthily and eat, there is exhibited not only the fruit and efficacy but the very essence of the body of Christ. He seems to speak as though he were affirming only that those who come worthily eat the body of Christ, which we too affirm. But afterwards he asserts that even those who come unworthily and without faith receive the true body and blood together with the godly.

units.la: Duplicem postea manducationem facit, vnam symbolorum, alteram corporis & sanguinis Christi, realiter & substantialiter verissime præsentis. Atq; ipsa quidem diuisio cum veterum doctrina congruit, quod autem ad manducationem corporis Christi requirit eiusdem realem & substantialem præsentiam, id ex sua & suorum opinione addidit, qui exist-mant corpus Christi non posse vere communicari, nisi realiter & corporaliter præsens fuerit. Porro hanc ipsam corporis Christi manducationem rursus duplicem facit, vnam fidei seu spiritualem, alteram qua ore etiam essentialiter, tialiter, seu corporaliter illud accipimus, atq; hanc ita definit. Corporalem autem intelligi mus, non tantum de naturali & sensibus sub- iecta, qua cibus dilaniatur & conteritur den tibus, sed etiam de arcana, mystica, & praeter- naturali, qua corpus Christi non conteritur dentibus, nec alteratur in nobis, sed nos po tius alterat, & substantiam corporis & animæ nostræ transmutat, & sibi agglutinat, & effi- cit nos participes vitæ æternæ, quæ etiam sa- cramentalis dici potest. Porro hæc eius definitio corporalis manducationis, cum his quæ postea subijcit pugnat. Primum enim hic statuit opus operatum, quod tamē postea se statuere negat, tribuit enim corporali manducationi qua ore sumimus corpus Christi, quod ea nos participes efficiat vitæ æternæ. Nam cum hanc manducationem separet ab ea quæ fide fit, iam non fidei sed operis operati ratione huic tribuit, quod orali hac manducatione per Christum ore sumptum vitæ æternæ participes reddamur. Deinde asserit postea, indigne accedentes ad cœnam Domini corpus Christi sumere sibi ad iudicium: & tamen hic absq; exceptione corporali manducationi vitam adscribit. Pugnant igitur Musculi propositiones non tantum aduersus nos, & veteris ecclesiæ doctrinam, sed ipsæ quoque sibi contradicunt.
units.tr: Next he makes a twofold eating: one of the signs, the other of the body and blood of Christ, which is truly present really and substantially. This division does agree with the teaching of the ancients. But what he adds, that there must be a real and substantial presence of the body of Christ for its eating, this he has added from his own opinion and that of his followers, who think that the body of Christ cannot truly be communicated unless it is present really and bodily. Again he makes this eating of the body of Christ twofold: one is by faith or spiritual, the other is that by which we receive it also essentially, that is, bodily, with the mouth. He defines this second eating thus. We understand the bodily eating not only as the natural one, subject to the senses, by which food is torn and ground by the teeth, but also as a secret, mystical and supernatural one, by which the body of Christ is not ground by the teeth nor altered in us, but rather alters us. It changes the substance of our body and soul, joins it to itself, and makes us partakers of eternal life, which may also be called sacramental. Now this definition of bodily eating clashes with what he goes on to say. For first he lays down an effect wrought by the act itself, which he afterwards denies he lays down. He ascribes to the bodily eating, by which we take the body of Christ with the mouth, that it makes us partakers of eternal life. For when he separates this eating from that which is done by faith, he then attributes to the oral eating, by the reasoning of an effect wrought by the act itself, that we become partakers of eternal life through Christ taken into the mouth. Next he afterwards asserts that those who come unworthily to the Lord's Supper eat the body of Christ to their own judgment. Yet here he ascribes life to the bodily eating without any exception. So Musculus' propositions clash not only with us and with the doctrine of the ancient Church, but they also contradict themselves.

units.la: Est autem hæc distinctio manducationis duplicis corporis Christi, seu triplicis, primæ qua symbola & sacramenta, secundæ qua corpus ipsum corporaliter, & tertiæ qua idem corpus spiritualiter manducatur, a Papistis inuenta. Veteres enim tantum duplicis manducationis meminerunt, vnius qua sacramentu, & alterius qua rem sacramenti percipimus. Sic Augustinus lib.21. de ciuit. Dei, cap. 26. Qui manducat inquit carnem meam & bibit sanguinem meum, in me manet & ego in eo: os itendit quid sit non sacramentotenus sed reue ra comedere corpus. Hoc enim sic dixit, tanquam si diceret, Qui non manet in me, & in quo ego non maneo, no se dicat aut existimet manducare corpus meum, & sanguinem meu bibere. Idem in Ioan. tract. 26. Huius rei sacramentum, id est, vnitatis corporis & sanguinis Christi, alicubi quotidie, alicubi certis interuallis dierum in mensa domini præparatur: & de mensa dominica sumitur quibusdam ad vitam, quibusdam ad exitium: res ipsa vero cuius sacramentum est, omni homini ad vitam, nulli ad exitium, quicunq; eius particeps fuerit. Alibi distinguit inter panem Domini, & panem Dominum. Videtur quidem alicubi impijs tribuere quod corpus Domini comedant, quoniam sacramenta sumunt corporis & sanguinis Domini, quæ nomen rerum acci piunt. Sed si quis diligenter cum ipsius, tum aliorum patrum scripta examinet, tantū duplicis plicis manducationis mentionem fieri inue*niet, vnius quæ pijs & impijs communis est, qua sacramenta seu symbola, siue corpus Christi in sacramento & sacramentotenus sumitur: alterius quæ fidelium est propria, qui non tantum sacramentum sed ipsam rem sacramenti, Christum ipsum spiritualiter per fidem sumunt. Porro inter has duas manducationes intermediam ponunt Aduersarij corporalem & oralem manducationem substantiæ corporis & sanguinis Christi realiter præsentis; ac non solum nouam hanc manducationem introducunt repugnantem veritati carnis Christi, & ipsius in cœlos ascensioni: sed naturam quoq; sacramentorum euertunt, illa enim instituta sunt vt terrenis signis cœlestia testificentur, & animos nostros in cœlos eue*hant: ipsi autem è cœlis rem sacramenti detrahentes, & coniungentes, ac quasi consubstantiales rei terrenæ, nos in terris retinet: atq; quod ferendum non est, ex corpore Christi sacramentum faciunt, cuius res sit ipsa efficacia & meritum corporis quod fide percipiatur, atque ita efficacia corporis horrenda impietate diuelluntur & separant ab ipso corpore, quando impios corpus sumere aiunt, efficacię autem illius participes esse negant. Videntur vero aliqui colorem afferre suę sententiæ, quod hac ratione discrimen statuatur inter veteris & noui Testamenti sacramenta, nam veteres quoq; fide
units.tr: This distinction of a twofold, or threefold, eating of the body of Christ is an invention of the Papists: the first, by which we eat the signs and sacraments; the second, by which the body itself is eaten bodily; and the third, by which the same body is eaten spiritually. For the ancients mentioned only a twofold eating: one by which we eat the sacrament, and another by which we receive the thing of the sacrament. So Augustine in book 21 of De civitate Dei, chapter 26: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me and I in him." He shows what it is to eat the body not merely sacramentally but in truth. For he said this as though he were saying: whoever does not abide in me, and in whom I do not abide, let him not say or think that he eats my body and drinks my blood. Likewise in his Tractate 26 on John: "The sacrament of this thing, that is, of the unity of the body and blood of Christ, is prepared on the Lord's table somewhere every day, somewhere at set intervals of days. From the Lord's table some take it to life, some to destruction. But the thing itself of which it is the sacrament is for every man to life, for no one to destruction, whoever shall be a partaker of it." Elsewhere he distinguishes between the bread of the Lord and the Lord the bread. It is true that somewhere he seems to ascribe to the wicked that they eat the body of the Lord, since they take the sacraments of the body and blood of the Lord, which receive the names of the things. But if anyone carefully examines both his writings and those of the other Fathers, he will find mention made of only a twofold eating: one common to the godly and the wicked, by which the sacrament or sign, or the body of Christ in the sacrament and sacramentally, is taken; and another proper to the faithful, who take not only the sacrament but the very thing of the sacrament, Christ himself, spiritually through faith. But the adversaries place between these two eatings an intermediate one, a bodily and oral eating of the substance of the body and blood of Christ really present. Not only do they introduce this new eating, which contradicts the truth of Christ's flesh and of his ascension into heaven, but they also overturn the nature of the sacraments. For these were instituted so that earthly signs might bear witness to heavenly things and lift our minds up to heaven. But they, drawing the thing of the sacrament down from heaven and joining it, as if consubstantial, to an earthly thing, hold us back on earth. And what is not to be endured, they make a sacrament out of the body of Christ, whose thing is the very efficacy and merit of the body, to be received by faith. Thus with horrible impiety they tear the efficacy of the body apart and separate it from the body itself, when they say that the wicked take the body but deny that they share in its efficacy.

units.la: R spiritualiter manducasse corpus Christi, sed corporaliter manducatione nouo testamento propriam esse. Sed si corporalis præsentia distinguere debet sacramenta noui fœderis àue ribus, oportet vt eadé præsentia in baptismo quoq; statuatur, scilicet vt sanguine Christi realiter & substantialiter in baptismo præsen-te à peccatis nostris abluamur, quod tamen nemo vnquam dixit. Est quidé magnū discrimen inter nostra & veteris populi sacramenta, de quo pręter alios veterū sępe & diligenter August. disserit, nusquam tamen corporale & reale præsentia Christi inter sacramentorū vtriusq; fœderis differentias nominat. Imo aduersus Faust.lib.20.ca.21. Huius sacrificij caro & sanguis, ante aduentū Christi per victimas similitudinum promittebatur: in passione Christi per ipsam veritatē reddebatur: post aduentū Christi per sacramentū memoriæ celebratur. Hic sacramento noui fœderis nō corporalem præsentiā, sed memoriā sacrificij semel à Christo oblati tribuit. Quod si discrimen aliquod in his quæ nobis in noui fœderis sacramentis offeruntur, siue in re ipsa, siue in modo offerēdi ponendum erat, tale proculdubio poni debuit, quod proprie ad eos pertineret qui vere sunt in nouo fœdere, at illi discrimen tale ponunt quod nō minus ad impios pertinet, qui reuera extra fœdus sunt, quam ad fideles ad quos proprie fœdus pertinet.
units.tr: ...spiritually eaten the body of Christ, but that eating with the mouth is peculiar to the New Testament. But if bodily presence must distinguish the sacraments of the New Covenant from the old, then this same presence must also be posited in baptism, namely that we are washed from our sins by the blood of Christ really and substantially present in baptism, which nobody has ever said. There is indeed a great difference between our sacraments and those of the ancient people, on which Augustine, among others, often and carefully writes; yet nowhere does he name a bodily and real presence of Christ as one of the differences between the sacraments of either covenant. Indeed, against Faustus (book 20, chapter 21) he says: "The flesh and blood of this sacrifice were promised before the coming of Christ through the victims of likenesses; in the passion of Christ they were rendered in the very truth; after the coming of Christ they are celebrated through the sacrament of memorial." Here he assigns to the sacrament of the New Covenant not a bodily presence but the memory of the sacrifice once offered by Christ. And if some difference was to be posited in what is offered to us in the sacraments of the New Covenant, whether in the thing itself or in the manner of offering, it undoubtedly ought to have been one that pertains properly to those who are truly in the New Covenant; but Musculus posits a difference that pertains no less to the wicked, who are really outside the covenant, than to the faithful, to whom the covenant properly belongs.

units.la: lam Iam quod asserit ipsum corpus & sanguinem Christi, esse certū sigillum, confirmationem & obsignationé fidei & spiritualis manducationis: item corporalé manducationé esse testificationem, pignus, & obsignationé manducationis spiritualis. Primum in eo peccat, quòd corpus Christi à manducatione corporis non distinguit. Deinde hęc quidem affirmat, sed non probat. Sacramenta esse sigilla fidei nostrę receptū est, quoniā Paulus circumcisionem σφραγίδα nominat: sed Musculus hoc quod externorū symbolorū est, corpori Christi tribuit, & id facit sacramentū, quod est res sacramenti. Quod si dicat se de interna & effi-caci obsignatione loqui, quomodo hanc tri-buit corporali manducationi, qua etiā impij corpus Christi manducant? Postremo videat ipse, quomodo cum suis gregalibus, qui cor-poralem manducationem propugnant, con-uenire queat: illi enim afferunt hoc esse novū testamentum quod Christus ecclesiæ legarit, corpus suum comedendum, & sanguinem suum bibendum, atque ipse hoc posuit discri-men veteris & noui Testamenti, hic autem corpus Christi, & eius manducationem tan-tum facit sigillum & obsignationem spiritua-lis manducationis, quam Patres etiam in vete-ri Testamento habuerunt.
units.tr: Now as to his assertion that the body and blood of Christ themselves are a certain seal, confirmation and attestation of faith and of spiritual eating; and likewise that bodily eating is a testimony, a pledge and a seal of spiritual eating. In the first place he errs in that he does not distinguish the body of Christ from the bodily eating of it. Next, he asserts these things but does not prove them. It is an accepted view that the sacraments are seals of our faith, since Paul calls circumcision a seal [σφραγίδα]; but Musculus ascribes to the body of Christ what belongs to the external symbols, and makes the sacrament the thing of the sacrament. But if he says that he is speaking of the inward and effective sealing, how does he ascribe this to bodily eating, which even the wicked perform with the body of Christ? Finally, let him consider how he can agree with his fellows who defend bodily eating: for they affirm that this is the New Testament which Christ bequeathed to the Church, that his body be eaten and his blood be drunk; yet he himself posits this as the difference between the Old and New Testaments, while here he makes the body of Christ and its eating merely a seal and attestation of the spiritual eating, which the Fathers had even under the Old Testament.

units.la: Similiter noua est eius interpretatio de recordatione seu commemoratione Christi in cœna.
units.tr: Likewise his interpretation of the remembrance or commemoration of Christ in the Supper is new.

units.la: Recordari Christi inquit, non est beneficia in panis & vini perceptione meminisse, ac sentire quod vere ea nobis exhibeantur, sed est meminisse, quod in manducatione panis, hoc ipsum corpus máducemus, hoc corpus nobis exhibeatur, quod pro nobis traditum est, hoc corpus quod pepedit in ligno, & hic sanguis qui in ara crucis effusus est in remissione peccatorum. Sed Paulus aliter intelexit verba Christi, qui praeceptum, Hoc facite in meam commemorationem, ita interpretatur: Quotiescunque enim manducabitis panem hunc, & calicem biberis, mortem domini annuntiabitis donec veniat. Et cum in coena Christus non absolute corpus suum nobis comedendum offerat, & sanguinem suum bibendum, sed corpus pro nobis traditum & fractum, & sanguinem effusum pro remissione peccatorum nostrorum, proculdubio etiam voluit ita commemorationem corporis sui fieri, ut maxime celebraremus summum hoc beneficium, quod nos corpore suo in mortem tradito, & sanguine effuso, a morte & damnatione redemit. Quomodo itaq; Musculus contedit in coena hanc praecipuam esse commemoratione, quod corpus Christi corporaliter nobis ad manducandum datum sit, & id corporaliter manducatu nos inquit participes efficere vitae aeternae.
units.tr: "To remember Christ," he says, "is not to call to mind, in the receiving of the bread and wine, the benefits and to feel that they are truly given to us; rather it is to recall that in eating the bread we eat this very body, that this body is offered to us which was delivered for us, this body which hung on the tree, and this blood which was poured out on the altar of the cross for the remission of sins." But Paul understood the words of Christ differently; he interprets the command, "Do this in remembrance of me," thus: "For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes" (1 Cor. 11). And since in the Supper Christ does not offer his body to be eaten and his blood to be drunk absolutely, but his body delivered and broken for us, and his blood shed for the remission of our sins, he undoubtedly also willed that the commemoration of his body be made in such a way that we most of all celebrate this supreme benefit, that by his body given up to death and his blood poured out he redeemed us from death and condemnation. How then does Musculus contend that in the Supper the chief remembrance is that the body of Christ was given to us bodily to eat, and that by eating it bodily we are made partakers of eternal life?

units.la: 19?Item hac corporali manducatione obsignatos propter pignus corporis Christi qd' manducatione ducatione hac acceperût, statuere iubet omnia peccata sibi remissa esse: reuera impiam opinionem, quod cœna domini sit opus quod ex opere operato mereatur remissionē peccatorum, confirmat, quamuis id ipsum verbis constanter neget, lubet nos certe statuere propter hanc obsignationem nobis condonata peccata, ad hanc autem obsignationem nō requirit fidem, quando corporalis hæc manducatio, quæ obsignatio est qua certi sumus iuxta illū de vita æterna, fit absq; fide, & communis est pijs atque impijs. Nam quod addit, fiducia operis operati Christi in cruce nobis remitti peccata, hoc etiam Pontificij dicunt: sed opus operatum Christi non tantum fide nobis applicat, sed opere operato manducationis carnalis. Similiter ea quæ subijcit, fide & ore manducari corpus Christi pro nobis traditum, ac nos fide confirmatos erigi corporali manducatione corporis Christi sub terroribus peccati & legis, vt agamus Deo gratias pro accepto corpore & sanguine Christi & omnibus beneficijs in ipso & per ipsum nobis exhibitis: pugnant quidem cum superioribus. Nam hic fide & ore corpus Christi manducari asserit, sua pra corporalem manducationem quæ etiam absq; fide fiat tantopere extulit, & tamē singula expendat, primas partes etiam hic corporali manducationi tribuit, quod illa erigat nos sub pauoribus & terroribus legis. Atque adeo totus huic vni addictus est, vt Eucharistiam inde dicta velit, cultum glorificationis merito Deo offerendum, propter tot ac tanta beneficia in cœna nobis exhibita, mâducatio ne corporis & sanguinis Christi, agere enim nos Deo gratias pro accepto corpore & sanguine Christi, & omnibus beneficijs in ipso. At longe aliter veteres docuerunt, qui conse-rentes Eucharistiam cum sacrificijs veteris te-stamenti, voluerunt sacrificiū Christi quo sei-psum pro peccatis nostris obtulit in cruce, suis-se adumbratū per veterū sacrificia, sed Eucha-ristiam esse memoriã & gratiarum actionem pro redemptione vnico Christi sacrificio no-bis parta. Sic enim D. Augustinus, In isto sa-crificio gratiarum actio atq; commemoratio est carnis Christi quam pro nobis obtulit, & sanguinis quem pro nobis idé Deus effudit. De quo beatus Paulus dicit in Actibus Apo-stolorū, Attendite vobis & vniuerso gregi, in quo vos spiritus sanctus posuit episcopos re-gere ecclesiam Dei, quam acquisiuit sanguine suo. Atq; vt Patres nunc omittamus, Augusta-na confessio saepe hoc vrget, cœnam institutā esse vt fides in ijs qui vtuntur sacramento re-cordetur quæ beneficia accipiat per Christū, atq; erigat & consoletur pauidā conscientiā. Promissione gratuitæ remissionis peccatorū in sacramento offerri & fide recipiendā esse. At Musculus docet recordatione Christi abs-que fide corporaliter manducati, hanc manducatione obsignatos de salute vult certos esse, hoc opere applicat nobis beneficia Christi.
units.tr: 19? Likewise, sealed by this bodily eating, on account of the pledge of the body of Christ which they have received by this eating, he bids them determine that all their sins are forgiven them. In truth he confirms the impious opinion that the Lord's Supper is a work which, by the work done (ex opere operato), merits the remission of sins, although he constantly denies this in words; he bids us indeed determine that our sins are forgiven us on account of this sealing; but for this sealing he does not require faith, since this bodily eating, which is the seal by which we are certain according to that saying about eternal life, takes place without faith and is common to the godly and the wicked. For when he adds that by the confidence in the work of Christ done on the cross our sins are remitted to us, the Papists also say this; but the work done by Christ applies it to us not only by faith but by the work done of carnal eating. Similarly, what he subjoins, that the body of Christ given for us is eaten by faith and by mouth, and that we, confirmed in faith, are raised up by the bodily eating of the body of Christ under the terrors of sin and of the law, so that we give thanks to God for the body and blood of Christ received and for all the benefits exhibited to us in him and through him: these things indeed clash with what went before. For here he asserts that the body of Christ is eaten by faith and by mouth, yet he so greatly extols bodily eating, which takes place even without faith, and though he weighs each point, he again assigns the first place to bodily eating, because it raises us up under the fears and terrors of the law. And so he is wholly devoted to this one thing, so that he wants the Eucharist to be named from it, the worship of glorification to be offered to God rightly, on account of so many and so great benefits exhibited to us in the Supper, namely by the eating of the body and blood of Christ; for he says we give thanks to God for the body and blood of Christ received and for all the benefits in him. But the ancients taught quite differently: they, comparing the Eucharist with the sacrifices of the Old Testament, held that the sacrifice of Christ by which he offered himself for our sins on the cross was foreshadowed by the sacrifices of the old covenant, but that the Eucharist is a memorial and thanksgiving for redemption obtained for us by the single sacrifice of Christ. For thus Augustine says: "In this sacrifice is the thanksgiving and commemoration of the flesh of Christ which he offered for us, and of the blood which the same God poured out for us." Of this the blessed Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to rule the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood" (Acts 20). And, to leave aside the Fathers for now, the Augsburg Confession often presses this: that the Supper was instituted so that faith in those who use the sacrament may recall what benefits they receive through Christ, and may raise up and console a frightened conscience; that the promise of the free remission of sins is offered in the sacrament and is to be received by faith. But Musculus teaches that those bodily eating without the remembrance of Christ, and sealed by this eating, wish to be certain of salvation; by this work he applies to us the benefits of Christ.

units.la: Quo autem apertius ostenderet Musculus se ad caitra Papistarum transfugiu sibi parare, multis propositionibus contendit praesentiam corporis & sanguinis Christi in coena Domini, ipsa pronunciatione verborum constitui, ita ut ad verborum pronunciationem in omni coena praesens sit corpus Christi, etiam ante fidem & manducationem. Priori disputatione praesentiae corporis Christi fundamentum constituit unionem personalem, cuius ea sit vis ut corpus Christi nullo loco circumscriptum ubique cum divinitate praesens statuat. Atque talem proprietatem praeternaturalem ex ipsa conceptione e spiritu sancto humana natura accepisse, ut ubique praesens esse possit. Caeterum nunc quasi oblitus priorum, Papistico more pronunciationi verborum attribuit, quod horum vi corpus Christi praesens constituatur. Ac argumentum affert a prima coena, in qua statim ad verborum sonum adfuerit corpus & sanguis Christi, eiusdem autem potentiae virtutis & efficaciae nunc quoque esse & semper fore verba Christi. Caeterum de verborum Christi veritate & virtute atque efficacia non est controversia, modo de sensu eorum constet. Aiunt Papistae sermone Christi operatorium esse, ideoque huius vi panem in corpus Christi convertisi, ... lis est opinio Musculi, tantum in hoc differt, quod loco transsubstantiatione fingit, consubstantiatione fingis.
units.tr: But in order to show more openly that Musculus is preparing for himself a passage over to the camp of the Papists, he contends in many propositions that the presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Lord's Supper is established by the very pronouncing of the words, so that at the pronouncing of the words the body of Christ is present in every supper, even before faith and eating. In the earlier disputation he laid down as the foundation of the presence of the body of Christ the personal union, whose force is such that it establishes the body of Christ, circumscribed in no place, to be present everywhere together with the divinity. And he says that the human nature received this supernatural property from the conception by the Holy Spirit, so that it can be present everywhere. But now, as if he had forgotten what went before, he attributes in the Papistical manner to the pronouncing of the words that by their force the body of Christ is made present. And he brings an argument from the first supper, in which at the sound of the words the body and blood of Christ were immediately present, and says that the words of Christ have the same power and efficacy now also and will always have. But there is no controversy about the truth, virtue and efficacy of the words of Christ, provided that their sense is agreed. The Papists say that the speech of Christ is operative, and that therefore by its force the bread is converted into the body of Christ; the opinion of Musculus is the same, except that in place of transubstantiation he invents consubstantiation.

units.la: Sed vtriq; primū in eo falluntur quod ambiguū pro confesso sumunt, Christi sermonē operatoriū esse: nō enim semper Christi sermo operatorius est, sed nonnunquā indicatiuus. Christus inquit, Ego sum vitis: Ioannes est Elias: quam absurde autem is faceret qui ita vellet concludere, verba Christi esse efficacia & operatoria, ideoq; Christū vere & reipsa vitem esse, & Ioanne substantialiter esse Eliam. Vbi sermo Dei earum rerum quę dicuntur est effector, id plerunq; scriptura ipsa indicat. Veluti quando ab initio dixit Dominus, Fiat lux, sub ijciunt diuinæ literæ, Et facta est lux. Sic aquā conuersam in vinum, virgam Mosis in serpentem versam, scriptura nō tacuerunt, at de verbis cœnæ nusquā legimus, Panis fiat corpus, aut panis factus est corpus domini. Et falsum est quod Musculus asserit, in prima cœna ad verborū pronunciatione statim adfuisse corpus et sanguinē domini. Christus mensę cū discipulis corpore suo assedit, panē acceptū benedixit, et illis distribuit ac dedit, dicēs: Accipite, edite, Hoc est corpus meū, neque vllius corporalis præsentię mētio fit ab Euangelistis præterquā illius qua vero corpore mēsę accubuit. Patres quidē dicūt Christū seipsum manibus suis gestasse, nēpe vt alibi docēt, quia sacrāmē tū corporis sui manibus suis gestauit. Sed esto sermonē Christi in cœna operatoriū fuisse, nū dicēmus hunc effecisse corporalē præsentiā, cū alioqui corpore suo, & quidé adhuc passibili localiter in prima cœna pręsens esset? Aut nũ sppterea statuemus verbo Christi, vt Papistę volùt, panè & vinū trāsubstantiari, mutari & conuerti in corpus & sanguinem Christi, aut cũ pane substantialiter coniungi corpus Chri sti & quasi companari? Neutrū horum concedere possumus, cum vtraq; sententia veritatē humanæ naturæ in Christo tollat, & sacramē torum naturæ repugnet: sed eam efficaciā & operatione verbis Christi tribuere oportet, quæ menti ipsius nó repugnet, & sensum verborū retineat sacramentis conuenienté: Népe quod panis & vinū facta sunt ex institutione Christi sacramēta corporis & sanguinis Chri sti, quod ante nõ erant. Ac cum opus hic nullum proferatur quod sensibus corporeis percipiatur, sequitur hęc spiritualiter accipienda esse, vt quod aliàs Dei verbo in corporib. effi citur vi naturæ à Deo conditæ, id in hoc mysterio vi spiritus sancti perficiatur in hominū mentibus. Atq; hoc modo verba Christi non modo tum quũ pronunciata sunt suā vim habuisse credimus, sed etiam nunc retinere, atq; retentura esse vsq; ad mundi dissolutionem. Sacramenta enim eam quā habent vim, ab instituentis auctoritate & mandato accipiunt, sicut & promissa omnia quibus fœdus quo Deo coiuncti sumus nituntur. Idcóq; quę Christi nomine hodie cœna celebratur in ecclesia, eadem pollet facultate qua illa ipsa quam ipse primam administrauit. Nam eam ideo initituit, vt non duntaxat temporarius, sed perpetuus eius visus in ecclesia esset. Itaque verba Chrysostomi quæ à Papistis nobis obiecta Musculus, vt & alia, ab illis mutuatur, opinio nem Papisticam Musculi non confirmant. Si cut, inquit, illa vox, qua dixit, Crescite, & multiplicamini, & replete terram, semel quidē dicta est, sed omni tempore sentit effectu, ad generationē operante natura: ita vox illa semelquidem dicta est, sed per omnes mensas ecclesiæ usq; ad hodiernū diem, & usq; ad eius aduentū præstat sacrificio firmitate. Neq; enim Chrysostomus dicit corpus Christi esse naturaliter & corporaliter in pane, cum eo modo tantum in cœlo sit, quo nos alibi mentibus nostris per fidem confscendere iubet, & ibi illum comedere. Sacramentaliter tamē tanquā in signo & figura, corpus & sanguis Christi sunt in pane & vino, quemadmodum etiam in aqua Baptismi. In illis autē qui rite recipiunt panem & vinū Eucharistiæ, corpus Christi est (spiritualiter per diuinam potentiam, illisq; vitam largitur. Et quemadmodū per verbum Dei omnia creata sunt, & virtute ac vi illorū verborū, Crescite & multiplicamini, huc usq; omnia generantur & crescunt ita virtute horum verborū Edite, Hoc est corpus meum: Bibite, Hic est sanguis meus: non autē virtute aut vi vllius hominis, panis & vinum sunt eo modo cõsecrata, vt quicūq; cū viua fide illum pane comederit, & illud vinū biberit, spiritua liter mäducet & bibat Christū sedentē cū Patre. Sacramentū vero nō ppriē fieri vi & effi cacia verborū idem perspicue docet, scribens: Verba sacerdotis ore pferūtur, Dei autē virtu te cōsecrātur & gratia: hoc enī significat, etiā si verba illa diuina ex Domini instituto admisceātur, tamē nō verborū vi sed Dei gratia & virtute sacramentū fieri, Christū ipsum diuinitate & spiritu suo adesse, & gratiā cōmunicantib. suppeditare, id qd ad conficiendū sacramentū satis est.
