Sic etiā Augſt. & Ambrof. alicubi tradūt per verba Christi ministro plata post panis & vini cōsecratione, sacramentū corporis & sanguinis Christi confici, verū nihil aliud significat quā pane et vinū vsui tā sacro per verbū Christi attributa, nō iam vulga res res et cibos vetris ac corporis nostri existe re, sed esse res planè sacras et sanctificatas, quę eas res nobis exhibeant quibus anima nostra spiritualiter saȷatur. Atq; idē docet Hieron. & Hilar. atq; alij veterū. Eodē modo Irenæus inquit mixtū calicē & fractū panē percepto verbo Dei fieri Eucharistiam corporis & sanguinis Christi. Ite panem qui est a terra percipiente vocatione Dei iam non esse cōmunē pane, sed Eucharistiā ex duabus rebus cōstan tem, terrena & cœlesti. Cæterum sicut Papiste existimant sacramentum fieri idem esse ac pané verti in corpus Christi, ita noster hic simili errore censet sacramentū confici idem esse ac vi verborum coniungi corpus Christi cum externo elemento panis:atq; suam fentē tiam confirmari existimat verbis Augustini, Accedat verbum ad elementū & fiet sacramē tum. Verum hęc ratio conficiendi sacramenti Augustino & veteri ecclefię ignota fuit. Quo modo autē Verbum accedens ad elementum faciat sacramentum, Augustinus ipse optime explicat: Accedat,inquit, Verbum ad elementum & fiet sacramentū. Vnde enim ista tanta virtus aquæ vt corpus tangat, & cor abluat, nisi faciente verbo: nō quia dicitur,sed quia creditur.Nam &in ipso verbo aliud est sonus transiens,aliud virtus manens. Hoc est verbū fidei quod prædicamus, inquit Apostolus. Vnde in Act. Apoft.Fide mundans corda eo• rū. Et Petrus Apostolus: Sic & nos baptisma saluos facit:non depositio sordium carnis,sed conscientiæ bonæ interrogatio. Hoc est ver• bum fidei quod prædicamus:quo fine dubio vt mundare possit consecratur & baptismus. Par omnino ratio est Baptismi & cœnæ Do• mini,& distum Auguft. Accedat verbum ad elementum & fiet sacramentū,non minus ad Baptif. quàm ad cœnā Domini pertinet,igi• tur vt in Baptismo nemo statuit ,pnũciatione verborū realiter in aqua præsens fieri corpus• Christi,quamuis omnes fateantur nos in Ba• ptismo consepeliri cum Christo, & cum ipso resurgere & Christũ induere, quod fit per fi•dě Spiritu sancto intus in cordibus nostris o•perāte: ita nulla necessitas nos cogit,vt cōtra tot loca scripturȩ,& veritatē humanæ naturæ in Christo,cōstituamus pronunciatione et vi verborū corpus Christi coniungi substantia•liter cum pane.Neq; magis probari potest ex scripturis hæc confubstantiatio quā Papisti•ca transsubstantiatio, quam tamē ipsi palam reijciunt. Ac primū superstitiosa & quodam•modo magica sunt omnia, quæ de efficacia quam pronūciationi verborum tribuunt, dis serunt: deinde à Papistis perparum hæc diffe runt.Illi enim etiā post actionem Cœnæ cor•pus Christi manere volunt, hi eodem modo quo illi prouunciatione verborū Christi cor•pus præsens fieri volunt non accedente fide, sed volunt præsentiam hāc tantū durare dum vsus cœnæ durat,non vltra. Hanc sententiam vt retineat Musculus, Regulam ab initio à se propositam, Nihil habere rationen sacramen ti extra vsum diuinitus institutū, libenter si modo liceret,reijceret, quam etiam recens na tam esse ait, vt ita eius auctoritatē eleuet, atq; cum reijcere non possit, saltem eam eludere conatur,quod ipse non loquatur de verborū pronunciatione extra cœnam, sed quæ ad vsum institutionis siue manducationis de•stinata sit, hanc pronuntiationem verborum Christi constituere corporis & sanguinis eius praesentiam etiam ante fidem & manducatio nem. Quasi vero absq; fide verborum vsus alius quis esse possit, aut ad vsum diutius instituendum abs q; fide adhibeatur? An enim verba sym bolorum causa proferuntur & ad illa dirigitur ac non potius ad homines, in quibus fide recepta suam demum habent efficaciam?
units.tr: But both sides are first mistaken in taking as granted what is in doubt, namely that the words of Christ are operative. For the words of Christ are not always operative; sometimes they are indicative. Christ says, "I am the vine"; John is Elias. How absurd would it be for someone to conclude from this that the words of Christ are effective and operative, and therefore that Christ truly and really is a vine, and that John is substantially Elias! Where God's word is the cause of the things spoken of, Scripture itself usually indicates this. Thus, when the Lord said at the beginning, "Let there be light," the divine letters add, "And there was light." Likewise, Scripture does not pass over in silence the water changed into wine or Moses' rod turned into a serpent, yet we nowhere read of the words of the Supper, "Let the bread become the body," or "the bread was made the body of the Lord." And it is false what Musculus asserts, that at the first Supper the body and blood of the Lord were present at the very pronouncing of the words. Christ sat at the table with his disciples in his body, took the bread, blessed it, distributed and gave it to them, saying, "Take, eat, this is my body." The Evangelists make no mention of any bodily presence except that of the true body that reclined at the table. The Fathers indeed say that Christ carried himself in his own hands, namely, as they teach elsewhere, because he carried the sacrament of his body in his own hands. But even if the words of Christ at the Supper were operative, shall we say that they brought about a bodily presence, when he was already present locally in his own body, and that body still passible, at the first Supper? Or shall we therefore hold, as the Papists wish, that by the word of Christ the bread and wine are transubstantiated, changed and converted into the body and blood of Christ, or that the body of Christ is substantially joined with the bread and, as it were, placed beside it? We can concede neither of these, since both opinions take away the truth of human nature in Christ and contradict the nature of the sacraments. Rather, we must attribute to the words of Christ an efficacy and operation that does not contradict his mind and that keeps the sense of the words suitable to a sacrament: namely, that the bread and wine, by the institution of Christ, have become sacraments of the body and blood of Christ, which they were not before. And since no work is here put forward that is perceived by the bodily senses, it follows that these things are to be understood spiritually, so that what is elsewhere effected in bodies by God's word, through the power of nature created by God, is in this mystery accomplished in the minds of men by the power of the Holy Spirit. In this way we believe that the words of Christ not only had their power when they were pronounced, but also still retain it now and will retain it until the dissolution of the world. For sacraments receive the power they have from the authority and command of the one who instituted them, just as all the promises on which the covenant by which we are joined to God rests. Therefore, the Lord's Supper celebrated today in the Church in Christ's name has the same power as that very Supper which he himself first administered. For he instituted it so that its use would be not merely temporary but perpetual in the Church. Thus the words of Chrysostom, which Musculus takes over from the Papists, along with others, do not confirm the Papist opinion of Musculus. "As," he says, "that word by which he said, 'Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,' was spoken once, yet at all times it still works its effect, nature operating for generation; so that word was spoken once, yet through all the tables of the Church, even to this day, and until his coming, it gives firmness to the sacrifice." Chrysostom does not say that the body of Christ is in the bread naturally and bodily, since he is in heaven only in the way in which he bids us elsewhere to ascend with our minds by faith and there to feed on him. Yet sacramentally, as in a sign and figure, the body and blood of Christ are in the bread and wine, just as they are also in the water of Baptism. In those who worthily receive the bread and wine of the Eucharist, the body of Christ is present spiritually through the divine power, and he grants life to them. And just as all created things were made through the word of God, and by the power and force of those words, "Increase and multiply," all things are generated and grow even to this day, so by the power of these words, "Eat, this is my body; drink, this is my blood," the bread and wine are consecrated, not by the virtue or power of any man, in such a way that whoever eats that bread with living faith and drinks that wine, spiritually eats and drinks Christ sitting with the Father. The same author clearly teaches that the sacrament is not properly made by the power and efficacy of the words, when he writes: "The words are uttered by the mouth of the priest, but the sacrament is consecrated by the power and grace of God." For this means that even if those divine words are added according to the Lord's institution, yet the sacrament is made not by the power of the words but by the grace and power of God, Christ himself being present by his divinity and Spirit and supplying grace to those who communicate, which is enough to make the sacrament. Thus also Augustine and Ambrose in some places hand down that, after the consecration of the bread and wine, the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ is made by the words of Christ spoken by the minister; but this means nothing other than that the bread and wine, set apart for sacred use through the word of Christ, cease to be common things and food for our belly and body, and become truly sacred and sanctified things, which convey to us those things by which our soul is spiritually fed. Jerome and Hilary, and other ancient writers, teach the same thing. In the same way Irenaeus says that the mixed cup and the broken bread, once the word of God has been received, become the Eucharist of the body and blood of Christ. He says that the bread which is from the earth, when it receives the calling of God, is no longer common bread, but a Eucharist consisting of two things, earthly and heavenly. But just as the Papists think that the making of the sacrament is the same as the bread being turned into the body of Christ, so our author here, in a similar error, thinks that the consecration of the sacrament is the same as the body of Christ being joined by the power of the words to the outward element of bread; and he thinks his view is confirmed by the words of Augustine, "Let the word come to the element and it becomes a sacrament." But this manner of making a sacrament was unknown to Augustine and to the ancient Church. How the word coming to the element makes a sacrament, Augustine himself explains very well: "Let the word," he says, "come to the element, and it becomes a sacrament. For whence does water have such great power, that it touches the body and washes the heart, unless the word works it? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed. For in the word itself there is one thing that is a passing sound and another that is a lasting power." This is the word of faith that we preach, says the Apostle. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles: "cleansing their hearts by faith." And the Apostle Peter: "So also baptism saves us, not the removal of the filth of the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience." This is the word of faith that we preach, by which, without doubt, baptism is consecrated so that it may cleanse. The reasoning for Baptism and for the Lord's Supper is wholly the same, and what Augustine said, "Let the word come to the element and it becomes a sacrament," pertains no less to Baptism than to the Lord's Supper. Therefore, just as no one holds that in Baptism the body of Christ is made really present in the water by the pronouncing of the words, although everyone confesses that in Baptism we are buried with Christ, rise with him, and put on Christ, which happens by faith, the Holy Spirit working inwardly in our hearts; so no necessity compels us, against so many passages of Scripture and against the truth of human nature in Christ, to hold that by the pronouncing and power of the words the body of Christ is substantially joined with the bread. Nor can this consubstantiation be proved from Scripture any better than the Papist transubstantiation, which they themselves openly reject. First, all the things they argue about the efficacy they attribute to the pronouncing of the words are superstitious and somewhat magical; second, these men differ very little from the Papists. For the Papists want the body of Christ to remain even after the action of the Supper, and these men want the body to become present by the pronouncing of Christ's words in the same way, not with faith coming in, but they want this presence to last only as long as the use of the Supper lasts, and no longer. In order to keep this opinion, Musculus, though he would gladly reject the rule he proposed at the start, that a sacrament has no meaning outside the divinely instituted use, if only he could, and though he says that rule is recent so as to lessen its authority, and since he cannot reject it, tries at least to evade it, by saying that he does not speak of the pronouncing of the words outside the Supper, but of the pronouncing directed to the use of the institution, or to the eating, and that this pronouncing of Christ's words establishes the presence of his body and blood even before faith and eating. As if there could be any use of the words without faith, or as if they were applied to a use to be carried on for longer without faith! For are the words of the symbols uttered for their own sake, and are they directed to those things, rather than to men, in whom they at last have their efficacy when received by faith?

units.la: Iraq; quod concludit, verborum vi statui preesse corpus Christi in pane, ideoq; etiam impios verum Christi corpus sumere, nos rectius inuertere & illi opponere possumus, ac dicere, impios nō sumere corpus Christi, quod est esca vitae, panis, quem qui manducat, Christo esse, viuet in aeternum: & omni homini ad vitam cedit, nulli ad exitium quicunq; eius partiteps fuerit, vt D. Augustin. scribit tract. 26. in Ioan. Atq; hanc sententiam Ambrosij & Augustini, atq; Hieron. & veterum quoq; Patrum vt Cypriani & Origenis testimonijs confirmare possumus, atq; ita demum concludere: cū impij & indigne accedentes firmant sacramentū rem aut sacramenti nō accipiant, hæc duo nō esse substantialiter coniuncta, neq; verborum pronunciatione ita panē factum esse corpus Christi vt substantialiter sit corpus Christi, aut illud substantialiter contineat, aut communicatum habeat, alioqui enim fieri non posset quin impij vno accepto alterum quoque acciperent.
units.tr: Moreover, as to their conclusion that by the power of the words the body of Christ is present in the bread, and therefore even the wicked receive the true body of Christ, we can turn this argument back on them more rightly and oppose it. We can say that the wicked do not receive the body of Christ, which is the food of life, the bread which whoever eats of it lives forever, which is Christ's, and which comes to life for every man, but to no one's destruction, whoever partakes of it, as Augustine writes in Tractate 26 on John. We can also confirm this view with the testimonies of Ambrose, Augustine and Jerome, and of the ancient Fathers too, such as Cyprian and Origen. And so we can conclude: when the wicked and unworthy approach and receive the sacrament, they receive the thing signified by the sacrament, or not at all. These two are not substantially joined together. Nor by the pronouncing of the words has the bread become the body of Christ in such a way that it is substantially the body of Christ, or substantially contains it, or has it in communion. Otherwise it could not happen that the wicked, having received the one, would not also receive the other.

units.la: Quod autem sacramentarios facit, qui negant impios manducare ipsum verum corpus Christi, oportet vt primum omnium Patres quos modo nominaui, & totam veterem ecclesiam sacramentarijs adnumeret, & ita de mutn ad nos damnandos accedat. Eiusdem ponderis est quod addit, eos qui negant indi gne accedentes manducare verū corpus Christi, ê sacramêto facere nudum ritū & ceremoniam. Satis enim hinc apparet, ita eū immersum esse crassis suis imaginationibus de corporali manducatione, vt spirituali & viuifi cam manducationem veri corporis Christi, rem nihili et imaginariam esse existimet, atq; adeo declarat se fidei efficaciam prorsus ignorare aut contemnere. Cum verò subiicit, hæc sua dogmata è scripturis & sanctis Patribus deducta esse, & cum Regula supra posita eon sentire: tum nobis persuadebit, cum meridie non lucere probauerit. Tot enim & tam aperta testimonia sunt Patrum quibus contrarium docent, vt in eo saltem pudori suo percerit, quod indefinite locutus neminem nominare ausus fuit, qui vna cum ipso sentiat, verborum vi & efficacia ita præsens fieri corpus Christi, vt illud etiam manducent impij. Atque tum demum hæc sententia cum regula ab ipso posita congruet, vbi vsus sacramenti diuinitus institutus fide carere poterit.
units.tr: As for their charge that we are sacramentarians because we deny that the wicked eat the true body of Christ itself, they should first count among sacramentarians all the Fathers I have just named, and the whole ancient Church, and so proceed to condemn us. Equally weighty is what he adds, that those who deny that the unworthy eat the true body of Christ make the sacrament a bare rite and ceremony. For it is plain enough from this that he is so immersed in his crude imaginings about a bodily eating that he judges the spiritual and life-giving eating of the true body of Christ to be a thing of nothing and imaginary. Thereby he declares that he is wholly ignorant of, or despises, the efficacy of faith. When he goes on to say that his doctrines are drawn from Scripture and the holy Fathers and agree with the rule set down above, he will persuade us of this only when he has shown that it is not as plain as noonday that they do not. For there are so many and such clear testimonies of the Fathers teaching the contrary that he should at least spare himself the shame of having spoken indefinitely and not dared to name anyone who agrees with him that by the power and efficacy of the words the body of Christ is so present that even the wicked eat it. And then at last this view will agree with the rule he has laid down, when the divinely instituted use of the sacrament can exist without faith.

units.la: Postremũ caput Disputationis est de adoratione Christi præsentis in cœna, quam tractat pluribus propositionibus, quarũ maior fere pars agit de Christo secundũ vtranq; naturam adorando vna adoratione, de quo non est controuersia. Initio autè ponit discrepantes opiniones eorum qui realem præsentiam corporis Christi constituentes, adorationem Christi in cœna præsentis, vel prorsus à cœnæ institutione alienam esse existimant, & proxime accedere ad explosam adorationẽ Papisticam, vel rem hanc liberam, indifferentem & quasi adiaphoram faciunt: vel postremo piam, rectam & licitam esse existimant. Hos omnes finit abundare in suo sensu, modo idé sibi concedatur. In quo vide quæso hominis ingenium. Opiniones quas ponit inter se pugnant: si enim adoratio res aliena est ab institutione cœnæ, & ad Papisticam superstitionẽ accedit non debet ferri in ecclesia, neq; cœna prophananda est, vt illi aliquis cultus à Christo non institutus affingatur. Rursus si adoratio hæc res pia est & recta, non videtur absq; impietate omitti posse. Sed hæc non movent Musculum, facile omnia ferre potest in suæ sationis hominibus: at si adorationem alij damnent, quibus cum nō per omnia consentit, illi crimen inexpiabile committent. Idipsum omnes facile vident, & animadvertunt quo consilio vtranque disputationem ediderit, Papisticam aut semipapisticam adorationem propugnandam susceperit. Credo equidem si hi quorum gloriæ inuidet & nomina odit, adoratione probassent, eum contra hanc improbaturum fuisse. Ea enim est hodie quorundam theologia, vt non ex doctrina de personis iudicium ferant, sed contra ex personis doctrinam æstiment, in illis quos amant & quibus fauent, omnia admirantur, contra eorum quos oderunt, omnia etiam rectissime dicta in alienum sensum detorquent & calumniantur. Sed nos hos suo relinquentes iudici, de rebus ipsis inter nos controuersis agamus.
units.tr: The last part of the Disputation concerns the adoration of Christ present in the Supper. He treats it in several propositions, most of which deal with adoring Christ according to both natures with one adoration, about which there is no dispute. At the outset, however, he sets out the differing opinions of those who, while affirming the real presence of Christ's body, think that the adoration of Christ present in the Supper is either wholly foreign to the institution of the Supper and comes close to the exploded Papist adoration, or they make this thing free, indifferent and, as it were, adiaphorous, or lastly they think it pious, right and lawful. He says all these may abound in their own sense, provided the same is granted to himself. Here, please, consider the character of the man. The opinions he sets out contradict one another. For if adoration is foreign to the institution of the Supper and approaches Papist superstition, it should not be tolerated in the Church, and the Supper must not be profaned by attaching to it a form of worship that Christ did not institute. Again, if this adoration is a pious and right thing, it does not seem that it can be omitted without impiety. But these points do not trouble Musculus. He can put up with everything in men of his own party. But if others condemn the adoration, with whom he does not agree in every respect, he will commit an unpardonable crime. Everyone easily sees this, and notices with what purpose he has published both disputations, taking up the defence of Papist or semi-Papist adoration. I believe indeed that if those whose glory he begrudges and whose names he hates had approved of adoration, he would have condemned it. For such is the theology of some people today that they do not judge doctrine by persons, but on the contrary judge persons by doctrine. In those whom they love and favour they admire everything, while against those whom they hate they twist and slander even the most rightly spoken words into a foreign sense. But leaving these men to their own judgment, let us deal with the matters themselves that are disputed between us.

units.la: Itaque quod adorationem Christi in sacramento attinet, non est controuersia, an aliqua reuerentia debeatur sacramento, fatemur enim monumenta & memorias rerum diuinarum aliquo modo coli & obseruari oportere: sed de adoratione hic quæritur, in qua sit proprius & peculiaris honor vnius & summi Dei. Hoc igitur quæritur, an Eucharistiam ita adorare liceat, propterea quod Christus in illa realiter & substantialiter præsens sit, vt ipse in Eucharistia hoc modo adoretur. Nos igitur qui scimus hanc realem & substantialem præsentiam ex scripturis ostendi non posse, negamus sacramenti adorationem: aduersariorum aliqui vt realem præsentiam ita adorationem quoque sacramenti defendunt. Est autem adoratio hæc à Papistis inuenta & in{?}
units.tr: So, as far as the adoration of Christ in the sacrament is concerned, there is no dispute whether some reverence is owed to the sacrament. For we confess that memorials and remembrances of divine things ought in some way to be honoured and observed. But the question here is about adoration, in which is the proper and particular honour of the one and highest God. The question, therefore, is whether it is lawful to adore the Eucharist for the reason that Christ is really and substantially present in it, so that he is adored in the Eucharist in this way. We, then, who know that this real and substantial presence cannot be shown from Scripture, deny the adoration of the sacrament. Some of our opponents defend the adoration of the sacrament just as they defend the real presence. This adoration was invented by the Papists and established

units.la: S ftituta,etenim Honorius mandauit sacerdotiâ bus vt plebem doceant,reuerenter coram Eu- charistia fe inclinare & eam venerari, Vrba- nus vero huius nominis IIII. peculiare insti- tuit festum corporis Christi, in quo prorsus gentili more in pompa circumfertur sacra- mentum,agri illo lustrantur,atque populus il- lud promiscuè adorat. Superstitionem hanc multum promouit Thomas Aquinas, hic e- nim totum illius festi officium, vt vocant, composuit,quod adeo Musculo nostro proba- tur, vt in vtraque Disputatione hymnu eius superstitiosum laudarit. Conantur autem qui- dam Patrum testimonio adorationem sacra- menti confirmare,et adducunt Augustinum, qui ait, Neminem illam carnem manducare nisi prius adorauerit:item Ambrosium, qui lib.3.cap.12.de spiritu sancto ita scribit:Itaque per scabellum terra intelligitur : per terram autem caro Christi, quam hodie quoque in mysterijs adoramus, & quam Apostoli in Christo Iesu, vt supra diximus, adorarunt. Neque enim diuisus est Christus, sed vnus. Idem scribit D. Augustinus in expositione Psal. 98. Sed Patres si Christum iubentes a- dorare in mysterijs,non hoc ad carnem Chri- sti referunt, quod illa realiter & substantiali- ter in his contineatur, nam eos aliter sensisse multis testimonijs dudum nostri probarunt: sed ad eos qui communicant hæc referunt.
units.tr: For Honorius ordered priests to teach the people to bow reverently before the Eucharist and to venerate it. Urban IV, moreover, instituted a special feast of the body of Christ, in which the sacrament is carried about in procession in a thoroughly pagan manner, fields are blessed with it, and the people adore it indiscriminately. Thomas Aquinas greatly promoted this superstition, for he composed the whole office of that feast, as they call it, and this so pleases our Musculus that in both Disputations he praised its superstitious hymn. Some, however, try to confirm the adoration of the sacrament by the testimony of the Fathers, and they cite Augustine, who says: No one eats that flesh unless he has first adored it; likewise Ambrose, who in Book 3, chapter 12, On the Holy Spirit, writes thus: So by the footstool is understood the earth, and by the earth the flesh of Christ, which we today also adore in the mysteries, and which the apostles adored in Christ Jesus, as we said above. For Christ is not divided, but one. Augustine writes the same in his exposition of Psalm 98. But when the Fathers bid us adore Christ in the mysteries, they do not refer this to the flesh of Christ in the sense that it is really and substantially contained in them. For our people have long since shown by many testimonies that the Fathers thought otherwise. Rather, they refer it to those who communicate.

units.la: Nos enim dum fumus in mysterijs, fide ac spi ritu percipimus carnem Christi pro nobis in mortem traditam, & sanguinem eius pro nobis effusum, atq; ea venerabundi colimus & adoramus.Adoramus etiam carnem Chri- fti in mysterijs, quod ea facramentali fignifi- catione fidei, atque spiritui nostro in myste- rijs adoranda quodammodo offeratur. Nam ita recte dicimur Deum adorare & colere in verbis Apostolorum & Prophetarum, cum illum adoramus & colimus, prout in illis fa- cris scriptis nobis ostenditur & significatur. Quemadmodum autem audita recitatione fa crorum verborum Deum adoramus, verba tamen ipsa non adoramus,ita in sacra commu nione adoramus quidem Christum, symbola tamen illa externa quae ponuntur ante ocu- los non adoramus, neq; etiam mentem ad illa dirigimus, Christum in illis substantialiter praefentem quaerentes. Chryfoftomus iubet nos corpus Christi non in altari sed in coelo animo & spiritu quaerere, atque aquilas fieri, vt in coelum aut supra coelos euolemus.Ac ve teres dicebant sursum corda,vt monerent a re bus visibilibus animum in coelos attollendu esse ad inuisibilia, quae nobis in sacramento offeruntur,& illic Christum quaerendu. Chri ftus etiam coenam instituens nusquam adora tionis mentionem fecit.Neq; valet quod obij ciunt,adorationem Christi in facrameto fan- § 2 ciri generali præcepto quo iubemur Deum, vbiq; in spiritu & veritate adorare: ad istam enim adorationem nihil opus est reali præsentia. Imo opinionibus Iudeorum & Samaritanorum qui præsentiam Dei ad certum aliquē locum alligabant, hanc sententiam Christus opponit. Vetat etiam ne patiamur nobis persuaderi, vt ipsum postquam a nobis abijt in certo aliquo terræ loco quæramus. Si quis (inquit) dixerit vobis, Ecce hic Christus, aut illic, nolite credere. Si dixerint vobis, ecce in deserto est, nolite exire: ecce in penetralibus, nolite credere. Scriptura docet Christum corpore suo in cœlos ascendisse, atque inde demum venturum in consummatione seculi ad judicandum viuos & mortuos, in cœlis igitur nos quærimus & adoramus Christum seruatorem non strum, neque alio nos ablegari patimur. Qui vero Christum in pane adorandum proponunt, necesse habent vt prius suam imaginationem firmioribus, quam hactenus fecerunt, argumentis probent. Deinde nunquam euitare poterunt, quin Papisticam ἀρτολάτρειαν aliqua ex parte confirmēt: Christi enim corpus etiam ante fidem & vsum pani coniungunt, & in eo adorant, atq; ita panē non tantum ad communionem vtuntur, sed prius ex eo idolum faciunt, quod adorent. Neq; reffert quod dicunt se creaturæ hunc honorem nō exhibere, nam ne Papistæ quidem creaturam s
units.tr: For while we are at the mysteries, we receive by faith and spirit the flesh of Christ, delivered to death for us, and his blood shed for us, and we worship and adore these with reverence. We also adore the flesh of Christ in the mysteries, because it is in a sacramental signification offered, in some sense, to our faith and spirit, to be adored in the mysteries. For we are rightly said to adore and worship God in the words of the apostles and prophets when we adore and worship him as he is shown and signified to us in those holy writings. Just as, on hearing the holy words recited, we adore God, yet we do not adore the words themselves, so in the holy communion we indeed adore Christ, but we do not adore those outward signs that are set before our eyes, nor do we direct our minds to them, seeking Christ substantially present in them. Chrysostom bids us seek the body of Christ not on the altar but in heaven, with mind and spirit, and to become eagles, so as to soar into heaven or above the heavens. And the ancients used to say "lift up your hearts," to warn that the mind must be raised from visible things to the invisible things offered to us in the sacrament, and that Christ must be sought there. Christ himself, instituting the Supper, never mentioned adoration. Nor is it valid what they object, that the adoration of Christ in the sacrament falls under the general precept by which we are commanded to adore God everywhere in spirit and truth. § 2 For for that adoration there is no need of a real presence. Indeed, Christ opposes this view to the opinions of the Jews and Samaritans, who tied the presence of God to a certain place. He also forbids us to allow ourselves to be persuaded to seek him in some particular place on earth after he has departed from us. "If anyone shall say to you, Behold, Christ is here or there, do not believe it. If they say to you, Behold, he is in the desert, do not go out; behold, he is in the inner chambers, do not believe it" (Matt. 24). Scripture teaches that Christ ascended into heaven in his body, and that from there he will at last come at the end of the age to judge the living and the dead. So we seek and adore Christ our Saviour in heaven, and we do not allow ourselves to be sent away to any other place. But those who propose that Christ is to be adored in the bread are bound first to prove their imagination by stronger arguments than they have hitherto used. Then they will never be able to avoid confirming, in some measure, the Papist artolatreia [ἀρτολατρεία, bread-worship]. For they join the body of Christ to the bread even before faith and use, and adore it in that, and so they not only use the bread for communion, but first make an idol of it to adore. Nor does it matter that they say they do not give this honour to a creature. For not even the Papists admit that they adore a creature. Indeed, they recognise no creature here at all, saying that the substances of bread and wine no longer remain, but have been turned into the body and blood of Christ.

units.la: s ram se adorare fatentur, imo creaturā nullam hic agnoscunt, dicentes panis & vini substan- tias non amplius superesse, sed in corpus & sanguinem Christi conuersas esse. Nihilomi- nus etiam aduersarij nostri eos horrendæ ido- lomaniæ accusant, & cœnam domini ab ipsis prophanatam conqueruntur. Testantur etiā Scholasticorum libri, quam multas spinosas quæstiones, ne quid grauius dicam, pepererit opinio de vi verborum consecrationis in con ficiendo sacramento, item adoratio Christi sub speciebus panis & vini: cum autem hæc omnia Aduersarijs nostris nota sint, videant ipsi quo consilio denuo in ecclesiam reducere conentur easdem opiniones. Etsi enim multos errorum riuulos obstruere conantur, tamen ijsdem fontibus patefactis nunquam prohibere poterunt, quominus similes superstitiones inde scaturiant. Ac verendum est ne qui in hac re cum Papistis colludunt, & eorū veteres superstitiones nouis coloribus pingunt, propius etiam ad illos accedant, & paulatim veterem papatum restituant: a cuius criminis suspicione si alieni esse volunt, factis non verbis se purgent, & principijs errorum valedicant, si nolint eos longius serpere.
units.tr: For they do not admit that they worship the bread itself; indeed they acknowledge no creature here at all, saying that the substances of bread and wine no longer remain, but have been changed into the body and blood of Christ. Nevertheless our opponents also accuse them of horrible idolatry, and complain that the Lord's Supper has been profaned by them. The books of the Scholastics also bear witness how many thorny questions, to say nothing stronger, the opinion about the power of the words of consecration in making the sacrament has brought forth, and likewise the adoration of Christ under the appearances of bread and wine. Since all these things are known to our opponents, let them see with what purpose they try once more to bring back into the Church the same opinions. For although they attempt to block up many small streams of error, yet, once the same springs have been opened, they will never be able to prevent similar superstitions from gushing forth from them. And there is cause to fear that those who collude with the Papists in this matter, and paint their old superstitions in new colours, will draw ever closer to them and gradually restore the old papacy. If they wish to be free of suspicion of this crime, let them clear themselves by deeds, not words, and renounce the principles of error, if they do not want it to creep further.

units.la: Multa quidem adhuc in hac disputatione Musculi notari poterat, & merebatur acrem reprehensorem, non tantum quod ad res ipsas spectat, & Papisticos errores quos denuo introducit in ecclesiam, sed etiam quoad consilium & scopum vtriusq; disputationis. Nam quod antea monui, hoc vnum spectat, vt viros longe se meliores & doctiores in inuidiã & odium adducat, quasi non recte de Sacramentis sentiant,& occultas hæreses alant: de inde maxime laborat ne vlla concordia & pacificatio constituatur inter ecclesias quæ Euangelium profitentes, hactenus tamè de modo præsentiæ Christi inter se dissentierunt. Verù ego hanc reprehensionem aliis relinquo, qui forte ipsum & similes ecclesiarum turbatores pro merito tractabunt, mihi tantum propositum fuit in simpliciorũ & mei similium gratiam, res præcipuas de quibus agitur in his disputationibus paucis examinare, indicare veram & orthodoxã doctrinam, & argumenta contraria si quæ allata fuerunt confutare. Qui prolixiorem tractationem requirit, libros plurimos habet unde eam petere poterit, & præsertim ex doctissimo libro quem Petrus Martyr, grauissimus theologus, contra Gardynerum quondam Vuintonienfem episcopum edidit: etenim pleraq; sua argumenta Musculus ab ipso Gardynero aut aliis Papistis mutuatus est.
units.tr: Much in this disputation of Musculus could still be noted, and it deserves a sharp critic, not only as regards the matters themselves, and the Popish errors which he reintroduces into the Church, but also as regards the aim and purpose of both disputations. For what I said before concerns this one thing: that he brings men far better and more learned than himself into envy and hatred, as if they did not hold sound views about the sacraments and nourished hidden heresies. Then he labours chiefly that no concord or peace may be established between the churches that profess the Gospel, which hitherto have nonetheless disagreed among themselves about the mode of Christ's presence. Truly, I leave this reproof to others, who will perhaps deal with him and similar disturbers of the churches as they deserve. My only purpose was, for the sake of the simpler folk and men like myself, to examine briefly the principal matters at issue in these disputations, to point out the true and orthodox doctrine, and to refute the contrary arguments, if any have been advanced. Whoever requires a fuller treatment has very many books from which he may seek it, and especially the most learned book which Peter Martyr, a most weighty theologian, published against Gardiner, once bishop of Winchester; for Musculus borrowed most of his arguments from Gardiner himself or from other Papists.
